System Design Mastery

The decisions that survive contact with scale. How to size a system before building it, choose a consistency model on purpose, partition data you cannot un-partition later, cache without serving lies, queue work without losing it, and keep a distributed system running when a third of it is broken and nobody is awake.

How to use this course

  • This course is about trade-offs, not products. Every mechanism here is explained by what it buys and what it costs, and the arithmetic is shown so you can check it against your own numbers. Redis, Kafka, PostgreSQL and Cassandra appear as examples of a category, never as an answer.
  • Every number comes from code you can run. The examples are runnable Python, and the output printed under each one is what that code produced — capacity arithmetic, consistent-hashing rings, quorum overlaps, Bloom filters, circuit breakers, saga orchestrators, back-pressure simulations, event-time windows and watermarks, Count-Min and HyperLogLog sketches, OAuth flows and architecture-decision linters. Where a demonstration needed a clock, the clock is injected, so the result is the same on every run.
  • It assumes you can read Python and have built something that talks over a network. If either is unfamiliar, work through the Foundations course first, then Networking and HTTP.
  • It builds on three courses and deliberately does not repeat them. Networking and HTTP covers what proxies, load balancers, CDNs and TLS actually do on the wire. Backend and API Design covers designing one HTTP service: idempotency keys, ETags, pagination, rate limits and the transactional outbox. Python covers the language. Where this course needs one of those, it names the course and the topic rather than re-teaching it.
  • Each section is Concept → Mechanism → Arithmetic → Practice → Exercises with solutions. The arithmetic matters more here than in most subjects, because the difference between a good design and a bad one is usually a number somebody did not compute.

Every example uses only the Python standard library, so there is nothing to install beyond Python itself. Every printed output was re-verified under Python 3.14.7 on 2026-09-25.

What you are actually learning

There are three separable skills hiding inside "system design", and confusing them is why the subject feels like trivia.

Estimation
Turning a vague request into numbers. Requests per second at peak, bytes per item, storage in three years, bandwidth, and how many machines that implies. This takes two minutes and eliminates most of the options — and it is the step most often skipped.
Mechanism
Knowing what each component actually does, and what it costs. What a quorum guarantees, why LRU is defeated by a scan, what a saga gives up, why an unbounded queue is worse than a rejection. This is the bulk of the course.
Judgement
Choosing the smallest design that meets the stated requirements, and being able to say what you traded. Most real systems are over-built, and the ability to defend leaving something out is worth more than the ability to add it.

The course is ordered so that each section can use the ones before it. Sections 1–3 establish the method and the two properties everything else serves — scalability and availability. Sections 4–8 are the distributed-data core: consistency, consensus, data stores, replication and partitioning, in that order because each depends on the last. Sections 9–11 are the three ways to avoid work: caching, asynchronism and event-driven architecture. Sections 12–15 are the parts that make a system operable: service boundaries, communication, resilience and operations. Sections 16–19 are what a system needs once it is large and has been handed on: processing data that never stops arriving (§16), counting what is too big to store (§17), knowing who is calling (§18) and leaving a design other people can understand (§19). Section 20 designs one system end to end using all of it.

What this course will not do

It will not give you a reference architecture. There isn't one. Every design here is derived from stated requirements, and the same feature list with different numbers produces a different system — §1.1 demonstrates exactly that.

It will not tell you which database to use. It will tell you which questions decide it (§6.1), and those questions have answers you can measure.

And it will not pretend the hard parts are easy. Distributed consensus is expensive, exactly-once delivery does not exist, cache invalidation is genuinely difficult, and a saga is worse than a transaction in every way except the one that matters. Where something is a real trade rather than a solved problem, it is presented as one.

SECTION 1

What System Design Is

System design is the practice of choosing a structure for software that has to keep working when it is large, when parts of it fail, and when nobody who wrote it is awake. It is not a body of facts to memorise — it is a set of trade-offs, and the skill being built here is making them deliberately and being able to say why. This section establishes the method: how to turn a vague request into requirements you can design against, how to size a system before building it, and the handful of numbers that make estimates possible.

1.1 Requirements Come First, and Most of Them Are Not About Features

Every system-design problem arrives underspecified. "Design a URL shortener" is not a problem statement; it is a topic. Requirements gathering is the first work — turning it into something with an answer — and it means separating what the system does from the conditions it must do it under.

Functional
What it does. "Shorten a URL, redirect a short code, show click counts." These are usually easy to enumerate and rarely determine the architecture.
Non-functional
The conditions: scale, latency, availability, consistency, durability, cost, and where the data may live. These decide the design, and they are the ones nobody states.
Explicitly out of scope
What you are choosing not to build. Naming it is not a formality — an unstated exclusion is a disagreement waiting to be discovered late.

The same feature list produces completely different systems depending on the second row:

def design_shape(reads_per_s, writes_per_s, availability, consistency):
    return {
        'storage': 'one relational node' if writes_per_s < 5_000 else 'partitioned (§8)',
        'reads': 'read replicas (§7.3)' if reads_per_s < 50_000 else 'CDN + cache (§9.2)',
        'redundancy': 'single region' if availability < 0.9999 else 'multi-region (§15.6)',
        'writes': 'strongly consistent' if consistency == 'strong' else 'eventual (§4.8)',
    }

SYSTEMS = [
    ('internal link shortener', 50, 1, 0.99, 'strong'),
    ('public link shortener', 400_000, 4_000, 0.9999, 'eventual'),
]
for name, reads, writes, availability, consistency in SYSTEMS:
    print(f'{name} — {reads:,}/s reads, {writes:,}/s writes, {availability:.2%}')
    for key, value in design_shape(reads, writes, availability, consistency).items():
        print(f'   {key:<12}{value}')
    print()

internal link shortener — 50/s reads, 1/s writes, 99.00%
   storage     one relational node
   reads       read replicas (§7.3)
   redundancy  single region
   writes      strongly consistent

public link shortener — 400,000/s reads, 4,000/s writes, 99.99%
   storage     one relational node
   reads       CDN + cache (§9.2)
   redundancy  multi-region (§15.6)
   writes      eventual (§4.8)

Identical functional requirements, and three of the four decisions differ. Only the storage choice survives — a shortener is write-light either way — and everything about how reads are served, how redundancy is arranged and what consistency is promised is decided by the second row of numbers rather than by the feature list. That is the point of asking before designing, and it is why "design a URL shortener" cannot be answered until someone says how many.

The questions worth asking, in the order that gets the most information soonest:

QUESTIONS = [
    ('Who uses it, and how many?',      'daily active users, and their growth rate'),
    ('What is the read:write ratio?',   'decides whether caching and replicas solve it'),
    ('How big is one item, and how many?', 'storage now, and in three years (§6.1)'),
    ('What latency is acceptable?',     'a p99 target, not an average (§15.2)'),
    ('What availability is needed?',    'in minutes per month, not in nines (§3.1)'),
    ('What must never be stale?',       'per operation, not for the whole system (§4.8)'),
    ('What must never be lost?',        'durability is separate from availability'),
    ('Where may the data live?',        'a legal constraint that can rule out designs'),
    ('What is the budget?',             'every answer above has a price'),
]
for question, why in QUESTIONS:
    print(f'{question:<38}{why}')

Who uses it, and how many?            daily active users, and their growth rate
What is the read:write ratio?         decides whether caching and replicas solve it
How big is one item, and how many?    storage now, and in three years (§6.1)
What latency is acceptable?           a p99 target, not an average (§15.2)
What availability is needed?          in minutes per month, not in nines (§3.1)
What must never be stale?             per operation, not for the whole system (§4.8)
What must never be lost?              durability is separate from availability
Where may the data live?              a legal constraint that can rule out designs
What is the budget?                   every answer above has a price

Two of these are asked less often than they should be. "What must never be lost?" is a durability question and is separate from availability: a system can be down for an hour and lose nothing, or be up continuously and silently drop writes, and the second is far worse. "Where may the data live?" is a legal constraint that can eliminate an entire architecture — a global database is not an option if EU personal data must stay in the EU (§15.6).

Requirements gathering ends when the answers are written down, and the design is then argued against those numbers rather than against preferences. Write them down and design against them. An architecture defended by "it scales" is defended by nothing; one defended by "it handles 40,000 writes a second because §8's partitioning gives us twelve shards at 3,300 each" is a claim someone can check.

1.2 Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation

Before designing anything, work out roughly how big it is. Capacity estimation — back-of-the-envelope arithmetic on load, storage and bandwidth — is the second step of the method and the one that eliminates whole categories of design in a couple of minutes. The arithmetic takes two minutes and it eliminates most of the options, because a design that is wrong by three orders of magnitude is wrong regardless of its elegance.

def estimate(dau, actions_per_user_per_day, read_write_ratio, bytes_per_item,
             peak_multiplier=3, retention_years=3):
    writes_per_day = dau * actions_per_user_per_day
    writes_per_s = writes_per_day / 86_400
    reads_per_s = writes_per_s * read_write_ratio
    return {
        'writes/day': f'{writes_per_day:,.0f}',
        'writes/s (average)': f'{writes_per_s:,.0f}',
        'writes/s (peak)': f'{writes_per_s * peak_multiplier:,.0f}',
        'reads/s (peak)': f'{reads_per_s * peak_multiplier:,.0f}',
        'storage/day': f'{writes_per_day * bytes_per_item / 1e9:,.1f} GB',
        f'storage/{retention_years}y': f'{writes_per_day * bytes_per_item * 365 * retention_years / 1e12:,.1f} TB',
    }

for key, value in estimate(dau=20_000_000, actions_per_user_per_day=2,
                           read_write_ratio=100, bytes_per_item=500).items():
    print(f'{key:<20}{value}')

writes/day          40,000,000
writes/s (average)  463
writes/s (peak)     1,389
reads/s (peak)      138,889
storage/day         20.0 GB
storage/3y          21.9 TB

Those six numbers determine the architecture, and each maps to a decision made elsewhere in this course: 1,389 writes a second fits comfortably on one database node (§6.1), so no partitioning; 138,889 reads a second at peak does not, so caching and replicas do the work (§9.1); and 21.9 TB over three years outgrows a single node, so archival or partitioning is needed eventually but not today.

Round aggressively and say so. Capacity estimation aims at an order of magnitude, not a forecast. A month is 2.5 million seconds, a day is 86,400 — call it 100,000. If the answer changes when you round, the estimate was too close to a boundary to be trusted anyway, and that itself is the finding.

And always compute the peak, not the average. Traffic is never uniform: a consumer service typically sees three to five times its average at peak, and an event-driven one — a ticket sale, a match kick-off, a payday — can see fifty times. Sizing for the average guarantees failure at the moment the system matters most.

def peak_profile(average_rps, shape):
    MULTIPLIERS = {'internal tool (working hours)': 4, 'consumer app (evening peak)': 3,
                   'e-commerce (seasonal)': 12, 'ticket sale (an instant)': 200}
    return average_rps * MULTIPLIERS[shape], MULTIPLIERS[shape]

for shape in ('internal tool (working hours)', 'consumer app (evening peak)',
              'e-commerce (seasonal)', 'ticket sale (an instant)'):
    peak, multiplier = peak_profile(2_000, shape)
    print(f'{shape:<32}{multiplier:>4}x  ->  {peak:>8,.0f} req/s at peak')

internal tool (working hours)      4x  ->     8,000 req/s at peak
consumer app (evening peak)        3x  ->     6,000 req/s at peak
e-commerce (seasonal)             12x  ->    24,000 req/s at peak
ticket sale (an instant)         200x  ->   400,000 req/s at peak

The last row is a different design, not a bigger one. Two hundred times the average cannot be provisioned for — the hardware would idle at 0.5% for all but a few minutes a year — so a ticket sale is built around a queue that absorbs the spike (§10.1) and admits users at a rate the system can serve. When the peak-to-average ratio is extreme, the answer is a change of shape rather than a change of size.

1.3 Powers of Two, and Reading Sizes

Storage and bandwidth estimates need a feel for magnitude. The table is short and worth knowing by sight.

UNITS = [(10, 'KB', 'a short text record, a small JSON object'),
         (20, 'MB', 'a photo, a minute of audio, a large log file'),
         (30, 'GB', 'a video, a small database, a machine\'s memory'),
         (40, 'TB', 'a large database, a day of logs at scale'),
         (50, 'PB', 'a data warehouse, a large object store')]

print(f'{"power":>7}{"exact bytes":>22}{"in SI units":>14}   typical')
for power, unit, example in UNITS:
    exact = 2 ** power
    si = exact / 10 ** (3 * (power // 10))
    print(f'2^{power:<5}{exact:>22,}{si:>11.2f} {unit:<2}   {example}')

print('\nthe approximation that makes mental arithmetic possible: 2^10 = 1,024 ~ 1,000')
print(f'error at 2^40: {(2 ** 40 / 1e12 - 1) * 100:.1f}% — small enough to ignore in an estimate')

  power           exact bytes   in SI units   typical
2^10                    1,024       1.02 KB   a short text record, a small JSON object
2^20                1,048,576       1.05 MB   a photo, a minute of audio, a large log file
2^30            1,073,741,824       1.07 GB   a video, a small database, a machine's memory
2^40        1,099,511,627,776       1.10 TB   a large database, a day of logs at scale
2^50    1,125,899,906,842,624       1.13 PB   a data warehouse, a large object store

the approximation that makes mental arithmetic possible: 2^10 = 1,024 ~ 1,000
error at 2^40: 10.0% — small enough to ignore in an estimate

Treat 2^10 as a thousand and the arithmetic becomes mental. The error compounds to 10% at the terabyte scale, which is far inside the precision of anything an estimate can claim.

Two conversions worth having automatically:

def sizes(items, bytes_each):
    total = items * bytes_each
    for unit, divisor in [('GB', 1e9), ('TB', 1e12), ('PB', 1e15)]:
        if total < divisor * 1000:
            return f'{total / divisor:,.1f} {unit}'
    return f'{total / 1e15:,.1f} PB'

CASES = [('1 billion user records', 1_000_000_000, 1_000),
         ('100 million photos', 100_000_000, 2_000_000),
         ('1 year of logs at 50k lines/s', 50_000 * 86_400 * 365, 300)]
for name, items, each in CASES:
    print(f'{name:<32}{sizes(items, each):>12}')

def bandwidth(requests_per_s, bytes_each):
    return requests_per_s * bytes_each / 1e6

print()
for rps, size_kb in [(10_000, 4), (400_000, 4), (10_000, 500)]:
    print(f'{rps:>8,} req/s x {size_kb:>4} KB = '
          f'{bandwidth(rps, size_kb * 1000):>8,.0f} MB/s '
          f'({bandwidth(rps, size_kb * 1000) * 8 / 1000:>6,.1f} Gbps)')

1 billion user records                1.0 TB
100 million photos                  200.0 TB
1 year of logs at 50k lines/s       473.0 TB

  10,000 req/s x    4 KB =       40 MB/s (   0.3 Gbps)
 400,000 req/s x    4 KB =    1,600 MB/s (  12.8 Gbps)
  10,000 req/s x  500 KB =    5,000 MB/s (  40.0 Gbps)

A billion small records is a terabyte; a hundred million photos is two hundred terabytes. The second is a different problem from the first, and the two-second calculation is what tells you so — it is the arithmetic that puts photos in object storage (§6.7) rather than in a database, before anyone has argued about it.

And bandwidth is the constraint people forget. Ten thousand requests a second at 500 KB is 5 GB/s — 40 Gbps, which is more than a single machine's network interface. That number changes the design (a CDN, §2.7) and it is invisible if you only count requests.

1.4 Latency Numbers Every Engineer Should Know

Estimating latency needs a sense of what operations cost. These are approximate and the ratios matter far more than the absolute values.

OPERATIONS = [
    ('L1 cache reference',                 0.000_001),
    ('main memory reference',              0.000_1),
    ('read 1 MB sequentially from memory', 0.03),
    ('SSD random read',                    0.1),
    ('read 1 MB sequentially from SSD',    0.5),
    ('round trip within a data centre',    0.5),
    ('disk seek (spinning)',               10.0),
    ('round trip London-New York',         56.0),
    ('round trip London-Sydney',           170.0),
]
baseline = OPERATIONS[1][1]                      # a main-memory reference
print(f'{"operation":<38}{"ms":>10}{"vs a memory reference":>24}')
for name, ms in OPERATIONS:
    ratio = ms / baseline
    shown = f'{ratio:,.0f}x' if ratio >= 1 else f'{ratio:.2f}x'
    print(f'{name:<38}{ms:>10.6f}{shown:>23}')

operation                                     ms   vs a memory reference
L1 cache reference                      0.000001                  0.01x
main memory reference                   0.000100                     1x
read 1 MB sequentially from memory      0.030000                   300x
SSD random read                         0.100000                 1,000x
read 1 MB sequentially from SSD         0.500000                 5,000x
round trip within a data centre         0.500000                 5,000x
disk seek (spinning)                   10.000000               100,000x
round trip London-New York             56.000000               560,000x
round trip London-Sydney              170.000000             1,700,000x

A cross-continental round trip is 560,000 memory references. That single ratio explains more architectural decisions than any other number: it is why caching works (§9.1), why chatty service calls are so expensive (§12.5), why CDNs exist (§2.7), and why a design is judged by how many network hops a request makes rather than by how much computation it does.

The rule that follows: count the round trips, not the CPU. A request doing three sequential cross-region calls has a floor of 168 milliseconds no matter how the code is written, and the only fixes are to remove a call, parallelise them, or move the data closer.

def budget(hops, hop_ms, parallel=False):
    return hop_ms if parallel else hops * hop_ms

for label, hops, hop_ms in [('3 sequential, same DC', 3, 0.5),
                            ('3 sequential, cross-region', 3, 56.0),
                            ('12 sequential, same DC', 12, 0.5)]:
    print(f'{label:<30}sequential {budget(hops, hop_ms):>7,.1f} ms   '
          f'parallel {budget(hops, hop_ms, parallel=True):>6,.1f} ms')

3 sequential, same DC         sequential     1.5 ms   parallel    0.5 ms
3 sequential, cross-region    sequential   168.0 ms   parallel   56.0 ms
12 sequential, same DC        sequential     6.0 ms   parallel    0.5 ms

Parallelising is the cheapest fix and is often available, because calls that do not depend on each other do not need to be sequential — and the reason they usually are is that the code was written as a series of statements rather than designed as a fan-out. Note what parallelising does not fix: the availability multiplication of §14.1 is unchanged, since all three services must still succeed.

1.5 How to Approach a Design Problem

A repeatable method, whether the problem is a real system or an interview question. The order matters, and the most common failure is starting at step four.

1
Clarify the requirements (§1.1). Ask the scale, the ratios, the latency and availability targets, and what must not be stale or lost. State what is out of scope. Five minutes here saves the whole design.
2
Estimate (§1.2). Requests per second at peak, storage now and in three years, bandwidth. These eliminate most options immediately.
3
Define the API and the data model. What are the operations, and what is stored? The access patterns you write down here choose the data store (§6.1) and the partition key (§8.3) — the two least reversible decisions in the system.
4
Draw the simplest thing that works, then scale it under pressure. Start with one server and one database; add a component only when you can name the number that forces it.
5
Find the bottleneck and address it. Then find the next one. A design is a sequence of these, and being able to say which constraint each component answers is what distinguishes a design from a diagram.
6
Say what breaks and what you traded. Every design has failure modes and costs; naming them is the strongest signal that the design was chosen rather than recalled.
def evolve(step, users, notes):
    return f'{step}. {users:>12,} users  {notes}'

STAGES = [
    (1,           100, 'one server, one database, done'),
    (2,        10_000, 'split app from database; add a load balancer (§2.4)'),
    (3,       500_000, 'add read replicas (§7.3) and a cache (§9.3); stateless app tier (§2.2)'),
    (4,     5_000_000, 'CDN for static and cacheable content (§2.7); async the slow work (§10.1)'),
    (5,    50_000_000, 'partition the write path (§8); extract the services that need it (§12.3)'),
    (6,   500_000_000, 'multi-region, with users pinned to a home region (§15.6)'),
]
for step, users, notes in STAGES:
    print(evolve(step, users, notes))

1.          100 users  one server, one database, done
2.       10,000 users  split app from database; add a load balancer (§2.4)
3.      500,000 users  add read replicas (§7.3) and a cache (§9.3); stateless app tier (§2.2)
4.    5,000,000 users  CDN for static and cacheable content (§2.7); async the slow work (§10.1)
5.   50,000,000 users  partition the write path (§8); extract the services that need it (§12.3)
6.  500,000,000 users  multi-region, with users pinned to a home region (§15.6)

Every step is forced by a number, and every step costs something. That is the honest version of the progression, and it is the opposite of how architecture diagrams are usually drawn — starting at step six because it looks serious. A system that serves 10,000 users from one machine is a correct design, and adding a message broker to it makes it worse.

Three habits that separate a good answer from a recited one:

Say what you are trading, every time. "Read replicas, which means reads can be stale by the replication lag, which is fine for the product catalogue and not for the checkout page." That sentence is worth more than the diagram.

Name the failure mode of each component you add. A cache introduces staleness and a stampede (§9.6); a queue introduces duplicates and a backlog (§10.6, §10.9); a new service introduces a network call that can fail (§14). If you cannot name it, you have not finished adding it.

Resist adding components. The most common error is a design with a message broker, a search cluster, a graph database and a service mesh for a system that has 200 requests a second. Each of those is a thing to run, monitor, upgrade and be woken up by (§12.3). The best design is the smallest one that meets the stated requirements, and the requirements are what §1.1 was for.

Exercises

Exercise 1.1 — Ask the questions. For "design a system for a supermarket chain to track stock across 400 stores", write the questions you would ask before designing, and show how two plausible sets of answers produce different architectures.

Solution 
QUESTIONS = [
    ('How many SKUs per store, and how many stores?', 'storage and partitioning (§8.3)'),
    ('How often does stock change per store?',        'write rate — the number that decides most of it'),
    ('Who reads it, and how fresh must it be?',       'a shelf-filler, head office and the website differ'),
    ('Must the website show live stock?',             'the hardest requirement here, if the answer is yes'),
    ('What happens when a store loses connectivity?', 'decides local-first vs central'),
    ('Is stock ever negative, and who reconciles?',   'consistency requirement, stated concretely'),
    ('How long is history kept, and for what?',       'audit and forecasting are different retentions'),
]
for question, why in QUESTIONS:
    print(f'{question:<48}{why}')

def architecture(live_website, offline_tolerant, writes_per_s):
    if not live_website and offline_tolerant:
        return ('store-local database + nightly batch to a central warehouse',
                'simple, cheap, robust to a broken link; head office sees yesterday')
    return ('per-store event stream (§10.2) -> central store; website reads a cache '
            'with a "may be inaccurate" caveat',
            'near-real-time, and every component in §9 through §14 is now needed')

for label, live, offline, writes in [('answers A', False, True, 40),
                                     ('answers B', True, True, 40)]:
    design, note = architecture(live, offline, writes)
    print(f'\n{label}: live website = {live}')
    print(f'   {design}')
    print(f'   {note}')

How many SKUs per store, and how many stores?   storage and partitioning (§8.3)
How often does stock change per store?          write rate — the number that decides most of it
Who reads it, and how fresh must it be?         a shelf-filler, head office and the website differ
Must the website show live stock?               the hardest requirement here, if the answer is yes
What happens when a store loses connectivity?   decides local-first vs central
Is stock ever negative, and who reconciles?     consistency requirement, stated concretely
How long is history kept, and for what?         audit and forecasting are different retentions

answers A: live website = False
   store-local database + nightly batch to a central warehouse
   simple, cheap, robust to a broken link; head office sees yesterday

answers B: live website = True
   per-store event stream (§10.2) -> central store; website reads a cache with a "may be inaccurate" caveat
   near-real-time, and every component in §9 through §14 is now needed

One question changes the entire architecture, and it is not a technical question. Whether the website shows live stock is a product decision, and answering it "yes" without examining it multiplies the cost of the system by an order of magnitude.

Answers A is a batch system, and it is genuinely correct if head office needs yesterday's numbers and shelf-fillers use in-store terminals. Four hundred stores at 40 writes a second is 16,000 writes a second in aggregate — but they never need to be in one place at one time, so the aggregate is a red herring. Store-local storage plus a nightly upload is robust, cheap, and unaffected by a broken link.

Answers B needs the whole course. Live website stock means per-store changes must reach a central system within seconds: an event stream per store (§10.2), an aggregation into a central store, a cache in front of the website (§9), and a decision about what happens when a store is offline — because the website is now showing stale data and must say so (§3.4).

And the question that saves the most money is the last-but-two: what happens when a store loses connectivity? If the answer is "the tills must keep working", the design is local-first with eventual synchronisation (§4.8) whatever else is decided — and that constraint, stated at the start, rules out any architecture that requires a round trip to head office to sell a tin of beans.

Exercise 1.2 — Estimate before designing. Estimate for a photo-sharing service: 50 million daily active users, each posting 0.5 photos and viewing 80 per day. Photos average 3 MB with three generated thumbnails totalling 400 KB. Compute writes, reads, storage, bandwidth, and say which numbers change the architecture.

Solution 
DAU, POSTS_PER_USER, VIEWS_PER_USER = 50_000_000, 0.5, 80
PHOTO_MB, THUMBS_KB, PEAK = 3, 400, 3

uploads_day = DAU * POSTS_PER_USER
views_day = DAU * VIEWS_PER_USER
uploads_s, views_s = uploads_day / 86_400, views_day / 86_400

print(f'{"uploads/day":<26}{uploads_day:>16,.0f}')
print(f'{"uploads/s average":<26}{uploads_s:>16,.0f}')
print(f'{"uploads/s peak":<26}{uploads_s * PEAK:>16,.0f}')
print(f'{"views/s average":<26}{views_s:>16,.0f}')
print(f'{"views/s peak":<26}{views_s * PEAK:>16,.0f}')
print(f'{"read:write ratio":<26}{views_day / uploads_day:>15,.0f}:1')

bytes_per_upload = PHOTO_MB * 1e6 + THUMBS_KB * 1e3
storage_day = uploads_day * bytes_per_upload
print(f'\n{"storage/day":<26}{storage_day / 1e12:>14,.1f} TB')
print(f'{"storage/year":<26}{storage_day * 365 / 1e15:>14,.1f} PB')
print(f'{"storage/5 years":<26}{storage_day * 365 * 5 / 1e15:>14,.1f} PB')

view_bytes = THUMBS_KB / 3 * 1e3                     # a feed view is one thumbnail
egress_peak = views_s * PEAK * view_bytes
ingress_peak = uploads_s * PEAK * bytes_per_upload
print(f'\n{"ingress at peak":<26}{ingress_peak / 1e9:>14,.1f} GB/s'
      f'  ({ingress_peak * 8 / 1e9:,.0f} Gbps)')
print(f'{"egress at peak (thumbs)":<26}{egress_peak / 1e9:>14,.1f} GB/s'
      f'  ({egress_peak * 8 / 1e9:,.0f} Gbps)')
print(f'{"egress at a 95% CDN hit":<26}{egress_peak * 0.05 / 1e9:>14,.1f} GB/s'
      f'  ({egress_peak * 0.05 * 8 / 1e9:,.0f} Gbps)')

uploads/day                     25,000,000
uploads/s average                      289
uploads/s peak                         868
views/s average                     46,296
views/s peak                       138,889
read:write ratio                      160:1

storage/day                         85.0 TB
storage/year                        31.0 PB
storage/5 years                    155.1 PB

ingress at peak                      3.0 GB/s  (24 Gbps)
egress at peak (thumbs)             18.5 GB/s  (148 Gbps)
egress at a 95% CDN hit              0.9 GB/s  (7 Gbps)

Four numbers change the architecture, and one of them is the one people miss.

The 160:1 read-to-write ratio says this is a read-heavy system, so the whole design is about serving reads cheaply: CDN, caching, read replicas (§2.7, §9.2). The write path at 868 uploads a second is unremarkable.

Six petabytes a year rules out storing photos in a database before any other consideration. Object storage, with the key in the metadata store (§6.7) — and this is the decision the estimate makes for you in ten seconds.

Egress at peak is the number that dominates the bill, and it is invisible if you only count requests. Serving thumbnails to 138,000 viewers a second is 18 GB/s, which is where the money goes — and a 95% CDN hit rate turns it into 0.9 GB/s from the origin, a twenty-fold reduction in the largest line item.

And the metadata is tiny. Nine million rows a day of a few hundred bytes is under a terabyte a year — a single relational node for years (§6.1). The instinct to reach for a distributed database here is driven by the photo volume, which is not in that database at all. Separating the bytes from the metadata makes a "petabyte-scale" problem into an object store plus an ordinary database, and that is the whole insight the estimate delivers.

Exercise 1.3 — Evolve a design under pressure. Start with a job board: one server, one PostgreSQL database, 500 users a day. Take it through 50,000, 5 million and 100 million users a day, naming at each step the number that forces the change, the component you add, and what it costs.

Solution 
def profile(dau, searches_per_user=6, applications_per_user=0.4, peak=3):
    reads = dau * searches_per_user / 86_400 * peak
    writes = dau * applications_per_user / 86_400 * peak
    return reads, writes

STEPS = [500, 50_000, 5_000_000, 100_000_000]
print(f'{"DAU":>13}{"peak reads/s":>15}{"peak writes/s":>15}   forced change')
FORCED = [
    'nothing — one server, one database',
    'split app from db; 2 app nodes behind a load balancer (§2.4)',
    'cache + read replicas (§9.3, §7.3); search moves to an index (§6.7)',
    'partition applications (§8.3); async the notifications (§10.1); CDN (§2.7)',
]
for dau, forced in zip(STEPS, FORCED):
    reads, writes = profile(dau)
    print(f'{dau:>13,}{reads:>15,.0f}{writes:>15,.0f}   {forced}')

          DAU   peak reads/s  peak writes/s   forced change
          500              0              0   nothing — one server, one database
       50,000             10              1   split app from db; 2 app nodes behind a load balancer (§2.4)
    5,000,000          1,042             69   cache + read replicas (§9.3, §7.3); search moves to an index (§6.7)
  100,000,000         20,833          1,389   partition applications (§8.3); async the notifications (§10.1); CDN (§2.7)

Read the second column against §6.1's thresholds. At 50,000 users the database is doing 10 reads a second — nothing. At 5 million it is 1,042, which one node still handles, but the search queries behind those reads are the expensive part, and that is what forces the change rather than the request count.

500 → 50,000: one number forces one change. Traffic is still trivial, and what actually forces the split is availability: one server means a deploy is downtime, and a hardware failure is an outage. Two application nodes behind a load balancer, database on its own machine. This is an availability change, not a capacity one, and confusing the two is why systems get scaled prematurely.

50,000 → 5,000,000: the search query is the bottleneck, not the row count. Job search is a full-text query with filters, and LIKE '%engineer%' cannot use an index (§6.7). Two changes: a search index fed from the database, and a cache in front of the popular queries — because job searches are extremely skewed, so a small cache absorbs most of them (§9.1's power-law arithmetic). Read replicas take the rest. The cost is that search results are now eventually consistent with the database, and a new job takes seconds to appear — which is fine, and must be stated as fine.

5,000,000 → 100,000,000: the write path finally matters. 13,889 peak writes a second is at the edge of one node (§6.1), and applications are the natural partition key — but note that partitioning by job_id and partitioning by applicant_id serve different queries, and this is the decision that is hardest to reverse (§8.3). Notification emails move to a queue (§10.1), assets to a CDN (§2.7), and the whole of §14's resilience machinery becomes necessary because there are now several services.

What was never needed: microservices. At a hundred million daily users this is still a system with a small number of capabilities and a team that can coordinate. §12.3's argument applies — services are an organisational answer, and nothing in this progression made the organisation the constraint.

SECTION 2

Scalability

Scalability is not speed. A system is scalable if you can serve more load by adding resources, and the useful question is never "is it fast?" but "what happens when this gets ten times bigger, and which part breaks first?" That question has an answer you can compute, and this section is about computing it — the two ways to add capacity, the one property that makes horizontal scaling possible at all, and the layer that distributes the work.

2.1 Two Kinds of Growth, and Why the Distinction Matters

Before the two kinds, one distinction that this section depends on. Performance is how fast a single request is; scalability is whether adding resources lets you serve more requests. They are independent properties, and conflating them sends optimisation effort to the wrong place: a system can have excellent performance and no scalability (one machine answering in a millisecond, with no way to add a second), or poor performance and perfect scalability (a batch job that takes an hour and takes thirty minutes with twice the workers). Tuning improves performance; adding capacity improves throughput only if the design is scalable, and a profiler cannot tell you which problem you have. Throughput — requests served per unit time — is the quantity scalability is about, and it is the one a capacity plan is written against.

Vertical scaling buys a bigger machine. Horizontal scaling buys more machines. They fail differently, and the difference is the whole design.

def vertical(cores, cost_multiplier_per_doubling=2.4):
    doublings = 0
    size, cost = 1, 1.0
    while size < cores:
        size, cost, doublings = size * 2, cost * cost_multiplier_per_doubling, doublings + 1
    return cost, doublings

print(f'{"cores":>8}{"relative cost":>16}{"cost per core":>16}')
for cores in (2, 8, 32, 128, 512):
    cost, _ = vertical(cores)
    print(f'{cores:>8}{cost:>16,.0f}{cost / cores:>16,.1f}')

   cores   relative cost   cost per core
       2               2             1.2
       8              14             1.7
      32              80             2.5
     128             459             3.6
     512           2,642             5.2

Cost per core rises with machine size, because the biggest machines are a specialist market — and above a point they simply stop existing. Horizontal scaling is linear in cost and has no ceiling, which is why every large system is horizontal.

But vertical scaling is not the poor relation, and treating it as one is a common and expensive mistake:

Vertical
Requires no code changes at all. A transaction still works, a join still works, in-memory state still works. It is a purchase, not a project — and a modern server with 128 cores and 2 TB of memory serves an enormous amount of traffic. Its limits are a hard ceiling, a single failure domain, and downtime to resize.
Horizontal
No ceiling and no single point of failure, and capacity can follow demand. It costs you statelessness (§2.2), a distribution layer (§2.4), and every problem in §4 through §14 — consistency, partitioning, replication, retries. That bill is paid once and paid forever.

Scale vertically first, and design so you can scale horizontally later. A day of resizing a database is cheaper than a quarter of re-architecting, and the number of systems that genuinely outgrow one large machine is much smaller than the number that assume they will.

The second thing that decides how far scaling goes is what fraction of the work is actually parallel, and this is the number people skip:

def amdahl(serial_fraction, workers):
    return 1 / (serial_fraction + (1 - serial_fraction) / workers)

print(f'{"workers":>9}' + ''.join(f'{f"{s:.0%} serial":>13}' for s in (0.0, 0.01, 0.05, 0.25)))
for workers in (1, 4, 16, 64, 256, 1_024):
    row = ''.join(f'{amdahl(s, workers):>12.1f}x' for s in (0.0, 0.01, 0.05, 0.25))
    print(f'{workers:>9}{row}')

  workers    0% serial    1% serial    5% serial   25% serial
        1         1.0x         1.0x         1.0x         1.0x
        4         4.0x         3.9x         3.5x         2.3x
       16        16.0x        13.9x         9.1x         3.4x
       64        64.0x        39.3x        15.4x         3.8x
      256       256.0x        72.1x        18.6x         4.0x
     1024      1024.0x        91.2x        19.6x         4.0x

Five per cent serial work caps you at twenty times, no matter how many machines you buy. That serial fraction is rarely labelled as such — it is the shared counter, the single leader that orders writes, the lock around the sequence generator, the one report that must scan everything. Find it before adding capacity, because past the knee every additional machine is pure cost.

And the same arithmetic explains something that surprises people: a system can get slower as it grows, because coordination between workers grows faster than the workers do (the USL's second term — coherence — is quadratic). Two hundred and fifty-six workers contending on one row is not a fast system.

2.2 Statelessness: the Property Everything Else Depends On

Horizontal scaling works only if any instance can serve any request. That requires the instance to hold no state that the next request needs — statelessness — and it is a property of where state lives, not of whether state exists.

class Stateful:
    """Sessions in process memory. Works perfectly with one instance."""
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name, self.sessions = name, {}

    def login(self, user):
        self.sessions[user] = {'cart': []}
        return f'{self.name}: logged {user} in'

    def add_to_cart(self, user, item):
        if user not in self.sessions:
            return f'{self.name}: NOT LOGGED IN'
        self.sessions[user]['cart'].append(item)
        return f'{self.name}: cart = {self.sessions[user]["cart"]}'

class Stateless:
    """Sessions in a shared store. Any instance can serve any request."""
    def __init__(self, name, store):
        self.name, self.store = name, store

    def login(self, user):
        self.store[user] = {'cart': []}
        return f'{self.name}: logged {user} in'

    def add_to_cart(self, user, item):
        if user not in self.store:
            return f'{self.name}: NOT LOGGED IN'
        self.store[user]['cart'].append(item)
        return f'{self.name}: cart = {self.store[user]["cart"]}'

nodes = [Stateful('app-1'), Stateful('app-2'), Stateful('app-3')]
print('--- in-process sessions, round-robin load balancing')
print(nodes[0].login('ada'))
print(nodes[1].add_to_cart('ada', 'book'))
print(nodes[2].add_to_cart('ada', 'pen'))

shared = {}
nodes = [Stateless(f'app-{i}', shared) for i in (1, 2, 3)]
print('\n--- shared session store, same routing')
print(nodes[0].login('ada'))
print(nodes[1].add_to_cart('ada', 'book'))
print(nodes[2].add_to_cart('ada', 'pen'))

--- in-process sessions, round-robin load balancing
app-1: logged ada in
app-2: NOT LOGGED IN
app-3: NOT LOGGED IN

--- shared session store, same routing
app-1: logged ada in
app-2: cart = ['book']
app-3: cart = ['book', 'pen']

The stateful version works flawlessly with one instance and breaks on the second, which is exactly why it survives so long: it passes every test on a developer's machine and fails the moment a second node exists. It also fails on every deploy, every autoscale-down, and every instance crash, because that memory is gone.

There are four places state can live, and only the first is a problem:

In the instance
Sessions, uploaded files on local disk, in-memory caches that must be consistent, scheduled jobs bound to one node. Every one of these blocks horizontal scaling, and each has a standard fix.
In the client
A signed token carrying the session (a JWT), so no server-side lookup is needed at all. Fast and free to scale — at the cost of not being revocable before it expires, which is a real security trade rather than a detail.
In a shared store
Redis for sessions, object storage for files (§6.7), the database for anything durable. The general answer, and the cost is a network hop plus a dependency you must run.
In a stateful tier, deliberately
Databases, caches and brokers are stateful, and pretending otherwise is how state ends up in the wrong place. The goal is not "no state anywhere" — it is state in a small number of components designed for it, with everything else disposable.

The test is one question: can you kill any instance at any moment and lose nothing but the requests in flight? If not, the state is in the wrong place, and it will be discovered during a deploy.

2.3 Sticky Sessions, and Why They Are a Trap

Sticky sessions — session affinity — route a user consistently to the same instance, so in-process state works. It is the fix that requires no application changes, and that is the problem.

def sticky_distribution(users_per_node, node_dies=None, new_node=False):
    nodes = dict(users_per_node)
    events = []
    if node_dies is not None:
        lost = nodes.pop(node_dies)
        events.append(f'{lost:,} users lost their session when {node_dies} died')
        for node in nodes:                              # they rehash onto the survivors
            nodes[node] += lost // len(nodes)
    if new_node:
        nodes['app-4'] = 0
        events.append('app-4 joined with 0 users and stays empty — affinity keeps '
                      'existing users where they are')
    return nodes, events

nodes = {'app-1': 3_000, 'app-2': 3_000, 'app-3': 3_000}
print(f'start           : {nodes}')
for label, kwargs in [('a node dies    ', dict(node_dies='app-2')),
                      ('a node is added', dict(new_node=True))]:
    nodes, events = sticky_distribution(nodes, **kwargs)      # cumulative
    print(f'{label} : {nodes}')
    for event in events:
        print(f'   -> {event}')

average = sum(nodes.values()) / len(nodes)
print(f'\nbusiest node is {max(nodes.values()) / average:.1f}x the average, '
      f'and the new node is serving {min(nodes.values())}')

start           : {'app-1': 3000, 'app-2': 3000, 'app-3': 3000}
a node dies     : {'app-1': 4500, 'app-3': 4500}
   -> 3,000 users lost their session when app-2 died
a node is added : {'app-1': 4500, 'app-3': 4500, 'app-4': 0}
   -> app-4 joined with 0 users and stays empty — affinity keeps existing users where they are

busiest node is 1.5x the average, and the new node is serving 0

Three failures, all of which arrive together on the day you most need capacity.

A node's death is a user-visible logout for everyone stuck to it. With state in a shared store, those users would have noticed nothing.

A new node stays empty. Affinity means existing users keep going where they were, so scaling out during a traffic spike adds a machine that serves nobody until new users arrive — which is precisely the wrong time for capacity to be useless.

Load drifts and stays drifted. Long-lived connections and uneven session lifetimes mean the distribution never re-evens, so you are provisioning for the busiest node rather than the average.

There is one legitimate use, and it is not sessions. Affinity is genuinely correct for a local cache — routing the same key to the same node so its cache stays warm (§9.8) — because there the state is disposable and a miss is merely slower. The distinction is exactly that: stick for performance, never for correctness. If losing the affinity loses data, the design is wrong.

2.4 Load Balancers: Layer 4 and Layer 7

Something has to spread requests across instances. Where it sits in the stack determines what it can do.

Layer 4
Forwards TCP or UDP. It sees addresses, ports and connection state, and nothing above that. Extremely fast — millions of connections per instance, minimal added latency, no TLS work — and correspondingly blind: it cannot route on a path, read a header, or retry a failed request, because it does not know where one request ends.
Layer 7
Terminates the connection and understands HTTP. It can route on path or header, retry an idempotent request against another instance, compress, rewrite, rate-limit and cache. Costs a full proxy per request, and it must hold the TLS certificates.
CAPABILITIES = [
    ('route by IP and port',       True,  True),
    ('spread TCP connections',     True,  True),
    ('route by URL path',          False, True),
    ('route by header or cookie',  False, True),
    ('retry a failed request',     False, True),
    ('terminate TLS',              False, True),
    ('per-request balancing',      False, True),
    ('handle non-HTTP protocols',  True,  False),
]
print(f'{"capability":<28}{"layer 4":>10}{"layer 7":>10}')
for name, l4, l7 in CAPABILITIES:
    print(f'{name:<28}{"yes" if l4 else "-":>10}{"yes" if l7 else "-":>10}')

capability                     layer 4   layer 7
route by IP and port               yes       yes
spread TCP connections             yes       yes
route by URL path                    -       yes
route by header or cookie            -       yes
retry a failed request               -       yes
terminate TLS                        -       yes
per-request balancing                -       yes
handle non-HTTP protocols          yes         -

"Per-request balancing" is the row that matters most and is the least obvious. A layer-4 balancer assigns a connection to a backend, and with HTTP/2 or a connection pool that connection carries thousands of requests over its lifetime — so a client that opened its connection when node 1 was idle keeps sending to node 1 forever, and the balancing you thought you had is balancing from ten minutes ago. A layer-7 balancer makes the decision per request, which is the only way keep-alive traffic spreads evenly.

The usual arrangement is both: layer 4 at the edge for raw throughput and DDoS absorption, layer 7 behind it for routing and retries. Networking and HTTP covers what a proxy does to a request in its reverse-proxy and load-balancer sections; the design question here is which algorithm it uses to choose, and that choice is not neutral:

from collections import Counter
import itertools

BACKENDS = ['fast-1', 'fast-2', 'slow-3']
SLOWDOWN = {'fast-1': 1.0, 'fast-2': 1.0, 'slow-3': 4.0}   # slow-3 takes 4x as long

def simulate(algorithm, arrivals, service_ms=10.0, gap_ms=4.0):
    """A timeline: each backend is busy until `free_at`. Wait = queueing delay."""
    free_at = {b: 0.0 for b in BACKENDS}
    in_flight = Counter()
    served, waits = Counter(), []
    cycle = itertools.cycle(BACKENDS)
    for n in range(arrivals):
        now = n * gap_ms
        for b in BACKENDS:                                  # release finished work
            if free_at[b] <= now:
                in_flight[b] = 0
        if algorithm == 'round robin':
            backend = next(cycle)
        elif algorithm == 'least connections':
            backend = min(BACKENDS, key=lambda b: (in_flight[b], b))
        elif algorithm == 'least response time':
            backend = min(BACKENDS, key=lambda b: (free_at[b], b))
        start = max(now, free_at[backend])
        free_at[backend] = start + service_ms * SLOWDOWN[backend]
        in_flight[backend] += 1
        served[backend] += 1
        waits.append(start - now)
    waits.sort()
    return served, waits[len(waits) // 2], waits[int(len(waits) * 0.99)]

print(f'{"algorithm":<22}{"p50 wait":>10}{"p99 wait":>11}   requests per backend')
for algorithm in ('round robin', 'least connections', 'least response time'):
    served, p50, p99 = simulate(algorithm, 900)
    print(f'{algorithm:<22}{p50:>7,.0f} ms{p99:>8,.0f} ms   {dict(sorted(served.items()))}')

algorithm               p50 wait   p99 wait   requests per backend
round robin                 0 ms   8,148 ms   {'fast-1': 300, 'fast-2': 300, 'slow-3': 300}
least connections          64 ms   2,316 ms   {'fast-1': 385, 'fast-2': 385, 'slow-3': 130}
least response time       200 ms     396 ms   {'fast-1': 400, 'fast-2': 400, 'slow-3': 100}

Round robin gives the slow backend exactly as much work as the fast ones — 300 requests each — so a queue builds in front of it that never drains, and the p99 wait for the whole system is eight seconds. This is the default in most configurations.

Least-connections needs to be told nothing about backend speed. It observes that work is piling up in front of slow-3 and sends 130 requests there instead of 300, cutting the p99 wait by more than three times — which is why it is the better default whenever request costs or backend speeds vary at all. Note the trade it makes: the p50 got worse, from 0 ms to 64 ms, because it packs the fast backends more tightly. Balancing algorithms move latency from the tail to the middle, and the tail is what users complain about.

Response-time-aware balancing goes furthest, reducing the p99 to under 400 ms by steering almost everything away from the slow backend — at the cost of the highest median of the three. Use it when backends are genuinely heterogeneous; least-connections is the right general default.

And the balancer must not itself be the single point of failure. One balancer in front of thirty application servers is a system with an availability of one machine. The standard answers are a pair sharing a floating address, DNS returning several balancer addresses, or a managed balancer that is already replicated — and whichever you use, the failure of one must be tested rather than assumed.

2.5 Health Checks, and the Ways They Lie

A balancer needs to know which backends can serve. That sounds simple and is the source of a whole category of outage, because a check that is too shallow keeps sending traffic to a broken node and one that is too deep takes the fleet down over a dependency.

def check(kind, process_alive, dependencies_up, thread_pool_free):
    if kind == 'TCP connect':
        return process_alive
    if kind == 'shallow HTTP (200 from /ping)':
        return process_alive
    if kind == 'readiness (can I serve?)':
        return process_alive and thread_pool_free
    if kind == 'deep (checks dependencies)':
        return process_alive and thread_pool_free and dependencies_up
    raise ValueError(kind)

SCENARIOS = [
    ('healthy',                     True, True,  True),
    ('thread pool exhausted',       True, True,  False),
    ('the shared database is down', True, False, True),
    ('process wedged',              False, True, False),
]
KINDS = ['TCP connect', 'shallow HTTP (200 from /ping)',
         'readiness (can I serve?)', 'deep (checks dependencies)']
print(f'{"scenario":<30}' + ''.join(f'{k.split()[0]:>12}' for k in KINDS))
for name, alive, deps, pool in SCENARIOS:
    row = ''.join(f'{("in" if check(k, alive, deps, pool) else "OUT"):>12}' for k in KINDS)
    print(f'{name:<30}{row}')

scenario                               TCP     shallow   readiness        deep
healthy                                 in          in          in          in
thread pool exhausted                   in          in         OUT         OUT
the shared database is down             in          in          in         OUT
process wedged                         OUT         OUT         OUT         OUT

Read the last column against the third row. When the shared database is down, a deep health check takes every single node out of the pool at once — and a balancer with no healthy backends returns errors for everything, including the requests that needed no database at all. The dependency failure has been amplified into a total outage by the mechanism meant to prevent one.

Four rules, each of which prevents a specific incident:

Check readiness, not dependencies. The question is "can this instance serve requests?", not "is the whole system healthy?". A shared dependency being down is identical on every node, so removing nodes for it cannot help — the traffic has nowhere else to go.

Separate liveness from readiness. Liveness asks "should I be restarted?" and must be very conservative, because a false positive kills a working process. Readiness asks "should I get traffic?" and can flap freely, because a false positive costs one node's capacity briefly. Kubernetes makes this distinction explicit, and conflating the two is how a struggling fleet gets restarted into a crash loop.

Make the check meaningful but cheap. A 200 from a handler that only proves the HTTP server is listening will happily report health while the thread pool is exhausted and every real request is timing out. Checking that a worker is available is one line and catches the common case.

Require several consecutive results before acting. One failed check is a network blip; three in a row is a signal. And require more consecutive successes to return a node than failures to remove it — coming back too eagerly produces a node that flaps in and out of the pool, which is worse than either state.

Then there is the case a health check cannot see: the node that is up and wrong. It responds, its pool is free, and it serves stale data or 500s from one endpoint because a deploy half-failed. That is what outlier detection is for — the balancer watching actual response codes and latencies and ejecting a backend whose error rate diverges from its peers. It is the circuit breaker from §14.5, applied by the balancer on the caller's behalf, and it catches what probing never will.

2.6 Single Points of Failure and Blast Radius

A single point of failure is any component whose loss stops the system. Finding them is a mechanical exercise, and the arithmetic tells you where to spend.

from math import prod

def component(name, instances, per_instance=0.99, shared_fate=False):
    """A replicated component fails only if all its instances do — unless they share fate."""
    if shared_fate:
        return name, per_instance, instances
    return name, 1 - (1 - per_instance) ** instances, instances

SYSTEM = [
    component('load balancer', 1),
    component('app servers', 6),
    component('database primary', 1),
    component('cache', 3),
    component('all of it in one availability zone', 1, per_instance=0.999, shared_fate=True),
]
print(f'{"component":<38}{"instances":>11}{"availability":>15}{"min/month down":>16}')
for name, availability, instances in SYSTEM:
    print(f'{name:<38}{instances:>11}{availability:>15.4%}'
          f'{(1 - availability) * 43_830:>13,.0f} min')

total = prod(a for _, a, _ in SYSTEM)
print(f'\n{"whole system":<38}{"":>11}{total:>15.4%}{(1 - total) * 43_830:>13,.0f} min')
print('the app tier contributes',
      f'{(1 - SYSTEM[1][1]) * 43_830:.2f} min — everything else dominates')

component                               instances   availability  min/month down
load balancer                                   1       99.0000%          438 min
app servers                                     6      100.0000%            0 min
database primary                                1       99.0000%          438 min
cache                                           3       99.9999%            0 min
all of it in one availability zone              1       99.9000%           44 min

whole system                                            97.9119%          915 min
the app tier contributes 0.00 min — everything else dominates

Six replicated app servers contribute almost nothing to downtime, and the two single instances contribute almost all of it. That is the general shape: replicating what is already replicated is the most common way to spend money on availability and get none. The load balancer and the database primary are where the minutes are.

The systematic way to find them is to ask, of every component, what happens when it disappears — and to include the ones that are not on the diagram:

The obvious ones
A single database primary, one load balancer, one message broker, one cache node holding something the system cannot serve without (§9.9). Each is a single point of failure in the strict sense: remove it and the system stops.
Shared fate
Three replicas in one availability zone, or on one physical host, are one replica for the purpose of a zone failure. Replication only helps across the boundary the failure crosses.
Off the diagram
DNS, the certificate that expires, the CI system you cannot deploy without, the secret store every service reads at boot, the container registry. These fail rarely and take everything with them, and none of them appears in an architecture drawing.
Correlated by design
The deploy that ships the same bug to every instance, the config change applied fleet-wide, the certificate every service shares. Redundancy does nothing here — staged rollout is the only defence, which is why canary deploys exist.

Blast radius is the other half of the question: not "will it fail?" but "how much fails with it?". The lever is partitioning failure domains — availability zones, shards (§8), cells, tenant groups — so that a failure is a fraction rather than everything:

def blast(users, cells):
    return users // cells, 1 / cells

for cells in (1, 2, 4, 16):
    affected, fraction = blast(8_000_000, cells)
    print(f'{cells:>3} cell(s): a single-cell failure affects {affected:>9,} users '
          f'({fraction:>6.1%})')

  1 cell(s): a single-cell failure affects 8,000,000 users (100.0%)
  2 cell(s): a single-cell failure affects 4,000,000 users ( 50.0%)
  4 cell(s): a single-cell failure affects 2,000,000 users ( 25.0%)
 16 cell(s): a single-cell failure affects   500,000 users (  6.2%)

Sixteen cells turns a total outage into a 6% one, and the cost is sixteen of everything plus a routing layer that maps a user to a cell. That is expensive, and it is why cell-based architecture belongs to systems where a total outage is genuinely unacceptable rather than merely bad. The general principle scales down, though: any boundary that stops a failure spreading is worth its price if the price is small — separate connection pools (§6.9), separate worker queues (§10.3), separate deploy waves.

2.7 Scaling the Edge: DNS and CDNs

Everything above scales the servers. Two mechanisms scale what happens before a request reaches them, and both remove load that no amount of capacity would otherwise handle.

DNS is the first routing decision, and it is a coarse but genuinely global load balancer. Returning several addresses for one name spreads clients across data centres; returning a different address depending on where the query came from sends users to the nearest region.

def dns_strategy(strategy, regions, user_region):
    if strategy == 'single A record':
        return [regions[0]], 'all traffic to one region; the others are cold'
    if strategy == 'round-robin A records':
        return regions, 'clients pick one, roughly evenly; ignores distance and health'
    if strategy == 'geo / latency-based':
        return [user_region], 'nearest region; needs health data to avoid a dead one'
    raise ValueError(strategy)

REGIONS = ['eu-west', 'us-east', 'ap-south']
for strategy in ('single A record', 'round-robin A records', 'geo / latency-based'):
    answer, note = dns_strategy(strategy, REGIONS, user_region='ap-south')
    print(f'{strategy:<24}{str(answer):<40}{note}')

single A record         ['eu-west']                             all traffic to one region; the others are cold
round-robin A records   ['eu-west', 'us-east', 'ap-south']      clients pick one, roughly evenly; ignores distance and health
geo / latency-based     ['ap-south']                            nearest region; needs health data to avoid a dead one

DNS's limitation is the same one §12.7 described: caching makes it slow to change. A TTL is a lower bound, resolvers and clients ignore it, and a connection pool resolves once at startup. So DNS is excellent for coarse, stable routing — region selection, spreading across data centres — and unsuitable as a failover mechanism that must act in seconds. Use it to choose a region, and something faster inside the region to choose a machine.

A CDN removes the request entirely. A network of points of presence near users serves cached responses without the origin being involved, which is both a latency win and a capacity win — and the capacity win is the larger one.

def cdn_effect(requests_per_s, hit_rate, origin_rtt_ms, edge_rtt_ms):
    origin_load = requests_per_s * (1 - hit_rate)
    mean_latency = hit_rate * edge_rtt_ms + (1 - hit_rate) * origin_rtt_ms
    return origin_load, mean_latency

print(f'{"CDN hit rate":>14}{"origin load/s":>16}{"mean latency":>15}')
for hit_rate in (0.0, 0.80, 0.95, 0.98, 0.995):
    load, latency = cdn_effect(400_000, hit_rate, origin_rtt_ms=140, edge_rtt_ms=15)
    print(f'{hit_rate:>13.1%}{load:>16,.0f}{latency:>12.0f} ms')

  CDN hit rate   origin load/s   mean latency
         0.0%         400,000         140 ms
        80.0%          80,000          40 ms
        95.0%          20,000          21 ms
        98.0%           8,000          18 ms
        99.5%           2,000          16 ms

At a 98% hit rate, 400,000 requests a second reaches the origin as 8,000 — the difference between a fleet and a rack. §9.1's warning applies unchanged: the interesting region is the far end, and a hit rate falling from 98% to 90% multiplies origin load fivefold.

There are two ways content gets to the edge, and choosing wrongly is a real cost:

Pull CDN
The edge fetches from the origin on the first miss and caches it. No publishing step and no wasted storage — only what people ask for is stored. Costs one slow request per object per POP, and a burst of origin traffic after a cache purge or a new deploy.
Push CDN
You upload content to the edge before anyone asks. No first-request penalty, and full control over when content appears — which matters for a coordinated launch. Costs a publishing pipeline and storage for everything, including what nobody requests.

A pull CDN is the default and is right for almost everything, because most catalogues are long-tailed and pushing them all is paying to store what nobody reads. A push CDN earns its keep for a small, high-value, known-in-advance set — the site's own assets, a launch video, a game patch every client will request within the same hour. And note that the first-request penalty is per POP, not global: with a hundred points of presence, a popular object is fetched from the origin a hundred times, which is exactly the cold-start arithmetic from §9.6 in a different costume.

The rule that decides what is cacheable at all: cache by URL, and put the version in it. An immutable URL (app.4f3c1e.js) can be cached for a year at every layer with no invalidation problem (§9.5), and a new version is a new URL. That single convention is what makes a 98% hit rate achievable rather than aspirational.

Exercises

Exercise 2.1 — Find the ceiling. A system runs on one application server and one database. Traffic is growing 15% a month. Current peak: 900 requests/s, 40% CPU on an 8-core app server, 25% CPU on the database, 180 GB of data growing 8% a month. Sessions are in process memory. Say what breaks first, when, and in what order — and give the fix for each.

Solution 
def project(value, monthly_growth, months):
    return value * (1 + monthly_growth) ** months

print(f'{"month":>6}{"req/s":>9}{"app CPU":>10}{"db CPU":>9}{"data GB":>10}')
for month in (0, 6, 12, 18, 24):
    rps = project(900, 0.15, month)
    print(f'{month:>6}{rps:>9,.0f}{project(0.40, 0.15, month):>9.0%}'
          f'{project(0.25, 0.15, month):>9.0%}{project(180, 0.08, month):>10,.0f}')

LIMITS = [
    ('app CPU hits 80%', 0.40, 0.15, 0.80),
    ('db CPU hits 80%',  0.25, 0.15, 0.80),
    ('data hits 2 TB',   180,  0.08, 2_000),
]
import math
print()
for name, start, growth, limit in LIMITS:
    months = math.log(limit / start) / math.log(1 + growth)
    print(f'{name:<20} in {months:>5.1f} months')

 month    req/s   app CPU   db CPU   data GB
     0      900      40%      25%       180
     6    2,082      93%      58%       286
    12    4,815     214%     134%       453
    18   11,138     495%     309%       719
    24   25,763    1145%     716%     1,141

app CPU hits 80%     in   5.0 months
db CPU hits 80%      in   8.3 months
data hits 2 TB       in  31.3 months

The order is app CPU, then database CPU, then storage — and the first one arrives in five months. But the honest answer to "what breaks first" is none of those:

Sessions in process memory break on the first day of the fix. The moment a second application server is added — which is the response to app CPU — every user routed to the new node is logged out (§2.2). This is the failure that is not on the graph, and it is first because it is triggered by the remedy rather than by growth. Move sessions to a shared store or a signed token now, while there is no urgency, because the alternative is doing it during a capacity incident.

Then, in order:

Month 5 — app CPU. Add application servers behind a layer-7 balancer (§2.4). This is easy if the sessions move first, and impossible if they do not. Least-connections rather than round robin, and readiness checks rather than deep ones (§2.5).

Month 13 — database CPU. Two moves, in this order: scale vertically (§2.1), which is a resize and no code change, and add read replicas (§7.3) for read traffic, which is a small change with a large effect if the workload is read-heavy. Neither of these is sharding, and sharding is not needed yet.

Month 31 — storage. Thirty-one months is a long way off, and the fix by then may be archival to object storage (§6.7) rather than partitioning. Do not shard now, but do choose a partition key now (§8.3) and make sure nothing in the schema makes it impossible.

The general lesson is the ordering. Every one of these is a routine change if done before it is urgent, and every one is an incident if done after. The single highest-value action on this list is the one the growth curve does not show.

Exercise 2.2 — Fix the load balancer configuration. Say what each of these five settings causes, in production, and give the correction.

(a) algorithm: round-robin, over backends of two different instance sizes
(b) health check: GET /health, which queries the database and the payment provider
(c) health check: interval 60s, unhealthy after 1 failure, healthy after 1 success
(d) session affinity: enabled, by client IP, because the app keeps sessions in memory
(e) one load balancer instance, with the database behind it replicated three ways
Solution 
FIXES = [
    ('(a) round robin, mixed sizes',
     'the small instances saturate while the large ones idle; tail latency tracks the small ones',
     'least-connections, or weighted round robin with weights set from capacity'),
    ('(b) health check hits dependencies',
     'the payment provider has a blip -> every node fails the check -> the fleet leaves the pool',
     'readiness = "can this instance serve?"; check dependencies in monitoring, not in the LB'),
    ('(c) 60s interval, 1 failure out, 1 success in',
     'up to 60s of traffic to a dead node, and a flapping node re-added on one lucky probe',
     'interval 5s, out after 3 consecutive failures, in after 5 — fast out, slow back'),
    ('(d) affinity by client IP',
     'a corporate NAT or mobile carrier puts thousands of users on one node; a node death logs them out',
     'move sessions to a shared store or a token, then disable affinity entirely'),
    ('(e) one LB, three DB replicas',
     'system availability equals one machine; the DB replication buys nothing above it',
     'a pair with a floating address, or a managed balancer; spend on the SPOF, not the replicated tier'),
]
for setting, effect, fix in FIXES:
    print(f'{setting}\n   causes: {effect}\n   fix   : {fix}\n')

(a) round robin, mixed sizes
   causes: the small instances saturate while the large ones idle; tail latency tracks the small ones
   fix   : least-connections, or weighted round robin with weights set from capacity

(b) health check hits dependencies
   causes: the payment provider has a blip -> every node fails the check -> the fleet leaves the pool
   fix   : readiness = "can this instance serve?"; check dependencies in monitoring, not in the LB

(c) 60s interval, 1 failure out, 1 success in
   causes: up to 60s of traffic to a dead node, and a flapping node re-added on one lucky probe
   fix   : interval 5s, out after 3 consecutive failures, in after 5 — fast out, slow back

(d) affinity by client IP
   causes: a corporate NAT or mobile carrier puts thousands of users on one node; a node death logs them out
   fix   : move sessions to a shared store or a token, then disable affinity entirely

(e) one LB, three DB replicas
   causes: system availability equals one machine; the DB replication buys nothing above it
   fix   : a pair with a floating address, or a managed balancer; spend on the SPOF, not the replicated tier

Three deserve more than a line.

(b) is the amplifier, and it is the most dangerous setting in the list. A dependency that is down is down identically for every node, so failing them all out of the pool converts a degraded system into a completely unavailable one — and it does so at the exact moment when serving the requests that do not need that dependency would have been most valuable (§2.5). The rule is worth stating absolutely: a health check must never fail for a reason that is the same on every instance.

(d) has a second problem beyond the ones in §2.3. Affinity by client IP is not affinity by user: a corporate NAT, a mobile carrier's gateway or a large VPN presents thousands of distinct users as one address, so they all pin to one backend. The load distribution is then determined by the shape of your users' networks, which is not something you control or can predict.

(e) is the arithmetic from §2.6. Three database replicas behind one load balancer is a system whose availability is the balancer's, and the replicas contribute essentially nothing to the total. Money spent on the replicated tier while a single instance sits in front of it is money spent on the wrong component — and the check is mechanical: list every component with an instance count of one.

Exercise 2.3 — Design for ten times the traffic. A read-heavy content site serves 20,000 requests/s from 12 application servers and one database with two read replicas, at a 60% CDN hit rate. Plan for 200,000 requests/s. Show the arithmetic, name what you would change in what order, and say which change buys the most.

Solution

Do the CDN arithmetic before anything else, because it changes every other number.

CURRENT_RPS, TARGET_RPS = 20_000, 200_000
APP_SERVERS, CURRENT_HIT = 12, 0.60

def origin(rps, hit_rate):
    return rps * (1 - hit_rate)

def servers_needed(origin_rps, per_server=(20_000 * (1 - 0.60)) / 12):
    return origin_rps / per_server

print(f'{"CDN hit rate":>14}{"origin req/s":>15}{"app servers":>14}')
for hit_rate in (0.60, 0.90, 0.98):
    o = origin(TARGET_RPS, hit_rate)
    print(f'{hit_rate:>13.0%}{o:>15,.0f}{servers_needed(o):>14,.0f}')

print(f'\ntoday: {origin(CURRENT_RPS, CURRENT_HIT):,.0f} origin req/s on {APP_SERVERS} servers'
      f' = {origin(CURRENT_RPS, CURRENT_HIT) / APP_SERVERS:,.0f} req/s per server')
print(f'raising the hit rate 60% -> 98% removes '
      f'{origin(TARGET_RPS, 0.60) - origin(TARGET_RPS, 0.98):,.0f} req/s at 10x traffic')

  CDN hit rate   origin req/s   app servers
          60%         80,000           120
          90%         20,000            30
          98%          4,000             6

today: 8,000 origin req/s on 12 servers = 667 req/s per server
raising the hit rate 60% -> 98% removes 76,000 req/s at 10x traffic

The CDN hit rate is worth more than everything else combined, and it is the cheapest change on the list. At 60% the target needs 120 application servers; at 98% it needs 6 — half the fleet you already have, at ten times the traffic. That is a caching and cache-header exercise (§9.5, §2.7), not a capacity purchase: immutable URLs for assets, sensible Cache-Control on content pages, stale-while-revalidate so an expiry never becomes a stampede (§9.6), and Vary headers narrow enough that the cache key is not fragmented into uselessness.

Then, in order of value per unit of effort:

1. Raise the CDN hit rate to 95%+. Days of work, removes 90% of the remaining load. Nothing else on this list is close.

2. Add an application-level cache for whatever still reaches the origin, so those requests mostly avoid the database too (§9.2's cascade — the layers multiply).

3. Scale the application tier horizontally, which is straightforward if it is already stateless (§2.2) and impossible if it is not. Verify that first.

4. Add read replicas. The site is read-heavy, so this scales the part that grows. Two replicas today; the number needed follows from what survives the caches, which is why it is fourth rather than first — sizing the database before fixing the caches sizes it for traffic that will never arrive.

5. Only then consider partitioning. A read-heavy content site behind a 98% CDN hit rate almost certainly never needs it, and §8.1's warning applies: the cost is permanent and the trigger has not occurred.

And the thing to check before any of it: the single points of failure (§2.6). Ten times the traffic on one load balancer and one database primary is ten times the traffic through two components whose failure is total. Growth makes an outage more expensive, so the availability work belongs in this plan and not in a later one.

SECTION 3

Availability

Availability is the property users actually experience, and it is the one most often stated as a number nobody has costed. "We need five nines" is a sentence that sounds like a requirement and is usually a wish — five nines is twenty-six seconds of downtime a month, less than a single deploy, and it constrains almost every other decision in the system. This section is about making availability a quantity you can reason about: what the numbers mean, what they cost, how a system fails when it is overloaded rather than broken, and what to do about it.

3.1 The Nines, and What They Cost

Start by making the number concrete, because a percentage is easy to agree to and a duration is not.

MINUTES = {'year': 525_960, 'month': 43_830, 'week': 10_080, 'day': 1_440}

def downtime(availability, period):
    return (1 - availability) * MINUTES[period]

print(f'{"nines":<18}{"availability":>14}{"per year":>13}{"per month":>14}{"per week":>13}')
for nines, availability in [('two', 0.99), ('three', 0.999), ('three and a half', 0.9995),
                            ('four', 0.9999), ('five', 0.99999)]:
    hours = downtime(availability, 'year') / 60
    month = downtime(availability, 'month')
    week = downtime(availability, 'week')
    print(f'{nines:<18}{availability:>13.5%}{hours:>10,.1f} h'
          f'{month:>10,.1f} min{week:>9,.1f} min')

nines               availability     per year     per month     per week
two                   99.00000%      87.7 h     438.3 min    100.8 min
three                 99.90000%       8.8 h      43.8 min     10.1 min
three and a half      99.95000%       4.4 h      21.9 min      5.0 min
four                  99.99000%       0.9 h       4.4 min      1.0 min
five                  99.99900%       0.1 h       0.4 min      0.1 min

Read the weekly column, because that is the horizon a team operates on. Three nines is ten minutes a week — one bad deploy, comfortably. Four nines is one minute a week, which means a deploy cannot cause user-visible downtime at all, so blue-green or canary is mandatory rather than nice.
