t=2   B and C notice, elect B as the new leader
t=3   A still believes it is leader — nothing has told it otherwise
t=4   a client reaches A and A accepts a write
t=31  A's lease expires; A steps down

Between t=2 and t=31 there are two leaders. The standard defence is fencing: every leader gets a monotonically increasing token, and every downstream service rejects anything carrying a token older than the highest it has seen.

class FencedStore:
    def __init__(self):
        self.highest_token = 0
        self.value = None

    def write(self, token, value):
        if token < self.highest_token:
            return f'REJECTED token {token} (already saw {self.highest_token})'
        self.highest_token = token
        self.value = value
        return f'accepted token {token}: {value!r}'

store = FencedStore()
print(store.write(7, 'from old leader A'))    # A, still holding token 7
print(store.write(8, 'from new leader B'))    # B elected, token 8
print(store.write(7, 'from old leader A'))    # A tries again — too late
print('final value:', store.value)

accepted token 7: 'from old leader A'
accepted token 8: 'from new leader B'
REJECTED token 7 (already saw 8)
final value: from new leader B

The zombie leader's write was rejected by the storage layer, which did not need to know anything about elections — only that tokens never go backwards. Fencing tokens are the thing most homegrown leader-election schemes leave out, and their absence is why "we use a distributed lock" is so often followed by "and we still got duplicate writes".

5.4 Leader Election and Raft

Raft is the consensus algorithm most systems use, because it was explicitly designed to be understandable. It has three states and one central idea: a term is a logical clock, and every term has at most one leader.

Follower
The default. Accepts entries from a leader, votes when asked. Becomes a candidate if it hears nothing for an election timeout.
Candidate
Increments the term, votes for itself, asks everyone else for a vote. Wins with a majority.
Leader
The only node that accepts writes. Replicates entries and sends heartbeats to suppress new elections.

The election rules are short enough to implement:

class Node:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.term = 0
        self.voted_for = None
        self.state = 'follower'

    def request_vote(self, candidate, term):
        """A node grants at most one vote per term, and never votes backwards."""
        if term < self.term:
            return False, f'{self.name}: no — term {term} is stale (mine is {self.term})'
        if term > self.term:
            self.term, self.voted_for, self.state = term, None, 'follower'
        if self.voted_for in (None, candidate):
            self.voted_for = candidate
            return True, f'{self.name}: yes to {candidate} in term {term}'
        return False, f'{self.name}: no — already voted for {self.voted_for} in term {term}'

cluster = {n: Node(n) for n in 'ABC'}

# A times out and stands for election in term 1
cluster['A'].term, cluster['A'].state, cluster['A'].voted_for = 1, 'candidate', 'A'
votes = 1
for name in 'BC':
    granted, why = cluster[name].request_vote('A', 1)
    votes += granted
    print(why)
print(f'A has {votes}/3 votes -> {"LEADER" if votes > 3 // 2 else "no majority"}\n')

# C also times out and stands, unaware. It cannot win term 1.
granted, why = cluster['B'].request_vote('C', 1)
print(why)
print('C cannot win term 1: B already voted, and a term has at most one leader')

B: yes to A in term 1
C: yes to A in term 1
A has 3/3 votes -> LEADER

B: no — already voted for A in term 1
C cannot win term 1: B already voted, and a term has at most one leader

One vote per node per term, plus a majority to win, is what makes two leaders in one term impossible — two majorities of the same cluster must share at least one node, and that node only voted once.

A split vote is possible, and Raft's answer is deliberately unglamorous: randomised election timeouts, so that the next attempt is very unlikely to collide again.

def split_vote_chance(cluster_size, simultaneous_candidates):
    """Two candidates in a 3-node cluster can deadlock at 1 vote each + their own."""
    return simultaneous_candidates > 1 and cluster_size % 2 == 1

print(split_vote_chance(3, 2), split_vote_chance(3, 1))
print('fix: each node waits a random 150-300 ms before standing, so collisions are rare')
print('and a collision only costs one more election timeout, not correctness')

True False
fix: each node waits a random 150-300 ms before standing, so collisions are rare
and a collision only costs one more election timeout, not correctness

The second half of Raft is log replication. The leader appends an entry, sends it to the followers, and commits it once a majority have stored it — at which point it is durable even if the leader dies immediately.

def commit_index(match_index, cluster_size):
    """The highest index stored on a majority of nodes."""
    ordered = sorted(match_index.values(), reverse=True)
    return ordered[cluster_size // 2]

# how far each follower has got, by log index
print(commit_index({'A': 7, 'B': 7, 'C': 5}, 3))
print(commit_index({'A': 7, 'B': 5, 'C': 5}, 3))
print(commit_index({'A': 9, 'B': 9, 'C': 9, 'D': 4, 'E': 4}, 5))
print(commit_index({'A': 9, 'B': 4, 'C': 4, 'D': 4, 'E': 4}, 5))

7
5
9
4

Entries below the commit index are safe; entries above it are not yet acknowledged and may be lost if the leader fails. Note the last case: a leader far ahead of everyone else has committed nothing beyond index 4, because the leader's own copy does not count as agreement.

5.5 Failure Detection

Every one of the mechanisms above starts with "if a node stops responding". How that is decided matters more than it looks.

Heartbeats are the basic mechanism: each node periodically announces it is alive, and silence past a threshold is treated as failure. The threshold is a direct trade:

def detection(heartbeat_ms, missed_allowed, p99_pause_ms):
    timeout = heartbeat_ms * missed_allowed
    return timeout, 'stable' if timeout > p99_pause_ms else 'FALSE POSITIVES'

for hb, missed in [(100, 3), (500, 3), (1000, 5), (50, 2)]:
    timeout, verdict = detection(hb, missed, p99_pause_ms=800)
    print(f'heartbeat {hb:>5} ms x {missed} missed = {timeout:>5} ms timeout   {verdict}')

heartbeat   100 ms x 3 missed =   300 ms timeout   FALSE POSITIVES
heartbeat   500 ms x 3 missed =  1500 ms timeout   stable
heartbeat  1000 ms x 5 missed =  5000 ms timeout   stable
heartbeat    50 ms x 2 missed =   100 ms timeout   FALSE POSITIVES

A timeout shorter than your worst normal pause manufactures failures. A 300 ms timeout on a service whose 99th-percentile garbage-collection pause is 800 ms will declare healthy nodes dead several times an hour, triggering elections, failovers and rebalances that are pure cost — and each of those makes the system slower, which makes more nodes miss their heartbeats. That feedback loop is a cascading failure, and a too-aggressive failure detector is one of its most common triggers.

The opposite error is just as real: a five-second timeout means five seconds of writes failing before anything is done about it.

For clusters larger than a handful of nodes, all-to-all heartbeats do not scale — the message count is quadratic:

for n in [3, 10, 100, 1000]:
    print(f'{n:>5} nodes: all-to-all = {n * (n - 1):>9,} msgs/interval'
          f'   gossip (fanout 3) = {n * 3:>6,}')

    3 nodes: all-to-all =         6 msgs/interval   gossip (fanout 3) =      9
   10 nodes: all-to-all =        90 msgs/interval   gossip (fanout 3) =     30
  100 nodes: all-to-all =     9,900 msgs/interval   gossip (fanout 3) =    300
 1000 nodes: all-to-all =   999,000 msgs/interval   gossip (fanout 3) =  3,000

Gossip is the answer at scale: each node tells a few random peers what it knows, and information spreads exponentially. It converges in about log(N) rounds rather than one, so it is slower to detect a failure and vastly cheaper.

import math

def rounds_to_converge(n, fanout):
    """Roughly how many gossip rounds until everyone has heard."""
    return math.ceil(math.log(n, fanout + 1))

for n in [10, 100, 1_000, 10_000]:
    print(f'{n:>6,} nodes, fanout 3 -> ~{rounds_to_converge(n, 3)} rounds to reach everyone')

    10 nodes, fanout 3 -> ~2 rounds to reach everyone
   100 nodes, fanout 3 -> ~4 rounds to reach everyone
 1,000 nodes, fanout 3 -> ~5 rounds to reach everyone
10,000 nodes, fanout 3 -> ~7 rounds to reach everyone

Ten thousand nodes, seven rounds. That logarithmic growth is why gossip underpins membership in Cassandra, Consul and Serf, and why a cluster of thousands is not qualitatively harder to monitor than a cluster of hundreds.

5.6 Ordering Without a Clock

Consensus tells you what was agreed. A related and separate question is what happened before what — and wall-clock timestamps cannot answer it, because clocks on different machines disagree.

def clock_skew_demo(events):
    """Two nodes, each stamping with its own slightly-wrong clock."""
    for label, node, local_clock, real_time in events:
        print(f'{label:<28} node {node}  stamped {local_clock:>6.1f}  (really {real_time:>5.1f})')

clock_skew_demo([
    ('A writes x=1',  'A', 100.0, 100.0),
    ('B writes x=2',  'B',  99.7, 100.4),   # B's clock is 700 ms behind
])
print()
print('by timestamp: A(100.0) is newer, so x=1 wins')
print('in reality:   B wrote later, so x=2 should win')
print('last-write-wins by wall clock silently discarded the newer write')

A writes x=1                 node A  stamped  100.0  (really 100.0)
B writes x=2                 node B  stamped   99.7  (really 100.4)

by timestamp: A(100.0) is newer, so x=1 wins
in reality:   B wrote later, so x=2 should win
last-write-wins by wall clock silently discarded the newer write

Last-write-wins conflict resolution loses data whenever clocks disagree, and clocks always disagree by some amount. NTP typically keeps machines within tens of milliseconds; a machine with a broken NTP client can be off by minutes, and nothing in the write path notices.

Lamport timestamps fix ordering without needing clocks at all. Each node keeps a counter, increments it on every event, and includes it in every message; a receiver sets its counter to max(mine, theirs) + 1.

class LamportClock:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name, self.counter = name, 0

    def local_event(self, what):
        self.counter += 1
        return f'{self.name}{self.counter} {what}'

    def send(self, what):
        self.counter += 1
        return self.counter, f'{self.name}{self.counter} send {what}'

    def receive(self, their_counter, what):
        self.counter = max(self.counter, their_counter) + 1
        return f'{self.name}{self.counter} recv {what}'

a, b = LamportClock('A'), LamportClock('B')
print(a.local_event('start'))
ts, line = a.send('x=1')
print(line)
print(b.local_event('unrelated work'))
print(b.receive(ts, 'x=1'))
print(b.local_event('x=2'))

A1 start
A2 send x=1
B1 unrelated work
B3 recv x=1
B4 x=2

B's counter jumped from 1 to 3 on receiving A2, which guarantees the property that matters: if event p caused event q, then p's timestamp is smaller than q's. So x=2 at B4 is correctly ordered after x=1 at A2.

The limitation is the converse. A smaller timestamp does not prove causality — B1 and A2 are concurrent, and Lamport timestamps cannot tell you so. Vector clocks can, at the cost of storing one counter per node:

def happened_before(v1, v2):
    """True if v1 causally precedes v2."""
    return all(v1.get(k, 0) <= v2.get(k, 0) for k in set(v1) | set(v2)) and v1 != v2

def relation(v1, v2):
    if v1 == v2:
        return 'identical'
    if happened_before(v1, v2):
        return 'v1 -> v2'
    if happened_before(v2, v1):
        return 'v2 -> v1'
    return 'CONCURRENT — a genuine conflict'

CASES = [
    ({'A': 2, 'B': 0}, {'A': 3, 'B': 0}),
    ({'A': 2, 'B': 1}, {'A': 2, 'B': 3}),
    ({'A': 2, 'B': 0}, {'A': 0, 'B': 2}),
    ({'A': 1, 'B': 1}, {'A': 1, 'B': 1}),
]
for v1, v2 in CASES:
    print(f'{str(v1):<18} vs {str(v2):<18} -> {relation(v1, v2)}')

{'A': 2, 'B': 0}   vs {'A': 3, 'B': 0}   -> v1 -> v2
{'A': 2, 'B': 1}   vs {'A': 2, 'B': 3}   -> v1 -> v2
{'A': 2, 'B': 0}   vs {'A': 0, 'B': 2}   -> CONCURRENT — a genuine conflict
{'A': 1, 'B': 1}   vs {'A': 1, 'B': 1}   -> identical

The third case is the valuable one. Two writes that neither preceded the other are a real conflict, and a vector clock says so instead of silently picking one. What to do about it is then an application decision — merge the values, keep both as siblings and let the user choose, or use a data type that merges automatically. Dynamo-style stores expose exactly this, and the reason many teams turn it off is that "handle sibling values" is real work; the reason they should not is that the alternative is losing writes.

5.7 Avoiding Consensus

Everything above is expensive, so the most valuable skill in this section is recognising when you do not need it.

Make the operation commutative. If order does not change the result, nothing needs to agree on order. Incrementing a counter, adding to a set, taking a maximum.
Partition so that one owner exists. If every key is owned by exactly one node, that node orders its own writes and no agreement is needed across nodes.
Use an existing consensus system. etcd, ZooKeeper and Consul exist so you can keep one small thing consistent — leadership, configuration, membership — and everything else eventually consistent.
Make it idempotent and retry. "Exactly once" needs agreement; "at least once, applied idempotently" needs none, and is indistinguishable from the outside.

The commutativity point is worth demonstrating, because it is the one people underuse:

def apply_all(initial, operations, order):
    value = initial
    for i in order:
        value = operations[i](value)
    return value

increments = [lambda v: v + 1, lambda v: v + 5, lambda v: v + 2]
print('commutative:', {apply_all(0, increments, o) for o in
                       [(0, 1, 2), (2, 1, 0), (1, 0, 2), (1, 2, 0)]})

assignments = [lambda v: 1, lambda v: 5, lambda v: 2]
print('not commutative:', sorted({apply_all(0, assignments, o) for o in
                                  [(0, 1, 2), (2, 1, 0), (0, 2, 1)]}))

commutative: {8}
not commutative: [1, 2, 5]

Every ordering of the increments gives 8, so replicas can apply them in any order, at any time, and converge without ever coordinating. The assignments give three different answers, so somebody has to decide the order — and that decision costs a round trip.

This is why counter += 1 scales and counter = n does not, why "add to cart" is easy to make available and "reserve the last item" is not, and why data types designed to merge — CRDTs — are built entirely out of commutative operations.

The last option is the one to reach for by default:

def needs_consensus(operation):
    return {
        'increment a view counter':        False,
        'append to an activity feed':      False,
        'add a tag to a document':         False,
        'elect the node that runs cron':   True,
        'allocate a globally unique id':   False,
        'sell the last concert ticket':    True,
        'decide which replica is primary': True,
    }[operation]

for op in ['increment a view counter', 'append to an activity feed',
           'add a tag to a document', 'allocate a globally unique id',
           'elect the node that runs cron', 'sell the last concert ticket',
           'decide which replica is primary']:
    print(f'{"CONSENSUS" if needs_consensus(op) else "no       "}  {op}')

no         increment a view counter
no         append to an activity feed
no         add a tag to a document
no         allocate a globally unique id
CONSENSUS  elect the node that runs cron
CONSENSUS  sell the last concert ticket
CONSENSUS  decide which replica is primary

"Allocate a globally unique id" is the interesting no. It sounds like it needs global agreement and does not: give each node a distinct prefix and let it allocate freely within its own range, and uniqueness falls out with zero coordination. A great many apparent consensus problems dissolve like that under one design change, and looking for that change before reaching for Raft is most of the craft.

Exercises

Exercise 5.1 — Size the cluster. For each requirement, give N, R and W, say how many failures it tolerates, and name what you gave up.

(a) A session store. Losing a session logs a user out. Reads vastly outnumber writes.
(b) A ledger of financial transactions. A lost write is unacceptable.
(c) A view counter on a news site, 50,000 writes per second.
(d) The record of which node is the primary for a database.
Solution 
def describe(n, r, w):
    return (f'N={n} R={r} W={w}  overlap={"yes" if r + w > n else "NO"}  '
            f'tolerates {n - max(r, w)} node failure(s)')

CHOICES = [
    ('(a) session store',   3, 1, 2, 'stale reads for a few ms after a write'),
    ('(b) ledger',          5, 3, 3, '160 ms cross-region writes; minority side unavailable'),
    ('(c) view counter',    3, 1, 1, 'any consistency guarantee at all'),
    ('(d) primary record',  5, 3, 3, 'availability during a partition, deliberately'),
]
for label, n, r, w, gave_up in CHOICES:
    print(f'{label:<22} {describe(n, r, w)}')
    print(f'{"":<22} gave up: {gave_up}\n')

(a) session store      N=3 R=1 W=2  overlap=NO  tolerates 1 node failure(s)
                       gave up: stale reads for a few ms after a write

(b) ledger             N=5 R=3 W=3  overlap=yes  tolerates 2 node failure(s)
                       gave up: 160 ms cross-region writes; minority side unavailable

(c) view counter       N=3 R=1 W=1  overlap=NO  tolerates 2 node failure(s)
                       gave up: any consistency guarantee at all

(d) primary record     N=5 R=3 W=3  overlap=yes  tolerates 2 node failure(s)
                       gave up: availability during a partition, deliberately

(a) N=3, R=1, W=2 deliberately breaks the overlap rule, and that is defensible here: reads are cheap and frequent, W=2 means a session survives one node dying, and the failure mode of a stale read is that a user is momentarily logged out — annoying, not dangerous. Naming the failure mode is the whole justification; if it were a permissions cache rather than a session store, the same numbers would be a security bug.

(b) N=5, R=3, W=3 is the classic majority configuration. Five rather than three because a ledger should survive two simultaneous failures, and because you want to be able to lose a node for maintenance and still tolerate one unplanned failure. Realistically a ledger should not be a quorum store at all — it should be a single-leader system with synchronous replication and a real transaction log.

(c) N=3, R=1, W=1 is right precisely because the data does not matter much. But the better answer changes the problem: a view counter is commutative (§5.7), so the correct design is not a quorum at all — accumulate increments locally, flush them periodically, and let them merge. Fifty thousand writes per second against a quorum store is an expensive way to be approximately right.

(d) is the one case where you should not implement this yourself. "Which node is primary" is exactly what etcd, ZooKeeper and Consul exist for, and using one gets you fencing tokens (§5.3), lease renewal and a tested implementation. The numbers above describe what etcd is doing internally.

The pattern across all four: the configuration follows from what a wrong answer costs, not from a preference for consistency or availability in the abstract.

Exercise 5.2 — Find the split-brain. This lock service is used to decide which worker processes a queue. Find every way it can allow two workers to run at once, and fix it.

class LockService:
    def __init__(self):
        self.holder = None

    def acquire(self, worker):
        if self.holder is None:
            self.holder = worker
            return True
        return False

    def release(self, worker):
        self.holder = None
Solution

Four faults, and each one independently allows two workers to run.

1. There is no lease. If the holder crashes, holder stays set forever and nothing ever runs again. The obvious fix — a timeout — introduces fault 2.

2. Once there is a timeout, the holder can be a zombie. The lock expires, a second worker acquires it, and the first worker — merely paused, not dead (§5.1) — wakes up and carries on believing it holds the lock. No lock service can prevent this; only fencing at the resource can (§5.3).

3. release does not check the caller. A late release() from an expired holder unlocks the lock that a different worker now holds.

4. The service is a single point of failure with no replication, so "the lock service is down" means "nothing runs".

class LockService:
    """A lease-based lock with fencing tokens. Clock is injected so this is testable."""
    def __init__(self, lease_seconds=30):
        self.lease_seconds = lease_seconds
        self.holder = None
        self.expires_at = 0.0
        self.token = 0

    def acquire(self, worker, now):
        if self.holder is not None and now < self.expires_at:
            return None                          # still held
        self.token += 1                          # monotonic, never reused
        self.holder, self.expires_at = worker, now + self.lease_seconds
        return self.token

    def renew(self, worker, token, now):
        if self.holder != worker or token != self.token or now >= self.expires_at:
            return False                         # lost it; do not pretend otherwise
        self.expires_at = now + self.lease_seconds
        return True

    def release(self, worker, token):
        if self.holder == worker and token == self.token:
            self.holder, self.expires_at = None, 0.0
            return True
        return False                             # a late release cannot unlock someone else

class Queue:
    """The resource. It fences, which is what actually provides safety."""
    def __init__(self):
        self.highest_token = 0
        self.processed = []

    def process(self, item, token):
        if token < self.highest_token:
            return f'REJECTED {item!r} (token {token} < {self.highest_token})'
        self.highest_token = token
        self.processed.append(item)
        return f'processed {item!r} with token {token}'

lock, queue = LockService(lease_seconds=30), Queue()

t1 = lock.acquire('w1', now=0)
print('w1 acquired, token', t1)
print(queue.process('job-1', t1))

print('w1 pauses for 40s — its lease expires at t=30')
t2 = lock.acquire('w2', now=40)
print('w2 acquired, token', t2)
print(queue.process('job-2', t2))

print('w1 wakes up, still believing it holds the lock:')
print(queue.process('job-3', t1))
print('w1 tries to renew:', lock.renew('w1', t1, now=41))
print('w1 tries to release:', lock.release('w1', t1))
print('processed:', queue.processed)

w1 acquired, token 1
processed 'job-1' with token 1
w1 pauses for 40s — its lease expires at t=30
w2 acquired, token 2
processed 'job-2' with token 2
w1 wakes up, still believing it holds the lock:
REJECTED 'job-3' (token 1 < 2)
w1 tries to renew: False
w1 tries to release: False
processed: ['job-1', 'job-2']

Three defences fired. The queue rejected the zombie's work — this is the one that matters, because it is the only one that does not depend on the zombie behaving well. renew refused, so w1 learns it has been deposed the next time it checks. release refused, so w1 could not unlock w2's lock.

Two notes on the design. The clock is a parameter, not time.time() — that is what makes the 40-second pause testable in a single deterministic run, and it is the same principle as injecting a clock anywhere else. And fault 4 is not fixed here: a real deployment replaces LockService with etcd or ZooKeeper, which is a replicated consensus system rather than one Python object. The fencing in Queue is still your job even then.

Exercise 5.3 — Order these events. Three nodes, no synchronised clocks. Assign Lamport timestamps, then vector clocks, and say which pairs are genuinely concurrent.

A1: A writes profile.name = "ada"
B1: B writes profile.email = "ada@x"     (B has not heard from A)
A2: A sends its state to C
C1: C receives A's message
C2: C writes profile.name = "grace"
B2: B sends its state to C
C3: C receives B's message
Solution

Each node keeps a Lamport counter and a vector with one entry per node. A local event bumps its own entry; a receive takes the element-wise maximum and then bumps its own.

class Node:
    def __init__(self, name, peers):
        self.name, self.lamport = name, 0
        self.vector = dict.fromkeys(peers, 0)

    def event(self, what):
        self.lamport += 1
        self.vector[self.name] += 1
        return self._show(what)

    def receive(self, their_lamport, their_vector, what):
        self.lamport = max(self.lamport, their_lamport) + 1
        self.vector[self.name] += 1
        for k, v in their_vector.items():
            self.vector[k] = max(self.vector[k], v)
        return self._show(what)

    def _show(self, what):
        vec = ','.join(f'{k}{v}' for k, v in sorted(self.vector.items()))
        return f'{self.name}  L={self.lamport}  V=({vec})  {what}'

a, b, c = Node('A', 'ABC'), Node('B', 'ABC'), Node('C', 'ABC')

print(a.event('name = "ada"'))
print(b.event('email = "ada@x"'))
print(a.event('send state to C'))
snap_a = (a.lamport, dict(a.vector))
print(c.receive(*snap_a, 'receive from A'))
print(c.event('name = "grace"'))
print(b.event('send state to C'))
snap_b = (b.lamport, dict(b.vector))
print(c.receive(*snap_b, 'receive from B'))

A  L=1  V=(A1,B0,C0)  name = "ada"
B  L=1  V=(A0,B1,C0)  email = "ada@x"
A  L=2  V=(A2,B0,C0)  send state to C
C  L=3  V=(A2,B0,C1)  receive from A
C  L=4  V=(A2,B0,C2)  name = "grace"
B  L=2  V=(A0,B2,C0)  send state to C
C  L=5  V=(A2,B2,C3)  receive from B

Note dict(a.vector) when taking the snapshot: a message carries a copy of the sender's vector, not a live reference to it. Sending a.vector itself would let later events at A alter a message that has already been sent — the aliasing trap, arriving in a distributed system.

Now the comparisons:

def relation(v1, v2):
    le = all(v1[k] <= v2[k] for k in v1)
    ge = all(v1[k] >= v2[k] for k in v1)
    if le and ge:
        return 'identical'
    if le:
        return 'first happened before second'
    if ge:
        return 'second happened before first'
    return 'CONCURRENT — a genuine conflict'

A1 = {'A': 1, 'B': 0, 'C': 0}
B1 = {'A': 0, 'B': 1, 'C': 0}
C2 = {'A': 2, 'B': 0, 'C': 2}
C3 = {'A': 2, 'B': 2, 'C': 3}

for label, v1, v2 in [('A1 vs B1', A1, B1), ('A1 vs C2', A1, C2),
                      ('B1 vs C2', B1, C2), ('C2 vs C3', C2, C3)]:
    print(f'{label}: {relation(v1, v2)}')

A1 vs B1: CONCURRENT — a genuine conflict
A1 vs C2: first happened before second
B1 vs C2: CONCURRENT — a genuine conflict
C2 vs C3: first happened before second

Three answers worth reading.

A1 and B1 are concurrent. Neither node had heard of the other, so nothing orders them. Here they happen to touch different fields, so merging is trivial — but had both written name, this is a real conflict that some rule or some human has to resolve.

A1 precedes C2. C received A's state before writing, so name = "grace" is a legitimate overwrite of name = "ada", and last-write-wins is safe for this pair.

B1 and C2 are concurrent — despite C2 having a much larger Lamport timestamp (L=4 against L=2). That is exactly the limitation stated in §5.6: a bigger Lamport number does not imply causality, only the reverse. The vector is what distinguishes them, and it costs one counter per node to store and to ship with every message.

The Lamport column is still useful, and for a reason worth knowing: it gives a total order — break ties by node name and every event has a distinct rank. That is enough for anything that needs an order rather than the causal order, and it is far cheaper than a vector.

The practical lesson is the last one. Vector clocks tell you that there is a conflict; they never tell you what to do about it. Designing so that concurrent writes touch different fields — or so the operations commute (§5.7) — is what turns a hard conflict into no conflict at all.

SECTION 6

Data Stores

"Which database should we use?" is the wrong question, and answering it in the abstract produces the architecture diagrams that have four databases and one that anybody actually queries. The right question is narrower and answerable: given these access patterns, at this volume, with these consistency requirements, what is the cheapest store that serves them? This section is about being able to answer it — what each family of store is genuinely good at, what it costs, and the small number of measurements that decide between them.

6.1 Start From the Access Patterns

Before naming any product, write down what the system will actually do to the data. Five properties settle most of the decision, and none of them is "is the data structured?".

Query shape
Lookup by key? Range scan? Arbitrary filters across several fields? Aggregation over millions of rows? Traversal of relationships? These have almost nothing in common, and a store that is excellent at one is usually mediocre at another.
Read/write ratio
A 1000:1 read-heavy workload can be denormalised and cached into almost any store. A write-heavy one cannot, and the write path becomes the design.
Volume and growth
Gigabytes on one machine forever, or terabytes needing partitioning (§8)? This is the question that eliminates the most options, and it is the one most often answered aspirationally.
Consistency requirement
Which of §4.2's three meanings, on which operations? "Strong for balances, eventual for the activity feed" is a normal answer and points at two different stores.
Access frequency
Uniform, or a hot 1% (§9.3's power law)? Skewed access means a small cache does most of the work, which changes what the store has to be good at.

The arithmetic that follows from those numbers usually decides the question before any product is named:

def profile(rows, row_bytes, reads_per_s, writes_per_s, growth_per_year):
    size_gb = rows * row_bytes / 1e9
    return {
        'size now': f'{size_gb:,.0f} GB',
        'size in 3 years': f'{size_gb * growth_per_year ** 3:,.0f} GB',
        'fits one node (2 TB)': size_gb * growth_per_year ** 3 < 2_000,
        'write rate': f'{writes_per_s:,}/s',
        'single-node writes OK (~20k/s)': writes_per_s < 20_000,
        'read:write': f'{reads_per_s // max(writes_per_s, 1)}:1',
    }

CASES = [
    ('user accounts',    5_000_000,    2_000,  8_000,     40, 1.6),
    ('order history',   80_000_000,    1_200, 20_000,  2_000, 2.0),
    ('sensor readings', 20_000_000_000,  100,    500, 400_000, 3.0),
]
for name, rows, row_bytes, reads, writes, growth in CASES:
    print(name)
    for key, value in profile(rows, row_bytes, reads, writes, growth).items():
        print(f'   {key:<32} {value}')

user accounts
   size now                         10 GB
   size in 3 years                  41 GB
   fits one node (2 TB)             True
   write rate                       40/s
   single-node writes OK (~20k/s)   True
   read:write                       200:1
order history
   size now                         96 GB
   size in 3 years                  768 GB
   fits one node (2 TB)             True
   write rate                       2,000/s
   single-node writes OK (~20k/s)   True
   read:write                       10:1
sensor readings
   size now                         2,000 GB
   size in 3 years                  54,000 GB
   fits one node (2 TB)             False
   write rate                       400,000/s
   single-node writes OK (~20k/s)   False
   read:write                       0:1

Three workloads, three different answers, and the deciding line is different in each. User accounts fit on one node for the foreseeable future — relational, no partitioning, and the discussion is over. Order history also fits — 768 GB of a 2 TB node in three years — but it is a third of the ceiling at fifty times the write rate, so it is a relational store with a partitioning plan written down now (§8.3) and a read-replica fan-out (§7.3). The distinction between accounts and orders is not whether it fits; it is how much headroom is left when it does. Sensor readings fail both tests immediately at 400,000 writes a second and 40 TB, which eliminates every single-node option before any preference is expressed.

Do this arithmetic first, in writing. It converts an argument about database preferences into a short list of stores that can physically do the job.

6.2 The Relational Store, and What It Actually Gives You

The default answer is a relational database, and it is the right default for a reason that is often stated backwards. What a relational database sells is not tables. Its value is not tables and rows — it is a bundle of guarantees that are extremely expensive to rebuild in application code.

Transactions
Multi-row atomicity with rollback. Every alternative to a transaction — a saga (§11.7), a compensating write, a reconciliation job — is more code and more failure modes than BEGIN … COMMIT.
Declared constraints
Foreign keys, uniqueness, checks, not-null. The database enforces these against every writer — including the migration script, the admin console and the intern's one-off fix — which application-level validation structurally cannot.
A query planner
You state what you want; the planner decides how. Add an index and every existing query gets faster with no code change. This is the feature people miss most after leaving.
Ad-hoc queries
A question nobody anticipated is answerable at 3 a.m. during an incident, without a schema change or a new index — slowly, but answerable.

That last one is worth dwelling on, because it is the property most often given away accidentally. A key-value store answers exactly the questions its keys were designed for. When the question changes, and it will, a relational store gives you a slow answer today and a fast one after an index; a key-value store gives you a migration.

The honest limits, stated plainly so the choice is real: writes are bounded by one node until you partition, and partitioning costs you the joins and the cross-row transactions that were the point (§8.1); joins across very large tables are expensive whatever the planner does; and a rigid schema means every shape change is a migration (§6.10). Note what is not on that list. "Does not scale" is false — a single well-tuned PostgreSQL node handles tens of thousands of writes a second and terabytes of data, which is more than most systems will ever need. The most common architecture mistake in this section is leaving relational too early, on the strength of a scale that never arrives.

6.3 Indexes, Selectivity, and Reading a Query Plan

Most "the database is slow" problems are one missing index, and most "we need a different database" conversations are one missing index that nobody looked for. An index is a sorted structure that turns a scan into a lookup, and the arithmetic is stark:

import math

def lookups(rows, fanout=200):
    """A B-tree of `fanout` children per node: depth is log_fanout(rows)."""
    scan = rows
    depth = max(1, math.ceil(math.log(rows, fanout)))
    return scan, depth

print(f'{"rows":>15}{"full scan reads":>18}{"B-tree depth":>15}{"speedup":>14}')
for rows in (1_000, 100_000, 10_000_000, 1_000_000_000):
    scan, depth = lookups(rows)
    print(f'{rows:>15,}{scan:>18,}{depth:>15}{scan // depth:>13,}x')

           rows   full scan reads   B-tree depth       speedup
          1,000             1,000              2          500x
        100,000           100,000              3       33,333x
     10,000,000        10,000,000              4    2,500,000x
  1,000,000,000     1,000,000,000              4  250,000,000x

A billion-row table is four page reads away from any row, and that is why the index exists. But an index only helps if the planner can use it, and two properties decide that.

Selectivity is the fraction of rows a condition keeps. Past some threshold a sequential scan is faster than an index scan, because random page reads cost more than sequential ones and the index adds a second structure to walk. Where that threshold sits depends entirely on the cost constants, and the model below — random pages four times the price of sequential ones — puts it at about a quarter of one per cent.

import math

def cost(rows, selectivity, random_page=4.0, sequential_page=1.0, rows_per_page=100):
    pages = rows / rows_per_page
    seq = pages * sequential_page
    matched = rows * selectivity
    idx = matched * random_page + math.log(rows, 200) * random_page
    return seq, idx

print(f'{"selectivity":>13}{"seq scan":>12}{"index scan":>13}{"planner picks":>16}')
for selectivity in (0.0001, 0.001, 0.01, 0.05, 0.20, 0.50):
    seq, idx = cost(10_000_000, selectivity)
    print(f'{selectivity:>12.2%}{seq:>12,.0f}{idx:>13,.0f}'
          f'{("index" if idx < seq else "seq scan"):>16}')

  selectivity    seq scan   index scan   planner picks
       0.01%     100,000        4,012           index
       0.10%     100,000       40,012           index
       1.00%     100,000      400,012        seq scan
       5.00%     100,000    2,000,012        seq scan
      20.00%     100,000    8,000,012        seq scan
      50.00%     100,000   20,000,012        seq scan

A sequential scan is not a bug in the plan. When a query matches a fifth of the table, reading it in order is genuinely the fastest way, and "why is it not using my index?" usually has the answer "because your WHERE clause is not selective". An index on a boolean, on a status column with three values, or on country = 'US' in a mostly-US dataset is an index the planner will correctly ignore.

Column order in a composite index is not a detail. An index on (a, b) is a sorted list of (a, b) pairs, so it serves WHERE a = ?, WHERE a = ? AND b = ?, and ORDER BY a, b — and cannot serve WHERE b = ? at all, because the b values are scattered throughout. The rule that follows is mechanical: equality columns first, then the range or sort column, then any column present only to make the index covering.

-- Serves: (tenant), (tenant, created_at), and ORDER BY created_at within a tenant.
-- Does NOT serve: a query filtering only on created_at.
CREATE INDEX orders_tenant_created ON orders (tenant_id, created_at DESC);

-- A covering index: the planner answers from the index alone, never touching the table.
CREATE INDEX orders_lookup ON orders (tenant_id, created_at DESC) INCLUDE (status, total_cents);

The plan is where you confirm all of this rather than assuming it, and the habit worth building is to run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) rather than reason about what the planner should do. Here is a real one, from PostgreSQL 18.6 against a 1.5-million-row orders table with the composite index above:

Limit  (cost=0.43..73.91 rows=20 width=32) (actual time=0.189..2.749 rows=20.00 loops=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=23 read=3
  ->  Index Scan using orders_tenant_created on orders
        (cost=0.43..11000.37 rows=2994 width=32) (actual time=0.136..0.786 rows=20.00 loops=1)
        Index Cond: (tenant_id = 42)
        Index Searches: 1
        Buffers: shared hit=23 read=3
Planning Time: 4.139 ms
Execution Time: 3.752 ms

Two numbers in there are the whole reason to read a plan rather than trust one. The Index Scan node estimates rows=2994 and reports actual rows=20.00 — not an error, but the plan telling you it would have produced 2,994 rows and stopped early because of the LIMIT. And Buffers: shared hit=23 read=3 says the entire query touched twenty-six 8 KB pages. Buffer counts are the most honest number in a plan, because unlike timings they do not depend on how busy the machine is — always ask for them with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS).

That is also the caveat on everything below: costs and timings are artefacts of the machine the plan ran on. The node types, the row counts and the buffer counts are the parts that transfer.

Seq Scan on a big table
The first thing to look for. Fine on a small table or a non-selective condition, and otherwise the missing index.
rows vs actual rows
The planner's estimate against reality. An estimate off by orders of magnitude means stale statistics, and every choice above that node was made on bad information. Below a Limit, expect actual to be smaller — that is early termination, not a bad estimate.
Buffers
hit came from the buffer cache, read from the operating system. The one number in the plan that does not change with machine load, and the one to compare across runs.
loops
A cheap node executed 10,000 times is not cheap. Multiply before believing a per-loop time.
Filter vs Index Cond
Index Cond is applied while walking the index; Filter is applied to rows already fetched. A Filter discarding most rows is work you paid for and threw away.

Two costs to weigh against all of this. Every index slows every write, because an insert must update each one — so an unused index is pure overhead, and production databases accumulate them. And an index is only as good as the statistics: after a bulk load, the planner is working from a description of a table that no longer exists until the statistics are refreshed.

6.4 Key-Value and Document Stores

"NoSQL" names a marketing category, not a technology, and the name is a historical accident — most NoSQL stores now have a query language, and several of them speak SQL. The stores in it have almost nothing in common except that they gave something up — usually joins, transactions or ad-hoc queries — to get something else, usually horizontal write scaling or schema flexibility. Judge each one by what it traded.

A key-value store is a distributed dictionary: get(key), put(key, value), and nothing else. That restriction is the feature — an operation that touches exactly one key can be routed to exactly one partition, so it scales horizontally without limit and answers in single-digit milliseconds. Redis, DynamoDB and Memcached are the common ones.

def kv_capability(query):
    """What a pure key-value store can and cannot answer."""
    SUPPORTED = {'get by key', 'put by key', 'delete by key', 'range scan on sort key'}
    return 'O(1)' if query in SUPPORTED else 'FULL SCAN or a second index you maintain'

for query in ['get by key', 'range scan on sort key',
              'find users in Berlin', 'count orders over 100 EUR',
              'join users to orders']:
    print(f'{query:<28} {kv_capability(query)}')

get by key                   O(1)
range scan on sort key       O(1)
find users in Berlin         FULL SCAN or a second index you maintain
count orders over 100 EUR    FULL SCAN or a second index you maintain
join users to orders         FULL SCAN or a second index you maintain

Every question that is not "by key" becomes your problem. You maintain a second table as an index, you keep it consistent yourself (§11.8), and you accept that it is eventually consistent with the first. That is a completely reasonable trade when there are two or three such questions and they are known in advance; it is a catastrophe when the questions keep arriving.

A document store — MongoDB, DynamoDB in its document mode, PostgreSQL's jsonb — stores nested records addressed by key, and adds secondary indexes and queries into the document's fields. Its real advantage is not "no schema"; it is that an aggregate is stored as one record. An order with its lines, addresses and payment is one read and one atomic write, where a normalised relational model needs a join across four tables.

ORDER_DOC = {
    'id': 'ord_9', 'customer': {'id': 'c_41', 'name': 'Ada'},
    'lines': [{'sku': 'a1', 'qty': 2, 'cents': 1_500},
              {'sku': 'b7', 'qty': 1, 'cents': 1_250}],
    'total_cents': 4_250, 'status': 'placed',
}

def reads_needed(model, query):
    if model == 'document':
        return {'whole order': 1, 'orders for a customer': 1,
                'all orders containing sku a1': 1, 'rename a customer': 'N documents'}[query]
    return {'whole order': 4, 'orders for a customer': 1,
            'all orders containing sku a1': 2, 'rename a customer': 1}[query]

for query in ['whole order', 'orders for a customer',
              'all orders containing sku a1', 'rename a customer']:
    print(f'{query:<32} document: {str(reads_needed("document", query)):<12}'
          f'relational: {reads_needed("relational", query)}')

whole order                      document: 1           relational: 4
orders for a customer            document: 1           relational: 1
all orders containing sku a1     document: 1           relational: 2
rename a customer                document: N documents relational: 1

The last row is the whole trade, and it is the one that decides. Embedded data is duplicated data, so changing it means finding and rewriting every copy — which is not a transaction, has no foreign key protecting it, and will eventually be partially applied. The rule that works: embed what is owned and copied by value, reference what is shared. An order's lines belong to the order and their prices are historical facts that must not change when the catalogue does — embed them. The customer's name is shared and mutable — reference it.

"Schemaless" deserves one blunt sentence. There is always a schema; the only question is whether it is declared in the database or implied by the code that reads the documents. A collection accumulating five versions of a record shape over three years has a schema — it is just written across every consumer, enforced nowhere, and discovered at 3 a.m.

6.5 Wide-Column, the LSM Tree, and Bloom Filters

Wide-column stores — Cassandra, ScyllaDB, HBase, BigTable — look like tables and behave nothing like them. The data model is a nested map: a partition key selects a node (§8.2), and within the partition, rows are stored sorted by a clustering key. That is the entire model, and every capability and limitation follows from it.

def cassandra_query(partition_key_given, clustering_prefix_given, other_filter):
    if not partition_key_given:
        return 'REFUSED — would need every node (ALLOW FILTERING lets you shoot yourself)'
    if other_filter and not clustering_prefix_given:
        return 'REFUSED — a filter on a non-key column cannot use the sort order'
    return 'one partition, one sequential read'

CASES = [
    ('WHERE device = ? AND ts > ?',       True,  True,  False),
    ('WHERE device = ?',                  True,  False, False),
    ('WHERE ts > ?',                      False, True,  False),
    ('WHERE device = ? AND status = ?',   True,  False, True),
]
for query, partition, clustering, other in CASES:
    print(f'{query:<34} {cassandra_query(partition, clustering, other)}')

WHERE device = ? AND ts > ?        one partition, one sequential read
WHERE device = ?                   one partition, one sequential read
WHERE ts > ?                       REFUSED — would need every node (ALLOW FILTERING lets you shoot yourself)
WHERE device = ? AND status = ?    REFUSED — a filter on a non-key column cannot use the sort order

You design the tables from the queries, one table per query, duplicating the data as many times as you have access patterns — which is the opposite of relational modelling and is not a mistake. What you buy is a write path that scales linearly with nodes and has no single leader (§7.6), which is why it is the standard answer for time-series ingestion, event logs and messaging at very large volume.

That write path is an LSM tree, and knowing its shape explains the store's whole performance profile. Writes go to an in-memory table and a write-ahead log — sequential, no seek, extremely fast. The write-ahead log is the same construction a relational database uses for durability and the same one §7.2 replicates from: the change is appended to a log before it is applied anywhere else, so a crash is recovered by replaying the tail. It is what lets an LSM store acknowledge a write that exists only in memory. When the memtable fills, it is flushed to an immutable sorted file. Reads may therefore have to check several files, and a background compaction merges them.

def lsm_reads(files, bloom_false_positive=0.01, bloom=True):
    """A read may touch every file on disk — unless a Bloom filter rules most out."""
    if not bloom:
        return files
    return 1 + (files - 1) * bloom_false_positive          # the real file, plus false positives

print(f'{"files on disk":>15}{"reads without bloom":>22}{"reads with bloom":>19}')
for files in (1, 4, 16, 64):
    print(f'{files:>15}{lsm_reads(files, bloom=False):>22}'
          f'{lsm_reads(files):>19.2f}')

  files on disk   reads without bloom   reads with bloom
              1                     1               1.00
              4                     4               1.03
             16                    16               1.15
             64                    64               1.63

Without a Bloom filter, a read on a 64-file table is 64 disk reads, which would make the whole design unusable. A Bloom filter is a small bit array that answers "is this key definitely absent, or possibly present?" — never a false negative, occasionally a false positive — so 63 of those 64 files are eliminated without being opened. It is worth building once, because it turns up everywhere: in LSM stores, in CDN cache-negative lookups, in "have we seen this URL" checks, and in §11.8's dedup problem.

import hashlib

class BloomFilter:
    def __init__(self, bits=8192, hashes=5):
        self.bits, self.hashes, self.array = bits, hashes, bytearray(bits // 8)

    def _positions(self, item):
        digest = hashlib.blake2b(item.encode(), digest_size=16).digest()
        base = int.from_bytes(digest[:8]), int.from_bytes(digest[8:])
        return [(base[0] + i * base[1]) % self.bits for i in range(self.hashes)]

    def add(self, item):
        for position in self._positions(item):
            self.array[position // 8] |= 1 << (position % 8)

    def __contains__(self, item):
        return all(self.array[p // 8] & (1 << (p % 8)) for p in self._positions(item))

bloom = BloomFilter()
present = [f'key{i}' for i in range(800)]
for key in present:
    bloom.add(key)

false_negatives = sum(1 for key in present if key not in bloom)
absent = [f'missing{i}' for i in range(10_000)]
false_positives = sum(1 for key in absent if key in bloom)

print('false negatives:', false_negatives, '(must be 0 — this is the guarantee)')
print(f'false positives: {false_positives} of 10,000 = {false_positives / 10_000:.2%}')
print('memory:', len(bloom.array), 'bytes for 800 keys =',
      f'{len(bloom.array) * 8 / 800:.1f} bits per key')

false negatives: 0 (must be 0 — this is the guarantee)
false positives: 85 of 10,000 = 0.85%
memory: 1024 bytes for 800 keys = 10.2 bits per key

Ten bits per key for a 1% false-positive rate, and zero false negatives by construction — a key that was added always tests present, because adding it set exactly the bits the test checks. That asymmetry is what makes it useful: "definitely not here, skip the disk read" is a decision you can act on, and "possibly here" costs only the read you would have done anyway.

The LSM tree's cost is the mirror of its benefit. Write amplification: every row is rewritten several times as compaction merges files. Read amplification on a key spread across many files. And space amplification, since an overwritten row occupies space until compaction removes it. A B-tree store makes the opposite trade — cheaper reads, more expensive random writes — which is the real difference between PostgreSQL and Cassandra underneath all the API differences.

6.6 Graph Databases

A graph store — Neo4j, or a relational schema with a recursive query — is for data whose value is in the relationships and whose queries traverse several hops. The distinguishing property is that a graph traverses by following pointers, so cost scales with the part of the graph you touch, while a relational join scales with the tables involved.

def hops_cost(hops, average_degree, rows_in_table=50_000_000):
    graph = average_degree ** hops                # touch only the neighbourhood
    relational = hops * rows_in_table // 1000     # a self-join per hop, index-assisted
    return graph, relational

print(f'{"hops":>6}{"graph: nodes visited":>24}{"relational: index probes":>27}')
for hops in (1, 2, 3, 4, 5):
    graph, relational = hops_cost(hops, average_degree=30)
    print(f'{hops:>6}{graph:>24,}{relational:>27,}')

  hops    graph: nodes visited   relational: index probes
     1                      30                     50,000
     2                     900                    100,000
     3                  27,000                    150,000
     4                 810,000                    200,000
     5              24,300,000                    250,000

One and two hops are a join, and every relational database does them well. "Friends of friends" is a self-join and needs no new technology. It is at three, four and five hops — fraud rings, dependency chains, "how is this account connected to that one" — that repeated self-joins become unmanageable to write and to plan, while a traversal stays proportional to the neighbourhood it visits.

Note the other side of the table. The graph's cost explodes too, just later and for a different reason: at degree 30, five hops is 24 million nodes, so a traversal on a well-connected graph must be bounded by a depth limit, a filter or a shortest-path algorithm rather than run to completion.

Do not adopt a graph database because your data has relationships. All data has relationships. Adopt one when the queries you cannot currently write are traversals of unbounded or variable depth — and check first whether a recursive query gets you there, because that is a WITH RECURSIVE away in a database you already run.

6.7 Object Storage, Search Indexes and Time Series

Three specialised stores, each of which solves a problem that general-purpose databases solve badly.

Object storage — S3, GCS, Azure Blob — stores immutable blobs addressed by key, at a cost per gigabyte roughly two orders of magnitude below block storage, with essentially unlimited capacity and durability that no self-run system will match. The rule is simple and rarely violated twice: files go in object storage, and the database holds the key.

def storage_cost(gb, store):
    RATES = {'object storage': 0.021, 'block storage (SSD)': 0.10, 'database (managed)': 0.23}
    return gb * RATES[store]

for gb in (100, 10_000, 500_000):
    row = '  '.join(f'{s}: ${storage_cost(gb, s):>10,.0f}/mo'
                    for s in ('object storage', 'block storage (SSD)', 'database (managed)'))
    print(f'{gb:>9,} GB   {row}')

      100 GB   object storage: $         2/mo  block storage (SSD): $        10/mo  database (managed): $        23/mo
   10,000 GB   object storage: $       210/mo  block storage (SSD): $     1,000/mo  database (managed): $     2,300/mo
  500,000 GB   object storage: $    10,500/mo  block storage (SSD): $    50,000/mo  database (managed): $   115,000/mo

Storing a 500 TB media library in a managed database costs $115,000 a month for something object storage does for $10,500 — eleven times the price — and the database is worse at it, because every backup, every replica and every restore now carries the bytes. What object storage will not do is update in place or answer a query, which is why the pattern is always "blob in the bucket, metadata in the database".

A search index — Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, PostgreSQL's full-text search — exists because LIKE '%term%' cannot use an index and therefore scans. An inverted index maps each term to the documents containing it, which is a different data structure, not a faster version of the same one.

from collections import defaultdict

DOCS = {
    1: 'red running shoes for trail running',
    2: 'blue trail shoes',
    3: 'red winter coat',
}

def build_inverted(docs):
    index = defaultdict(set)
    for doc_id, text in docs.items():
        for term in text.split():
            index[term].add(doc_id)
    return index

index = build_inverted(DOCS)
print('term -> docs')
for term in ('red', 'trail', 'shoes'):
    print(f'  {term:<8} {sorted(index[term])}')

query = ['red', 'shoes']
matches = set.intersection(*(index[term] for term in query))
print(f'\nquery {query}: docs {sorted(matches)} — set intersection, not a scan')
print('a LIKE scan would read all', len(DOCS), 'documents; the index reads',
      len(query), 'posting lists')

term -> docs
  red      [1, 3]
  trail    [1, 2]
  shoes    [1, 2]

query ['red', 'shoes']: docs [1] — set intersection, not a scan
a LIKE scan would read all 3 documents; the index reads 2 posting lists

Real search adds relevance scoring, stemming (running matching run), synonyms and typo tolerance on top of that structure — none of which a LIKE can express at all. The cost is that a search index is a derived, eventually-consistent copy fed from your source of truth, usually by change data capture (§11.2). Never make it authoritative: it is rebuildable by design, and a rebuild is the standard fix for half its problems.

A time-series store — TimescaleDB, InfluxDB, Prometheus — is optimised for a workload with an unusual shape: append-only writes in roughly timestamp order, queries that are always a time range plus an aggregation, and old data that gets less valuable rather than being deleted.

def retention_plan(raw_per_day_gb, policies):
    total, kept = 0.0, []
    for name, days, resolution_divisor in policies:
        size = raw_per_day_gb * days / resolution_divisor
        total += size
        kept.append((name, days, size))
    return kept, total

POLICIES = [('raw (10s)', 7, 1), ('1-minute rollup', 90, 6),
            ('1-hour rollup', 730, 360)]
kept, total = retention_plan(120, POLICIES)
for name, days, size in kept:
    print(f'{name:<18}{days:>5} days{size:>12,.0f} GB')
print(f'{"total":<18}{"":>5}     {total:>12,.0f} GB')
print(f'raw for 2 years would be {120 * 730:,.0f} GB')

raw (10s)             7 days         840 GB
1-minute rollup      90 days       1,800 GB
1-hour rollup       730 days         243 GB
total                              2,883 GB
raw for 2 years would be 87,600 GB

Downsampling is the whole idea. Two years of full-resolution data is 87 TB; two years with rollups is under 2 TB, and nobody has ever needed ten-second resolution from eighteen months ago. Add columnar compression — adjacent timestamps and slowly-changing values compress extraordinarily well — and the storage question stops being a question.

6.8 Denormalisation, and Writing for the Read

Normalisation stores each fact once, which makes writes cheap and correct and makes reads do joins. Denormalisation trades that: store the fact where it will be read, pay more on write, and accept that copies can diverge.

def read_cost(model, joins, rows_scanned_per_join=1_000):
    if model == 'normalised':
        return joins, joins * rows_scanned_per_join
    return 1, rows_scanned_per_join

def write_cost(model, copies):
    return 1 if model == 'normalised' else copies

for reads_per_write in (1, 10, 1_000, 100_000):
    n_reads, n_scan = read_cost('normalised', joins=4)
    d_reads, d_scan = read_cost('denormalised', joins=4)
    normalised = reads_per_write * n_scan + write_cost('normalised', 6)
    denormalised = reads_per_write * d_scan + write_cost('denormalised', 6)
    better = 'denormalise' if denormalised < normalised else 'normalise'
    print(f'{reads_per_write:>7,}:1 read:write  normalised {normalised:>12,}  '
          f'denormalised {denormalised:>12,}  -> {better}')

      1:1 read:write  normalised        4,001  denormalised        1,006  -> denormalise
     10:1 read:write  normalised       40,001  denormalised       10,006  -> denormalise
  1,000:1 read:write  normalised    4,000,001  denormalised    1,000,006  -> denormalise
100,000:1 read:write  normalised  400,000,001  denormalised  100,000,006  -> denormalise

The crossover is early, which is why denormalisation is so common — but the units above are work, not risk, and the risk is the part that decides. Four rules keep it from becoming a correctness problem:

Normalise first, denormalise from measurements. A denormalisation put in before the query was slow is a permanent maintenance cost bought with a guess.

Keep one authoritative copy. Every derived copy must be reproducible from it, and there must be a job that can rebuild them. A denormalised field with no rebuild path is a field that will be wrong and unfixable.

Update copies through one path. A total stored on a row, updated by three different code paths, will diverge — usually within a month. Make it a projection driven by events (§11.5), or a trigger, or a single service method. Not three.

Reconcile on a schedule. A nightly job comparing derived values against a recomputation catches divergence while it is a small correction rather than a year of wrong invoices.

Two specific forms deserve naming. A counter column (comment_count on a post) avoids a COUNT(*) per read and needs the discipline above. And a materialised view is the database's own supported version of the same trade — it knows how to refresh it, so it cannot silently diverge, and that is a substantial advantage over doing it by hand.

6.9 Connection Pools and Federation

A database connection is not cheap. It is a TCP connection, a TLS handshake, an authentication round trip and — in PostgreSQL — a whole backend process with megabytes of memory. Creating one per request is a mistake the pool exists to prevent, and sizing that pool wrong is a mistake the pool cannot prevent.

def pool_behaviour(app_nodes, pool_per_node, db_max_connections,
                   arrival_rate, service_time_ms):
    demanded = app_nodes * pool_per_node
    concurrency_needed = arrival_rate * service_time_ms / 1000     # Little's law
    return {
        'connections demanded': demanded,
        'database limit': db_max_connections,
        'over limit': demanded > db_max_connections,
        'actually needed': round(concurrency_needed),
        'wasted': max(0, demanded - round(concurrency_needed)),
    }

for nodes, per_node in [(40, 20), (40, 5), (200, 20)]:
    result = pool_behaviour(nodes, per_node, 200, arrival_rate=6_000, service_time_ms=8)
    print(f'{nodes:>4} nodes x {per_node:>2} = ', end='')
    print('  '.join(f'{k}: {v}' for k, v in result.items()))

  40 nodes x 20 = connections demanded: 800  database limit: 200  over limit: True  actually needed: 48  wasted: 752
  40 nodes x  5 = connections demanded: 200  database limit: 200  over limit: False  actually needed: 48  wasted: 152
 200 nodes x 20 = connections demanded: 4000  database limit: 200  over limit: True  actually needed: 48  wasted: 3952

Forty nodes with a pool of twenty demands 800 connections against a limit of 200, so 600 requests are refused outright — and the workload only ever needed 48 concurrent connections. This is the single most common database misconfiguration there is, and it gets worse on every autoscale event, which is exactly when the system is already under stress.

Three rules, and the second is counter-intuitive enough that it is worth stating as a number:

Size the pool from Little's law: concurrency = arrival rate × service time, plus headroom. Six thousand requests a second at 8 ms is 48. A pool of 10 per node is usually generous, and one of 100 is almost always a misunderstanding.

A bigger pool is slower past the crossover. A database with 8 cores executes 8 queries at a time; 400 connections means 392 of them are context-switching, contending for locks and thrashing cache. Throughput falls as the pool grows past a small multiple of the core count. The pool is a bulkhead (§14.6), and its whole job is to say no.

Use a proxy pooler when node count is the problem. PgBouncer in transaction mode multiplexes thousands of client connections onto a few dozen server ones, and it is the standard answer for a large fleet or for serverless functions, where connection count is otherwise unbounded by construction.

Federation is the other lever: split by function rather than by row. Users in one database, orders in another, analytics in a third. Each gets its own connections, its own cache, its own tuning and its own failure domain, and the write load divides without any of §8's key-choice difficulty. What it costs is exactly what partitioning costs — no joins across the boundary and no cross-database transactions — so federate along the seams where you were not joining anyway, which is usually where a service boundary would go too (§12).

6.10 Schema Migration Without Downtime

A schema change on a live system is a distributed problem: old code and new code run simultaneously during a deploy, and both must work against whatever the schema is at that moment. The pattern that solves it is expand / migrate / contract, and the discipline is that each phase deploys separately.

PHASES = [
    ('expand',   'add the new column, nullable, no constraint',
     'old code ignores it; new code can write it', True),
    ('backfill', 'copy data in batches, throttled',
     'both column versions readable; no lock held', True),
    ('migrate',  'deploy code writing BOTH and reading NEW',
     'a rollback is still safe — old column is current', True),
    ('verify',   'compare old and new for a period',
     'the step everyone skips, and the only one that catches a bad backfill', True),
    ('contract', 'stop writing OLD, then drop it',
     'only after no deployed code reads it', True),
]

for index, (name, action, note, both_versions_work) in enumerate(PHASES):
    print(f'{index + 1}. {name:<9} {action}')
    print(f'{"":13}{note}')
    print(f'{"":13}old and new code both work: {both_versions_work}')

1. expand    add the new column, nullable, no constraint
             old code ignores it; new code can write it
             old and new code both work: True
2. backfill  copy data in batches, throttled
             both column versions readable; no lock held
             old and new code both work: True
3. migrate   deploy code writing BOTH and reading NEW
             a rollback is still safe — old column is current
             old and new code both work: True
4. verify    compare old and new for a period
             the step everyone skips, and the only one that catches a bad backfill
             old and new code both work: True
5. contract  stop writing OLD, then drop it
             only after no deployed code reads it
             old and new code both work: True

The rule underneath every phase: a deploy is never atomic, so every intermediate state must be a working system. Two versions of the application run at once during a rolling deploy, and if a migration requires them to disagree about the schema, there is no ordering of the deploy that works.

The migrations that go wrong are the ones that take a lock:

Add a nullable column
Instant in PostgreSQL — metadata only. Safe.
Add a column with a default
Instant in PostgreSQL 11+ — the default is stored in the catalogue and materialised lazily. Measured on the 1.5-million-row table above: ADD COLUMN note text DEFAULT 'none' NOT NULL took 7.9 ms. On older versions and on some other engines the same statement rewrites the whole table under an exclusive lock. Check your version rather than assuming.
Add an index
Locks writes for the duration unless built concurrently. Use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, accept that it is slower and can fail, and remember it cannot run inside a transaction.
Add a NOT NULL constraint
Scans the whole table under a lock. Add it as NOT VALID, then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT, which takes a much weaker lock. PostgreSQL 18 is the first version where a not-null constraint itself can be NOT VALID — before it, the same effect needed a CHECK (col IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID. Verify what your version supports.
Change a column type
Usually a full rewrite. Do it as expand/contract with a new column, never in place on a large table.
Rename anything
There is no safe in-place rename on a live system, because old and new code disagree instantly. Expand/contract is the only correct answer.

Two operational rules that are cheap and prevent most incidents. Set a lock timeout — a migration that waits for a lock queues every subsequent query behind it, so a five-second migration turns into an outage while it waits for one long-running transaction. SET lock_timeout = '3s' makes it fail instead, and failing a migration is nothing. And backfill in batches with a pause, never as one UPDATE: a single statement over ten million rows holds locks, bloats the write-ahead log and stalls replication (§7.4) for as long as it runs.

Exercises

Exercise 6.1 — Choose the stores. Design the storage for a video platform: user accounts and subscriptions; video files up to 4 GB; view counts updated 300,000 times a second; comments; full-text search over titles and descriptions; per-video watch-time metrics at 10-second resolution; and a "viewers also watched" recommendation traversal. Name a store per concern and justify each from the access pattern, not the data shape.

Solution 
DESIGN = [
    ('accounts, subscriptions', 'relational',
     'transactions, constraints, ad-hoc queries; small and will stay small'),
    ('video files', 'object storage + key in the relational row',
     '4 GB blobs; cost, durability, and the CDN can read it directly'),
    ('view counts', 'in-process counter -> Redis -> periodic flush',
     '300k writes/s of a value read approximately; write-behind (§9.4)'),
    ('comments', 'relational, partitioned by video_id',
     'moderation, threading and deletion want transactions; §8.3 gives locality'),
    ('search', 'search index fed by CDC (§11.2)',
     'relevance, stemming and typo tolerance are not expressible in SQL LIKE'),
    ('watch-time metrics', 'time-series store with rollups',
     'append-only, always queried by time range, and downsamples (§6.7)'),
    ('recommendations', 'precomputed lists in a key-value store',
     'the traversal is a nightly batch job; serving it is a lookup by key'),
]
for concern, store, why in DESIGN:
    print(f'{concern:<26} {store}')
    print(f'{"":26} {why}')

accounts, subscriptions    relational
                           transactions, constraints, ad-hoc queries; small and will stay small
video files                object storage + key in the relational row
                           4 GB blobs; cost, durability, and the CDN can read it directly
view counts                in-process counter -> Redis -> periodic flush
                           300k writes/s of a value read approximately; write-behind (§9.4)
comments                   relational, partitioned by video_id
                           moderation, threading and deletion want transactions; §8.3 gives locality
search                     search index fed by CDC (§11.2)
                           relevance, stemming and typo tolerance are not expressible in SQL LIKE
watch-time metrics         time-series store with rollups
                           append-only, always queried by time range, and downsamples (§6.7)
recommendations            precomputed lists in a key-value store
                           the traversal is a nightly batch job; serving it is a lookup by key

Four of these deserve the reasoning spelled out.

View counts are not a database problem, they are a write-rate problem. Three hundred thousand increments a second against any transactional store is hopeless, and the requirement quietly says it does not need to be exact or immediate. Count in application memory, flush to Redis every second, persist periodically. This is §9.4's write-behind, and the coalescing is what makes the number affordable.

Comments are relational despite the volume, because the operations on them are the ones relational stores exist for: cascade a delete when a video is removed, enforce that a reply's parent exists, moderate transactionally. Partition by video_id so a video's whole thread is one partition (§8.8) and the common query stays local.

Recommendations do not need a graph database, and this is the trap in the exercise. The traversal is real, but it runs nightly in a batch job — where the appropriate tool is a graph processing framework or a plain join, not a graph database serving live queries. What serves live traffic is video_id -> [list of ids], which is a key-value lookup. Distinguish the store that computes an answer from the store that serves it; they are usually different, and conflating them is how a system acquires a database it does not need.

And what deliberately is not here: a separate store for subscriptions. Accounts and subscriptions are joined constantly, are transactional together, and are small. Splitting them would buy a distributed transaction and nothing else.

Exercise 6.2 — Diagnose the slow query. This query takes fifteen seconds. The plan below is real — PostgreSQL 18.6, a 1.5-million-row orders table, 42,000 customers, work_mem = 1MB. Name every problem, say which of them the LIMIT already solves, and give the fix.

SELECT o.id, o.total_cents, c.name
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.status = 'pending'
  AND o.created_at > now() - interval '7 days'
ORDER BY o.created_at DESC
LIMIT 50;

Limit  (cost=49628.96..49629.08 rows=50 width=38)
       (actual time=15521.782..15526.508 rows=50.00 loops=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=13427 read=1996, temp read=287 written=287
  ->  Sort  (cost=49628.96..49768.72 rows=55907 width=38)
            (actual time=15521.731..15523.702 rows=50.00 loops=1)
        Sort Key: o.created_at DESC
        Sort Method: top-N heapsort  Memory: 32kB
        ->  Hash Join  (cost=1460.00..47771.77 rows=55907 width=38)
                       (actual time=3199.460..13547.335 rows=54978.00 loops=1)
              Hash Cond: (o.customer_id = c.id)
              ->  Seq Scan on orders o  (cost=0.00..45152.00 rows=55907 width=32)
                                        (actual time=685.608..3327.864 rows=54978.00 loops=1)
                    Filter: ((status = 'pending'::text)
                             AND (created_at > (now() - '7 days'::interval)))
                    Rows Removed by Filter: 1445022
                    Buffers: shared hit=13168 read=1984
              ->  Hash  (cost=688.00..688.00 rows=42000 width=22)
                        (actual time=2513.026..2513.300 rows=42000.00 loops=1)
                    Buckets: 32768  Batches: 2  Memory Usage: 1410kB
                    Buffers: shared hit=256 read=12, temp written=112
Planning Time: 3.314 ms
Execution Time: 15528.483 ms
Solution

Three real problems, one non-problem that looks like one, and one thing the plan does right.

1. Seq Scan on orders with Rows Removed by Filter: 1445022. The database read all 1.5 million rows and threw away 96% of them. This is the fifteen seconds. There is no usable index for (status, created_at), so there is nothing else the planner could have done.

2. The join runs over the whole matching set, not over 50 rows. The Hash Join node reports actual rows=54978.00: every matching order was joined to a customer, and then 50 survived. LIMIT can only stop early if the node below it produces rows in the required order, and a hash join does not.

3. Buckets: 32768 Batches: 2 … temp written=112. The hash on customers did not fit in the 1 MB work_mem, so it was split into two batches and spilled to a temporary file. That is 42,000 rows — a tiny table — and it is spilling, which is a work_mem that is too small for this query rather than a schema problem.

Now the one that looks like a problem and is not. Sort Method: top-N heapsort Memory: 32kB is exactly right: because of the LIMIT 50, PostgreSQL does not sort 54,978 rows at all — it keeps a 50-element heap and discards the rest as they stream past, in 32 KB of memory. A LIMIT converts a sort into a bounded top-N sort, which is why the sort node costs almost nothing here. Guessing that the sort was the problem, and raising work_mem to fix it, would have changed nothing.

And the estimate is good: rows=55907 against actual rows=54978.00, within 2%. This is the part worth internalising, because it contradicts the usual instinct. The planner understood the query perfectly and still produced a terrible plan — not because its statistics were stale, but because the only access path available was a full scan. ANALYZE would not have helped. When the estimate is accurate and the plan is still bad, the answer is an index, not statistics.

All three problems have one fix, and it is a single index:

CREATE INDEX orders_status_created ON orders (status, created_at DESC);

Column order is the entire point (§6.3). status is the equality predicate and goes first; created_at is the range and the sort key and goes second, descending to match the ORDER BY. The planner can now walk the index in exactly the order requested and stop after 50 rows — so the scan is gone, the sort node disappears entirely, and only 50 customers are ever looked up. Here is what it actually did:

Limit  (cost=0.73..58.35 rows=50 width=38) (actual time=0.503..15.226 rows=50.00 loops=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=155 read=5
  ->  Nested Loop  (cost=0.73..65540.92 rows=56873 width=38)
                   (actual time=0.417..12.313 rows=50.00 loops=1)
        ->  Index Scan using orders_status_created on orders o
              (cost=0.43..49585.26 rows=56873 width=32)
              (actual time=0.095..1.661 rows=50.00 loops=1)
              Index Cond: ((status = 'pending'::text)
                           AND (created_at > (now() - '7 days'::interval)))
              Buffers: shared hit=7 read=3
        ->  Memoize  (cost=0.30..0.34 rows=1 width=22)
                     (actual time=0.113..0.118 rows=1.00 loops=50)
              Cache Key: o.customer_id
              Hits: 0  Misses: 50  Evictions: 0  Memory Usage: 7kB
              ->  Index Scan using customers_pkey on customers c
                    (cost=0.29..0.33 rows=1 width=22)
                    (actual time=0.053..0.053 rows=1.00 loops=50)
                    Index Cond: (id = o.customer_id)
Planning Time: 1.273 ms
Execution Time: 16.924 ms

15,528 ms to 17 ms, and 15,423 buffers to 160. Read the buffer counts rather than the timings, since the timings belong to that machine: the query went from touching fifteen thousand pages to touching a hundred and sixty.

Three changes in that plan, all consequences of the one index. The Sort node is gone — the index is already in created_at DESC order within status = 'pending', so there is nothing to sort. The Hash Join became a Nested Loop, because with only 50 outer rows a per-row index lookup is cheaper than hashing 42,000 customers — the planner switched strategy on its own, which is §6.2's point about a query planner being a feature. And Memoize appeared above the customer lookup, caching results in case an outer row repeats.

Two further improvements, in the order worth trying them.

Make the index covering so the table heap is never touched for the columns being selected:

CREATE INDEX orders_covering ON orders (status, created_at DESC)
  INCLUDE (id, total_cents, customer_id);

Limit  (cost=0.43..3.04 rows=50 width=24) (actual time=0.245..5.476 rows=50.00 loops=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=1 read=3
  ->  Index Only Scan using orders_covering on orders o
        (cost=0.43..2915.75 rows=55966 width=24)
