print('all readable DURING migration:', all(c.get(f'user{i}') == i for i in range(2_000)))

for i in range(2_000):                                   # the background copier
    key = f'user{i}'
    if partition_for(key) in c.migrating:
        c.node_for(key)[key] = c.node_for(key, c.previous)[key]
c.finish_migration()
print('all readable after: ', all(c.get(f'user{i}') == i for i in range(2_000)))

all readable before: True
816 of 1024 partitions are moving
all readable DURING migration: True
all readable after:  True

The three True values are the claims that matter. No key was unreadable at any point — before the migration, during it with 816 of 1,024 partitions reassigned but not yet copied, or after it. That is the property the dual read exists to provide, and it is the difference between a rebalance and an outage.

Note that 816 partitions move because the reassignment here is the naive p % nodes from §8.6. A real cluster would use the minimal planner, move ~205, and finish four times sooner — but the dual-read window is what makes either of them safe.

The three fixes, restated:

blake2b instead of hash() — stable across processes, machines and Python versions, forever. Any cryptographic or non-cryptographic named hash works; the language's built-in one does not.

PARTITIONS is fixed at 1024 and never changes. Nodes come and go; partitions are merely reassigned. This is §8.6's fixed-partition scheme, and it is why the key-to-partition mapping is stable for the life of the system.

A dual-read window means a key that has not yet been copied is still found at its old home. Without it, the interval between "reassign" and "finish copying" returns None for every un-migrated key — which is the outage the original code guarantees.

Exercise 8.3 — Kill the hotspot. A leaderboard shards by game_id. One game is 80% of traffic: 400,000 reads/s and 20,000 writes/s of score updates. Reads want the top 100. Design it.

Solution

Sharding cannot help: game_id is one key, so the hot game is one shard however many shards exist (§8.5). The fix is to change what is stored and where the work happens.

import hashlib
import heapq
from collections import Counter

SALTS = 64

def salt_for(player):
    digest = hashlib.blake2b(player.encode(), digest_size=8).digest()
    return int.from_bytes(digest) % SALTS

def rank_key(kv):
    player, score = kv
    return (score, player)          # TOTAL order: score, then name to break ties

class Leaderboard:
    """Writes fan out across SALTS partitions; reads come from a periodic rollup."""
    def __init__(self):
        self.buckets = [dict() for _ in range(SALTS)]
        self.top_cache = None

    def submit(self, player, score):
        bucket = self.buckets[salt_for(player)]
        if score > bucket.get(player, -1):
            bucket[player] = score
            self.top_cache = None

    def rebuild_top(self, n=100):
        """Run every couple of seconds, NOT per request."""
        partial = [heapq.nlargest(n, b.items(), key=rank_key) for b in self.buckets]
        self.top_cache = heapq.nlargest(n, [kv for p in partial for kv in p], key=rank_key)
        return self.top_cache

    def top(self, n=100):
        if self.top_cache is None:
            self.rebuild_top()
        return self.top_cache[:n]

lb = Leaderboard()
for i in range(50_000):
    lb.submit(f'player{i}', (i * 7919) % 100_000)

spread = Counter(salt_for(f'player{i}') for i in range(50_000))
shares = sorted(v / 50_000 for v in spread.values())
print(f'write load per bucket: {shares[0]:.2%} to {shares[-1]:.2%} (even is {1/SALTS:.2%})')

reference = heapq.nlargest(5, [(f'player{i}', (i * 7919) % 100_000)
                               for i in range(50_000)], key=rank_key)
print('top 5:', lb.top(5))
print('exactly the global top 5:', lb.top(5) == reference)

write load per bucket: 1.45% to 1.69% (even is 1.56%)
top 5: [('player46963', 99997), ('player29284', 99996), ('player11605', 99995), ('player40889', 99991), ('player23210', 99990)]
exactly the global top 5: True

The merged answer is exactly the global answer, and one detail is what guarantees that: rank_key returns a tuple, not a bare score. Two players on the same score would otherwise be ordered arbitrarily by heapq.nlargest, differently in the per-bucket pass and in the final merge, and the merged top-100 would occasionally disagree with the true one. Any ranking that is displayed, compared or tested needs a tiebreak on something unique — the same rule as any sort whose output someone will look at.

Four design decisions, and the arithmetic that justifies them:

SALTS = 64

def budget(reads, writes, salts, cache_hit, rebuild_seconds):
    return {
        'writes per bucket/s': writes // salts,
        'reads reaching storage/s': int(reads * (1 - cache_hit)),
        'rebuilds/s': round(1 / rebuild_seconds, 2),
        'staleness': f'up to {rebuild_seconds}s',
    }

for name, value in budget(400_000, 20_000, SALTS,
                          cache_hit=0.999, rebuild_seconds=2).items():
    print(f'{name:<26} {value}')

writes per bucket/s        312
reads reaching storage/s   400
rebuilds/s                 0.5
staleness                  up to 2s

Salting spreads the writes from 20,000/s on one shard to 312/s on each of sixty-four — comfortably within a single node, with room to grow.

The top-100 is a rollup, not a query. Computing it per request would mean merging 64 buckets 400,000 times a second; computing it every two seconds means half a merge per second. Reads then hit a cached list.

Caching does the heavy lifting, exactly as §8.5 argued: at a 99.9% hit rate — trivially achievable for one list that changes every two seconds — 400,000 reads/s become 400.

The leaderboard is two seconds stale, deliberately. That is an eventual-consistency choice (§4.8) and the right one: nobody can perceive a two-second lag in a leaderboard, and pretending otherwise would cost three orders of magnitude more hardware.

SECTION 9

Caching

A cache is a bet that the recent past predicts the near future. It is the cheapest performance win available — usually a few lines of code against an order-of-magnitude reduction in load — and it is also the place where the most confusing production bugs live, because a cache introduces a second copy of data and every second copy can be wrong. This section is about making that bet deliberately: what a cache actually buys, the five ways to wire one in, and the four failure modes that put caches in incident reports.

9.1 The Arithmetic That Decides Everything

Two numbers decide whether caching is worth doing at all: the hit rate and the ratio between the cost of a hit and the cost of a miss. Everything else about caching is detail on top of those two.

def effective(hit_rate, hit_ms, miss_ms, requests_per_second):
    latency = hit_rate * hit_ms + (1 - hit_rate) * miss_ms
    return latency, requests_per_second * (1 - hit_rate)

print(f'{"hit rate":>9} {"mean latency":>13} {"origin load":>12} {"load removed":>13}')
for h in (0.0, 0.50, 0.80, 0.90, 0.95, 0.99, 0.999):
    latency, origin = effective(h, hit_ms=0.5, miss_ms=40.0, requests_per_second=50_000)
    print(f'{h:>9.1%} {latency:>10.2f} ms {origin:>9,.0f}/s {1 - origin / 50_000:>12.1%}')

 hit rate  mean latency  origin load  load removed
     0.0%      40.00 ms    50,000/s         0.0%
    50.0%      20.25 ms    25,000/s        50.0%
    80.0%       8.40 ms    10,000/s        80.0%
    90.0%       4.45 ms     5,000/s        90.0%
    95.0%       2.48 ms     2,500/s        95.0%
    99.0%       0.90 ms       500/s        99.0%
    99.9%       0.54 ms        50/s        99.9%

Read the third column rather than the second, because it is the one that decides whether your database survives. The interesting region is the far end. Going from no cache to a 50% hit rate halves the origin load; going from 99% to 99.9% halves it again — and those two changes are worth exactly the same amount to the database, even though the first looks like an enormous improvement and the second looks like a rounding error.

The corollary is the one that catches people out: a small drop in hit rate is a large jump in origin load. A cache running at 99% that degrades to 95% has not lost 4% of anything; it has multiplied the traffic reaching the database by five, which is the difference between a healthy database and an outage. This is why cache hit rate is a page-worthy metric and not a dashboard curiosity, and why §9.6's stampede — a momentary collapse of the hit rate to zero — is dangerous out of all proportion to how long it lasts.

The second number matters just as much and gets less attention:

def worth_it(hit_ms, miss_ms, hit_rate):
    uncached, cached = miss_ms, hit_rate * hit_ms + (1 - hit_rate) * (hit_ms + miss_ms)
    return uncached, cached, uncached / cached

CASES = [
    ('database query over the network', 0.4, 40.0, 0.95),
    ('a value already in local memory', 0.4,  0.5, 0.95),
    ('an expensive report',             0.4, 4_000.0, 0.60),
    ('a rarely-repeated search',        0.4, 40.0, 0.05),
]
for name, hit, miss, rate in CASES:
    uncached, cached, speedup = worth_it(hit, miss, rate)
    verdict = 'cache it' if speedup > 1.2 else 'DO NOT CACHE'
    print(f'{name:<32} {uncached:>8.1f} -> {cached:>7.2f} ms  {speedup:>5.1f}x  {verdict}')

database query over the network      40.0 ->    2.40 ms   16.7x  cache it
a value already in local memory       0.5 ->    0.43 ms    1.2x  DO NOT CACHE
an expensive report                4000.0 -> 1600.40 ms    2.5x  cache it
a rarely-repeated search             40.0 ->   38.40 ms    1.0x  DO NOT CACHE

A miss costs more than no cache at all, because a miss pays the lookup and the origin. Setting cached = uncached and solving gives the break-even hit rate: hit_ms / miss_ms — 1% for the 40 ms query, 80% for the 0.5 ms one. The last two rows clear that bar and are still not worth building: 1.2× and 1.0× buy you a network dependency, a second copy to keep correct, and a component to operate, in exchange for a difference nobody can measure. The threshold that matters is not break-even, it is whether the win is large enough to pay for the complexity, which is why the verdict column asks for 1.2× rather than 1.0×.

Read the two rejected rows for why they fail, because both are common designs. Caching a value already in local memory adds a network hop to save a memory read — the break-even hit rate is 80%, so there is almost no room. Caching a search that is almost never repeated pays the lookup on every request to remove the origin from 5% of them; the cache is a tax collector, and it also fills memory with entries that will never be read again.

9.2 The Layers, and What Each One Is Good At

A request passes several places a cache can live, and they are not interchangeable. Each one is closer to the user, so it is faster and serves more traffic — and further from the truth, so it is harder to invalidate.

Client / browser
Free and infinitely scalable — the request never leaves the device. Completely uninvalidatable: once a response is in a browser cache with a one-year max-age, it is there until it expires. Only for content addressed by an immutable URL.
CDN / edge
Serves from a POP near the user, removing both origin load and round-trip latency. Purge is possible but takes seconds to minutes to propagate globally. Networking and HTTP covers the mechanics in its proxies and CDNs section.
Reverse proxy
One shared cache in front of your fleet, holding whole HTTP responses. Cheap, immediately purgeable, and blind to anything below the HTTP layer.
In-process
A dictionary in the application. Nanoseconds, no serialisation, no network. Its two costs are that every node has a different copy (§9.8) and that it dies with the process.
Distributed cache
Redis or Memcached: one shared copy, invalidatable in one place, survives a deploy. Costs a network round trip and becomes a dependency you must run.
Database buffer pool
The one you did not write. The database already keeps hot pages in memory, which is why "add a cache" sometimes measures as no improvement at all — you were hitting a cache already.

Caches compose multiplicatively, and that is the reason to use several. Each layer only sees what the layer above it missed:

def cascade(requests, layers):
    remaining = requests
    for name, hit_rate in layers:
        served = remaining * hit_rate
        remaining -= served
        print(f'{name:<22} serves {served:>10,.0f}/s   passes on {remaining:>9,.0f}/s')
    print(f'{"database":<22} serves {remaining:>10,.0f}/s')

cascade(1_000_000, [('CDN', 0.90), ('reverse proxy', 0.50),
                    ('in-process', 0.40), ('redis', 0.80)])

CDN                    serves    900,000/s   passes on   100,000/s
reverse proxy          serves     50,000/s   passes on    50,000/s
in-process             serves     20,000/s   passes on    30,000/s
redis                  serves     24,000/s   passes on     6,000/s
database               serves      6,000/s

No individual layer is impressive — 90%, 50%, 40%, 80% — and together they turn a million requests a second into six thousand. That is the shape of every large read-heavy system: not one heroic cache, but four ordinary ones in series.

Cache as close to the user as the invalidation requirements allow. That is the whole design rule, and it runs in the opposite direction to the instinct, which is to cache where it is easiest to write the code.

9.3 Cache-Aside

Cache-aside — also called lazy loading — puts the application in charge: look in the cache, and on a miss, fetch from the store and put it back. It is by far the most common pattern, and worth writing out in full because its two flaws are not obvious.

class Origin:
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data, self.reads = dict(data), 0

    def get(self, key):
        self.reads += 1
        return self.data.get(key)

    def put(self, key, value):
        self.data[key] = value

def cache_aside(cache, origin, key):
    if key in cache:                       # hit
        return cache[key], 'hit'
    value = origin.get(key)                # miss: read through by hand
    if value is not None:
        cache[key] = value
    return value, 'miss'

origin = Origin({'u1': 'Ada', 'u2': 'Grace'})
cache = {}
for key in ['u1', 'u1', 'u2', 'u1', 'u3', 'u3']:
    value, outcome = cache_aside(cache, origin, key)
    print(f'get {key} -> {str(value):<6} ({outcome})')
print('origin reads:', origin.reads, '| cached keys:', sorted(cache))

get u1 -> Ada    (miss)
get u1 -> Ada    (hit)
get u2 -> Grace  (miss)
get u1 -> Ada    (hit)
get u3 -> None   (miss)
get u3 -> None   (miss)
origin reads: 4 | cached keys: ['u1', 'u2']

Its virtues are real: the cache holds only data somebody actually asked for, the application survives a cache outage (every request becomes a miss and the system is merely slow), and the cache and the store need not share a schema.

Now the flaws.

Every distinct key costs one guaranteed miss, so a cold cache after a deploy or a Redis restart sends the full read volume to the origin at once. That is §9.6.

u3 was never cached, and was read from the origin twice. The code only caches non-None values, so a key that does not exist is looked up every single time. If those requests are attacker-controlled — a scraper walking random product ids — you have a cache that provides no protection at all against exactly the traffic you most want to absorb. The fix is negative caching: store a tombstone for a missing key with a short TTL.

The write path is not shown, and that is where the bug is. Cache-aside says nothing about writes, so the application must invalidate by hand, and the ordering is subtle enough to have its own subsection (§9.5).

9.4 Read-Through, Write-Through, Write-Behind and Refresh-Ahead

The alternative to cache-aside is to make the cache itself responsible for talking to the store. The application then only ever talks to the cache, which is simpler to use and harder to operate.

class Origin:                                   # the store behind the cache
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data, self.reads = dict(data), 0

    def get(self, key):
        self.reads += 1
        return self.data.get(key)

    def put(self, key, value):
        self.data[key] = value

class Cache:
    def __init__(self, origin):
        self.data, self.origin, self.pending = {}, origin, []

    def read_through(self, key):
        """The cache loads on a miss. The caller never sees the origin."""
        if key not in self.data:
            self.data[key] = self.origin.get(key)
        return self.data[key]

    def write_through(self, key, value):
        """Origin first, then cache. Slower writes, never a stale entry."""
        self.origin.put(key, value)
        self.data[key] = value

    def write_behind(self, key, value):
        """Cache first, origin later, in batches. Fast writes, a durability window."""
        self.data[key] = value
        self.pending.append((key, value))

    def flush(self):
        coalesced = dict(self.pending)              # last write per key wins
        for key, value in coalesced.items():
            self.origin.put(key, value)
        written, self.pending = len(coalesced), []
        return written

origin = Origin({'p1': 10})
cache = Cache(origin)

print('read-through p1 :', cache.read_through('p1'), '| origin reads:', origin.reads)
print('read-through p1 :', cache.read_through('p1'), '| origin reads:', origin.reads)

cache.write_through('p1', 11)
print('write-through   : cache', cache.data['p1'], '| origin', origin.data['p1'])

for price in (12, 13, 14, 15):
    cache.write_behind('p1', price)
print('write-behind    : cache', cache.data['p1'], '| origin', origin.data['p1'],
      '| pending', len(cache.pending))
print('flush wrote     :', cache.flush(), 'row(s) for', 4, 'writes | origin', origin.data['p1'])

read-through p1 : 10 | origin reads: 1
read-through p1 : 10 | origin reads: 1
write-through   : cache 11 | origin 11
write-behind    : cache 15 | origin 11 | pending 4
flush wrote     : 1 row(s) for 4 writes | origin 15
Read-through
Cache-aside with the loading moved inside. Same behaviour, less duplicated code, and one important difference: the application can no longer keep working when the cache is down, because it has no path to the origin.
Write-through
Write the store, then the cache. The cache is never stale and reads after a write are correct. Every write pays both costs, and it fills the cache with data nobody may ever read.
Write-behind
Write the cache, acknowledge, persist later. Four writes to the same key became one origin write — an enormous saving for counters, view tallies and session updates. And there is a window in which acknowledged data exists only in the cache.
Refresh-ahead
Refresh a popular entry before it expires, so a hot key is never missed. It works when access is predictable and wastes origin reads when it is not.

Write-behind is the one to think hardest about, because the coalescing is genuinely dramatic and so is the failure. Losing the last few seconds of a view counter is nothing; losing the last few seconds of an order is a company problem. Use it for data whose loss is tolerable, or put the durability somewhere else first — which is precisely the outbox construction from §11.2, with the cache playing the role of the fast path.

Refresh-ahead is worth one concrete note, because it is the pattern most often reinvented badly. Refreshing everything is a self-inflicted load spike; refreshing only what is about to expire and is being read is the version that works, and it is a two-line change to a read path:

class Origin:                                   # the store behind the cache
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data, self.reads = dict(data), 0

    def get(self, key):
        self.reads += 1
        return self.data.get(key)

    def put(self, key, value):
        self.data[key] = value

def get_with_refresh_ahead(cache, origin, key, now, ttl, refresh_at=0.8):
    """Serve from cache; when the entry is >80% through its TTL, refresh it too."""
    entry = cache.get(key)
    if entry is None:
        cache[key] = (origin.get(key), now)
        return cache[key][0], 'miss'
    value, stored_at = entry
    age = now - stored_at
    if age >= ttl:
        cache[key] = (origin.get(key), now)
        return cache[key][0], 'expired'
    if age >= ttl * refresh_at:
        cache[key] = (origin.get(key), now)         # serve the old value, refresh anyway
        return value, 'hit + refreshed'
    return value, 'hit'

origin, cache = Origin({'hot': 'v1'}), {}
for now in (0, 30, 60, 85, 95, 130):
    value, outcome = get_with_refresh_ahead(cache, origin, 'hot', now, ttl=100)
    print(f't={now:>3}s  {outcome:<15} origin reads so far: {origin.reads}')

t=  0s  miss            origin reads so far: 1
t= 30s  hit             origin reads so far: 1
t= 60s  hit             origin reads so far: 1
t= 85s  hit + refreshed origin reads so far: 2
t= 95s  hit             origin reads so far: 2
t=130s  hit             origin reads so far: 2

The entry never expires under load, because it is renewed at 85 seconds while still valid — so no request ever waits for the origin, which is the point. Note the injected now: a cache is a time-dependent object, and testing one against the wall clock produces a test that passes on a fast machine and fails in CI.

9.5 Invalidation, and the Race Nobody Sees in Review

Cache invalidation is the problem of deciding when a cached copy has stopped being true, and there are only three ways to do it. They have very different properties.

Expiry (TTL)
Bounded staleness, no coordination. The cache forgets on a timer, so a writer need do nothing at all. Correct by construction and the right default. Its cost is that you are always either serving data older than you would like or expiring entries that had not changed.
Explicit invalidation
Fresh immediately, at the cost of coordination. The writer deletes the key. Every writer everywhere must remember to do it, for every key the value appears in — including derived and aggregated ones.
Versioned keys
No invalidation at all. Put a version or content hash in the key, so a new value has a new key and the old one simply ages out. There is no race, because nothing is ever mutated. This is what asset fingerprinting does, and it is the most robust of the three wherever you can arrange it.

Prefer a short TTL to clever invalidation, and prefer a versioned key to both. Almost every cache invalidation bug in production is in the second row.

Here is the one that survives code review. A reader misses, reads the origin, and is descheduled. A writer updates the origin and deletes the cache key. The reader wakes up and stores the value it read — which is now old — and there is no TTL short enough to make this a small problem, because the entry was just written and its TTL has restarted.

class Store:
    def __init__(self, value):
        self.value = value

store, cache = Store('price=10'), {}

print('--- the interleaving that breaks delete-on-write')
value_read_by_reader = store.value                      # 1. reader misses, reads origin
print('1. reader read       :', value_read_by_reader)
store.value = 'price=99'                                # 2. writer updates the origin
cache.pop('price', None)                                # 3. writer deletes the cache key
print('2. writer wrote      :', store.value, '(cache now empty)')
cache['price'] = value_read_by_reader                   # 4. reader stores what it read
print('3. reader populated  :', cache['price'])
print('   origin says       :', store.value)
print('   STALE FOR THE FULL TTL:', cache['price'] != store.value)

--- the interleaving that breaks delete-on-write
1. reader read       : price=10
2. writer wrote      : price=99 (cache now empty)
3. reader populated  : price=10
   origin says       : price=99
   STALE FOR THE FULL TTL: True

The cache now holds the old price and will keep holding it until the TTL expires — potentially hours, and no subsequent write will fix it, because writes delete a key that is repopulated with stale data by the very next reader. Four defences, in ascending order of cost:

Delete after writing, never update in place. Writing cache[key] = new_value on the write path makes the race worse: two concurrent writers can leave the cache holding the value of the one whose origin write lost. Deleting is idempotent and cannot invert the order.

Give every entry a short TTL anyway. It does not prevent the race; it bounds the damage to something survivable, and it is one line. This is the single highest-value cache configuration decision there is.

Delete twice — once on write, once again a second later, after any in-flight read has finished. Crude, effective, widely deployed, and known as delayed double delete.

Version the key. price:v7 and price:v8 are different entries and there is no interleaving that can confuse them. The reader storing a stale value stores it under the old version's key, which nobody will ever ask for again.

The deeper point: a cache is a replica, so everything §7 says about replication lag applies to it. Delete-on-write is asynchronous single-leader replication with no ordering guarantee, and it fails for exactly the reasons that construction always fails.

9.6 The Stampede

A popular key expires. In the microsecond before anything repopulates it, every request for that key is a miss, and every one of them goes to the origin.

def stampede(concurrent_requests, protection):
    """One expired hot key, many simultaneous readers. Count the origin calls."""
    origin_calls, lock_held, served = 0, False, []
    for _ in range(concurrent_requests):
        if protection == 'none':
            origin_calls += 1
            served.append('fresh')
        elif protection == 'lock':
            if not lock_held:
                lock_held = True
                origin_calls += 1
                served.append('fresh')
            else:
                served.append('waited')
        elif protection == 'stale-while-revalidate':
            if not lock_held:
                lock_held = True
                origin_calls += 1
                served.append('fresh')
            else:
                served.append('stale')
    return origin_calls, served.count('fresh'), served.count('waited'), served.count('stale')

print(f'{"protection":<24}{"origin calls":>13}{"fresh":>8}{"waited":>8}{"stale":>7}')
for protection in ('none', 'lock', 'stale-while-revalidate'):
    calls, fresh, waited, stale = stampede(5_000, protection)
    print(f'{protection:<24}{calls:>13,}{fresh:>8}{waited:>8,}{stale:>7,}')

protection               origin calls   fresh  waited  stale
none                            5,000    5000       0      0
lock                                1       1   4,999      0
stale-while-revalidate              1       1       0  4,999

Five thousand identical queries arriving simultaneously at a database that was comfortably serving zero of them a moment ago. This is a cache stampede — also called a thundering herd — and it is how a cache turns into an outage: the origin slows under the load, so the requests take longer, so more requests pile up behind them, so the origin slows further — the cascading failure §3 describes, triggered by a cache doing exactly what it was told.

The three defences differ in what they do to the 4,999 requests that lost the race.

A lock — single-flight — makes one request fetch and the rest wait for it. Origin load is exactly one query. Every waiting request pays the full origin latency, so a slow origin becomes a latency spike for everyone, and the lock itself needs a timeout or one crashed holder stalls the key forever.

Stale-while-revalidate serves the expired value to everyone else while one request refreshes in the background. Nobody waits, the origin sees one query, and the price is that 4,999 users got data that was a few hundred milliseconds past its expiry — almost always the right trade, and the reason the pattern is in HTTP's Cache-Control as a standard directive.

Probabilistic early expiration avoids the synchronisation entirely: each read independently decides, with a probability rising as the entry ages, to refresh early. No lock, no coordination, and expiries spread out instead of aligning.

import math
import random

def xfetch(age, ttl, delta_ms, rng, beta=1.0):
    """Refresh early with probability rising near expiry (Vattani et al., 2015)."""
    return age - delta_ms * beta * math.log(rng.random()) >= ttl

rng = random.Random(20260825)
print(f'{"age":>5}{"early refreshes / 10,000 reads":>32}')
for age in (30, 50, 70, 85, 95, 99):
    early = sum(xfetch(age, ttl=100, delta_ms=8, rng=rng) for _ in range(10_000))
    print(f'{age:>4}s{early:>26,}')

  age  early refreshes / 10,000 reads
  30s                         2
  50s                        19
  70s                       221
  85s                     1,504
  95s                     5,347
  99s                     8,832

The probability is negligible early and rises steeply as the entry approaches expiry, so refreshes are spread over the last few seconds of the TTL rather than all landing on the instant it ends. Read the column as a per-read probability, not a count of refreshes: in a live cache the first read that returns true refreshes the entry and resets its age to zero, so the whole ramp collapses to roughly one early refresh per TTL. delta_ms is the knob — set it to the time the origin actually takes, so the refresh starts about one origin-latency before the entry would have expired.

The other stampede is the cold one, and it has no clever fix. A Redis restart, a deploy that changes a key prefix, or a cache flush drops the hit rate to zero for every key at once, and single-flight does not help because the requests are for different keys. What helps is warming the cache before taking traffic, replacing the cache gradually rather than all at once, and — the honest one — making sure the origin can survive its full traffic for the minutes it takes to refill. A system that cannot survive a cold cache has made its cache a single point of failure, whatever the architecture diagram says.

9.7 Eviction

A cache is finite, so something must be discarded. The policy decides which, and the differences are much larger than they look.

from collections import OrderedDict, Counter

def lru(trace, capacity):
    cache, hits = OrderedDict(), 0
    for key in trace:
        if key in cache:
            cache.move_to_end(key); hits += 1
        else:
            if len(cache) >= capacity:
                cache.popitem(last=False)          # evict least recently used
            cache[key] = True
    return hits

def lfu(trace, capacity):
    cache, freq, hits = set(), Counter(), 0
    for key in trace:
        freq[key] += 1
        if key in cache:
            hits += 1
        else:
            if len(cache) >= capacity:
                victim = min(cache, key=lambda k: (freq[k], k))
                cache.discard(victim)
            cache.add(key)
    return hits

def belady(trace, capacity):
    """Optimal: evict whatever is used furthest in the future. Not implementable live."""
    cache, hits = set(), 0
    for i, key in enumerate(trace):
        if key in cache:
            hits += 1
            continue
        if len(cache) >= capacity:
            def next_use(k):
                try: return trace.index(k, i + 1)
                except ValueError: return len(trace) + 1
            cache.discard(max(cache, key=next_use))
        cache.add(key)
    return hits

hot = ['a', 'b', 'c'] * 40                                  # 3 keys, read constantly
scan = [f'x{i}' for i in range(120)]                        # 120 keys, read once each
trace = [k for pair in zip(hot, scan) for k in pair]        # interleaved

print(f'{"policy":<10}{"hits":>7}{"hit rate":>11}')
for name, fn in [('LRU', lru), ('LFU', lfu), ('Belady', belady)]:
    hits = fn(trace, capacity=4)
    print(f'{name:<10}{hits:>7}{hits / len(trace):>10.1%}')

policy       hits   hit rate
LRU             0      0.0%
LFU           114     47.5%
Belady        117     48.8%

That gap is the single most useful thing to know about eviction. The trace is deliberately LRU's worst case — a cyclic working set slightly larger than the cache, which is the pattern LRU is provably bad at — and a real workload is kinder. The shape, though, is entirely real. LRU is defeated by a scan: a batch job reading 120 rows once each walks through the cache and evicts the three keys the entire workload actually depends on, because each of those single-use rows is, briefly, the most recently used thing in the cache. LFU is immune here, because a key read forty times outranks a key read once no matter how recently the once happened.

That is not a general verdict on LFU, which has its own well-known failure: it clings to keys that were popular yesterday and is slow to admit anything new. Real systems use hybrids for exactly this reason — W-TinyLFU, used by Caffeine and by parts of Redis, admits a new key only if a frequency sketch says it is likely to be used more than the key it would evict, which gets LFU's scan resistance without its inability to forget. Belady's optimal is unimplementable — it requires knowing the future — but it is the right yardstick: if your policy is far below it on your real trace, there is something to win.

Two practical notes. TTL and eviction are different mechanisms and you need both: TTL bounds staleness, eviction bounds memory, and a cache with only one of them either serves stale data forever or runs out of memory. And watch what the cache does when it is full — a Redis instance with no maxmemory-policy set will start refusing writes rather than evicting, which turns a full cache into a write outage in a component you were treating as optional.

9.8 Hot Keys, Coherence, and the Cost of Being Distributed

A single shared cache has its own version of §8.5's problem: one key can be hotter than one machine.

def hot_key_load(total_rps, key_share, cache_nodes, per_node_capacity):
    hottest = total_rps * key_share                     # one key lives on ONE node
    even = total_rps / cache_nodes
    return hottest, even, hottest > per_node_capacity

for share in (0.001, 0.02, 0.30):
    hottest, even, overloaded = hot_key_load(2_000_000, share, 20, 200_000)
    print(f'key is {share:>5.1%} of traffic: {hottest:>9,.0f}/s on one node '
          f'(even would be {even:,.0f}/s)  overloaded: {overloaded}')

key is  0.1% of traffic:     2,000/s on one node (even would be 100,000/s)  overloaded: False
key is  2.0% of traffic:    40,000/s on one node (even would be 100,000/s)  overloaded: False
key is 30.0% of traffic:   600,000/s on one node (even would be 100,000/s)  overloaded: True

Consistent hashing (§8.4) spreads keys evenly and can do nothing about one key being 30% of the traffic — the celebrity user, the front-page product, the feature flag every request reads. Three fixes, and they are the same shape as §8.5's:

Replicate the hot key under several names (flag:v3#0 … flag:v3#9) and have clients pick one at random, dividing the load by ten at the cost of ten copies to invalidate.

Put a small in-process cache in front of the distributed one. A key hot enough to overload a Redis node is hot enough to have a near-perfect hit rate in a 100-entry local cache with a 1-second TTL. This is the standard answer and it is very effective — 2,000,000 requests a second across 200 application nodes is 10,000 per node per second, and a one-second local TTL turns that into one Redis call per node per second.

Or accept a little staleness by design, which is what the second fix really is.

That local cache is also where coherence becomes a problem, and it is worth being precise about the trade:

class Node:
    def __init__(self, name): self.name, self.local = name, {}

def read(node, shared, key):
    if key not in node.local:
        node.local[key] = shared[key]
    return node.local[key]

shared = {'flag': 'on'}
nodes = [Node('app-1'), Node('app-2'), Node('app-3')]
for node in nodes:
    read(node, shared, 'flag')

shared['flag'] = 'off'                       # a write, and one node happens to re-read
nodes[0].local.pop('flag')
read(nodes[0], shared, 'flag')

print('shared store :', shared['flag'])
for node in nodes:
    print(f'{node.name:<7} sees : {node.local["flag"]}')
print('nodes disagree:', len({n.local["flag"] for n in nodes}) > 1)

shared store : off
app-1   sees : off
app-2   sees : on
app-3   sees : on
nodes disagree: True

Three application nodes, three local caches, two different answers to the same question, and a user's experience now depends on which node their request lands on — a feature that flickers on and off as they click. There are two honest responses and one bad one.

The bad one is trying to keep local caches globally coherent by broadcasting invalidations to every node. It works until a node misses a message, and then it is silently wrong with no mechanism to recover.

The two that work: make the TTL short enough that the divergence window is acceptable — one second of flicker is invisible, one minute is a support ticket — and broadcast invalidations as an optimisation on top of a short TTL, never as the correctness mechanism. A missed message then costs you one extra second of staleness instead of permanent divergence. This is the same principle as §7.4's read-your-writes handling: the fallback must be correct on its own, and the fast path is only ever an improvement.

9.9 What Not to Cache

The decision to cache is usually made by asking whether it will be fast. That is the second question. The first is what a stale answer does.

Anything that answers "is this allowed?" Permissions, blocks, bans, feature entitlements, revoked tokens. A stale "yes" is a security incident, and §4.8's exercise makes the same point: the test is not "is staleness acceptable" but "what is the worst concrete outcome". Cache these with explicit invalidation and a TTL measured in seconds, or do not cache them.
Anything with a hit rate below the break-even in §9.1. A per-user key on a site with millions of one-visit users is not a cache, it is a write-only memory that adds latency to every request.
A query that is slow because it is missing an index. The cache hides it, the query stays slow, and the day the cache is cold the system does not come back up. Fix the query; then decide whether it still needs a cache.
Anything the system cannot run without. The moment the origin cannot serve full traffic, the cache has stopped being an optimisation and become a component whose failure is your failure — at its availability, not your database's. That may be a perfectly deliberate choice; it must not be an accidental one.

The last one deserves a sentence more, because it is the difference between a cache and an architecture. Ask the question directly, in a review, out loud: "if this cache is empty, do we serve or do we fall over?" If the answer is "we fall over", the cache is now a tier of the system and needs the same treatment as any other — replication, monitoring, capacity headroom, a failure drill. Most teams discover which answer applies to them during an incident.

Exercises

Exercise 9.1 — Choose the strategy. For each workload, choose a layer, a write strategy and an invalidation strategy, and name the failure you are accepting.

(a) A product catalogue: 500,000 reads/s, updated a few times a day by staff,
    and a price shown to a user must be the price they are charged.
(b) A per-video view counter: 40,000 increments/s, displayed rounded to the nearest
    thousand, and exact-to-the-second accuracy is not required.
(c) A user's permission set: read on every request, changed rarely, and a revoked
    permission must stop working promptly.
(d) A machine-learning feature vector recomputed nightly, 8 KB per user,
    read once per session by 200 million users.
Solution 
ANSWERS = [
    ('(a) catalogue', 'CDN + reverse proxy', 'write-through on staff edit',
     'versioned keys, purge on publish',
     'a purge that fails leaves an old price at one POP — so charge from the database, not the cache'),
    ('(b) view counter', 'in-process, flushed to Redis', 'write-behind, coalesced',
     'TTL only — nothing to invalidate',
     'a crash loses the last few seconds of counts, which is acceptable by the requirement'),
    ('(c) permissions', 'distributed cache, short TTL', 'write-through on change',
     'explicit invalidation AND a 5-30s TTL',
     'up to one TTL of stale access — the TTL is the security parameter, so it is small'),
    ('(d) feature vector', 'distributed cache, no local copy', 'batch-loaded nightly',
     'versioned by the training run date',
     '1.6 TB of cache and a ~0% hit rate if sessions do not repeat — measure before building'),
]
for label, layer, write, invalidation, failure in ANSWERS:
    print(f'{label}\n  layer      : {layer}\n  writes     : {write}'
          f'\n  invalidate : {invalidation}\n  accepting  : {failure}\n')

(a) catalogue
  layer      : CDN + reverse proxy
  writes     : write-through on staff edit
  invalidate : versioned keys, purge on publish
  accepting  : a purge that fails leaves an old price at one POP — so charge from the database, not the cache

(b) view counter
  layer      : in-process, flushed to Redis
  writes     : write-behind, coalesced
  invalidate : TTL only — nothing to invalidate
  accepting  : a crash loses the last few seconds of counts, which is acceptable by the requirement

(c) permissions
  layer      : distributed cache, short TTL
  writes     : write-through on change
  invalidate : explicit invalidation AND a 5-30s TTL
  accepting  : up to one TTL of stale access — the TTL is the security parameter, so it is small

(d) feature vector
  layer      : distributed cache, no local copy
  writes     : batch-loaded nightly
  invalidate : versioned by the training run date
  accepting  : 1.6 TB of cache and a ~0% hit rate if sessions do not repeat — measure before building

(a) turns on one sentence in the requirement. "The price shown must be the price charged" does not mean the cache must be perfectly fresh — it means the charge must be computed from the database, with the cached price used only for display and re-validated at checkout. That decouples the two entirely and lets you cache aggressively at the edge, which is the only way 500,000 reads/s is affordable. Trying to make a globally distributed CDN cache strongly consistent to protect a pricing invariant is the expensive wrong answer.

(b) is the write-behind case, and the requirement says so outright: rounded to the nearest thousand, no second-level accuracy needed. Increment in process memory, flush to Redis every second or two, and let a durable store take periodic snapshots. Forty thousand increments a second becomes a few hundred writes a second. Note the compounding: coalescing in the application and in Redis before the database sees anything.

(c) is the one where the TTL is a security control. Both mechanisms are needed and neither is sufficient: explicit invalidation is fast but can be missed, and the TTL is the guarantee that a missed invalidation heals. Choose the TTL by asking how long a revoked administrator may keep administrator access, and write the answer down — that number is the design.

(d) is the trap. The arithmetic disqualifies it before any strategy question: 200 million users at 8 KB is 1.6 TB of cache, and if each user reads their vector once per session the hit rate is roughly zero — every entry is loaded to serve exactly one read. This is §9.1's second table, at scale. Read it from the store the nightly job wrote it to, and cache only the small subset of users who are active repeatedly.

Exercise 9.2 — Find the four bugs. This cache layer is in production. Every line looks reasonable and four things are wrong. Name each, say what a user experiences, and give the fix.

import time

CACHE = {}

def get_user(db, user_id):
    if user_id in CACHE:
        return CACHE[user_id]
    user = db.query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?', user_id)
    CACHE[user_id] = user
    return user

def update_user(db, user_id, fields):
    db.execute('UPDATE users SET ... WHERE id = ?', user_id)
    CACHE[user_id] = db.query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?', user_id)

def get_permissions(db, user_id):
    key = f'perm:{user_id}'
    if key in CACHE and CACHE[key]['at'] > time.time() - 86400:
        return CACHE[key]['value']
    value = db.query('SELECT * FROM permissions WHERE user_id = ?', user_id)
    CACHE[key] = {'value': value, 'at': time.time()}
    return value
Solution

Fault 1 — the cache is unbounded and has no TTL. CACHE is a module-level dictionary that only ever grows: one entry per user ever seen, held until the process restarts. The user-visible symptom is a process whose memory climbs all day and is OOM-killed overnight, taking live requests with it — and because it dies and restarts empty, it also produces a cold stampede (§9.6) every time. The fix is a bounded cache with an eviction policy and a TTL on every entry (§9.7): both mechanisms, not one.

Fault 2 — update_user writes the fresh value into the cache instead of deleting the key. Two concurrent updates can interleave so that the origin ends with writer B's value and the cache ends with writer A's, and nothing will ever correct it. del CACHE[user_id] is idempotent and cannot invert the ordering (§9.5). It also removes the pointless extra SELECT on the write path.

Fault 3 — the permission TTL is 86,400 seconds. A revoked permission keeps working for up to a day. This is §9.9's first row: the TTL on an authorisation decision is the security parameter, and a day is not a cache-tuning choice, it is a stated policy that a fired employee retains access until tomorrow. Seconds, plus explicit invalidation on change.

Fault 4 — it is a per-process cache treated as if it were shared. There is no invalidation path between processes at all, so update_user on node 1 leaves node 2 serving the old row until its process restarts — indefinitely, since there is no TTL. The user edits their profile, reloads, and the change appears and disappears depending on which node answers (§9.8). Either move the cache to a shared store, or keep it local with a TTL short enough that the divergence is invisible.

A version with all four fixed:

from collections import OrderedDict

class Origin:                                   # the store behind the cache
    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data, self.reads = dict(data), 0

    def get(self, key):
        self.reads += 1
        return self.data.get(key)

    def put(self, key, value):
        self.data[key] = value

class TTLCache:
    """Bounded, LRU-evicting, TTL'd. `now` is injected so it is testable."""
    def __init__(self, capacity, ttl):
        self.data, self.capacity, self.ttl = OrderedDict(), capacity, ttl

    def get(self, key, now):
        entry = self.data.get(key)
        if entry is None:
            return None
        value, stored_at = entry
        if now - stored_at >= self.ttl:
            del self.data[key]                       # expired
            return None
        self.data.move_to_end(key)
        return value

    def put(self, key, value, now):
        if key in self.data:
            del self.data[key]
        elif len(self.data) >= self.capacity:
            self.data.popitem(last=False)            # evict least recently used
        self.data[key] = (value, now)

    def delete(self, key):
        self.data.pop(key, None)


users = TTLCache(capacity=3, ttl=60)
perms = TTLCache(capacity=3, ttl=10)                 # seconds: this TTL is a security control

def get_user(origin, user_id, now):
    hit = users.get(user_id, now)
    if hit is not None:
        return hit, 'hit'
    value = origin.get(user_id)
    users.put(user_id, value, now)
    return value, 'miss'

def update_user(origin, user_id, value):
    origin.put(user_id, value)
    users.delete(user_id)                            # delete, never write

origin = Origin({'u1': 'Ada', 'u2': 'Grace', 'u3': 'Katherine', 'u4': 'Dorothy'})

print(get_user(origin, 'u1', now=0))
print(get_user(origin, 'u1', now=30), '  <- still inside the 60s TTL')
print(get_user(origin, 'u1', now=90), '  <- expired, refetched')

update_user(origin, 'u1', 'Ada Lovelace')
print(get_user(origin, 'u1', now=91), '  <- delete-on-write, so no stale read')

for user_id in ('u2', 'u3', 'u4'):                   # capacity is 3
    get_user(origin, user_id, now=92)
print('cached keys, oldest first:', list(users.data))
print('bounded at capacity:', len(users.data) == 3)
print('permission TTL is', perms.ttl, 'seconds, not', 86_400)

('Ada', 'miss')
('Ada', 'hit')   <- still inside the 60s TTL
('Ada', 'miss')   <- expired, refetched
('Ada Lovelace', 'miss')   <- delete-on-write, so no stale read
cached keys, oldest first: ['u2', 'u3', 'u4']
bounded at capacity: True
permission TTL is 10 seconds, not 86400

The eviction line is the one to read: u1 is gone despite having been read four times, because the capacity is three and it was the least recently used when u4 arrived. That is LRU behaving correctly, and it is also §9.7's warning in miniature — a scan of four keys through a three-key cache evicts the hottest entry in it.

Exercise 9.3 — Size and defend a cache. A product page is read 300,000 times a second across 2 million distinct products, following a power law: the top 1% of products get 60% of the traffic. A page costs 45 ms to build from the database and the entry is 4 KB. Size the cache, predict the hit rate, decide the stampede protection, and state what happens on a cold start.

Solution

The whole exercise is one insight: a power-law workload means a small cache gets almost all of the benefit, and the arithmetic tells you where to stop paying.

def zipf_share(fraction_cached, top_share=0.60, top_fraction=0.01):
    """Traffic served if you cache the hottest `fraction_cached` of the catalogue."""
    if fraction_cached <= top_fraction:
        return top_share * (fraction_cached / top_fraction)
    tail = (fraction_cached - top_fraction) / (1 - top_fraction)
    return top_share + (1 - top_share) * tail

CATALOGUE, ENTRY_KB, RPS, MISS_MS = 2_000_000, 4, 300_000, 45

print(f'{"cached":>10}{"entries":>11}{"memory":>10}{"hit rate":>10}'
      f'{"origin/s":>11}{"origin threads":>16}')  # threads = Little\'s law
for fraction in (0.001, 0.005, 0.01, 0.05, 0.20, 1.00):
    entries = int(CATALOGUE * fraction)
    hit = zipf_share(fraction)
    origin = RPS * (1 - hit)
    print(f'{fraction:>9.1%}{entries:>11,}{entries * ENTRY_KB / 1000:>7,.0f} MB'
          f'{hit:>10.1%}{origin:>11,.0f}{origin * MISS_MS / 1000:>16,.0f}')

    cached    entries    memory  hit rate   origin/s  origin threads
     0.1%      2,000      8 MB      6.0%    282,000          12,690
     0.5%     10,000     40 MB     30.0%    210,000           9,450
     1.0%     20,000     80 MB     60.0%    120,000           5,400
     5.0%    100,000    400 MB     61.6%    115,152           5,182
    20.0%    400,000  1,600 MB     67.7%     96,970           4,364
   100.0%  2,000,000  8,000 MB    100.0%          0               0

Cache 1% of the catalogue. Twenty thousand entries, 80 MB — small enough to sit in the application's own memory, let alone Redis — and it absorbs 60% of the traffic. The next 4% of the catalogue costs five times the memory and buys 1.6 percentage points of hit rate. The origin threads column is the one that makes the decision concrete: it is the concurrency the database must sustain (Little's law — arrival rate times service time), and it is the number that turns "the cache helps" into "the database needs 5,400 concurrent queries, which it cannot do".

Note what the table also says: even a 100%-cached catalogue is only the steady state. Every row still has a miss column, and §9.1's warning applies — the hit rate does not have to fall far to multiply the origin load.

Now defend it:

def defend(rps, hot_key_share, ttl_s, protection):
    hottest_key_rps = rps * hot_key_share
    if protection == 'none':
        burst = hottest_key_rps                       # everyone misses at once
    elif protection == 'single-flight':
        burst = 1 / ttl_s                             # one refetch per TTL
    elif protection == 'stale-while-revalidate':
        burst = 1 / ttl_s
    return hottest_key_rps, burst

print(f'{"protection":<26}{"reads/s for the hot key":>25}{"origin calls/s":>16}')
for protection in ('none', 'single-flight', 'stale-while-revalidate'):
    reads, burst = defend(300_000, hot_key_share=0.02, ttl_s=60, protection=protection)
    rate = f'{burst:,.0f}/s' if burst >= 1 else f'1 per {1 / burst:,.0f}s'
    print(f'{protection:<26}{reads:>25,.0f}{rate:>16}')

protection                  reads/s for the hot key  origin calls/s
none                                          6,000         6,000/s
single-flight                                 6,000       1 per 60s
stale-while-revalidate                        6,000       1 per 60s

Stale-while-revalidate, with a 60-second TTL. The single hottest product takes 6,000 reads a second; at expiry, unprotected, all 6,000 hit a query that takes 45 milliseconds, which is 270 concurrent database queries for one product page. With stale-while-revalidate it is one query every sixty seconds and no request ever waits. Single-flight gives the same origin figure but makes 6,000 users wait 45 ms; for a product page, serving a value a moment past its expiry is obviously better than serving a spinner.

The cold start is the answer that matters most, and it is not reassuring. With an empty cache the hit rate is zero, so the origin sees the full 300,000 reads a second at 45 ms each — 13,500 concurrent queries, against a database sized for the 5,400 in the steady state. The system does not come back up. Three things make that survivable, and they must be designed in rather than discovered:

Do not empty the cache all at once. Replace Redis nodes one at a time (consistent hashing, §8.4, means each replacement invalidates only its own share), and never change a global key prefix in a single deploy.

Warm before taking traffic. The top 20,000 products are known in advance — they are the previous hour's top 20,000. Loading them takes seconds and covers 60% of traffic before the first user arrives.

Shed load on the way up. If the cache is cold and the origin is saturated, serving 20% of requests correctly and rejecting the rest quickly is strictly better than serving none of them slowly (§3). A concurrency limit in front of the database — a bulkhead (§14.6) — is what turns "the site is down for twenty minutes" into "the site is degraded for two".

The point the exercise is built to make: the steady-state arithmetic is easy and the cold-start arithmetic is the one that decides the architecture. Everyone computes the first. The second is what an incident review computes for you afterwards.

SECTION 10

Asynchronism

The fastest way to answer a request is not to do the work. Asynchronism is the decision to accept a request, record the intent durably, answer immediately, and do the work afterwards — and it is one of the highest-leverage moves in system design, because it decouples what the user waits for from what the system has to do. It is also the move that introduces queues, workers, backlogs and duplicate delivery, so it comes with a set of problems that have to be designed for rather than discovered.

10.1 What Moving Work Off the Request Path Buys

Start with the numbers, because they are what makes the argument for asynchronism.

def request_latency(steps):
    return sum(ms for _, ms, _ in steps)

STEPS = [
    ('validate and write the order',   12, 'synchronous — the user needs the order id'),
    ('charge the card',               850, 'synchronous — the user needs to know it worked'),
    ('generate the invoice PDF',      600, 'asynchronous'),
    ('send the confirmation email',   400, 'asynchronous'),
    ('update the search index',       120, 'asynchronous'),
    ('notify the warehouse',          300, 'asynchronous'),
    ('recompute recommendations',   2_400, 'asynchronous'),
]
sync = [s for s in STEPS if s[2].startswith('synchronous')]
everything = request_latency(STEPS)
print(f'everything inline : {everything:>6,} ms')
print(f'only what the user waits for: {request_latency(sync):>6,} ms')
print(f'moved off the request path  : {everything - request_latency(sync):>6,} ms '
      f'({1 - request_latency(sync) / everything:.0%})')

everything inline :  4,682 ms
only what the user waits for:    862 ms
moved off the request path  :  3,820 ms (82%)

A 4.7-second checkout becomes 862 milliseconds, and nothing was made faster — the same work still happens. What changed is who waits. Three further gains follow from that and are worth naming separately, because each is a reason on its own:

Failure isolation
The email service being down no longer fails checkout. The message sits in the queue and is delivered when it comes back — which converts a hard dependency into a soft one, the single most valuable move in §14.1.
Load smoothing
A queue absorbs a spike that the workers process at their own pace. A synchronous system must be provisioned for the peak; an asynchronous one can be provisioned nearer the average, with latency absorbing the difference.
Independent scaling
PDF generation is CPU-heavy, email is network-bound and the search index needs memory. As queue consumers they scale separately, on different hardware, without touching the web tier.

And the costs, which are not small. The user does not know it worked — you have replaced a result with a promise, and the interface must now express "in progress" and eventually surface failure. Debugging is harder, because a failure happens later, in a different process, with no user waiting to report it. Two more things can break: the broker, and the workers. And everything downstream must tolerate duplicates, because every queue that survives a crash delivers at least once (§10.6).

The test for whether a step belongs off the request path is a single question: does the user's next action depend on it? They need the order id and they need to know the payment succeeded. They do not need the PDF to exist before the page renders.

10.2 Queues and Logs Are Different Things

"Message queue" is used loosely for two designs with genuinely different semantics, and choosing the wrong one is the most common architectural mistake in this section.

A queue
RabbitMQ, SQS, Celery's broker. The broker holds messages and hands each one to exactly one consumer, which acknowledges it; the broker then deletes it. Consumers compete for work, adding one is instant throughput, and the queue's natural state is empty. The message is gone once handled.
A log
Kafka, Redpanda, Kinesis. The broker holds an ordered, immutable sequence and every consumer group tracks its own offset. Nothing is deleted on read — messages age out on a retention policy. Many independent consumers read the same stream, and a new one can start from the beginning. The message stays.
class Queue:
    """Competing consumers. Delivered once, then gone."""
    def __init__(self):
        self.messages = []

    def publish(self, message):
        self.messages.append(message)

    def consume(self, worker):
        if not self.messages:
            return None
        message = self.messages.pop(0)
        return f'{worker} got {message}'

class Log:
    """Independent consumer groups, each with its own offset. Nothing is removed."""
    def __init__(self):
        self.entries, self.offsets = [], {}

    def publish(self, message):
        self.entries.append(message)

    def consume(self, group):
        offset = self.offsets.get(group, 0)
        if offset >= len(self.entries):
            return None
        self.offsets[group] = offset + 1
        return f'{group} got {self.entries[offset]}'

queue = Queue()
for message in ('m1', 'm2', 'm3'):
    queue.publish(message)
print('queue :', [queue.consume(w) for w in ('worker-a', 'worker-b', 'worker-a')])
print('        remaining:', queue.messages, '- a second team cannot read these')

log = Log()
for message in ('m1', 'm2', 'm3'):
    log.publish(message)
print('\nlog   :', [log.consume('billing') for _ in range(3)])
print('        :', [log.consume('analytics') for _ in range(3)], '- same messages, own offset')
print('        entries still present:', log.entries)
print('        a new group starting from 0:', log.consume('fraud-team-deployed-today'))

queue : ['worker-a got m1', 'worker-b got m2', 'worker-a got m3']
        remaining: [] - a second team cannot read these

log   : ['billing got m1', 'billing got m2', 'billing got m3']
        : ['analytics got m1', 'analytics got m2', 'analytics got m3'] - same messages, own offset
        entries still present: ['m1', 'm2', 'm3']
        a new group starting from 0: fraud-team-deployed-today got m1

The last line is the property people most often want and most often discover they do not have. A team that deploys a new consumer next month can read last month's events from a log and cannot read them from a queue, because the queue deleted them the moment the first consumer acknowledged.

Choosing between them is not a matter of taste:

Use a message queue for work — one thing must happen once. Resize this image, send this email, run this report. Competing consumers give you free horizontal scaling, and per-message acknowledgement means a failed message is retried without affecting its neighbours.

Use a log for facts — something happened and any number of parties may care, now or later. Order placed, user signed up, price changed. Replay, multiple independent consumers and ordering within a partition are the features, and this is the substrate every pattern in §11 is built on.

The seductive mistake is using a log as a task queue. It looks like it works: publish tasks, have workers read. Then a single slow message blocks its partition — a log has no per-message acknowledgement, only an offset — so the messages behind it wait, and adding consumers does not help because a partition is consumed by exactly one member of a group. A queue handles this natively; a log makes you build head-of-line blocking into your own design.

10.3 Task Queues and Sizing the Worker Pool

A task queue is a queue plus a pool of workers, and the only real question is how many workers. It is answered by Little's law, not by intuition:

def workers_needed(tasks_per_second, seconds_per_task, target_utilisation=0.7):
    concurrency = tasks_per_second * seconds_per_task           # Little's law
    return concurrency, concurrency / target_utilisation

print(f'{"task":<22}{"rate/s":>9}{"seconds":>9}{"concurrency":>13}{"workers @70%":>14}')
TASKS = [
    ('send email',            200, 0.4),
    ('generate PDF',           40, 2.5),
    ('transcode video',         2, 180.0),
    ('recompute recs',          5, 12.0),
]
for name, rate, seconds in TASKS:
    concurrency, workers = workers_needed(rate, seconds)
    print(f'{name:<22}{rate:>9}{seconds:>9.1f}{concurrency:>13,.0f}{workers:>14,.0f}')

task                     rate/s  seconds  concurrency  workers @70%
send email                  200      0.4           80           114
generate PDF                 40      2.5          100           143
transcode video               2    180.0          360           514
recompute recs                5     12.0           60            86

Provision for utilisation well below 1, and the reason is queueing theory rather than caution. As utilisation approaches 100%, waiting time does not rise gently — it goes to infinity, because there is no idle capacity to absorb the natural variation in arrivals.

def wait_multiplier(utilisation):
    """M/M/1: mean time in system is service_time / (1 - utilisation)."""
    return 1 / (1 - utilisation)

print(f'{"utilisation":>12}{"mean wait, x service time":>28}')
for utilisation in (0.5, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9, 0.95, 0.99):
    print(f'{utilisation:>11.0%}{wait_multiplier(utilisation):>25.1f}x')

 utilisation   mean wait, x service time
        50%                      2.0x
        70%                      3.3x
        80%                      5.0x
        90%                     10.0x
        95%                     20.0x
        99%                    100.0x

At 50% utilisation a task waits twice its own service time; at 95% it waits twenty times; at 99%, a hundred. The last 10% of capacity costs more latency than the first 90% combined, which is why "the workers are only 70% busy, we are wasting money" is one of the more expensive optimisations available.

Three design rules follow from the same arithmetic:

Separate queues by task duration, never by importance alone. A 180-second transcode and a 0.4-second email in one queue means the email waits behind the transcode — head-of-line blocking, and the fix is separate queues with separate pools, which is §14.6's bulkhead applied to workers.

Make every task idempotent and give it a timeout. A worker will be killed mid-task by a deploy, an OOM or a network partition, and the task will be redelivered. A task with no timeout that hangs holds its worker forever, which removes capacity permanently and silently.

Keep the payload small: send an id, not the data. A message carrying a 4 MB image is a broker storing your images badly. Put the object in object storage (§6.7), put the key in the message, and the broker stays fast.

10.4 Ordering, Partitions, and What a Guarantee Costs

Global ordering across a distributed queue is not something you should want. It requires every message to pass through one place, which caps throughput at one machine and makes that machine a single point of failure — a total order is a consensus problem (§5.1), with consensus's price.

What real systems provide instead is ordering within a partition, with the partition chosen by a key:

def partition_for(key, partitions):
    return sum(key.encode()) % partitions          # a real system uses a proper hash

MESSAGES = [
    ('order-7', 'created'), ('order-9', 'created'), ('order-7', 'paid'),
    ('order-9', 'cancelled'), ('order-7', 'shipped'), ('order-4', 'created'),
]
PARTITIONS = 3
lanes = {p: [] for p in range(PARTITIONS)}
for key, event in MESSAGES:
    lanes[partition_for(key, PARTITIONS)].append(f'{key}:{event}')

for partition, messages in lanes.items():
    print(f'partition {partition}: {messages}')

print('\nper-key order preserved:',
      all(lane == sorted(lane, key=lambda m: [f'{k}:{e}' for k, e in MESSAGES].index(m))
          for lane in lanes.values()))
print('order-7 events, in order:',
      [m for lane in lanes.values() for m in lane if m.startswith('order-7')])

partition 0: ['order-9:created', 'order-9:cancelled']
partition 1: ['order-7:created', 'order-7:paid', 'order-7:shipped', 'order-4:created']
partition 2: []

per-key order preserved: True
order-7 events, in order: ['order-7:created', 'order-7:paid', 'order-7:shipped']

Every event for order-7 is in one partition, in the order it was produced. That is exactly the guarantee the domain needs — paid must not be processed before created — and nothing weaker is required, because order-9's events have no meaningful relationship to order-7's.

Partition 2 is empty, and that is not a flaw in the example. Three keys over three partitions will not distribute evenly, exactly as §8.2's hashing demonstration showed — evenness is a property that appears at volume, and a partition scheme should be judged on ten thousand keys rather than on six. What does need judging at any scale is whether one key carries a disproportionate share of the traffic, which is the third consequence below.

Three consequences follow, and each is a trap if it is not designed for.

A partition is consumed by exactly one member of a consumer group. That is what makes the ordering guarantee possible, and it means the partition count is the ceiling on consumer parallelism. Thirty consumers against twelve partitions leaves eighteen idle. Choose the partition count for the parallelism you will eventually want, because increasing it later re-hashes keys and breaks ordering across the change — the same problem, and the same reason, as §8.6's rebalancing.

A hot key is a hot partition. One high-volume tenant, one celebrity account, one popular product concentrates on a single consumer while the others idle. This is §8.5 exactly, and it has the same fixes: a compound key, salting, or a dedicated partition.

Ordering is only preserved if you do not concurrently process within a partition. A consumer that reads a batch and hands it to a thread pool has thrown away the guarantee it paid for — and this is a bug that only appears under load, which is when it costs the most.

Retries break ordering too, and this one surprises people. A message that fails and is retried after its successors have been processed is now out of order. If ordering genuinely matters, a failure must stop the partition until it is resolved, and that is a deliberate choice to trade availability for correctness — see §10.7, where the alternative is to send it to a dead-letter queue and accept the gap.

10.5 Pub/Sub and Fan-Out

Publish/subscribe decouples a producer from an unknown set of consumers: the producer publishes to a topic, and every subscriber gets a copy. The producer does not know who is listening, which is exactly §11.1's coupling reversal, and it is what makes adding a consumer a deployment rather than a code change upstream.

The design question underneath is when the fan-out happens, and it is one of the classic system-design decisions.

def fan_out_on_write(followers, posts_per_day, read_cost=1):
    return {'writes per post': followers,
            'writes per day': followers * posts_per_day,
            'reads': f'{read_cost} — the timeline is precomputed'}

def fan_out_on_read(following, posts_per_day):
    return {'writes per post': 1,
            'writes per day': posts_per_day,
            'reads': f'{following} — merge every followed feed at read time'}

def row(label, result):
    print(f'  fan-out on {label:<6}{result["writes per post"]:>14,}'
          f'{result["writes per day"]:>16,}   reads: {result["reads"]}')

print('ordinary user: 300 followers, follows 300, posts 2/day')
print(f'{"":17}{"writes/post":>14}{"writes/day":>16}')
row('write', fan_out_on_write(300, 2))
row('read', fan_out_on_read(300, 2))

print('\ncelebrity: 90,000,000 followers, follows 300, posts 5/day')
print(f'{"":17}{"writes/post":>14}{"writes/day":>16}')
row('write', fan_out_on_write(90_000_000, 5))
row('read', fan_out_on_read(300, 5))

ordinary user: 300 followers, follows 300, posts 2/day
                    writes/post      writes/day
  fan-out on write            300             600   reads: 1 — the timeline is precomputed
  fan-out on read               1               2   reads: 300 — merge every followed feed at read time

celebrity: 90,000,000 followers, follows 300, posts 5/day
                    writes/post      writes/day
  fan-out on write     90,000,000     450,000,000   reads: 1 — the timeline is precomputed
  fan-out on read               1               5   reads: 300 — merge every followed feed at read time

Fan-out on write precomputes each follower's timeline, so a read is one lookup. For an ordinary user that is 600 writes a day to make every read free — an excellent trade in a read-heavy system.

Fan-out on read stores the post once and merges at read time. Cheap writes, expensive reads, and the reads are the common operation.

For the celebrity it is 450 million writes a day for five posts, arriving as five spikes of ninety million. No amount of queue capacity makes that a good idea, and it is why the real answer in every large system is hybrid: fan out on write for ordinary accounts, and for the small number of accounts above a follower threshold, store the post once and merge it in at read time. A reader's timeline is then "my precomputed feed, plus the handful of celebrities I follow, merged" — which is a small merge, because nobody follows thousands of celebrities.

The threshold is a tuning parameter, not a principle, and it should be a configuration value you can move. The lesson that generalises past timelines: when a workload has a power-law shape, the right design is usually two designs with a threshold between them, because a single strategy must be sized for the tail and is then wrong for the body.

10.6 Delivery Semantics

Every asynchronous system has to answer "how many times will this be delivered?", and there are exactly three possible answers — one of which does not exist.

def deliver(semantics, failure):
    """What happens to one message under each policy when something goes wrong."""
    if semantics == 'at-most-once':          # ack FIRST, then work
        return {'none': 'once', 'crash mid-work': 'LOST', 'ack lost': 'once'}[failure]
    if semantics == 'at-least-once':         # work FIRST, then ack
        return {'none': 'once', 'crash mid-work': 'DUPLICATE',
                'ack lost': 'DUPLICATE'}[failure]
    raise ValueError(semantics)

FAILURES = ('none', 'crash mid-work', 'ack lost')
print(f'{"":<16}' + ''.join(f'{f:>17}' for f in FAILURES))
for semantics in ('at-most-once', 'at-least-once'):
    print(f'{semantics:<16}' + ''.join(f'{deliver(semantics, f):>17}' for f in FAILURES))

                             none   crash mid-work         ack lost
at-most-once                 once             LOST             once
at-least-once                once        DUPLICATE        DUPLICATE
At-most-once
Acknowledge before doing the work. Never duplicated, sometimes lost. Legitimate for metrics samples, presence pings and log lines where a gap is invisible — and wrong for everything else. Choose it deliberately or not at all.
At-least-once
Do the work, then acknowledge. Never lost, sometimes duplicated. The default in every real broker, and the one to design for.
Exactly-once
Not achievable in delivery. The acknowledgement can always be lost after the work and before the record of it, and no protocol removes that window — §5.7 is the proof, and it is a theorem rather than an engineering gap.

What is achievable, and what every system advertising exactly-once actually implements, is at-least-once delivery plus an idempotent consumer — effectively-once. §11.8 builds it: a dedup record written in the same transaction as the effect, so the second delivery has no effect. The distinction is not pedantry. The guarantee holds only inside the store the receipt is written to, so a consumer that dedups in one database and then calls a payment API has two systems again and needs the API's own idempotency key as well.

One operational detail that causes more duplicates than crashes do: the visibility timeout. A broker hands a message to a worker and hides it for a fixed period; if no acknowledgement arrives in time, it assumes the worker died and redelivers. A task that regularly takes longer than the timeout is therefore delivered again while the first worker is still running it — two workers, same message, concurrently. Set the timeout above the worst-case task duration, extend it by heartbeat for long tasks, and treat a rising redelivery count as the alarm it is.

10.7 Dead Letters and Poison Messages

Some messages can never be processed: a malformed payload, a reference to a deleted row, a bug in the consumer. Retrying forever is not resilience — it is an infinite loop consuming a worker.

class Broker:
    def __init__(self, max_attempts=3):
        self.queue, self.dlq, self.max_attempts = [], [], max_attempts
        self.attempts, self.processed = {}, []

    def publish(self, message_id, payload):
        self.queue.append((message_id, payload))

    def run(self, handler):
        while self.queue:
            message_id, payload = self.queue.pop(0)
            self.attempts[message_id] = self.attempts.get(message_id, 0) + 1
            try:
                handler(payload)
                self.processed.append(message_id)
            except ValueError as exc:
                if self.attempts[message_id] >= self.max_attempts:
                    self.dlq.append({'id': message_id, 'payload': payload,
                                     'attempts': self.attempts[message_id],
                                     'error': str(exc)})
                else:
                    self.queue.append((message_id, payload))     # retry, behind the others

def handler(payload):
    if payload.get('amount') is None:
        raise ValueError('missing amount')
    return payload['amount'] * 2

broker = Broker()
broker.publish('m1', {'amount': 10})
broker.publish('m2', {})                                  # poison: will never succeed
broker.publish('m3', {'amount': 30})

broker.run(handler)
print('processed :', broker.processed)
print('attempts  :', broker.attempts)
print('dead-letter queue:')
for entry in broker.dlq:
    print('  ', entry)
print('queue drained:', broker.queue == [])

processed : ['m1', 'm3']
attempts  : {'m1': 1, 'm2': 3, 'm3': 1}
dead-letter queue:
   {'id': 'm2', 'payload': {}, 'attempts': 3, 'error': 'missing amount'}
queue drained: True

m1 and m3 were processed once; m2 was attempted three times and set aside, and the queue drained. Without the dead-letter queue, m2 would still be retrying, and every message behind it would be waiting.

Four rules for a dead-letter queue that is worth having:

A dead letter must carry its context. The payload, the error, the attempt count, the timestamp, and the trace id. A DLQ of bare payloads is a pile of messages nobody can act on, and it will be ignored.

Alert on the DLQ, and treat depth as a first-class metric. A dead-letter queue nobody watches is a slow data-loss mechanism with a reassuring name. dlq_depth > 0 is a real alert; dlq_depth rising quickly is an incident.

Make replay a routine operation, not a script someone writes during the incident. Most dead letters are caused by a bug or a transient dependency failure, so the fix is: deploy the fix, replay the DLQ. That path should be one command and should itself be idempotent.

Distinguish retryable from permanent before retrying at all. A timeout is retryable; a malformed payload is not. Retrying a permanently-broken message three times wastes a worker and delays everything else — the sensible design routes a validation failure straight to the DLQ and retries only what could plausibly succeed. This is the same distinction §14.3 makes about which HTTP status codes are worth retrying.

10.8 Back Pressure: What a Full Queue Should Do

A queue is a buffer, and every buffer eventually fills. Back pressure is what happens then, and the default — grow without limit — is the one choice that is always wrong.

def policy_outcome(policy, capacity, arrivals, service_rate, seconds=60):
    """One minute of overload: arrivals exceed what the workers can drain."""
    queued, rejected, dropped = 0, 0, 0
    for _ in range(seconds):
        queued += arrivals - service_rate
        if queued > capacity:
            overflow = queued - capacity
            queued = capacity
            if policy == 'unbounded':
                queued += overflow                       # no limit at all
            elif policy == 'reject new':
                rejected += overflow
            elif policy == 'drop oldest':
                dropped += overflow
    return queued, rejected, dropped

OUTCOMES = {
    'unbounded': 'everything accepted, hours late; memory grows until the broker dies',
