    'reject new': 'a fast 503 with Retry-After; accepted work still completes on time',
    'drop oldest': 'silent loss of the oldest work — almost never what you want',
}
print(f'{"policy":<14}{"queue depth":>14}{"rejected":>11}{"dropped":>10}')
for policy in ('unbounded', 'reject new', 'drop oldest'):
    depth, rejected, dropped = policy_outcome(policy, 10_000, 5_000, 3_000)
    print(f'{policy:<14}{depth:>14,}{rejected:>11,}{dropped:>10,}')
    print(f'{"":14}{OUTCOMES[policy]}')

policy           queue depth   rejected   dropped
unbounded            120,000          0         0
              everything accepted, hours late; memory grows until the broker dies
reject new            10,000    110,000         0
              a fast 503 with Retry-After; accepted work still completes on time
drop oldest           10,000          0   110,000
              silent loss of the oldest work — almost never what you want

An unbounded queue does not prevent failure; it converts a fast, visible failure into a slow, invisible one. The requests are accepted, the user is told everything is fine, and the work happens two hours later — or never, when the broker runs out of memory and the whole backlog is lost. Every one of those messages was past its deadline (§14.2) long before a worker touched it.

The policies, and when each is right:

Reject new work
Return 429 or 503 with Retry-After. The producer knows immediately, and the work already accepted still completes within its expected time. The right default, and the only policy that keeps a promise to the requests it did accept.
Block the producer
Make the publish call wait for space. Natural back pressure, and it works when the producer is a batch job that can simply go slower. It is dangerous when the producer is serving users, because you have moved the queue into your request threads (§14.6).
Shed by priority
Drop or reject low-value work first: analytics before payments, free tier before paid. The most sophisticated option and the most useful under real overload, and it requires classifying every message.
Drop oldest
Only for streams where recency is the value — a metrics feed, a position update. Silent data loss anywhere else.

Back pressure must propagate all the way to the source or it does nothing. A worker slowing down is only useful if the queue fills, the producer is rejected, and the client is told — a chain in which any link that silently buffers absorbs the signal and hides the problem until it is much larger. This is the same argument §14 makes about deadlines: a signal that stops at the first hop is not a signal.

10.9 Queue Depth, and the Arithmetic of a Backlog

Queue depth is the most useful metric an asynchronous system has, and it is routinely misread. Depth alone means nothing; depth divided by drain rate is the number that matters.

def backlog(depth, arrival_rate, service_rate):
    net = service_rate - arrival_rate
    if net <= 0:
        return None, 'GROWING — the backlog never drains at this rate'
    return depth / net, f'drains in {depth / net:,.0f}s at {net:,}/s net'

print(f'{"depth":>10}{"arrivals/s":>12}{"capacity/s":>12}   verdict')
for depth, arrivals, capacity in [
        (50_000, 1_000, 3_000), (50_000, 2_900, 3_000),
        (50_000, 3_000, 3_000), (50_000, 3_200, 3_000)]:
    _, verdict = backlog(depth, arrivals, capacity)
    print(f'{depth:>10,}{arrivals:>12,}{capacity:>12,}   {verdict}')

     depth  arrivals/s  capacity/s   verdict
    50,000       1,000       3,000   drains in 25s at 2,000/s net
    50,000       2,900       3,000   drains in 500s at 100/s net
    50,000       3,000       3,000   GROWING — the backlog never drains at this rate
    50,000       3,200       3,000   GROWING — the backlog never drains at this rate

A depth of 50,000 is fine, alarming or fatal depending entirely on the other two numbers, and they are the ones that are usually not on the dashboard. At 1,000 arrivals a second it clears in 25 seconds. At 2,900 it takes 500 seconds — half an hour of stale results, from a graph that looks identical. At 3,200 it never clears, and no amount of waiting helps.

That leads to the rule for alerting on queues: alert on the age of the oldest message, not on the depth. Age is the number that maps directly to user experience — "the oldest unprocessed order is nine minutes old" is immediately actionable, while "the queue has 50,000 messages" requires three more lookups before anyone knows whether to care. It is also robust to traffic growth, where a depth threshold set last year fires constantly this year.

Two more numbers belong on the same dashboard:

def capacity_plan(peak_rate, seconds_per_task, target_wait_s, spike_multiple=3):
    steady = peak_rate * seconds_per_task
    spike_depth = peak_rate * (spike_multiple - 1) * 60          # a 1-minute 3x spike
    drain_workers = spike_depth / target_wait_s * seconds_per_task
    return {
        'steady-state workers': round(steady / 0.7),
        'backlog from a 1-min 3x spike': f'{spike_depth:,.0f} messages',
        f'workers to clear it in {target_wait_s}s': round(steady / 0.7 + drain_workers),
    }

for key, value in capacity_plan(peak_rate=500, seconds_per_task=0.8, target_wait_s=120).items():
    print(f'{key:<38} {value}')

steady-state workers                   571
backlog from a 1-min 3x spike          60,000 messages
workers to clear it in 120s            971

Autoscaling workers on queue depth is the standard answer and it has one sharp edge: workers take time to start, so scaling begins after the backlog has already formed. Scale on the rate of change of depth as well as on depth, keep a warm floor of workers so the first spike does not wait for a cold start, and remember that scaling up consumers past the partition count does nothing at all in a log-based system (§10.4).

Exercises

Exercise 10.1 — Split the work. A photo-sharing upload does: store the file, generate three thumbnails, extract EXIF, run content moderation, update the user's gallery, notify followers, and update a trending-hashtags counter. Decide what is synchronous, what is asynchronous, which mechanism each asynchronous piece uses, and what the user sees while it is pending.

Solution 
PLAN = [
    ('store the file',        'SYNC',  'the id is the response; nothing else can start without it'),
    ('content moderation',    'SYNC*', 'a fast automated check inline; the slow model async'),
    ('generate thumbnails',   'queue', 'CPU-bound, one-per-image, must happen exactly once'),
    ('extract EXIF',          'queue', 'cheap; batch it with the thumbnail job, same worker'),
    ('update the gallery',    'queue', "the owner's own view — do it first, it is the one they check"),
    ('notify followers',      'log',   'fan-out on write, hybrid above the celebrity threshold'),
    ('trending hashtags',     'log',   'a stream consumer with a windowed count; approximate is fine'),
]
for step, mechanism, why in PLAN:
    print(f'{step:<24}{mechanism:<8}{why}')

store the file          SYNC    the id is the response; nothing else can start without it
content moderation      SYNC*   a fast automated check inline; the slow model async
generate thumbnails     queue   CPU-bound, one-per-image, must happen exactly once
extract EXIF            queue   cheap; batch it with the thumbnail job, same worker
update the gallery      queue   the owner's own view — do it first, it is the one they check
notify followers        log     fan-out on write, hybrid above the celebrity threshold
trending hashtags       log     a stream consumer with a windowed count; approximate is fine

Only the store is truly synchronous, and the response is the photo id plus a processing status. Everything else can complete after the user has seen the page.

Moderation is the interesting call, and it is a split. Making the user wait for a full moderation model is unacceptable latency; publishing unmoderated content is unacceptable risk. The design that works is a fast inline check — hash matching against known-bad content, a few milliseconds — plus an asynchronous deep check, with the photo visible only to its owner until that completes. The trade is stated in the product, not hidden in the architecture: "your photo is being processed" is a normal thing for a user to read.

Thumbnails and EXIF are one job, not two. Both need the decoded image, and decoding is most of the cost. Two queue messages means decoding twice — a real and common waste, and the reason to think about task boundaries in terms of the expensive shared step.

Notifications are a log, not a queue, because "photo posted" is a fact that several independent consumers care about — notifications, the recommendation trainer, analytics — and each wants its own offset. A queue would let exactly one of them have it. This is §10.2's distinction, and it is the decision that is most expensive to reverse.

Trending hashtags is deliberately approximate. A windowed count over the stream, tolerant of duplicates because at-least-once means it will see some, and reset periodically. Exact counting here would need coordination that buys nothing a user can perceive.

And the ordering that matters: update the owner's gallery before notifying followers. A follower who arrives before the gallery write finds a photo that does not appear to exist. Within one partition keyed by photo id, the events are consumed in order and this is free — which is §10.4 doing real work rather than being a nicety.

Exercise 10.2 — Find the five bugs. This worker is in production. Name each fault, say what a user experiences, and rewrite it.

import json

def worker_loop(broker, db, mailer):
    while True:
        message = broker.receive()
        broker.acknowledge(message)
        payload = json.loads(message.body)
        db.execute('UPDATE orders SET status = ? WHERE id = ?',
                   ('confirmed', payload['order_id']))
        mailer.send(payload['email'], 'Order confirmed')
        for follower in db.query('SELECT id FROM followers WHERE user_id = ?',
                                 payload['user_id']):
            broker.publish('notify', json.dumps({'to': follower, 'order': payload}))
Solution

Fault 1 — it acknowledges before doing the work. This is at-most-once (§10.6), almost certainly by accident rather than by choice. A crash anywhere below that line loses the message permanently: the order is never confirmed, no email is sent, and there is no record that anything went wrong. Acknowledge after the work.

Fault 2 — no error handling at all, so one bad message kills the loop. A malformed body raises out of json.loads, the while True exits, and the worker process dies. Under a supervisor it restarts, receives the same message, and dies again — a crash loop that consumes the whole worker pool. This needs a try/except, bounded retries and a dead-letter queue (§10.7).

Fault 3 — the effect is not idempotent with respect to the notifications. Fixing fault 1 makes this at-least-once, and then a redelivery re-publishes a notification to every follower. The UPDATE is a status assignment and survives repetition; the fan-out does not. A user with 800 followers generates 800 duplicate notifications per redelivery.

Fault 4 — the email is sent before the transaction is durable, and is not deduplicated. If the UPDATE is rolled back, the customer has been told about a confirmation that did not happen. And on redelivery they get the email again.

Fault 5 — the fan-out is inline and unbounded. A user with two million followers produces two million publish calls inside one message's processing, holding the worker for minutes and blowing past any visibility timeout — so the message is redelivered while it is still being processed, and a second worker starts the same two-million-message fan-out. This is the failure that takes the whole system down, and §10.5's hybrid threshold is the fix.

The rewrite:

import json

class Rewritten:
    def __init__(self, db, broker, max_attempts=3, celebrity_threshold=10_000):
        self.db, self.broker = db, broker
        self.max_attempts, self.celebrity_threshold = max_attempts, celebrity_threshold

    def handle(self, message):
        try:
            payload = json.loads(message.body)
        except json.JSONDecodeError as exc:
            self.broker.dead_letter(message, f'unparseable: {exc}')   # permanent: no retry
            self.broker.acknowledge(message)
            return 'dead-lettered'

        try:
            with self.db:                                  # ONE transaction
                seen = self.db.execute(
                    'SELECT 1 FROM processed WHERE consumer = ? AND message_id = ?',
                    ('order-confirm', message.id)).fetchone()
                if seen:
                    self.broker.acknowledge(message)
                    return 'duplicate'
                self.db.execute('INSERT INTO processed VALUES (?, ?)',
                                ('order-confirm', message.id))
                self.db.execute('UPDATE orders SET status = ? WHERE id = ?',
                                ('confirmed', payload['order_id']))
                # side effects go in the outbox, not out of the process (§11.2)
                self.db.execute(
                    'INSERT INTO outbox (topic, dedup_key, payload) VALUES (?, ?, ?)',
                    ('email.order_confirmed', f'confirm:{message.id}',
                     json.dumps({'to': payload['email']})))
                self.db.execute(
                    'INSERT INTO outbox (topic, dedup_key, payload) VALUES (?, ?, ?)',
                    ('fanout.requested', f'fanout:{message.id}',
                     json.dumps({'user_id': payload['user_id'],
                                 'order_id': payload['order_id']})))
        except Exception as exc:                           # transient: let it be redelivered
            if message.attempts >= self.max_attempts:
                self.broker.dead_letter(message, str(exc))
                self.broker.acknowledge(message)
                return 'dead-lettered'
            return 'retry'                                 # NOT acknowledged
        self.broker.acknowledge(message)                   # ack LAST
        return 'processed'

Five changes, each matching a fault:

Acknowledge last (fault 1), so a crash means redelivery rather than loss.

A parse failure goes straight to the DLQ (fault 2) without consuming three retries, because it can never succeed. A database error is retried, because it might.

A dedup receipt in the same transaction as the effect (faults 3 and 4) makes the whole handler effectively-once (§11.8).

Side effects go into an outbox (fault 4) rather than leaving the process mid-transaction, and each carries a dedup_key so the relay's own at-least-once delivery cannot double-send.

The fan-out becomes one message, not two million (fault 5). A separate fan-out service reads fanout.requested, looks up the follower count, and either fans out in bounded batches or — above the celebrity threshold — writes nothing and lets readers merge at read time:

def fanout_plan(followers, threshold=10_000, batch=500):
    if followers > threshold:
        return {'strategy': 'read-time merge', 'messages published': 0,
                'why': 'writing 90M rows for one post is never the cheaper side'}
    return {'strategy': 'write-time fan-out',
            'messages published': -(-followers // batch),
            'why': f'{batch} followers per message, each independently retryable'}

for followers in (300, 9_500, 90_000_000):
    print(f'{followers:>12,} followers -> {fanout_plan(followers)}')

         300 followers -> {'strategy': 'write-time fan-out', 'messages published': 1, 'why': '500 followers per message, each independently retryable'}
       9,500 followers -> {'strategy': 'write-time fan-out', 'messages published': 19, 'why': '500 followers per message, each independently retryable'}
  90,000,000 followers -> {'strategy': 'read-time merge', 'messages published': 0, 'why': 'writing 90M rows for one post is never the cheaper side'}

Batching matters as much as the threshold. Nine thousand five hundred followers becomes nineteen messages rather than 9,500, so a failure retries five hundred notifications instead of one, and the worker is never held for more than a batch. The message that triggers the fan-out stays small and fast, which is what keeps the visibility timeout honest.

Exercise 10.3 — Size and defend a pipeline. An order pipeline takes 800 orders a second at peak, each requiring a 1.2-second enrichment call. Black Friday brings a sustained 6× spike for four hours. Choose the queue or log, size the workers, set the back-pressure policy, define the alerts, and say exactly what happens in the first ten minutes of the spike.

Solution 
PEAK, SERVICE_S, SPIKE, SPIKE_HOURS = 800, 1.2, 6, 4

def size(rate, service_s, utilisation=0.7):
    concurrency = rate * service_s
    return concurrency, concurrency / utilisation

steady_c, steady_w = size(PEAK, SERVICE_S)
spike_c, spike_w = size(PEAK * SPIKE, SERVICE_S)
print(f'steady peak {PEAK:>5,}/s -> {steady_c:>7,.0f} concurrent, {steady_w:>7,.0f} workers')
print(f'spike       {PEAK * SPIKE:>5,}/s -> {spike_c:>7,.0f} concurrent, {spike_w:>7,.0f} workers')

print('\n--- if the fleet does NOT scale ---')
arrivals, capacity = PEAK * SPIKE, PEAK
net = arrivals - capacity
for minutes in (1, 10, 60, SPIKE_HOURS * 60):
    depth = net * minutes * 60
    oldest_s = depth / capacity
    print(f'  after {minutes:>3} min: depth {depth:>12,}  oldest message '
          f'{oldest_s / 60:>8,.0f} min old')

print('\n--- with the queue capped at 10 minutes of work ---')
CAP = PEAK * 600
print(f'  cap                = {CAP:,} messages (10 min at {PEAK:,}/s)')
print(f'  cap reached after  = {CAP / net:,.0f}s of the spike')
print(f'  then: {net:,}/s rejected with 503 + Retry-After')
print(f'  accepted work still completes within 10 minutes, throughout')

steady peak   800/s ->     960 concurrent,   1,371 workers
spike       4,800/s ->   5,760 concurrent,   8,229 workers

--- if the fleet does NOT scale ---
  after   1 min: depth      240,000  oldest message        5 min old
  after  10 min: depth    2,400,000  oldest message       50 min old
  after  60 min: depth   14,400,000  oldest message      300 min old
  after 240 min: depth   57,600,000  oldest message    1,200 min old

--- with the queue capped at 10 minutes of work ---
  cap                = 480,000 messages (10 min at 800/s)
  cap reached after  = 120s of the spike
  then: 4,000/s rejected with 503 + Retry-After
  accepted work still completes within 10 minutes, throughout

A log, partitioned by order_id. Orders have a lifecycle whose events must stay in order per order (§10.4), several teams want the stream, and replay after a bad deploy is worth having. Partition count is set from the eventual consumer parallelism — at 5,760 spike workers, a few hundred partitions, not the twelve someone picks by default.

Size for the steady peak, autoscale to the spike, and keep a warm floor. 1,371 workers steady, 8,229 at the spike. Provisioning 8,229 permanently to serve one weekend is a bad trade; provisioning 1,371 and scaling reactively is one too, because the first minutes are spent scaling while the backlog builds. Pre-scale before a known event — Black Friday is on the calendar — and autoscale for the unknown ones.

Read the un-scaled table, because it is the argument for the cap. At 6× arrivals against 1× capacity the backlog grows by 4,000 a second: after ten minutes the oldest message is 50 minutes old, and after four hours it is twenty hours old. The pipeline is not slow at that point, it is broken, and every order in it was past its deadline long before a worker saw it — but nothing has errored, and the dashboard is green.

Cap the queue at ten minutes of work and reject beyond it. 480,000 messages, reached two minutes into the spike; after that, 4,000 a second get an immediate 503 with Retry-After. That sounds worse and is much better: every accepted order completes within ten minutes, and the client knows immediately which ones were not accepted and can retry them with backoff and jitter (§14.4). The alternative accepts everything and silently fails all of it.

Alert on age, not depth (§10.9). oldest_message_age > 5 min is the page; queue depth goes on the dashboard as context. Add rejection_rate > 0 as a warning, because the cap doing its job is still information the business needs, and dlq_depth > 0 as its own alert (§10.7).

And the first ten minutes, concretely. t=0: arrivals jump to 4,800/s and depth starts climbing at 4,000/s. t≈30s: the depth-derivative alarm fires and autoscaling begins; workers take one to two minutes to become useful. t=2min: the cap is hit and rejection starts — the first visible errors, and the moment the system starts keeping its promises rather than breaking them quietly. t≈4min: the new workers are draining, net rate turns positive, depth falls. t=10min: back inside the age SLO with the fleet at spike size, and the rejected orders were retried by clients that were told to.

SECTION 11

Event-Driven Architecture

Every section so far has been about making a distributed system agree on state. This one is about a different move: stop trying to agree, and record what happened instead. An event-driven system publishes facts about the past — an order was placed, a payment was captured — and lets each service decide what those facts mean for it. That buys decoupling, replay and an audit trail. It costs you transactions, and everything in this section is a way of paying that bill.

11.1 Commands, Events, and What a Message Carries

A command is a request to do something in the future, addressed to one recipient, and it can be refused. An event is a statement that something already happened, addressed to nobody in particular, and it cannot be refused — only ignored. The grammar gives it away: ChargeCard is a command, CardCharged is an event.

Command
Imperative, one recipient, may fail. The sender knows who will handle it and usually waits for an answer. Coupling points from sender to receiver.
Event
Past tense, any number of recipients, already true. The publisher does not know who is listening and does not wait. Coupling points from receiver to publisher — the opposite direction.

That reversal is the entire architectural argument. In a command-driven design, adding a "send a loyalty-points update when an order is placed" feature means editing the order service. In an event-driven one it means deploying a new consumer of order.placed and touching nothing that already works.

What the event carries is a separate decision, and there are three common answers with genuinely different consequences.

ORDER = {'id': 'ord_9', 'customer': 'c_41', 'total_cents': 4250, 'status': 'placed'}

def notification(order):
    return {'type': 'order.placed', 'order_id': order['id']}

def carried_state(order):
    return {'type': 'order.placed', 'version': 3, **order}

def delta(order):
    return {'type': 'orders.insert', 'before': None, 'after': order}

STYLES = [
    ('notification', notification(ORDER), True,  'schema is one field'),
    ('carried state', carried_state(ORDER), False, 'schema is the public contract'),
    ('delta (CDC)',   delta(ORDER),        False, 'schema is your table'),
]
for name, event, callback, note in STYLES:
    print(f'{name:<14} {len(str(event)):>3} bytes  call back: {str(callback):<5} {note}')
    print(f'{"":14} {event}')

notification    45 bytes  call back: True  schema is one field
               {'type': 'order.placed', 'order_id': 'ord_9'}
carried state  114 bytes  call back: False schema is the public contract
               {'type': 'order.placed', 'version': 3, 'id': 'ord_9', 'customer': 'c_41', 'total_cents': 4250, 'status': 'placed'}
delta (CDC)    128 bytes  call back: False schema is your table
               {'type': 'orders.insert', 'before': None, 'after': {'id': 'ord_9', 'customer': 'c_41', 'total_cents': 4250, 'status': 'placed'}}

A notification is the smallest and the most decoupled: it says something changed, ask me if you care. Its hidden cost is a read amplification — a thousand orders a second with four interested consumers becomes four thousand extra reads a second against the order service, arriving in a burst immediately after each write, which is the worst possible moment. It also has a subtle correctness trap: by the time the consumer calls back, the order may have changed again, so the consumer sees a later state than the event announced.

Event-carried state transfer puts everything the consumer needs in the payload. No callback, no read amplification, and consumers keep working while the producer is down — the strongest form of decoupling available. Its cost is that the payload is now a published contract you cannot change casually (§11.9), and that the data is a snapshot which is stale from the instant it is written.

A delta, typically produced by change data capture, mirrors the row before and after. It is the cheapest to produce — the database is already writing this to its replication log (§7.2) — and the most coupled, because your consumers now depend on your table layout. Rename a column and every consumer breaks. Use it for data pipelines and analytics; be very cautious about using it as the integration contract between teams.

Default to event-carried state, with the identifier always present. The payload should be a deliberately designed subset — the fields the domain considers public — rather than the row, and it should always include the id so a consumer that needs the freshest version can still call back.

11.2 The Dual-Write Problem, and Why It Has Only One Good Answer

Here is the bug that sits underneath every event-driven system. The Backend and API Design course builds the fix in detail — its transactions and asynchronism section writes the outbox table and its relay against a real database — so this section spends its words on the part that is a distributed systems question: what guarantee you end up with, and what it forces on everyone downstream.

The bug is writing to two systems with no transaction spanning them:

def place_order_broken(db, broker, order):
    db.insert(order)                       # (1) committed
    broker.publish('order.placed', order)  # (2) crash here and the event is gone forever

There is no ordering of those two lines that is safe. Publish first and a crash leaves an event for an order that does not exist; commit first and a crash leaves an order nobody hears about. Retrying does not help, because after a network timeout you do not know which side happened.

The transactional outbox removes the second system from the write path. The event is inserted into an ordinary table in the same transaction as the business data, so there is exactly one commit and therefore nothing to be inconsistent about. A separate relay then reads that table and publishes. Watch what the relay's own crash does:

class Outbox:
    """One table, written in the business transaction."""
    def __init__(self):
        self.rows, self.seq = [], 0

    def commit(self, key, payload):
        self.seq += 1
        self.rows.append({'seq': self.seq, 'key': key, 'payload': payload, 'sent': False})

    def unsent(self):
        return [r for r in self.rows if not r['sent']]

def relay(outbox, broker, crash_before_marking=None):
    """Publish, then mark. A crash between the two republishes on restart."""
    for row in outbox.unsent():
        broker.append((row['key'], row['payload']))
        if row['seq'] == crash_before_marking:
            return 'crashed after publishing seq %d' % row['seq']
        row['sent'] = True
    return 'drained'

box, broker = Outbox(), []
for order_id, customer in [('ord_1', 'c_7'), ('ord_2', 'c_7'), ('ord_3', 'c_9')]:
    box.commit(customer, {'id': order_id, 'customer': customer})

print(relay(box, broker, crash_before_marking=2))
print(relay(box, broker))
print('published:', [p['id'] for _, p in broker])
print('duplicates:', len(broker) - len({p['id'] for _, p in broker}))

crashed after publishing seq 2
drained
published: ['ord_1', 'ord_2', 'ord_2', 'ord_3']
duplicates: 1

The outbox gives you at-least-once delivery, never exactly-once. The relay published ord_2 and died before recording that it had; on restart it publishes it again. You could try to make the mark atomic with the publish, and you would be back at the dual-write problem you just solved — the two systems have simply changed names. §5.7 made the same point about consensus: the achievable guarantee is at least once, applied idempotently, and §11.8 is where the "applied idempotently" half gets built.

Two properties of the outbox are worth naming because the rest of this section depends on them.

Ordering is per key, and only if you publish in sequence order. The relay above walks rows by seq, so ord_1 and ord_2 — both for customer c_7 — reach the broker in the order they were committed. Run two relay instances for throughput and that guarantee evaporates unless each instance owns a disjoint set of keys. This is the same constraint partitioned queues impose (§10.4), and the same reason a partition key exists at all (§8.3).

The table is a log, so replay is free. Resetting sent to false republishes history, which is how you backfill a consumer that was deployed a month late — and it is a hint at the much larger idea in §11.3.

The alternative to a polling relay is change data capture: read the database's write-ahead log directly, as Debezium does against PostgreSQL's logical replication slots. The WAL already exists (§7.2), so CDC adds no write cost and no polling latency, and it cannot miss a row because it is the durability mechanism. What it costs is operational surface — a connector, a replication slot that will fill your disk if the consumer stalls — and the coupling of §11.1's delta style, since what the log contains is rows. Poll the outbox for integration events between services; use CDC for pipelines into analytics and search.

11.3 Event Sourcing: the Log Is the Database

Ordinary storage keeps current state and throws away how it got there. Event sourcing inverts that: the sequence of events is the source of truth, and current state is a fold over it — derived, disposable, and reconstructible at any time.

def apply(state, event):
    kind, e = event['type'], event
    if kind == 'opened':
        return {'balance': 0, 'held': 0, 'status': 'open'}
    if kind == 'deposited':
        return state | {'balance': state['balance'] + e['cents']}
    if kind == 'held':
        return state | {'held': state['held'] + e['cents']}
    if kind == 'captured':
        return state | {'balance': state['balance'] - e['cents'],
                        'held': state['held'] - e['cents']}
    if kind == 'frozen':
        return state | {'status': 'frozen'}
    raise ValueError(f'unknown event {kind!r}')

def fold(events):
    state = None
    for event in events:
        state = apply(state, event)
    return state

LOG = [
    {'type': 'opened'},
    {'type': 'deposited', 'cents': 10_000},
    {'type': 'held', 'cents': 2_500},
    {'type': 'deposited', 'cents': 4_000},
    {'type': 'captured', 'cents': 2_500},
    {'type': 'frozen'},
]

for n in range(1, len(LOG) + 1):
    s = fold(LOG[:n])
    print(f'after {n} events: balance {s["balance"]:>6}  held {s["held"]:>5}  {s["status"]}')

print('\navailable now       :', fold(LOG)['balance'] - fold(LOG)['held'])
print('available at event 3:', fold(LOG[:3])['balance'] - fold(LOG[:3])['held'])

after 1 events: balance      0  held     0  open
after 2 events: balance  10000  held     0  open
after 3 events: balance  10000  held  2500  open
after 4 events: balance  14000  held  2500  open
after 5 events: balance  11500  held     0  open
after 6 events: balance  11500  held     0  frozen

available now       : 11500
available at event 3: 7500

Four things fall out of this that are genuinely hard to get any other way.

Time travel
fold(LOG[:n]) is the state at any past moment, exactly. Not an approximation reconstructed from an audit table — the real state, because the events are what happened.
A free audit log
The question "why is this balance 11,500?" has a complete answer that cannot drift from reality, because there is no second copy to drift from.
New questions, retroactively
A metric nobody thought of in January can be computed over January's data, because the raw facts were never discarded.
Debugging by replay
A production bug reproduces by folding the real event stream through the fixed code. Nothing else gives you that.

The costs are equally real and are the reason this is a specialist tool rather than a default.

Queries are hard. "All accounts with a balance over 10,000" means folding every account. That is not a tuning problem, it is structural — and §11.5 is the standard answer.

Events are immutable, including the wrong ones. You cannot fix a bad event with an UPDATE; you append a compensating event (corrected, reversed). This is how double-entry bookkeeping has worked for centuries — a mistaken ledger entry is corrected by a reversing entry, never by an erasure — and accountants are right about it, but it surprises people.

The schema is forever. A five-year-old event must still be readable by today's code — §11.9.

Deleting data is genuinely difficult. "Erase this user" against an append-only log conflicts with the GDPR right to erasure. The workable pattern is crypto-shredding: encrypt personal fields with a per-subject key, keep the keys in mutable storage, and delete the key. The events remain, and become undecryptable noise.

Use event sourcing where the history is the product — ledgers, order lifecycles, medical records, anything audited or regulated. Do not use it for a user profile table.

11.4 Snapshots, and the Cost of Replay

Folding is O(n) in the number of events, and n only grows. An account with 200,000 events is a slow read on every request, so event-sourced systems periodically persist the fold and replay only what came after.

def apply(state, event):                      # the fold from §11.3, unchanged
    if event['type'] == 'opened':
        return {'balance': 0, 'held': 0, 'status': 'open'}
    if event['type'] == 'deposited':
        return state | {'balance': state['balance'] + event['cents']}
    raise ValueError(event['type'])

def rebuild(log, snapshots, upto):
    """Return (state, events_read). Start from the newest snapshot at or before `upto`."""
    base, start = None, 0
    for offset in sorted(snapshots):
        if offset <= upto:
            base, start = dict(snapshots[offset]), offset
    state, read = base, 0
    for event in log[start:upto]:
        state = apply(state, event)
        read += 1
    return state, read

log = [{'type': 'opened'}] + [{'type': 'deposited', 'cents': 100}] * 199_998
snapshots = {}
state = None
for i, event in enumerate(log):
    state = apply(state, event)
    if (i + 1) % 1_000 == 0:
        snapshots[i + 1] = dict(state)

cold, cold_read = rebuild(log, {}, len(log))
warm, warm_read = rebuild(log, snapshots, len(log))
print(f'no snapshots : balance {cold["balance"]:,}  events replayed {cold_read:,}')
print(f'every 1,000  : balance {warm["balance"]:,}  events replayed {warm_read:,}')
print('identical    :', cold == warm)
print(f'snapshots stored: {len(snapshots):,}  ({len(snapshots)/len(log):.2%} of the log)')

no snapshots : balance 19,999,800  events replayed 199,999
every 1,000  : balance 19,999,800  events replayed 999
identical    : True
snapshots stored: 199  (0.10% of the log)

Same answer, 199,999 events read versus 999. Three rules keep snapshots from becoming a source of bugs.

A snapshot is a cache, never a truth. Deleting every snapshot must leave the system correct and merely slow. The moment a snapshot holds something not derivable from the log, you have silently stopped being event-sourced.

A snapshot must record the version of the code that produced it. Fix a bug in apply and every existing snapshot is now wrong in exactly the way the bug was. Stamping each snapshot with a fold-logic version, and ignoring snapshots whose version is not current, turns a data-corruption incident into a slow morning.

Snapshot on a count, not a clock. Every thousand events gives a bounded replay cost regardless of how busy an entity is; every hour gives you a 5-event snapshot for a dormant account and a 400,000-event replay for a hot one.

11.5 CQRS: Separating the Write Model from the Read Models

CQRS — Command Query Responsibility Segregation — is the observation that the model you need to validate a change and the model you need to answer a question are rarely the same shape, and that forcing one structure to do both makes it bad at both.

The write side needs whatever enforces invariants: for a bank account, the balance and the holds, nothing more. The read side needs whatever the screens ask for: a monthly statement, a per-customer total, a search index. In an event-sourced system these are built from the same log by different folds, called projections.

from collections import defaultdict

LOG = [
    {'seq': 1, 'account': 'a1', 'type': 'opened',    'customer': 'c_7'},
    {'seq': 2, 'account': 'a1', 'type': 'deposited', 'cents': 10_000, 'day': '2026-03-01'},
    {'seq': 3, 'account': 'a2', 'type': 'opened',    'customer': 'c_7'},
    {'seq': 4, 'account': 'a2', 'type': 'deposited', 'cents':  2_500, 'day': '2026-03-01'},
    {'seq': 5, 'account': 'a1', 'type': 'captured',  'cents':  1_500, 'day': '2026-03-02'},
    {'seq': 6, 'account': 'a1', 'type': 'deposited', 'cents':  4_000, 'day': '2026-03-02'},
]

def balances(log):                       # read model 1: one row per account
    out = defaultdict(int)
    for e in log:
        if e['type'] == 'deposited': out[e['account']] += e['cents']
        if e['type'] == 'captured':  out[e['account']] -= e['cents']
    return dict(out)

def customer_totals(log):                # read model 2: one row per customer
    owner, out = {}, defaultdict(int)
    for e in log:
        if e['type'] == 'opened':    owner[e['account']] = e['customer']
        if e['type'] == 'deposited': out[owner[e['account']]] += e['cents']
        if e['type'] == 'captured':  out[owner[e['account']]] -= e['cents']
    return dict(out)

def daily_volume(log):                   # read model 3: one row per day
    out = defaultdict(int)
    for e in log:
        if e['type'] in ('deposited', 'captured'): out[e['day']] += e['cents']
    return dict(out)

CAUGHT_UP = 4                            # the projector has processed seq 1..4
for name, fn in [('balances', balances), ('customer totals', customer_totals),
                 ('daily volume', daily_volume)]:
    live = fn(LOG)
    lagging = fn([e for e in LOG if e['seq'] <= CAUGHT_UP])
    print(f'{name:<16} live {live}')
    print(f'{"":16} at seq {CAUGHT_UP} {lagging}')

balances         live {'a1': 12500, 'a2': 2500}
                 at seq 4 {'a1': 10000, 'a2': 2500}
customer totals  live {'c_7': 15000}
                 at seq 4 {'c_7': 12500}
daily volume     live {'2026-03-01': 12500, '2026-03-02': 5500}
                 at seq 4 {'2026-03-01': 12500}

Three read models, one log, no joins at query time — each is already the exact shape its screen wants, so the read is a primary-key lookup. They can live in different stores, too: balances in a key-value store, customer totals in the relational database, daily volume in a time-series store (§6).

A projection is eventually consistent with the write model, and this is not a detail you can hide. The at seq 4 rows are what a user would see if they read immediately after writing — a balance missing the two most recent events. Everything §4.6 said about session guarantees applies directly, and there are only three honest responses:

Read your own writes
The command returns the sequence number it wrote; the client sends it with the next read, and the read waits for the projection to reach it or is routed to the write model. Bounded, explicit, and the right default for anything a user just changed.
Show the lag
"Updated 3 seconds ago." Honest, cheap, and perfectly acceptable for dashboards and reports.
Read the write model
For the one screen that genuinely cannot tolerate staleness, query the authoritative side and accept the cost. CQRS does not forbid this; it just makes it a decision.

Projections are rebuildable, and that is their best property. A bug in daily_volume is fixed by deploying the corrected fold, truncating the read model and replaying the log — no migration, no backfill script, no reconciliation against a system of record. This is why a projection must be a pure fold with no side effects: a projector that sends an email cannot be replayed, and you will need to replay it.

Track the offset in the same transaction as the projection's own write. A projector that updates its read model and then records its position can crash between the two and reprocess the last event on restart, which is at-least-once again — fine for out[account] = x, wrong for out[account] += x. Committing both together makes the projector exactly-once with respect to its own store, which is the one place in a distributed system where exactly-once is genuinely achievable.

CQRS does not require event sourcing, and event sourcing does not require CQRS. A perfectly ordinary application can maintain a denormalised read table from the outbox and get most of the benefit. They are paired so often because event sourcing makes queries hard and CQRS makes them easy again.

11.6 Two-Phase Commit, and the Window Where It Stops

The obvious way to make a change span two services is a distributed transaction. Two-phase commit is the classical protocol: a coordinator asks every participant to prepare, and only if all of them vote yes does it tell them to commit.

Phase 1 — prepare
Each participant does the work, writes it durably, takes the locks, and promises it can commit. It may no longer decide on its own; it has given up its autonomy.
Phase 2 — commit
The coordinator durably records the decision, then tells everyone. Any participant that does not hear must ask, and must keep asking.

The promise is real: 2PC gives genuine atomicity across heterogeneous systems, which is why XA exists and why it is still used inside a single data centre between a database and a message broker. The failure mode is equally real.

class Participant:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name, self.state, self.locks = name, 'idle', 0

    def prepare(self):
        self.state, self.locks = 'prepared', 1     # durable, locks HELD
        return 'yes'

    def commit(self):
        self.state, self.locks = 'committed', 0

def two_phase_commit(participants, coordinator_crashes_after_prepare=False):
    votes = [p.prepare() for p in participants]
    if not all(v == 'yes' for v in votes):
        return 'aborted by vote'
    if coordinator_crashes_after_prepare:
        return 'coordinator crashed with the decision unrecorded'
    for p in participants:
        p.commit()
    return 'committed'

for crash in (False, True):
    ps = [Participant(n) for n in ('inventory', 'payments', 'shipping')]
    print(two_phase_commit(ps, crash))
    print('  ', [(p.name, p.state, f'{p.locks} lock') for p in ps])

committed
   [('inventory', 'committed', '0 lock'), ('payments', 'committed', '0 lock'), ('shipping', 'committed', '0 lock')]
coordinator crashed with the decision unrecorded
   [('inventory', 'prepared', '1 lock'), ('payments', 'prepared', '1 lock'), ('shipping', 'prepared', '1 lock')]

Look at the second line: three services are prepared, holding locks, and none of them may decide. They cannot commit — the coordinator might have decided to abort. They cannot abort — it might have decided to commit. They cannot time out and guess, because guessing wrong breaks atomicity, which was the entire point. So they wait, holding row locks that block every unrelated request touching the same rows, until the coordinator comes back. This is 2PC's blocking window, and it is not an implementation defect: it is a theorem. A commit protocol that never blocks on a coordinator failure requires consensus among the participants themselves (§5.4), which is what modern systems like Spanner actually do — running Paxos groups per shard so the "coordinator" is itself a replicated, failure-tolerant thing rather than a single process.

The second problem is arithmetic, and it is the one that decides most architectures:

from math import prod

def transaction_availability(service_availability, participants):
    return prod([service_availability] * participants)

for n in (1, 2, 3, 5, 10):
    a = transaction_availability(0.999, n)
    plural = 'participants' if n > 1 else 'participant '
    print(f'{n:>2} {plural} at 99.9%: {a:.4%}  ->  {(1 - a) * 525_960:>6.1f} min/year down')

 1 participant  at 99.9%: 99.9000%  ->   526.0 min/year down
 2 participants at 99.9%: 99.8001%  ->  1051.4 min/year down
 3 participants at 99.9%: 99.7003%  ->  1576.3 min/year down
 5 participants at 99.9%: 99.5010%  ->  2624.5 min/year down
10 participants at 99.9%: 99.0045%  ->  5236.0 min/year down

Every participant multiplies into the failure probability. A synchronous transaction across five services is less available than any of them, and adding a service to the flow makes every existing flow worse. That is the structural reason microservice architectures abandon distributed transactions rather than tuning them.

Use 2PC when the participants are few, co-located and long-lived — a database and a broker in one data centre, with an XA transaction manager that has genuinely been operated before. Do not use it across service or organisational boundaries, across regions, or anywhere a participant might be down for an hour. For those, the answer is the next subsection.

11.7 Sagas: Trading Atomicity for Availability

A saga is a sequence of local transactions, each of which commits immediately in its own service, plus a compensating action for each one that semantically undoes it. If step four fails, the saga runs the compensations for steps three, two and one, in reverse.

def run_saga(steps, fail_at=None):
    """steps: [(name, do, undo)]. Returns (outcome, trace)."""
    trace, done = [], []
    for name, do, undo in steps:
        if name == fail_at:
            trace.append(f'FAIL   {name}')
            for undo_name, undo_fn in reversed(done):
                trace.append(f'UNDO   {undo_name} -> {undo_fn()}')
            return 'compensated', trace
        trace.append(f'ok     {name} -> {do()}')
        done.append((name, undo))
    return 'completed', trace

STEPS = [
    ('reserve stock', lambda: 'sku_44 x1 held',      lambda: 'stock released'),
    ('charge card',   lambda: 'auth_9f captured',    lambda: 'refund issued'),
    ('book courier',  lambda: 'courier slot booked', lambda: 'slot cancelled'),
    ('send receipt',  lambda: 'receipt emailed',     lambda: 'apology emailed'),
]

for failure in (None, 'book courier'):
    outcome, trace = run_saga(STEPS, fail_at=failure)
    print(f'--- fail_at={failure!r}: {outcome}')
    for line in trace:
        print('   ', line)

--- fail_at=None: completed
    ok     reserve stock -> sku_44 x1 held
    ok     charge card -> auth_9f captured
    ok     book courier -> courier slot booked
    ok     send receipt -> receipt emailed
--- fail_at='book courier': compensated
    ok     reserve stock -> sku_44 x1 held
    ok     charge card -> auth_9f captured
    FAIL   book courier
    UNDO   charge card -> refund issued
    UNDO   reserve stock -> stock released

The trace shows the property that matters and the property that bites. Nothing was ever locked across services — each step committed alone, so charge card was a complete, visible, durable transaction the moment it ran. And the undo of charge card is not a rollback: it is a refund, a new fact appended to history. Money left the customer's account and came back, and both events are on their statement.

A compensating action is semantic, not mechanical, and some things cannot be compensated. The last step above is the honest illustration: an email that has been sent cannot be unsent, and the compensation is an apology. Order the steps so the irreversible ones come last, and where you cannot, replace the irreversible action with a reversible one — hold the money with an authorisation and capture it only when the saga completes, rather than charging at step two.

A saga has no isolation. Between "stock reserved" and "order confirmed" the system is in a state no single transaction would ever expose: stock is gone, no order exists. Another request can see it. The standard countermeasure is a semantic lock — a status field (pending, confirmed, cancelled) that tells every reader this row is mid-saga, so the UI can show "processing" instead of a contradiction. §4.4's warning applies exactly: the anomaly does not disappear because you stopped calling it one.

There are two ways to drive a saga, and choosing wrongly is a common and expensive mistake.

Orchestration
One component holds the workflow, calls each service and knows how to compensate — the code above. The flow is readable in one file, the state is queryable ("where is order 91?"), and testing it is testing one object. The orchestrator becomes a component that must itself be available and whose state must itself be durable, and there is a real risk of it accumulating business logic that belongs in the services.
Choreography
No central component: each service listens for the previous step's event and emits its own. Maximum decoupling, minimum ceremony, and genuinely the right choice for two or three steps. Past that it becomes a system whose behaviour exists in no file — answering "what happens when a payment fails?" means reading every service, and cyclic dependencies appear that nobody designed.

Choreograph two or three steps; orchestrate anything longer, anything with compensations, and anything a support engineer will be asked about. The orchestrator's durable state is the thing that makes "order 91 is stuck at step 3, retrying since 14:02" an answerable question — and it should itself be event-sourced, which is exactly what workflow engines like Temporal provide.

Every step and every compensation must be idempotent and retryable. The orchestrator will crash mid-saga and resume, and it cannot know whether the step it was running took effect. A compensation that fails is worse: there is no compensation for a compensation, so the only options are retry with backoff (§14.4) forever and, ultimately, an alert and a human. Design compensations to be the simplest possible operations for exactly this reason.

11.8 Idempotent Consumers

Everything above delivers at least once. The outbox republishes after a relay crash, the broker redelivers when an ack is lost, the orchestrator retries a step whose response timed out. The consumer is where duplicates are made harmless, and there are two ways to do it.

The first is to make the operation naturally idempotent, which requires no bookkeeping at all:

state = {}

def set_status(order_id, status):          # assignment: idempotent
    state[order_id] = status

def add_points(customer, n):               # accumulation: NOT idempotent
    state[customer] = state.get(customer, 0) + n

for _ in range(3):
    set_status('ord_1', 'shipped')
    add_points('c_7', 50)
print(state)

{'ord_1': 'shipped', 'c_7': 150}

Assignment survives repetition; accumulation does not. Where the domain allows it, send the new value rather than the delta — this is the same rule that makes PUT idempotent and POST not, and it is the cheapest fix available.

Where the operation is genuinely not repeatable — charging a card, incrementing a counter, sending an email — the consumer needs a dedup store: a record of the message ids it has already processed, written in the same transaction as the effect.

class Consumer:
    def __init__(self):
        self.points, self.seen, self.work_done = {}, set(), 0

    def handle(self, message):
        if message['id'] in self.seen:                 # already applied
            return 'duplicate'
        # one transaction: the effect and the receipt commit together
        self.points[message['customer']] = self.points.get(message['customer'], 0) + message['points']
        self.seen.add(message['id'])
        self.work_done += 1
        return 'applied'

STREAM = [
    {'id': 'm1', 'customer': 'c_7', 'points': 50},
    {'id': 'm2', 'customer': 'c_9', 'points': 20},
    {'id': 'm1', 'customer': 'c_7', 'points': 50},     # relay crash replay
    {'id': 'm3', 'customer': 'c_7', 'points': 10},
    {'id': 'm2', 'customer': 'c_9', 'points': 20},     # lost ack, redelivered
    {'id': 'm1', 'customer': 'c_7', 'points': 50},     # and again
]

c = Consumer()
print([c.handle(m) for m in STREAM])
print('deliveries', len(STREAM), '| applied', c.work_done, '| points', c.points)
print('same as no duplicates:', c.points == {'c_7': 60, 'c_9': 20})

['applied', 'applied', 'duplicate', 'applied', 'duplicate', 'duplicate']
deliveries 6 | applied 3 | points {'c_7': 60, 'c_9': 20}
same as no duplicates: True

Six deliveries, three effects, and the result is identical to a perfect broker's. This is what "exactly-once" means in every system that claims it. Kafka's exactly-once semantics, the projector offset in §11.5, and this dedup table are all the same construction: at-least-once delivery plus an atomic dedup record on the consumer's own store. Nothing anywhere removes the duplicate from the network — §5.7 explains why it cannot be done — the duplicate is simply made to have no effect. The accurate name is effectively-once, and knowing the difference matters, because the guarantee holds only within the store the receipt is written to. A consumer that dedups in Redis and then charges a card via Stripe has two systems again, and needs Stripe's idempotency key as well.

Four practical requirements, each of which has caused a real outage somewhere:

The id must be assigned by the producer and stable across redeliveries. A consumer-generated id, a timestamp, or a hash of the payload that includes a retry_count all defeat the mechanism entirely.

The receipt and the effect must commit together. Write the effect, crash, and the redelivery applies it twice; write the receipt first, crash, and the message is lost. Same transaction, same store, or you have re-created the dual-write problem inside the consumer.

The dedup store needs a retention window, and it must exceed the maximum redelivery age. Keeping ids forever is not viable at a million messages a day. Keeping them for an hour is fine until a message sits in a dead-letter queue for a day and is replayed — the classic double-charge, and the argument for a window measured in weeks, or for a natural key (payment for order 91) with no expiry at all.

Duplicates and out-of-order delivery are different problems. Dedup handles repeats; it does nothing about a stale event arriving after a newer one. For that, carry a version or sequence number in the event and drop anything not newer than what the read model already holds — the last-writer-wins rule from §4.7, applied at the consumer.

11.9 Events Are a Contract, and They Live Forever

An event that has been published cannot be recalled, and in an event-sourced system it will still be read in five years. That makes event schemas the longest-lived contracts in the architecture — longer-lived than your API, which at least has a deprecation path.

The rule is the same one that governs any wire format: additive changes are safe, everything else is a new event type. Adding an optional field with a default is invisible to old consumers. Removing a field, renaming one, narrowing a type, or changing what a value means are all breaking, and the last one is the dangerous case because no schema registry will catch it.

Since old events cannot be rewritten, the read path has to cope, and the standard mechanism is an upcaster: a small function per version step that migrates an old event to the next shape, chained on load.

def v1_to_v2(e):
    """v2 added an explicit currency; v1 was implicitly EUR."""
    return e | {'version': 2, 'currency': 'EUR'}

def v2_to_v3(e):
    """v3 renamed `total` (a float of euros) to `total_cents` (an int)."""
    out = e | {'version': 3, 'total_cents': round(e['total'] * 100)}
    del out['total']
    return out

UPCASTERS = {1: v1_to_v2, 2: v2_to_v3}
CURRENT = 3

def load(event):
    while event['version'] < CURRENT:
        event = UPCASTERS[event['version']](event)
    return event

STORED = [
    {'version': 1, 'type': 'order.placed', 'id': 'ord_1', 'total': 42.50},
    {'version': 2, 'type': 'order.placed', 'id': 'ord_2', 'total': 99.00, 'currency': 'GBP'},
    {'version': 3, 'type': 'order.placed', 'id': 'ord_3', 'total_cents': 1250, 'currency': 'EUR'},
]
for stored in STORED:
    print(f'v{stored["version"]} -> {load(dict(stored))}')

v1 -> {'version': 3, 'type': 'order.placed', 'id': 'ord_1', 'currency': 'EUR', 'total_cents': 4250}
v2 -> {'version': 3, 'type': 'order.placed', 'id': 'ord_2', 'currency': 'GBP', 'total_cents': 9900}
v3 -> {'version': 3, 'type': 'order.placed', 'id': 'ord_3', 'total_cents': 1250, 'currency': 'EUR'}

Every event reaching the domain logic is v3, and the domain logic contains no version checks at all — that is the whole point. The alternative, if event.get('version', 1) < 2: scattered through the handlers, is how a codebase becomes unmaintainable one migration at a time.

Three things the upcaster chain demands:

Every event carries its version, from the first one you ever publish. Retrofitting this means guessing, and dict.get('version', 1) is a guess that will eventually be wrong.

Upcasters are pure and are never deleted. v1_to_v2 must still exist when the current version is nine, because a v1 event is still in the log. They are cheap — a few lines each — and deleting one silently breaks the oldest data you have.

An upcaster cannot invent information. v1_to_v2 could supply EUR only because v1 genuinely was euros; if v1 had mixed currencies with no field to say which, no upcaster can recover it, and the honest answer is a new event type consumed alongside the old one until the old one is exhausted. Test upcasters against real archived events, not fixtures written today — a fixture is written by someone who knows the current schema, which is exactly the knowledge the test is supposed to check.

Finally, a message that no version of the consumer can handle must not block the stream. Retry with backoff, then move it to a dead-letter queue (§10.7) with the full context and alert on it. A poison message that halts a partition takes down every well-formed message behind it, which turns one bad payload into an outage.

Exercises

Exercise 11.1 — Choose the pattern. For each requirement, choose between an orchestrated saga, a choreographed saga, two-phase commit, and event sourcing with CQRS. Give the deciding reason and the main cost.

(a) Debiting one account and crediting another inside a single bank's core ledger,
    where regulators require every historical balance to be reproducible.
(b) A signup flow: create the user, provision a workspace, send a welcome email.
(c) An order flow across inventory, payments, fraud, shipping and notifications,
    where support staff must be able to answer "where is my order?".
(d) Writing a row and publishing a message to a broker, both inside one data centre,
    with an existing XA transaction manager the team already operates.
Solution 
ANSWERS = [
    ('(a) ledger', 'event sourcing + CQRS',
     'the audit requirement is the product; a fold gives any past balance exactly',
     'queries need projections, and erasure needs crypto-shredding'),
    ('(b) signup', 'choreographed saga',
     'three steps, no compensation worth writing, teams stay decoupled',
     'the flow exists in no single file — acceptable at three steps'),
    ('(c) orders', 'orchestrated saga',
     'five steps with real compensations, and the state must be queryable',
     'the orchestrator is a component to build, run and keep available'),
    ('(d) row + message', 'outbox — or 2PC if the manager is already run well',
     'one data centre, two long-lived participants, short-held locks',
     '2PC blocks if the coordinator dies; the outbox is simpler and needs no manager'),
]
for label, choice, why, cost in ANSWERS:
    print(f'{label}\n  choose : {choice}\n  because: {why}\n  cost   : {cost}\n')

(a) ledger
  choose : event sourcing + CQRS
  because: the audit requirement is the product; a fold gives any past balance exactly
  cost   : queries need projections, and erasure needs crypto-shredding

(b) signup
  choose : choreographed saga
  because: three steps, no compensation worth writing, teams stay decoupled
  cost   : the flow exists in no single file — acceptable at three steps

(c) orders
  choose : orchestrated saga
  because: five steps with real compensations, and the state must be queryable
  cost   : the orchestrator is a component to build, run and keep available

(d) row + message
  choose : outbox — or 2PC if the manager is already run well
  because: one data centre, two long-lived participants, short-held locks
  cost   : 2PC blocks if the coordinator dies; the outbox is simpler and needs no manager

(a) is the case event sourcing was invented for. "Every historical balance must be reproducible" is not a reporting requirement that a nightly snapshot job can satisfy — it is a statement that the history is the record. Note what it is not: the debit and the credit are inside one ledger, so they are one local transaction, and no distributed protocol is involved at all. The hard part is §11.5's read models and §11.3's erasure problem, not atomicity.

(b) is where choreography is genuinely correct and where teams over-engineer most often. Three steps, and the compensations are trivial or unnecessary — a workspace that failed to provision can be retried, and there is no money to refund. An orchestrator here is a component to build, deploy and monitor in exchange for nothing. The honest caveat: if the flow grows to seven steps, migrate before it becomes unreadable, and expect that to be unpleasant.

(c) is the orchestration case, and the deciding clause is the support requirement. Five services with compensating actions (release stock, refund, cancel the courier slot) is already at the edge of what choreography can express; "where is my order?" settles it, because that question needs a durable record of saga position, which only an orchestrator has. 2PC across five services is disqualified by §11.6's arithmetic before any other consideration — five participants at 99.9% each give 99.50% together, which is about three and a half hours of downtime a month.

(d) is the one place 2PC is still a reasonable answer, and the qualifier matters. Two participants, one data centre, sub-millisecond phases, and an operations team that already runs the transaction manager. The blocking window is real but short and rare. If the team does not already run XA, use the outbox — it achieves the same practical outcome with a table and a loop, at the cost of at-least-once instead of exactly-once, which §11.8 makes harmless anyway.

Exercise 11.2 — Find the four bugs. This consumer processes payment events. Every line is plausible and four of them are wrong. Name each fault, say what a user experiences, and rewrite it.

import uuid

class PaymentConsumer:
    def __init__(self, db, mailer):
        self.db, self.mailer, self.seen = db, mailer, set()

    def handle(self, event):
        key = uuid.uuid4()
        if key in self.seen:
            return
        self.mailer.send(event['customer'], 'Payment received')
        self.db.execute('UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + ? WHERE id = ?',
                        (event['amount'], event['account']))
        self.db.commit()
        self.seen.add(key)
Solution

Fault 1 — the dedup key is generated, not received. uuid.uuid4() is a fresh random value on every call, so key in self.seen is never true and the dedup does nothing whatsoever. Every redelivery is fully reprocessed. The key must come from the producer and be stable across redeliveries (§11.8).

Fault 2 — the effect is not idempotent and the receipt is not atomic with it. balance = balance + ? is accumulation, and self.seen.add(key) happens after commit(). Crash between them — or simply restart the process, since self.seen is in memory — and the balance is credited twice. The receipt must be a row in the same database, written in the same transaction as the update.

Fault 3 — the email is sent before the transaction commits. If the UPDATE fails, the customer has been told about a payment that did not land. Side effects that leave the system must happen after the commit that makes them true, and because a crash can then lose them, they belong in an outbox rather than in the handler.

Fault 4 — the email is not deduplicated even once the dedup works. It is outside the transaction, so it is at-least-once no matter what the database does. A customer with a flapping consumer receives the same "Payment received" mail nine times. The mailer needs its own idempotency key.

The rewrite, with the dedup receipt in the database and the notification in an outbox:

class PaymentConsumer:
    def __init__(self, db):
        self.db = db

    def handle(self, event):
        message_id = event['message_id']          # from the producer, stable on redelivery
        with self.db:                             # ONE transaction
            already = self.db.execute(
                'SELECT 1 FROM processed WHERE consumer = ? AND message_id = ?',
                ('payments', message_id)).fetchone()
            if already:
                return 'duplicate'
            self.db.execute('INSERT INTO processed VALUES (?, ?)', ('payments', message_id))
            self.db.execute('UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + ? WHERE id = ?',
                            (event['amount'], event['account']))
            self.db.execute(
                'INSERT INTO outbox (topic, dedup_key, payload) VALUES (?, ?, ?)',
                ('email.payment_received', f'receipt:{message_id}', event['customer']))
        return 'applied'

Running it against a stream with duplicates, with a real table for the receipts:

import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE processed (consumer TEXT, message_id TEXT, PRIMARY KEY (consumer, message_id));
CREATE TABLE accounts  (id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, balance INTEGER NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE outbox    (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT, topic TEXT,
                        dedup_key TEXT UNIQUE, payload TEXT);
INSERT INTO accounts VALUES ('acc_1', 0);
""")

class PaymentConsumer:
    def __init__(self, db):
        self.db = db

    def handle(self, event):
        message_id = event['message_id']
        with self.db:
            already = self.db.execute(
                'SELECT 1 FROM processed WHERE consumer = ? AND message_id = ?',
                ('payments', message_id)).fetchone()
            if already:
                return 'duplicate'
            self.db.execute('INSERT INTO processed VALUES (?, ?)', ('payments', message_id))
            self.db.execute('UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + ? WHERE id = ?',
                            (event['amount'], event['account']))
            self.db.execute(
                'INSERT INTO outbox (topic, dedup_key, payload) VALUES (?, ?, ?)',
                ('email.payment_received', f'receipt:{message_id}', event['customer']))
        return 'applied'

STREAM = [
    {'message_id': 'p1', 'account': 'acc_1', 'amount': 2500, 'customer': 'c_7'},
    {'message_id': 'p1', 'account': 'acc_1', 'amount': 2500, 'customer': 'c_7'},
    {'message_id': 'p2', 'account': 'acc_1', 'amount': 1000, 'customer': 'c_7'},
    {'message_id': 'p1', 'account': 'acc_1', 'amount': 2500, 'customer': 'c_7'},
]

consumer = PaymentConsumer(db)
print([consumer.handle(e) for e in STREAM])
print('balance:', db.execute('SELECT balance FROM accounts').fetchone()[0])
print('emails queued:', db.execute('SELECT count(*) FROM outbox').fetchone()[0])

['applied', 'duplicate', 'applied', 'duplicate']
balance: 3500
emails queued: 2

Four deliveries, two effects, one email per real payment. The UNIQUE constraint on dedup_key is the second line of defence: even if the receipt logic were bypassed, the duplicate notification could not be enqueued twice.

Exercise 11.3 — Build a saga with a failing compensation. Write an orchestrator that runs a three-step booking saga (hold seat, charge card, issue ticket), resumes correctly after a crash, and handles the case where a compensation itself fails. Show it recovering from a crash in the middle of step 2, and show what happens when the refund fails twice before succeeding.

Solution

Two requirements drive the design. Resuming after a crash means the orchestrator's position must be durable and every step must be idempotent, because a step that was running when the process died may or may not have taken effect. A failing compensation has no compensation of its own, so the only available strategy is retry with a bounded budget, then escalate to a human — and the saga must stay durably marked as unresolved until that happens.

class Services:
    """Idempotent by construction: every operation is keyed on the booking id."""
    def __init__(self, refund_failures=0):
        self.seats, self.charges, self.tickets = {}, {}, {}
        self.refund_failures = refund_failures
        self.calls = []

    def hold_seat(self, booking, seat):
        self.calls.append('hold_seat')
        self.seats[booking] = seat                      # assignment, not append
        return f'seat {seat} held'

    def release_seat(self, booking):
        self.calls.append('release_seat')
        self.seats.pop(booking, None)
        return 'seat released'

    def charge(self, booking, cents):
        self.calls.append('charge')
        self.charges.setdefault(booking, cents)         # idempotency key = booking
        return f'{self.charges[booking]} charged'

    def refund(self, booking):
        self.calls.append('refund')
        if self.refund_failures > 0:
            self.refund_failures -= 1
            raise RuntimeError('payment gateway timeout')
        self.charges.pop(booking, None)
        return 'refunded'

    def issue_ticket(self, booking):
        self.calls.append('issue_ticket')
        raise RuntimeError('ticketing system rejected the booking')


class Orchestrator:
    """`state` stands in for a durable row: everything here would be committed."""
    def __init__(self, services, max_compensation_attempts=3):
        self.svc, self.max_attempts = services, max_compensation_attempts

    def plan(self, booking, seat, cents):
        return [
            ('hold_seat', lambda: self.svc.hold_seat(booking, seat),
                          lambda: self.svc.release_seat(booking)),
            ('charge',    lambda: self.svc.charge(booking, cents),
                          lambda: self.svc.refund(booking)),
            ('issue',     lambda: self.svc.issue_ticket(booking), None),
        ]

    def run(self, state, steps, crash_at=None, log=None):
        log = log if log is not None else []
        for index in range(state['position'], len(steps)):
            name, do, _ = steps[index]
            if name == crash_at:
                log.append(f'CRASH during {name} (position {state["position"]} is durable)')
                return 'crashed', state, log
            try:
                log.append(f'ok    {name}: {do()}')
            except RuntimeError as exc:
                log.append(f'FAIL  {name}: {exc}')
                state['status'] = 'compensating'
                return self.compensate(state, steps, index, log)
            state['position'] = index + 1               # committed with the step's effect
        state['status'] = 'completed'
        return 'completed', state, log

    def compensate(self, state, steps, failed_at, log):
        for index in range(failed_at - 1, -1, -1):
            name, _, undo = steps[index]
            if undo is None:
                continue
            for attempt in range(1, self.max_attempts + 1):
                try:
                    log.append(f'undo  {name}: {undo()} (attempt {attempt})')
                    break
                except RuntimeError as exc:
                    log.append(f'RETRY {name}: {exc} (attempt {attempt})')
            else:
                state['status'] = 'needs_operator'
                log.append(f'ESCALATE {name}: {self.max_attempts} attempts exhausted')
                return 'needs_operator', state, log
        state['status'] = 'compensated'
        return 'compensated', state, log


print('=== crash during step 2, then resume ===')
svc = Services()
orch = Orchestrator(svc)
steps = orch.plan('bk_1', '14C', 8_900)
state = {'position': 0, 'status': 'running'}

outcome, state, log = orch.run(state, steps, crash_at='charge')
for line in log:
    print('  ', line)
print('   durable state after crash:', state)

log = []
outcome, state, log = orch.run(state, steps, log=log)     # restart, same durable state
for line in log:
    print('  ', line)
print('   outcome:', outcome, '| seats:', svc.seats, '| charges:', svc.charges)
print('   hold_seat called', svc.calls.count('hold_seat'), 'time(s) — not repeated')

print('\n=== the refund fails twice before succeeding ===')
svc2 = Services(refund_failures=2)
orch2 = Orchestrator(svc2)
outcome, state2, log2 = orch2.run({'position': 0, 'status': 'running'},
                                  orch2.plan('bk_2', '3A', 12_500))
for line in log2:
    print('  ', line)
print('   outcome:', outcome, '| charges left:', svc2.charges)

print('\n=== the refund never succeeds ===')
svc3 = Services(refund_failures=99)
orch3 = Orchestrator(svc3)
outcome, state3, log3 = orch3.run({'position': 0, 'status': 'running'},
                                  orch3.plan('bk_3', '9F', 4_000))
for line in log3:
    print('  ', line)
print('   outcome:', outcome, '| durable status:', state3['status'])
print('   charge still outstanding:', svc3.charges)

=== crash during step 2, then resume ===
   ok    hold_seat: seat 14C held
   CRASH during charge (position 1 is durable)
   durable state after crash: {'position': 1, 'status': 'running'}
   ok    charge: 8900 charged
   FAIL  issue: ticketing system rejected the booking
   undo  charge: refunded (attempt 1)
   undo  hold_seat: seat released (attempt 1)
   outcome: compensated | seats: {} | charges: {}
   hold_seat called 1 time(s) — not repeated

=== the refund fails twice before succeeding ===
   ok    hold_seat: seat 3A held
   ok    charge: 12500 charged
   FAIL  issue: ticketing system rejected the booking
   RETRY charge: payment gateway timeout (attempt 1)
   RETRY charge: payment gateway timeout (attempt 2)
   undo  charge: refunded (attempt 3)
   undo  hold_seat: seat released (attempt 1)
   outcome: compensated | charges left: {}

=== the refund never succeeds ===
   ok    hold_seat: seat 9F held
   ok    charge: 4000 charged
   FAIL  issue: ticketing system rejected the booking
   RETRY charge: payment gateway timeout (attempt 1)
   RETRY charge: payment gateway timeout (attempt 2)
   RETRY charge: payment gateway timeout (attempt 3)
   ESCALATE charge: 3 attempts exhausted
   outcome: needs_operator | durable status: needs_operator
   charge still outstanding: {'bk_3': 4000}

Four design decisions are doing the work here.

position advances only after the step's effect is durable, and in a real system both would be in one transaction — the same rule §11.5 gives projectors. That is what makes the resume correct: the restart re-runs charge rather than skipping it, and re-running is safe because charge is keyed on the booking id.

Every service operation is idempotent by construction, not by a dedup table. hold_seat assigns, charge uses setdefault with the booking as the key, release_seat uses pop(..., None). This is §11.8's first strategy, and it is available here because the orchestrator has a natural idempotency key — the booking id — for every call. Where it is available, prefer it: there is no receipt store to size or expire.

Compensations run in reverse and skip steps that have none. The failing step (issue) needs no undo — it did not take effect — and the loop starts from failed_at - 1 for exactly that reason.

An exhausted compensation leaves the saga durably needs_operator. The third run is the important one: the money is still charged, and the system says so rather than reporting success or silently dropping the saga. That row is what an alert fires on and what a support engineer queries. A saga that cannot compensate is not a bug to be coded around; it is an incident, and the design's job is to make it visible.

One thing deliberately left out: the retry loop has no delay. A real one uses exponential backoff with jitter (§14.4) — retrying a gateway timeout three times in three microseconds tests nothing and hits a rate limit.

SECTION 12

Service Architecture

Every section so far has been about a mechanism — how to replicate, partition, cache, queue or retry. This one is about a decision that comes before all of them: where the boundaries between components go. It is the most consequential choice in a system's design and the least reversible, because a boundary in the wrong place makes every subsequent decision harder and moving one means moving data, teams and deployments at the same time. It is also the choice most often made for the wrong reasons.

12.1 The Question Is Not "Microservices or Not"

Ask it that way and the answer will be a preference. Ask what boundaries buy and what they cost, and it becomes a decision with an answer.

A boundary between two components gives you exactly three things, and each has a price attached.

Independent deployment
Ship one part without the rest. Costs: every call across the boundary is now a network call that can fail, be slow, or be duplicated — §14's entire subject.
Independent scaling
Give the CPU-heavy part different hardware from the memory-heavy part. Costs: two things to provision, monitor and keep available.
Independent failure
One part can be down while the others serve. Costs: only if you build it — a boundary with a synchronous required call across it makes availability worse, not better (§14.1).

And it takes away one thing that is difficult to get back: a transaction cannot span it. Everything inside one database is BEGIN … COMMIT; everything across a boundary is a saga, a compensating action or an eventual-consistency argument (§11.7). That single loss accounts for most of the accidental complexity in distributed systems.

The arithmetic of a change is the clearest way to see the trade:

def change_cost(services_touched, deploys_needed, coordination_hours_per_extra_deploy=2):
    return {
        'code changes': services_touched,
        'deploys': deploys_needed,
        'must be ordered': deploys_needed > 1,
        'coordination hours': (deploys_needed - 1) * coordination_hours_per_extra_deploy,
    }

SCENARIOS = [
    ('add a field, one service owns it',        1, 1),
    ('add a field the UI and API both read',    2, 2),
    ('a change spanning 5 services',            5, 5),
]
for name, services, deploys in SCENARIOS:
    result = change_cost(services, deploys)
    print(f'{name:<40}' + '  '.join(f'{k}: {v}' for k, v in result.items()))
