add a field, one service owns it        code changes: 1  deploys: 1  must be ordered: False  coordination hours: 0
add a field the UI and API both read    code changes: 2  deploys: 2  must be ordered: True  coordination hours: 2
a change spanning 5 services            code changes: 5  deploys: 5  must be ordered: True  coordination hours: 8

A feature that requires five coordinated deploys is not a feature, it is a project. And this number — how many services a typical change touches — is the single best measure of whether your boundaries are in the right place. If most changes touch one service, the boundaries match the domain. If most changes touch four, they do not, and no amount of tooling will fix it.

12.2 Bounded Contexts: Where the Seams Actually Are

The reliable way to find a boundary is to look for where the language changes. A bounded context is a region within which a term has one unambiguous meaning — and the discovery that the same word means different things to different parts of the business is the discovery of a seam.

MEANINGS = {
    'Sales':     ('a prospect with a budget', ['company', 'contact', 'deal size', 'stage']),
    'Billing':   ('a legal entity with a payment method', ['tax id', 'invoice address', 'terms']),
    'Support':   ('a person who can raise a ticket', ['email', 'entitlement', 'timezone']),
    'Analytics': ('a row in a fact table', ['cohort', 'first seen', 'lifetime value']),
}
print('The word "customer" in four contexts:\n')
for context, (meaning, fields) in MEANINGS.items():
    print(f'{context:<11}{meaning}')
    print(f'{"":11}fields: {", ".join(fields)}')

shared = set.intersection(*(set(fields) for _, fields in MEANINGS.values()))
print(f'\nfields shared by all four: {shared or "{}"}')
print('-> there is no single "customer" table that serves all four well')

The word "customer" in four contexts:

Sales      a prospect with a budget
           fields: company, contact, deal size, stage
Billing    a legal entity with a payment method
           fields: tax id, invoice address, terms
Support    a person who can raise a ticket
           fields: email, entitlement, timezone
Analytics  a row in a fact table
           fields: cohort, first seen, lifetime value

fields shared by all four: {}
-> there is no single "customer" table that serves all four well

Four contexts, one word, and not a single field in common. The unified customer model that tries to serve all four ends up with sixty nullable columns, four sets of validation rules that contradict each other, and a table every team is afraid to change. Splitting along the language boundary gives each context the model it actually needs, joined only by a shared identifier.

Three techniques find these seams in practice, in rough order of how much they cost to run:

Follow the language. Where a word changes meaning, or where one team says "customer" and another says "account" for the same thing, there is a boundary. This is free and works surprisingly well.

Follow the change history. Files that always change together belong together, and a module that changes for four unrelated reasons is four modules. git log answers this directly, and it is evidence rather than opinion.

Follow the data ownership. Exactly one context should be able to write a given piece of data. Two services writing the same table is not a boundary — it is a shared database with extra steps, and it is the most common way a "microservice" architecture ends up worse than the monolith it replaced.

And the anti-patterns are just as identifiable. Splitting by technical layer — a "database service", an "API service", a "business logic service" — produces boundaries that every single feature must cross, which is the worst possible arrangement. Splitting by entity — a service per table — produces the same problem at finer grain, because real operations touch several entities at once. Split by capability: "placing an order", "arranging delivery", "collecting payment". Each owns its data and its rules, and most changes fit inside one.

12.3 Monolith, Modular Monolith, Microservices

These are three points on one axis, and the middle one is missing from most arguments.

Monolith
One deployable, one database, in-process calls. Transactions work. Refactoring across boundaries is a compiler-checked rename. One deploy pipeline, one place to look during an incident. Scales as one unit, and internal boundaries erode unless something enforces them.
Modular monolith
One deployable, enforced internal modules, each owning its own schema and reachable only through a declared interface. Keeps transactions and gets most of the boundary discipline. The boundaries are cheap to move because they are still compile-time. Needs real enforcement — a build rule, not a convention.
Microservices
Many deployables, each with its own data, communicating over the network. Independent deploys, scaling and failure domains, and the ability for teams to work without coordinating. Every in-process call becomes a distributed systems problem, and the operational surface multiplies.

The cost of the third option is usually underestimated because it is spread across things that do not look like costs:

def operational_surface(services, per_service):
    return {name: services * count for name, count in per_service.items()}

PER_SERVICE = {'deploy pipelines': 1, 'dashboards': 1, 'on-call runbooks': 1,
               'sets of alerts': 1, 'databases': 1, 'dependency upgrades/yr': 12}

for services in (1, 8, 40):
    surface = operational_surface(services, PER_SERVICE)
    print(f'{services:>3} service(s): ' + '  '.join(f'{k} {v}' for k, v in surface.items()))

def call_paths(services):
    return services * (services - 1) // 2         # potential pairwise interactions

print()
for services in (1, 4, 8, 40):
    label = 'service ' if services == 1 else 'services'
    print(f'{services:>3} {label} -> up to {call_paths(services):>4,} pairwise call paths')

  1 service(s): deploy pipelines 1  dashboards 1  on-call runbooks 1  sets of alerts 1  databases 1  dependency upgrades/yr 12
  8 service(s): deploy pipelines 8  dashboards 8  on-call runbooks 8  sets of alerts 8  databases 8  dependency upgrades/yr 96
 40 service(s): deploy pipelines 40  dashboards 40  on-call runbooks 40  sets of alerts 40  databases 40  dependency upgrades/yr 480

  1 service  -> up to    0 pairwise call paths
  4 services -> up to    6 pairwise call paths
  8 services -> up to   28 pairwise call paths
 40 services -> up to  780 pairwise call paths

Forty services is 480 pipelines, dashboards, runbooks and alert sets, and up to 780 possible call paths. None of that is visible in the design document, all of it is real, and most of it needs a platform team to make tolerable — which is the honest prerequisite that goes unstated. Microservices are an organisational solution with a technical cost. They pay off when independent teams need to deploy without coordinating; they do not pay off because a system is "complex".

Start with the modular monolith, and mean it. Enforce the module boundaries with something mechanical — a dependency rule in the build, a schema-per-module convention, an architecture test that fails the build on a cross-module import. Then, when a module genuinely needs its own deploy cadence or its own scaling profile, extracting it is mostly a matter of replacing an in-process call with a network one, because the boundary already exists and has been tested by daily use. A boundary you have lived with for a year is one you can trust; one you drew in a design meeting is a guess.

12.4 Coupling, and the Four Kinds Worth Naming

"Loosely coupled" is used as a synonym for "good", which makes it useless. There are several distinct kinds of coupling, they have different cures, and a design can be excellent on one and disastrous on another.

Temporal
A must be up for B to work. Created by every synchronous call. Cured by asynchrony (§10) — a queued message decouples in time completely.
Data / schema
B depends on A's internal shape. Created by a shared database or a leaked table structure. Cured by a published contract that is deliberately narrower than the internal model (§11.9).
Deployment
A and B must ship together. Created by a breaking change with no compatibility window. Cured by versioning and expand/contract (§6.10) — the same discipline, applied to an API.
Behavioural
B depends on how A works, not just its interface — an ordering, a timing, an implicit side effect. The hardest kind, because it is invisible in every artefact. Cured only by making the assumption explicit in the contract and testing it.
def assess(design):
    return {k: design[k] for k in ('temporal', 'data', 'deployment', 'behavioural')}

DESIGNS = {
    'shared database':        dict(temporal='low',  data='EXTREME', deployment='high', behavioural='high'),
    'synchronous REST':       dict(temporal='HIGH', data='medium',  deployment='medium', behavioural='medium'),
    'REST + circuit breaker': dict(temporal='medium', data='medium', deployment='medium', behavioural='medium'),
    'events on a log':        dict(temporal='low',  data='medium',  deployment='low',   behavioural='low'),
}
print(f'{"design":<26}{"temporal":>10}{"data":>9}{"deployment":>13}{"behavioural":>14}')
for name, design in DESIGNS.items():
    print(f'{name:<26}' + ''.join(f'{v:>{w}}' for v, w in
                                  zip(assess(design).values(), (10, 9, 13, 14))))

design                      temporal     data   deployment   behavioural
shared database                  low  EXTREME         high          high
synchronous REST                HIGH   medium       medium        medium
REST + circuit breaker        medium   medium       medium        medium
events on a log                  low   medium          low           low

A shared database is the worst of these and the most common. Two services reading and writing the same tables are coupled on schema absolutely: neither can change a column without checking the other, neither can choose a different store, and a migration must be coordinated across both. It looks loosely coupled on the architecture diagram because there is no arrow between the services — the arrow goes through the database, and it is the tightest one in the system.

The rule that prevents it is one line and is worth enforcing mechanically: one service owns each table, and everyone else asks that service. Read replicas for reporting are fine; a second service writing your tables is not a boundary at all.

Events on a log score best on every axis, which is why §11 spends so long on them — and it is not free. Their cost is not coupling but consistency: the consumer is eventually consistent by construction, and everything §4.6 says about session guarantees becomes the caller's problem.

12.5 The Distributed Monolith

The failure mode worth being able to recognise by name: services split at the wrong boundaries, so they must all deploy together and all be up together. Every cost of microservices, no benefit of either option.

def diagnose(signals):
    score = sum(signals.values())
    verdict = ('DISTRIBUTED MONOLITH' if score >= 4 else
               'boundaries need work' if score >= 2 else 'healthy')
    return score, verdict

SYSTEMS = {
    'system A': dict(shared_database=1, deploys_must_be_ordered=1, a_change_touches_many=1,
                     one_service_down_takes_all_down=1, cannot_test_alone=1, chatty_sync_calls=1),
    'system B': dict(shared_database=0, deploys_must_be_ordered=1, a_change_touches_many=1,
                     one_service_down_takes_all_down=0, cannot_test_alone=0, chatty_sync_calls=1),
    'system C': dict(shared_database=0, deploys_must_be_ordered=0, a_change_touches_many=0,
                     one_service_down_takes_all_down=0, cannot_test_alone=0, chatty_sync_calls=0),
}
for name, signals in SYSTEMS.items():
    score, verdict = diagnose(signals)
    present = [k for k, v in signals.items() if v]
    print(f'{name}: {score}/6 -> {verdict}')
    print(f'{"":10}{present or "none"}')

system A: 6/6 -> DISTRIBUTED MONOLITH
          ['shared_database', 'deploys_must_be_ordered', 'a_change_touches_many', 'one_service_down_takes_all_down', 'cannot_test_alone', 'chatty_sync_calls']
system B: 3/6 -> boundaries need work
          ['deploys_must_be_ordered', 'a_change_touches_many', 'chatty_sync_calls']
system C: 0/6 -> healthy
          none

Each of those six signals is individually diagnostic, and the first two are close to conclusive on their own.

A shared database means the boundary is decorative (§12.4).

Deploys that must be ordered mean the services are one deployable wearing several process names — and the cure is a compatibility window on every change, not better release tooling.

Chatty synchronous calls are the one that turns a design problem into a latency problem, and the arithmetic is unforgiving:

def chain_latency(hops, per_hop_ms, in_process_us=2):
    return hops * per_hop_ms, hops * in_process_us / 1000

for hops in (1, 5, 12, 30):
    network, in_process = chain_latency(hops, per_hop_ms=8)
    print(f'{hops:>3} calls: {network:>5,} ms over the network vs '
          f'{in_process:>6.3f} ms in process  ({network / in_process:>9,.0f}x)')

  1 calls:     8 ms over the network vs  0.002 ms in process  (    4,000x)
  5 calls:    40 ms over the network vs  0.010 ms in process  (    4,000x)
 12 calls:    96 ms over the network vs  0.024 ms in process  (    4,000x)
 30 calls:   240 ms over the network vs  0.060 ms in process  (    4,000x)

An in-process function call is roughly four thousand times cheaper than a network one, so a loop that made 30 calls without anyone noticing becomes 240 milliseconds when it crosses a boundary — and that is the happy path, before §14's timeouts, retries and availability multiplication apply. When a request fans out across many services synchronously, the boundary is in the wrong place: those calls were one operation, and they should be inside one component.

The way out is to merge, not to add tooling. A distributed monolith is usually treated as an operations problem and given a service mesh, better tracing and a release train. Those help you observe it. Recombining the services that always change together, and then re-splitting along a seam found from the change history (§12.2), is what actually fixes it — and it is a normal, respectable move rather than an admission of failure.

12.6 The API Gateway

Once there are several services, something has to face the client, and it should not be the services themselves. An API gateway is one entry point that handles what every service would otherwise implement separately.

CROSS_CUTTING = ['TLS termination', 'authentication', 'rate limiting', 'request logging',
                 'CORS', 'request size limits', 'compression', 'routing']

def implementations(services, at_gateway):
    return len(CROSS_CUTTING) if at_gateway else len(CROSS_CUTTING) * services

for services in (3, 12, 40):
    print(f'{services:>3} services: {implementations(services, False):>4} implementations '
          f'without a gateway, {implementations(services, True):>3} with one')
print(f'\nconcerns handled once: {", ".join(CROSS_CUTTING)}')

  3 services:   24 implementations without a gateway,   8 with one
 12 services:   96 implementations without a gateway,   8 with one
 40 services:  320 implementations without a gateway,   8 with one

concerns handled once: TLS termination, authentication, rate limiting, request logging, CORS, request size limits, compression, routing

Forty services each doing their own authentication is forty chances to do it differently and one of them wrongly — and the security concerns in particular should exist in exactly one place, reviewed once.

The gateway also solves a client-side problem that is easy to underestimate. A mobile screen assembled from six services means six round trips over a high-latency link, six connections, and six chances of partial failure that the client must handle:

def client_cost(calls, rtt_ms, concurrent=False):
    latency = rtt_ms if concurrent else calls * rtt_ms
    return latency, calls, 1 - 0.999 ** calls

for label, calls in [('direct to 6 services', 6), ('one call to a gateway', 1)]:
    latency, requests, failure = client_cost(calls, rtt_ms=180)
    print(f'{label:<24}{latency:>6,} ms  {requests} request(s)  '
          f'{failure:.2%} chance at least one fails')

direct to 6 services     1,080 ms  6 request(s)  0.60% chance at least one fails
one call to a gateway      180 ms  1 request(s)  0.10% chance at least one fails

Two warnings, because the gateway is also a well-known way to make things worse.

It is a single point of failure and sits on every request path. It needs the same treatment as any other tier — replication, health checks, capacity headroom and a deliberate answer to what happens when it is degraded.

It must not accumulate business logic. A gateway that starts routing, then transforms a payload, then applies a discount rule, then knows about order states has become the monolith you split up, with the added property that every team now needs a change in it. Keep it to cross-cutting concerns, and put the assembly logic in a backend for frontend — a small service per client type that composes calls and owns the shaping — which is a service you can own, test and deploy like any other.

12.7 Service Discovery

Services move. They autoscale, get rescheduled, roll during a deploy, and fail. Hard-coded addresses stop working within a day of the first autoscale event, so something must answer "where is the order service right now?".

class Registry:
    """Instances register, heartbeat, and are evicted when they stop. `now` is injected."""
    def __init__(self, ttl=30):
        self.instances, self.ttl = {}, ttl

    def register(self, service, address, now):
        self.instances[(service, address)] = now

    def heartbeat(self, service, address, now):
        if (service, address) in self.instances:
            self.instances[(service, address)] = now

    def healthy(self, service, now):
        return sorted(address for (name, address), seen in self.instances.items()
                      if name == service and now - seen < self.ttl)

registry = Registry()
for address in ('10.0.0.1', '10.0.0.2', '10.0.0.3'):
    registry.register('orders', address, now=0)
print('t=0   healthy:', registry.healthy('orders', now=0))

for now in (10, 20):                                  # .3 stops heartbeating after t=0
    for address in ('10.0.0.1', '10.0.0.2'):
        registry.heartbeat('orders', address, now)
print('t=20  healthy:', registry.healthy('orders', now=20))
print('t=35  healthy:', registry.healthy('orders', now=35), '- .3 aged out after its TTL')

registry.register('orders', '10.0.0.4', now=36)       # a new instance scales up
print('t=36  healthy:', registry.healthy('orders', now=36))

t=0   healthy: ['10.0.0.1', '10.0.0.2', '10.0.0.3']
t=20  healthy: ['10.0.0.1', '10.0.0.2', '10.0.0.3']
t=35  healthy: ['10.0.0.1', '10.0.0.2'] - .3 aged out after its TTL
t=36  healthy: ['10.0.0.1', '10.0.0.2', '10.0.0.4']

Notice that 10.0.0.3 was still being returned at t=20, twenty seconds after it stopped heartbeating — it only aged out at t=30, when its TTL expired. That gap — between an instance failing and the registry noticing — is unavoidable and is the reason a caller must handle a dead address regardless of how good discovery is: retry the next instance (§14.3), and let the circuit breaker (§14.5) stop calling one that keeps failing. Discovery reduces the window; it does not close it.

There are two places the lookup can happen, and the choice matters more than the product choice:

Client-side
The caller fetches the instance list and picks one itself. No extra hop, and the client can do smart balancing — least-connections, latency-aware, zone-preferring. Costs a discovery library in every language you use, which is the reason most teams eventually leave it.
Server-side
The caller sends to a stable address — a load balancer or a DNS name — and something else resolves it. Language-agnostic, one place to change policy, and the standard: Kubernetes Services are exactly this. Costs an extra hop and a component on the request path.

DNS is the discovery mechanism you already have, and its trap is caching. A record's TTL is a lower bound, not a promise: JVMs have historically cached DNS forever by default, connection pools hold sockets to an address that was resolved once at startup, and an intermediate resolver may ignore your TTL entirely. A deploy that moves an address and relies on DNS to propagate it can therefore route traffic to a machine that no longer exists for far longer than the TTL suggests. Networking and HTTP covers the resolution path in its DNS section; the design consequence here is that DNS is fine for coarse, slow-changing routing and bad for anything that changes in seconds.

12.8 The Service Mesh

At forty services, every one needs mTLS, retries with jitter, circuit breaking, timeouts, load balancing and distributed tracing. Implementing that in each service, in each language, and keeping it consistent is not achievable. A service mesh moves it into a proxy deployed beside every instance — a sidecar — so the behaviour is configured centrally and the application code contains none of it.

def mesh_tradeoff(services, languages, hops_per_request, sidecar_latency_ms=0.6,
                  sidecar_memory_mb=60, instances_per_service=6):
    return {
        'library implementations avoided': services * languages,
        'added latency per request': f'{hops_per_request * 2 * sidecar_latency_ms:.1f} ms',
        'sidecar instances': services * instances_per_service,
        'extra memory': f'{services * instances_per_service * sidecar_memory_mb / 1024:.1f} GB',
    }

for services, languages in [(6, 1), (40, 4)]:
    print(f'{services} services, {languages} language(s):')
    for key, value in mesh_tradeoff(services, languages, hops_per_request=4).items():
        print(f'   {key:<34} {value}')

6 services, 1 language(s):
   library implementations avoided    6
   added latency per request          4.8 ms
   sidecar instances                  36
   extra memory                       2.1 GB
40 services, 4 language(s):
   library implementations avoided    160
   added latency per request          4.8 ms
   sidecar instances                  240
   extra memory                       14.1 GB

Read both rows before deciding. At forty services in four languages, a mesh replaces 160 library implementations — that is the case where it is clearly correct. At six services in one language, it replaces six, and costs 4.8 milliseconds per request, 36 extra processes and 2 GB of memory to do it. A library is the right answer at small scale, and a mesh becomes right when the number of language-and-service combinations makes a library impossible to keep consistent.

What a mesh gives you, stated precisely so the trade is legible:

mTLS everywhere
Encrypted, mutually authenticated service-to-service traffic with certificate rotation handled for you. Genuinely hard to do well by hand, and the strongest single argument for a mesh.
Uniform resilience
Timeouts, retries with jitter, circuit breaking and outlier ejection (§14), configured once and applied identically to every service regardless of language.
Traffic control
Canary releases by percentage, mirroring production traffic to a new version, and fault injection for testing — all without redeploying anything.
Observability
Consistent metrics and trace propagation for every call, without instrumenting each service. The most immediately useful benefit and the one teams notice first.

And the honest costs: latency on every hop, a control plane that is now critical infrastructure, a substantial increase in what can go wrong — a misconfigured mesh policy can break every service at once — and a debugging surface that now includes the proxy, which means every incident has one more layer to rule out. Adopt it when the number of services makes the alternative unmanageable, not before, and remember that the retry and circuit-breaker configuration a mesh applies is the same design work from §14; the mesh moves where it lives, and does not decide it for you.

12.9 Getting There: the Strangler Fig

Nobody designs the right boundaries first. The realistic path is extracting a service from a system that already works, and the pattern that does it without a rewrite is the strangler fig: put a facade in front, route one capability at a time to the new service, and let the old system shrink.

class Strangler:
    """A routing facade. Each capability moves independently and can move back."""
    def __init__(self, capabilities):
        self.routes = {name: 'monolith' for name in capabilities}
        self.calls = {'monolith': 0, 'service': 0}

    def route(self, capability):
        target = self.routes[capability]
        self.calls[target] += 1
        return target

    def migrate(self, capability, target):
        self.routes[capability] = target          # one routing change, no deploy
        return f'{capability} -> {target}'

CAPABILITIES = ['browse', 'cart', 'checkout', 'invoicing', 'shipping']
facade = Strangler(CAPABILITIES)

print('step 0:', {c: facade.routes[c] for c in CAPABILITIES})
for step, capability in enumerate(['invoicing', 'shipping', 'cart'], start=1):
    facade.migrate(capability, 'service')
    remaining = [c for c in CAPABILITIES if facade.routes[c] == 'monolith']
    print(f'step {step}: moved {capability:<10} still in the monolith: {remaining}')

for capability in CAPABILITIES:
    facade.route(capability)
print('\nrouting after 3 extractions:', facade.calls)
print('rollback is one routing change:', facade.migrate('cart', 'monolith'))

step 0: {'browse': 'monolith', 'cart': 'monolith', 'checkout': 'monolith', 'invoicing': 'monolith', 'shipping': 'monolith'}
step 1: moved invoicing  still in the monolith: ['browse', 'cart', 'checkout', 'shipping']
step 2: moved shipping   still in the monolith: ['browse', 'cart', 'checkout']
step 3: moved cart       still in the monolith: ['browse', 'checkout']

routing after 3 extractions: {'monolith': 2, 'service': 3}
rollback is one routing change: cart -> monolith

The last line is the entire reason to work this way. Every step is independently reversible by a routing change, with no code deploy and no data migration to undo — which means an extraction that turns out to be wrong costs an afternoon rather than a quarter.

Five rules that make it work in practice:

Extract the leaves first. invoicing and shipping are downstream of everything and depended on by little, so they have the fewest inbound calls to redirect. Extracting checkout first — the thing everything touches — is how a migration stalls in a half-finished state.

Move the data with the capability, not before or after. A service extracted while still reading the monolith's tables is §12.4's shared database, and you have added a network hop to a design that got no better.

Run both and compare before switching. Send the request to both implementations, serve the old answer, and log the differences. This catches behavioural coupling (§12.4) that no contract test would — the undocumented ordering, the rounding rule, the special case for one customer that has been there for six years.

Keep the facade dumb. The moment it holds business logic it becomes a component that must change for every feature, and the migration now has a permanent extra step in it.

Finish. A strangler migration abandoned halfway is the worst of all states: two systems, two deploy pipelines and a facade nobody dares remove. Either complete the extraction or route the capability back and delete the service — both are fine, and the half-finished state is not.

12.10 Trust Boundaries Between Services

Splitting a system creates a question a monolith never had to answer: when service B receives a call claiming to be from service A on behalf of user U, what makes any of that true? An in-process call was trusted because it could not be forged. A network call can be.

The naive answer — the network is private, so calls on it are trusted — is the flat trust model, and it fails in a specific and well-documented way:

def blast_radius(model, services, compromised=1):
    if model == 'flat / network trust':
        return services, 'one compromised service can call every other as anyone'
    if model == 'authenticated callers (mTLS)':
        return services, 'the caller is known, but is still authorised for everything'
    if model == 'authenticated + authorised per call':
        return compromised, 'a compromised service can do only what it was granted'
    raise ValueError(model)

for model in ('flat / network trust', 'authenticated callers (mTLS)',
              'authenticated + authorised per call'):
    reach, note = blast_radius(model, services=40)
    print(f'{model:<36}reaches {reach:>3} of 40   {note}')

flat / network trust                reaches  40 of 40   one compromised service can call every other as anyone
authenticated callers (mTLS)        reaches  40 of 40   the caller is known, but is still authorised for everything
authenticated + authorised per call reaches   1 of 40   a compromised service can do only what it was granted

Authentication alone does not reduce the blast radius; authorisation does. Knowing that a call came from the recommendations service is only useful if something then refuses to let the recommendations service issue refunds. Both halves are needed, and they are different mechanisms.

Two identities travel with an internal request, and conflating them is the most common design error here:

Who is calling
Service identity. Established by mTLS — each service holds a short-lived certificate, and the mutual handshake proves both ends. This is what a service mesh provides for free (§12.8) and what is otherwise a certificate-rotation project.
On whose behalf
User identity. Established at the gateway (§12.6) and propagated inward as a signed token, so every downstream service can verify the user without calling back to the auth service. The gateway is the only component that validates the original credential.

Authentication for external callers is a different problem, and OAuth 2.0 is the standard answer to it. OAuth is an authorisation delegation protocol rather than an authentication one, which is the source of most confusion about it — OpenID Connect is the thin layer on top that adds authentication. Its value in a system design is one specific property: it lets a user grant a third party limited access without giving it their password. The third party receives a scoped, expiring access token; the user's credential never leaves the authorisation server, and the grant can be revoked without a password change. Backend and API Design builds the authorization-code flow with PKCE in detail; the system-level consequences are these:

def token_check(where, calls_auth_server, latency_ms, revocation_delay_s):
    return where, calls_auth_server, latency_ms, revocation_delay_s

STRATEGIES = [
    token_check('opaque token, introspected on every call', True, 12, 0),
    token_check('signed JWT, verified locally', False, 0.05, 900),
    token_check('signed JWT + a revocation list check', True, 1.5, 5),
]
print(f'{"strategy":<44}{"auth call?":>11}{"added ms":>10}{"revocation lag":>16}')
for where, calls, ms, revocation in STRATEGIES:
    lag = 'immediate' if revocation == 0 else f'up to {revocation}s'
    print(f'{where:<44}{str(calls):>11}{ms:>10.2f}{lag:>16}')

strategy                                     auth call?  added ms  revocation lag
opaque token, introspected on every call           True     12.00       immediate
signed JWT, verified locally                      False      0.05      up to 900s
signed JWT + a revocation list check               True      1.50        up to 5s

That table is the whole trade, and it has no free option. An opaque token introspected on every call is revocable instantly and puts the authorisation server on the critical path of every request — a hard dependency (§14.1) with its own availability, latency and capacity. A locally-verified JWT costs nothing and cannot be revoked before it expires, which is why token lifetimes are short and why "log out everywhere" is genuinely hard. The middle row is what most systems settle on: verify locally, and check a small, cached revocation list for the cases that matter.

Defence in depth is the principle underneath all of this: assume every individual control will fail, and arrange that no single failure is sufficient. Defence in depth is not the same as having many controls — it is having controls that fail independently, so that whatever bypassed one does not also bypass the next. A gateway that authenticates is one layer; a service that re-checks authorisation for the specific object being accessed is another; a database user with only the permissions that service needs is a third; and network policy restricting which services may connect at all is a fourth.

LAYERS = [
    ('network policy', 'only the services that need to talk may connect'),
    ('mTLS', 'the caller is cryptographically identified'),
    ('gateway authentication', 'the user credential is validated exactly once'),
    ('per-service authorisation', 'this caller may perform this operation'),
    ('per-object authorisation', 'this user may access THIS record'),
    ('least-privilege database user', 'the service can only touch its own tables'),
    ('encryption at rest', 'a stolen disk is not a stolen database'),
    ('audit log', 'what happened is reconstructable afterwards'),
]

def survives(layers_present, layers_bypassed):
    return max(0, layers_present - layers_bypassed)

print(f'{"layer":<32}protects against')
for name, protects in LAYERS:
    print(f'{name:<32}{protects}')

print()
for bypassed in (1, 2, 4):
    print(f'{bypassed} layer(s) bypassed -> {survives(len(LAYERS), bypassed)} still standing')

layer                           protects against
network policy                  only the services that need to talk may connect
mTLS                            the caller is cryptographically identified
gateway authentication          the user credential is validated exactly once
per-service authorisation       this caller may perform this operation
per-object authorisation        this user may access THIS record
least-privilege database user   the service can only touch its own tables
encryption at rest              a stolen disk is not a stolen database
audit log                       what happened is reconstructable afterwards

1 layer(s) bypassed -> 7 still standing
2 layer(s) bypassed -> 6 still standing
4 layer(s) bypassed -> 4 still standing

The layer most often missing is per-object authorisation, and it is the one that matters most. A service that checks "is this caller allowed to read orders?" and not "is this user allowed to read this order?" will happily return anyone's order to anyone with a valid token — which is the top entry on the OWASP API list precisely because it is so easy to omit and so trivial to exploit. The check belongs next to the data, in the service that owns it, and it cannot be delegated to the gateway, because the gateway does not know which record is being requested.

And the boundary itself is where trust is established, not assumed. Everything §12.4 said about coupling has a security counterpart: a service reading another service's tables bypasses that service's authorisation entirely, which is one more reason the one-owner-per-table rule is not merely about schema changes.

Exercises

Exercise 12.1 — Draw the boundaries. A logistics company runs one monolith. It handles: quoting a shipment price, booking a shipment, assigning a courier, tracking parcels in real time, invoicing, customs paperwork, and a customer support console. Real-time tracking is 90% of the traffic and needs different scaling from everything else. Customs rules change weekly and are written by a separate compliance team. Propose the boundaries, say which are services and which are modules, and name what you deliberately keep together.

Solution 
PROPOSAL = [
    ('tracking',        'SERVICE',   '90% of traffic, write-heavy, needs its own scaling and store'),
    ('customs',         'SERVICE',   'a separate team ships weekly; deploy independence is the point'),
    ('quoting+booking', 'one module', 'a quote becomes a booking; they share pricing rules'),
    ('courier assignment', 'module',  'changes with booking more often than with anything else'),
    ('invoicing',       'module -> service later', 'a natural leaf; extract when billing needs its own cadence'),
    ('support console', 'module',    'reads everything, owns nothing — a UI concern, not a domain'),
]
for name, kind, why in PROPOSAL:
    print(f'{name:<20}{kind:<26}{why}')

print('\ndeliberately NOT split:')
for line in ['quoting from booking — a change to pricing touches both, every time',
             'booking from courier assignment — one transaction, one consistency boundary',
             'the support console into per-domain services — it is a reader, not an owner']:
    print('  \u00b7', line)

tracking            SERVICE                   90% of traffic, write-heavy, needs its own scaling and store
customs             SERVICE                   a separate team ships weekly; deploy independence is the point
quoting+booking     one module                a quote becomes a booking; they share pricing rules
courier assignment  module                    changes with booking more often than with anything else
invoicing           module -> service later   a natural leaf; extract when billing needs its own cadence
support console     module                    reads everything, owns nothing — a UI concern, not a domain

deliberately NOT split:
  · quoting from booking — a change to pricing touches both, every time
  · booking from courier assignment — one transaction, one consistency boundary
  · the support console into per-domain services — it is a reader, not an owner

Two services, and the reason for each is different. That is the point of the exercise: a boundary needs a specific justification, and "it is a different noun" is not one.

Tracking is a service because of scaling and workload shape. Ninety per cent of traffic, high write volume, and a query pattern that wants a time-series or wide-column store (§6.5) rather than the relational database the rest of the business runs on. It also has a completely different availability requirement — tracking being down is annoying, booking being down is lost revenue — so an independent failure domain is worth real money.

Customs is a service because of the organisation. A separate compliance team shipping weekly rule changes should not need a release slot in the main deploy pipeline, and the main system should not be blocked by a compliance deploy. This is §12.3's point that microservices are an organisational solution: nothing about customs is technically demanding, and the boundary still earns its cost.

Quoting and booking stay together, because a quote becomes a booking and both are governed by the same pricing rules. Splitting them means every pricing change is a two-service coordinated deploy — §12.1's arithmetic, and the clearest possible signal that the boundary is wrong.

The support console is a reader. It owns no data and needs a view across everything, so making it a service that calls five others gives it §12.5's chatty synchronous fan-out. A read model built from events (§11.5) is the right shape if it needs to be independent, and a module is the right shape until then.

And invoicing is the one marked for later. It is a genuine leaf, it has an obvious seam, and there is no reason to extract it today — which is the most common mistake this exercise is built to surface. Note the boundary in the code, enforce it as a module, and extract it when there is a reason.

Exercise 12.2 — Diagnose and fix. A team split their monolith into eight services eighteen months ago. Today: a release train ships all eight every Thursday, a feature averages 3.4 services, all eight share one PostgreSQL instance, the p99 checkout latency went from 400 ms to 2.1 s, and an outage in any one service takes checkout down. They are asking whether a service mesh would help. Answer them.

Solution

No. A mesh would let them watch this happen in higher resolution. Every symptom described is a boundary problem, and a mesh does not move boundaries.

SIGNALS = {
    'release train ships all eight':      ('deployment coupling', 'boundaries do not match change'),
    'a feature averages 3.4 services':    ('wrong seams',         '§12.1: the key measure, and 3.4 is bad'),
    'one shared PostgreSQL':              ('data coupling',       '§12.4: the tightest kind, invisible on the diagram'),
    'p99 400 ms -> 2.1 s':                ('chatty sync calls',   '§12.5: in-process calls became network calls'),
    'any service down takes checkout down': ('no failure isolation', '§14.1: all dependencies are hard'),
}
for signal, (kind, note) in SIGNALS.items():
    print(f'{signal:<38}{kind:<24}{note}')

print(f'\ndistributed-monolith signals present: {len(SIGNALS)}/6')

latency_budget = 2_100 - 400
print(f'latency added by the split: {latency_budget:,} ms')
print(f'at ~8 ms per hop that is roughly {latency_budget // 8} extra network calls per checkout')

release train ships all eight         deployment coupling     boundaries do not match change
a feature averages 3.4 services       wrong seams             §12.1: the key measure, and 3.4 is bad
one shared PostgreSQL                 data coupling           §12.4: the tightest kind, invisible on the diagram
p99 400 ms -> 2.1 s                   chatty sync calls       §12.5: in-process calls became network calls
any service down takes checkout down  no failure isolation    §14.1: all dependencies are hard

distributed-monolith signals present: 5/6
latency added by the split: 1,700 ms
at ~8 ms per hop that is roughly 212 extra network calls per checkout

Five of §12.5's six signals. This is a textbook distributed monolith, and the mesh question is a symptom of the usual response — treating a design problem as an operations problem.

What to do instead, in order:

1. Give each service its own schema, today. One PostgreSQL instance is acceptable; one schema shared between eight services is not. Assign every table an owner, and replace every cross-service read with an API call or an event. This is unglamorous and it is the change that makes every other change possible, because until it is done no service can be deployed or moved independently of any other.

2. Measure which services always change together, from eighteen months of git log. Services that appear in the same commit most of the time are one service. Expect to find that three or four of the eight should be merged — merging is the fix, and it is not a retreat.

3. Re-cut the remaining boundaries from the change history, not from the original design. The original was a guess made before anyone had lived with it; there is now real evidence (§12.2).

4. Kill the release train. It is both a symptom and a cause: while everything ships together there is no pressure to make anything independently deployable, and the coupling is never felt by the people creating it. Requiring each service to deploy on its own forces the compatibility windows to be built.

5. Attack the latency by removing calls, not by making them faster. Roughly 210 extra network calls' worth of latency was added to checkout. Some can be parallelised and some cached, but the real answer is that those calls were one operation and belong in one component.

And then, possibly, a mesh. Once the boundaries are right and there are still enough services to make consistent retry, timeout and mTLS configuration hard, a mesh is a reasonable answer to a real problem (§12.8). Adopting it now would add latency to a system whose complaint is latency, add a control plane to a team already struggling with operational surface, and make the boundary problem harder to see.

Exercise 12.3 — Plan an extraction. Take the logistics monolith from Exercise 12.1 and plan the extraction of real-time tracking, end to end: the facade, the order of steps, the data move, how you verify each step, and what you can roll back at each point. Tracking currently writes to a parcel_events table that the support console and invoicing both read.

Solution

The two readers are the whole problem. Extracting a service whose table other components read is not one migration, it is three: move the writer, move the readers, then move the data — and doing them in the wrong order leaves a shared database (§12.4) with a network hop added.

PLAN = [
    ('0. facade',
     'route /tracking/* through a facade that still calls the monolith',
     'no behaviour change; the routing layer is now in place',
     'delete the facade'),
    ('1. publish',
     'monolith writes parcel_events AND publishes to a log, via the outbox (§11.2)',
     'the stream exists and can be verified against the table before anything depends on it',
     'stop the relay; the table is still authoritative'),
    ('2. build',
     'the new service consumes the log and builds its own store; serves nothing yet',
     'compare its answers with the monolith offline for a week',
     'delete the service; nothing reads it'),
    ('3. shadow',
     'the facade sends every read to BOTH, serves the monolith, logs differences',
     'behavioural coupling surfaces here or nowhere (§12.9)',
     'stop shadowing — one config change'),
    ('4. shift reads',
     '1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% of reads served by the new service',
     'error rate and p99 watched at each step',
     'move the percentage back down; the monolith is still fully current'),
    ('5. move the writer',
     'ingestion writes to the new service; the monolith consumes the log to keep its table',
     'the monolith table is now a derived copy, not the source',
     'point ingestion back — the harder rollback, and the first one that is'),
    ('6. move the readers',
     'support console and invoicing read the tracking API or their own projections',
     'no component outside tracking touches parcel_events',
     'point them back at the table, which is still being maintained'),
    ('7. contract',
     'stop maintaining parcel_events; drop it a release later',
     'the extraction is finished',
     'NOT REVERSIBLE — which is why it is last and waits a release'),
]
for step, action, verify, rollback in PLAN:
    print(f'{step}\n   do      : {action}\n   verify  : {verify}\n   rollback: {rollback}\n')

print('reversible steps:', sum(1 for s in PLAN if not s[3].startswith('NOT')), 'of', len(PLAN))

0. facade
   do      : route /tracking/* through a facade that still calls the monolith
   verify  : no behaviour change; the routing layer is now in place
   rollback: delete the facade

1. publish
   do      : monolith writes parcel_events AND publishes to a log, via the outbox (§11.2)
   verify  : the stream exists and can be verified against the table before anything depends on it
   rollback: stop the relay; the table is still authoritative

2. build
   do      : the new service consumes the log and builds its own store; serves nothing yet
   verify  : compare its answers with the monolith offline for a week
   rollback: delete the service; nothing reads it

3. shadow
   do      : the facade sends every read to BOTH, serves the monolith, logs differences
   verify  : behavioural coupling surfaces here or nowhere (§12.9)
   rollback: stop shadowing — one config change

4. shift reads
   do      : 1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% of reads served by the new service
   verify  : error rate and p99 watched at each step
   rollback: move the percentage back down; the monolith is still fully current

5. move the writer
   do      : ingestion writes to the new service; the monolith consumes the log to keep its table
   verify  : the monolith table is now a derived copy, not the source
   rollback: point ingestion back — the harder rollback, and the first one that is

6. move the readers
   do      : support console and invoicing read the tracking API or their own projections
   verify  : no component outside tracking touches parcel_events
   rollback: point them back at the table, which is still being maintained

7. contract
   do      : stop maintaining parcel_events; drop it a release later
   verify  : the extraction is finished
   rollback: NOT REVERSIBLE — which is why it is last and waits a release

reversible steps: 7 of 8

Four decisions in that ordering are the ones worth defending.

The facade goes first and does nothing. Step 0 changes no behaviour at all, and it is what makes every later step a routing change rather than a deploy. Teams routinely skip it and then discover that shifting 1% of reads requires a code change in the caller.

Dual-writing via the outbox precedes the new service existing. The log is built and verified against the existing table while nothing depends on it, so by the time the service consumes it, the stream is known to be correct. Building the service first and then wondering whether the stream is complete is the version that fails.

Shadowing is the step that earns its keep and is always the first to be cut. Running both and comparing is the only way to find the behaviour nobody wrote down — the deduplication rule for repeated scans, the timezone the timestamps are actually in, the one carrier whose events arrive out of order. A contract test cannot find these, because the contract does not mention them.

The writer moves after the reads, not before. While the monolith is the writer, its table is current and every rollback is free. Once ingestion moves, the monolith's copy is derived and rolling back means reconciling — the first genuinely expensive reversal, which is why six of the eight steps come before it.

And the property that makes the whole plan safe: seven of the eight steps are reversible without a data migration. The one that is not is the last, is separated from the rest by a release, and does nothing except delete something already unused.

SECTION 13

Communication

Two components need to exchange information. That is one decision with several parts — which protocol, which direction, which encoding, what happens when the shape changes — and each part has a default that is right most of the time and wrong in a way that is expensive to discover late. Backend and API Design covers designing one HTTP API in depth, and Networking and HTTP covers what the protocols actually do on the wire. This section is about choosing between them when the callers are other services and the volume is large.

13.1 The First Question Is Synchronous or Not

Before any protocol choice, decide whether the caller waits. It is the decision that determines availability (§14.1), coupling (§12.4) and how the failure is handled, and the protocol follows from it rather than the other way round.

def interaction(style, caller_waits, needs_answer_now, tolerates_delay):
    return {
        'request/response': caller_waits and needs_answer_now,
        'fire and forget': not caller_waits,
        'request/async reply': caller_waits is False and needs_answer_now,
        'streaming': tolerates_delay is False and not needs_answer_now,
    }[style]

CASES = [
    ('is this card valid?',        'request/response', 'the user cannot proceed without it'),
    ('send the receipt email',     'fire and forget',  'nobody is waiting; it must not fail checkout'),
    ('generate a 400-page report', 'request/async reply', 'accept, return a job id, notify later'),
    ('live driver position',       'streaming',        'continuous updates, no request per update'),
]
for question, style, why in CASES:
    print(f'{question:<28}{style:<22}{why}')

is this card valid?         request/response      the user cannot proceed without it
send the receipt email      fire and forget       nobody is waiting; it must not fail checkout
generate a 400-page report  request/async reply   accept, return a job id, notify later
live driver position        streaming             continuous updates, no request per update

The default should be asynchronous, and synchronous should need a justification — which is the opposite of how most systems are built. A synchronous call couples the caller's availability to the callee's, adds the callee's latency to the caller's, and needs every mechanism in §14 to be safe. An asynchronous one needs a queue and idempotent handling (§10), which is a smaller and better-understood bill.

The justification, when it exists, is usually one of two things: the user is waiting for the answer, or the caller must not proceed if the operation failed. Card authorisation is both. Sending a receipt is neither, and making it synchronous is how a mail provider's outage becomes a checkout outage.

And "request with an asynchronous reply" is the option most often forgotten. Accept the work, return 202 with a job id and a status URL, and notify by webhook or push when it finishes. The client is not blocked, the server holds no connection for four minutes, and a timeout somewhere in the middle does not lose the work — Backend and API Design builds this pattern in its long-running-operations section, and it is the correct shape for anything measured in seconds rather than milliseconds.

13.2 REST, RPC and gRPC

For synchronous calls there are three styles, and they differ in what they make easy rather than in what they make possible.

REST over HTTP
Resources and standard verbs. Its leverage is everything that already understands HTTP — caches, proxies, load balancers, browsers, every debugging tool ever written. Human-readable, no code generation required, and the universal choice for a public API.
RPC (JSON over HTTP)
Call a named procedure. Natural for actions that are not nouns, and it gives up HTTP's caching and intermediary semantics because everything is a POST to one endpoint.
gRPC
Binary Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2, with a generated client from a schema. Fast, strongly typed, and it supports streaming in both directions. Costs a build step, poor browser support without a proxy, and payloads no human can read from a packet capture.

The performance difference is real and is smaller than the arguments about it suggest:

def payload(style, fields=12, mean_field_bytes=14, name_bytes=11):
    if style == 'JSON':
        return fields * (name_bytes + mean_field_bytes + 4)     # quotes, colon, comma
    if style == 'protobuf':
        return fields * (1 + mean_field_bytes)                  # tag byte, no field names
    raise ValueError(style)

json_bytes, proto_bytes = payload('JSON'), payload('protobuf')
print(f'JSON     {json_bytes:>5} bytes')
print(f'protobuf {proto_bytes:>5} bytes  ({json_bytes / proto_bytes:.1f}x smaller)')

for rps, rtt_ms in [(100, 8), (50_000, 8)]:
    saved_mb_s = rps * (json_bytes - proto_bytes) / 1e6
    print(f'at {rps:>6,} req/s: {saved_mb_s:>7.2f} MB/s of bandwidth saved')

JSON       348 bytes
protobuf   180 bytes  (1.9x smaller)
at    100 req/s:    0.02 MB/s of bandwidth saved
at 50,000 req/s:    8.40 MB/s of bandwidth saved

At a hundred requests a second the saving is a rounding error; at fifty thousand it is real. That is the shape of the whole decision: gRPC's advantages are proportional to volume, and its costs — the build step, the debugging difficulty, the browser proxy — are fixed. Below a certain traffic level you are paying the fixed cost for a benefit you cannot measure.

The rule that holds up in practice: REST at the edge, gRPC between services, if you have enough services for it to matter. Public and browser-facing APIs get HTTP and JSON, because compatibility with everything is worth more than bytes. Internal service-to-service calls in a large system get gRPC, because the schema, the generated clients and the streaming are genuinely valuable when there are forty services and four languages (§12.8).

There is one more gRPC feature that is underrated and is often the deciding one: the schema is a build-time contract. A .proto file is checked in, both sides generate from it, and a field removed on one side fails to compile on the other. That catches at build time what §13.7 otherwise has to catch in production.

13.3 GraphQL, and the Problem It Actually Solves

GraphQL exists for a specific problem: a client that needs data from several places and wants to say so in one request. It is not a faster REST, and adopting it for the wrong reason is a common and costly mistake.

SCREEN = {'user profile': 1, 'their last 10 orders': 1, 'each order\'s items': 10,
          'product details per item': 30, 'shipping status per order': 10}

rest_calls = sum(SCREEN.values())
print(f'REST, naive          : {rest_calls} requests  <- the N+1 problem, over the network')
print(f'REST, purpose-built  : 1 request   <- a backend-for-frontend endpoint (§12.6)')
print(f'GraphQL              : 1 request   <- the client declares the shape it needs')

for rtt_ms in (12, 180):
    print(f'\nat {rtt_ms} ms RTT: naive {rest_calls * rtt_ms:>6,} ms   single request {rtt_ms:>4} ms')

REST, naive          : 52 requests  <- the N+1 problem, over the network
REST, purpose-built  : 1 request   <- a backend-for-frontend endpoint (§12.6)
GraphQL              : 1 request   <- the client declares the shape it needs

at 12 ms RTT: naive    624 ms   single request   12 ms

at 180 ms RTT: naive  9,360 ms   single request  180 ms

On a mobile network the naive version is nine and a half seconds. That is the problem, and it has two solutions: a purpose-built endpoint per screen, or a query language that lets the client describe what it needs. A backend-for-frontend is the simpler answer and should be tried first, because it needs no new technology and the endpoint can be optimised as a single query.

GraphQL earns its complexity when the number of clients makes purpose-built endpoints unmanageable — several mobile versions in the wild, a web app, partner integrations, all wanting different shapes of the same graph. Then a single schema that each client queries differently is genuinely better than twenty endpoints nobody can retire.

What it costs, stated so the trade is legible:

HTTP caching is gone
Every query is a POST to one URL, so no CDN, proxy or browser cache can help (§9.2). You rebuild caching inside the resolvers, per field, yourself.
Query cost is unbounded
A client can request a deeply nested query that is expensive in a way no endpoint ever was. Depth limits, complexity scoring and persisted queries are mandatory, not optional.
N+1 moves, it does not vanish
The network round trips became resolver calls. Without batching — a DataLoader — you have the same problem inside one process, which is better and still bad.
Observability is harder
Every request has the same URL and status code, so per-endpoint latency and error rates stop meaning anything. Instrumentation has to be per-field or per-operation-name.

13.4 Getting Data to a Client That Is Waiting

When the server has news, four mechanisms deliver it, and the choice is usually made by habit rather than by the numbers.

def cost(mechanism, clients, events_per_client_s, poll_interval_s=5,
         connection_memory_kb=12):
    """HTTP requests/s (setup cost), messages/s (useful work), and held memory."""
    held = clients * connection_memory_kb / 1e6
    if mechanism == 'polling':
        requests = clients / poll_interval_s
        useful = clients * events_per_client_s
        return requests, useful, 0.0, f'{1 - useful / requests:.0%} of requests return nothing'
    if mechanism == 'long polling':
        requests = clients * events_per_client_s
        return requests, requests, held, 'one request per event, plus a held connection'
    return 0.0, clients * events_per_client_s, held, 'no new requests after the first'

print(f'{"mechanism":<16}{"requests/s":>12}{"messages/s":>12}{"held GB":>10}   note')
for mechanism in ('polling', 'long polling', 'SSE / WebSocket'):
    requests, messages, memory, note = cost(mechanism, clients=200_000,
                                            events_per_client_s=0.02)
    print(f'{mechanism:<16}{requests:>12,.0f}{messages:>12,.0f}{memory:>10.1f}   {note}')

mechanism         requests/s  messages/s   held GB   note
polling               40,000       4,000       0.0   90% of requests return nothing
long polling           4,000       4,000       2.4   one request per event, plus a held connection
SSE / WebSocket            0       4,000       2.4   no new requests after the first

Polling 200,000 clients every five seconds is 40,000 requests a second of which 90% return nothing. That is the cost of not knowing when something happened, and it is paid continuously whether or not anything is going on.

Polling
Ask repeatedly. Simple, stateless, works everywhere, and the load is constant regardless of activity. Genuinely the right answer for infrequent updates and small client populations — and the interval is a direct trade between staleness and load.
Long polling
The server holds the request open until it has something. Near-real-time with ordinary HTTP, and it holds a connection per client while adding a request per event. A reasonable fallback where nothing better is available.
Server-sent events
One long-lived HTTP response streaming events, server to client only. Automatic reconnection with Last-Event-ID, works through most proxies, and it is plain HTTP. The right default for notifications, live feeds and progress — and it is consistently underused because WebSocket is better known.
WebSocket
A full-duplex connection after an HTTP upgrade. Necessary when the client also sends frequently — chat, collaborative editing, games. Costs you a protocol outside HTTP: your own reconnection, heartbeats, authentication and message framing, and load balancers that must be configured for long-lived connections.

Choose SSE unless the client needs to send. That single sentence resolves most of these decisions correctly, and the reason is that everything SSE gives up — bidirectionality — is not needed for the majority of push use cases, while everything it keeps (HTTP semantics, proxy compatibility, automatic reconnection) is work you would otherwise write.

Two consequences of persistent connections that apply to SSE and WebSocket alike. They make your servers stateful (§2.2) in a specific way: a connection is bound to one instance, so a deploy disconnects everyone, and 200,000 clients reconnecting simultaneously is a self-inflicted thundering herd — stagger the reconnect with jitter (§14.4) and drain deliberately (§14.9). And they consume file descriptors and memory rather than CPU, so capacity planning is about connection count, not request rate, which is a different graph than the one on the dashboard.

13.5 The Transport Underneath

Almost every service-to-service call is TCP, and the cases where it is not are worth recognising.

def transport(requirement):
    NEEDS = {
        'every byte must arrive':        ('TCP', 'ordered, reliable, retransmitted'),
        'late data is worthless':        ('UDP', 'no retransmission; a stale packet is dropped'),
        'many parallel streams':         ('HTTP/2 or QUIC', 'one connection, no per-stream handshake'),
        'head-of-line blocking hurts':   ('QUIC (UDP)', 'a lost packet stalls one stream, not all'),
        'the client moves networks':     ('QUIC (UDP)', 'a connection id survives an address change'),
    }
    return NEEDS[requirement]

for requirement in ['every byte must arrive', 'late data is worthless',
                    'many parallel streams', 'head-of-line blocking hurts',
                    'the client moves networks']:
    choice, why = transport(requirement)
    print(f'{requirement:<30}{choice:<18}{why}')

every byte must arrive        TCP               ordered, reliable, retransmitted
late data is worthless        UDP               no retransmission; a stale packet is dropped
many parallel streams         HTTP/2 or QUIC    one connection, no per-stream handshake
head-of-line blocking hurts   QUIC (UDP)        a lost packet stalls one stream, not all
the client moves networks     QUIC (UDP)        a connection id survives an address change

TCP is the default and is almost always right, because almost all application data is worthless if it arrives corrupted or out of order. UDP is for the narrow case where latency beats completeness: live audio and video, real-time game state, and metrics where a lost sample is invisible. The test is simple — would you rather have this packet late, or not at all? For a video frame, not at all; retransmitting a frame that should already be on screen is worse than skipping it.

The design consequence that matters most at scale is connection reuse. A new TCP connection costs a round trip, and a new TLS connection costs one or two more:

def handshake_cost(rtt_ms, tls_version, reused=False):
    if reused:
        return 0.0
    tcp = rtt_ms
    tls = {'1.2': 2 * rtt_ms, '1.3': rtt_ms, '1.3 resumed': 0}[tls_version]
    return tcp + tls

for label, rtt in [('same data centre', 0.5), ('cross-region', 80)]:
    print(f'{label} (RTT {rtt} ms):')
    for version in ('1.2', '1.3', '1.3 resumed'):
        print(f'   TLS {version:<12} new connection {handshake_cost(rtt, version):>6.1f} ms'
              f'   reused {handshake_cost(rtt, version, reused=True):>4.1f} ms')

same data centre (RTT 0.5 ms):
   TLS 1.2          new connection    1.5 ms   reused  0.0 ms
   TLS 1.3          new connection    1.0 ms   reused  0.0 ms
   TLS 1.3 resumed  new connection    0.5 ms   reused  0.0 ms
cross-region (RTT 80 ms):
   TLS 1.2          new connection  240.0 ms   reused  0.0 ms
   TLS 1.3          new connection  160.0 ms   reused  0.0 ms
   TLS 1.3 resumed  new connection   80.0 ms   reused  0.0 ms

Cross-region, a new TLS 1.2 connection costs 240 milliseconds before a single byte of your request is sent. A client that opens a connection per request is paying that on every call, and the fix is a connection pool with keep-alive — which is one configuration setting and one of the largest latency wins available in a service that does not have it. Networking and HTTP covers the handshakes themselves; the system-design point is that connection reuse is a capacity decision, not a micro-optimisation, and it interacts with §2.4's warning that a layer-4 balancer cannot rebalance a reused connection.

13.6 Serialisation, and Where the Bytes Go

The encoding choice is usually made once and lived with forever, so it is worth making deliberately.

FORMATS = [
    ('JSON',          'text',   1.00, 'universal, debuggable, no schema required'),
    ('JSON+gzip',     'text',   0.18, 'the same bytes, 5x smaller, at some CPU on both ends'),
    ('MessagePack',   'binary', 0.55, 'JSON-shaped, no schema, modestly smaller'),
    ('Protobuf',      'binary', 0.28, 'schema required, generated code, very fast to parse'),
    ('Protobuf+gzip', 'binary', 0.12, 'the smallest of these, and the most machinery'),
    ('Avro',          'binary', 0.25, 'schema travels with the data — built for logs (§10.2)'),
]
BASE_KB = 4.0
print(f'{"format":<14}{"kind":>8}{"size":>10}{"at 50k req/s":>15}   note')
for name, kind, ratio, note in FORMATS:
    size = BASE_KB * ratio
    print(f'{name:<14}{kind:>8}{size:>8.2f} KB{size * 50_000 / 1_000:>12.0f} MB/s   {note}')

format            kind      size   at 50k req/s   note
JSON              text    4.00 KB         200 MB/s   universal, debuggable, no schema required
JSON+gzip         text    0.72 KB          36 MB/s   the same bytes, 5x smaller, at some CPU on both ends
MessagePack     binary    2.20 KB         110 MB/s   JSON-shaped, no schema, modestly smaller
Protobuf        binary    1.12 KB          56 MB/s   schema required, generated code, very fast to parse
Protobuf+gzip   binary    0.48 KB          24 MB/s   the smallest of these, and the most machinery
Avro            binary    1.00 KB          50 MB/s   schema travels with the data — built for logs (§10.2)

Gzipped JSON is smaller than raw Protobuf here, which is the row that settles most arguments about this. Compression is one header on the request and needs no schema, no build step and no code generation, so it is the move to make first whenever the complaint is bandwidth. Protobuf's real advantages are the schema, the generated clients and the parse speed — a binary format is several times faster to decode than JSON, and at high request rates that is the number that matters, not the bytes.

Three rules that hold regardless of format:

Never put large binary data in a message. A base64-encoded image inflates by a third and turns your broker or API into a file server (§10.3). The object goes in object storage (§6.7); the key goes in the message.

Choose a format with a schema for anything long-lived. Events in a log are read years later by code that does not exist yet (§11.9), and a schema is what makes that possible. Avro is designed for exactly this, carrying a schema identifier with each record so a reader can resolve an old one.

Watch what the parser costs. At high request rates JSON parsing can be a measurable fraction of CPU, and it is invisible in application profiling that only looks at handler code. If a service is mysteriously CPU-bound, measure serialisation before rewriting business logic.

13.7 Versioning Between Services

API versioning for a public interface means a compatibility policy and a deprecation timetable, which Backend and API Design covers in its versioning section: URI versions, media-type versions, and the definition of a breaking change. Between internal services the problem is different in one specific way, and it is why API versioning between services is usually not a version number at all: you deploy both sides, but never at the same instant.

def deploy_window(old_version_still_running, change_kind):
    COMPATIBLE = {
        'add an optional field': True,
        'add a new endpoint': True,
        'widen an accepted value': True,
        'remove a field': False,
        'rename a field': False,
        'narrow a type': False,
        'change a field\'s meaning': False,
    }
    safe = COMPATIBLE[change_kind]
    if not old_version_still_running:
        return 'safe (nothing old is running)'
    return 'SAFE' if safe else 'BREAKS during the rollout window'

print('during a rolling deploy, both versions run at once:')
for change in ['add an optional field', 'add a new endpoint', 'widen an accepted value',
               'remove a field', 'rename a field', 'narrow a type',
               "change a field's meaning"]:
    print(f'   {change:<26}{deploy_window(True, change)}')

during a rolling deploy, both versions run at once:
   add an optional field     SAFE
   add a new endpoint        SAFE
   widen an accepted value   SAFE
   remove a field            BREAKS during the rollout window
   rename a field            BREAKS during the rollout window
   narrow a type             BREAKS during the rollout window
   change a field's meaning  BREAKS during the rollout window

There is no ordering of two deploys that makes a breaking change safe, because there is always a window in which both versions are running. That is the same constraint §6.10 imposed on schema migrations, and it has the same answer — expand and contract, in three separate releases:

1
Expand. The producer adds the new field alongside the old one and populates both. Nothing consumes it yet, and nothing breaks.
2
Migrate. Every consumer is updated to read the new field, with a fallback to the old one. Deploy them in any order — that is the point of the fallback.
3
Contract. Once no deployed consumer reads the old field — verified, not assumed — the producer stops writing it and removes it.

Step 3's "verified" is where this goes wrong, and the way to make it real is to instrument it: log or count every read of the deprecated field, tagged with the caller, and remove it only when that counter has been zero for longer than your longest deploy cycle. Asking around is not evidence, and a consumer nobody remembers is exactly the one that breaks.

The change that has no safe version is a change of meaning. Renaming price to price_cents is caught by every schema check; silently changing price from euros to cents is caught by nothing, compiles everywhere, and produces orders that are a hundred times wrong. A change of meaning must be a new field with a new name, always, without exception — and it is the single most valuable rule in this section.

And consumer-driven contract tests are what turn all of this from a policy into a check. Each consumer publishes the shape it actually depends on; the producer's build runs every consumer's expectations against the new version and fails if one breaks. That converts "we think nobody uses that field" into a build error, which is the only form of that sentence worth trusting.

13.8 Pagination at Scale

Any endpoint returning a collection must paginate, and the choice between the two mechanisms is decided by the size of the collection.

def page_cost(mechanism, page_size, page_number, total_rows):
    if mechanism == 'offset':
        offset = page_size * (page_number - 1)
        return offset + page_size, 'the database walks every skipped row'
    return page_size, 'an index seek straight to the cursor'

print(f'{"page":>7}{"offset: rows read":>20}{"cursor: rows read":>20}')
for page in (1, 10, 1_000, 50_000):
    offset_rows, _ = page_cost('offset', 50, page, 5_000_000)
    cursor_rows, _ = page_cost('cursor', 50, page, 5_000_000)
    print(f'{page:>7}{offset_rows:>20,}{cursor_rows:>20,}')

   page   offset: rows read   cursor: rows read
      1                  50                  50
     10                 500                  50
   1000              50,000                  50
  50000           2,500,000                  50

Offset pagination reads every row it skips. Page 50,000 costs 2.5 million row reads to return fifty, so the endpoint gets slower the deeper anyone goes — and a crawler or an export script goes all the way down, which is how a "slow endpoint" turns out to be one client walking a list.

Offset also has a correctness problem that is easy to demonstrate:

ITEMS = [f'item-{i:02d}' for i in range(1, 11)]

page1 = ITEMS[0:3]
ITEMS.insert(0, 'item-00')                       # something is added while paging
page2_offset = ITEMS[3:6]

after = 'item-03'
start = ITEMS.index(after) + 1
page2_cursor = ITEMS[start:start + 3]

print('page 1            :', page1)
print('page 2 by offset  :', page2_offset, '<- item-03 appears twice')
print('page 2 by cursor  :', page2_cursor, '<- correct, unaffected by the insert')

page 1            : ['item-01', 'item-02', 'item-03']
page 2 by offset  : ['item-03', 'item-04', 'item-05'] <- item-03 appears twice
page 2 by cursor  : ['item-04', 'item-05', 'item-06'] <- correct, unaffected by the insert

An insert shifts every offset, so a client walking the list sees an item twice — or, on a delete, misses one entirely. A cursor names a position in the ordering rather than a count, so nothing before it can move it.

Backend and API Design builds cursor pagination in detail, including the requirement that the ordering be total. The system-design points that go beyond one API are these:

A cursor must encode the full sort key, and the sort must be unique. Ordering by created_at alone breaks whenever two rows share a timestamp — the cursor cannot say which of them it meant. (created_at, id) is unique and is the standard shape.

Cap the page size and the total. An endpoint that accepts limit=100000 has a client that will send it. And there is rarely a legitimate reason to reach page 50,000 of a UI: if someone needs the whole collection, give them an export job (§13.1's asynchronous reply) rather than letting them walk it a page at a time, which is slower for them and far more expensive for you.

Offset is still fine for small, bounded collections. A user's own addresses, a team's members, a menu's items — a few hundred rows at most, where the deep-page problem cannot occur. The rule is about size, not about principle: offset for what fits on a few pages, cursor for anything a machine will walk.

Exercises

Exercise 13.1 — Choose the mechanism. For each, choose the interaction style, the protocol and the transport, and name the failure you are designing for.

(a) A payment service confirming a card authorisation for a checkout page.
(b) A warehouse system telling 3,000 handheld scanners about new picking tasks.
(c) A video call between two participants.
(d) An internal recommendation service called 40,000 times a second by the product page.
(e) An export of a customer's entire order history, 400,000 rows.
Solution 
ANSWERS = [
    ('(a) card authorisation', 'synchronous request/response', 'REST over HTTP/TLS (TCP)',
     'a timeout is ambiguous — needs an idempotency key and a reconciliation job'),
    ('(b) picking tasks',      'server push', 'server-sent events over HTTP (TCP)',
     '3,000 scanners reconnecting after a deploy — stagger with jitter'),
    ('(c) video call',         'peer-to-peer streaming', 'WebRTC over UDP',
     'packet loss: drop the frame, never retransmit it'),
    ('(d) recommendations',    'synchronous, with a fallback', 'gRPC over HTTP/2 (TCP)',
     'it is a SOFT dependency — short timeout, static fallback, no retry'),
    ('(e) 400k-row export',    'request with an async reply', 'REST + a job id + object storage',
     'never stream 400k rows through a request; the connection will not survive it'),
]
for case, style, protocol, failure in ANSWERS:
    print(f'{case}\n   style   : {style}\n   protocol: {protocol}\n   designing for: {failure}\n')

(a) card authorisation
   style   : synchronous request/response
   protocol: REST over HTTP/TLS (TCP)
   designing for: a timeout is ambiguous — needs an idempotency key and a reconciliation job

(b) picking tasks
   style   : server push
   protocol: server-sent events over HTTP (TCP)
   designing for: 3,000 scanners reconnecting after a deploy — stagger with jitter

(c) video call
   style   : peer-to-peer streaming
   protocol: WebRTC over UDP
   designing for: packet loss: drop the frame, never retransmit it

(d) recommendations
   style   : synchronous, with a fallback
   protocol: gRPC over HTTP/2 (TCP)
   designing for: it is a SOFT dependency — short timeout, static fallback, no retry

(e) 400k-row export
   style   : request with an async reply
   protocol: REST + a job id + object storage
   designing for: never stream 400k rows through a request; the connection will not survive it

Four of these turn on a specific detail.

(a) is synchronous because the user cannot proceed, and the interesting part is the failure. A timeout on a payment authorisation does not tell you whether the money moved, so the design needs an idempotency key on the request (§11.8) and a reconciliation job that compares your records against the processor's. A synchronous call whose timeout is ambiguous needs an asynchronous safety net, and payments is the canonical case.

(b) is SSE, not WebSocket, and this is the choice most often made wrongly. The scanners receive tasks; they report completion over ordinary HTTP requests, which are infrequent. There is no need for a bidirectional protocol, and SSE brings automatic reconnection with Last-Event-ID — precisely what a handheld device walking in and out of Wi-Fi coverage needs.
