Choosing WebSocket here means writing reconnection and replay logic that SSE provides.

(c) is the UDP case, and it is a genuine one. A retransmitted video frame arrives after the moment it depicted has passed, so TCP's reliability is actively harmful: it stalls the stream to deliver something that will be discarded. Loss is handled by concealment, not retransmission.

(d) is the most consequential answer, and it is not about the protocol. gRPC is right at 40,000 requests a second — the volume makes the binary encoding and the connection reuse worth the build step (§13.2). But the design decision is that recommendations is a soft dependency (§14.1): a 50 ms timeout, a static bestsellers fallback, no retry, and a circuit breaker. Making the product page's availability depend on the recommendation service is the mistake that Exercise 14.1 is entirely about.

(e) must not be a request at all. Four hundred thousand rows will not survive a request timeout, a load balancer's idle limit or a proxy's buffer, and paginating it is 8,000 requests. Accept the request, return 202 with a job id, generate the file into object storage (§6.7), and give the client a signed URL when it is ready.

Exercise 13.2 — Find the four problems. This internal API is called by six services. Name each problem, say who it breaks and when, and give the fix.

GET /api/orders?page=847&size=500&sort=created_at
    -> {"orders": [...500 orders, each with the full customer record...]}

The team plans to rename "total" to "total_cents" next Tuesday, and to change
"total" from euros to cents in the same release. They will deploy the producer
first, then the six consumers over the following two weeks.
Solution 
PROBLEMS = [
    ('offset page 847 with size 500',
     'the database reads 423,500 rows to return 500',
     'cursor pagination on (created_at, id); cap size at 100'),
    ('sort=created_at alone',
     'not a total order — rows sharing a timestamp paginate unstably',
     'sort on (created_at, id); the cursor must encode both'),
    ('the full customer record embedded in every order',
     '500 duplicated customer objects per page; a customer rename is now in a cache somewhere',
     'embed the id and a display name; let the consumer fetch what it needs'),
    ('rename AND change units in one release',
     'a consumer reading "total" for two weeks sees euros, then cents — 100x wrong, silently',
     'never change a meaning in place: add total_cents, expand/contract over three releases'),
]
for problem, breaks, fix in PROBLEMS:
    print(f'{problem}\n   breaks: {breaks}\n   fix   : {fix}\n')

rows_read = 500 * (847 - 1) + 500
print(f'offset page 847 x 500: {rows_read:,} rows read to return 500 '
      f'({rows_read // 500}x waste)')

offset page 847 with size 500
   breaks: the database reads 423,500 rows to return 500
   fix   : cursor pagination on (created_at, id); cap size at 100

sort=created_at alone
   breaks: not a total order — rows sharing a timestamp paginate unstably
   fix   : sort on (created_at, id); the cursor must encode both

the full customer record embedded in every order
   breaks: 500 duplicated customer objects per page; a customer rename is now in a cache somewhere
   fix   : embed the id and a display name; let the consumer fetch what it needs

rename AND change units in one release
   breaks: a consumer reading "total" for two weeks sees euros, then cents — 100x wrong, silently
   fix   : never change a meaning in place: add total_cents, expand/contract over three releases

offset page 847 x 500: 423,500 rows read to return 500 (847x waste)

The fourth is the serious one and would be a production incident. Deploying the producer first means that for two weeks, consumers that have not yet been updated read total and get a number that is a hundred times larger than it was, in a field whose name and type did not change. Nothing fails, nothing logs an error, and every downstream calculation is wrong — invoices, reports, fraud thresholds, the lot.

A change of meaning is not a schema change and no schema check will catch it (§13.7). The only safe version is a new field:

Release 1 (expand). Add total_cents alongside total, populate both. total keeps meaning euros. Nothing breaks and nothing needs coordinating.

Release 2..7 (migrate). Each consumer moves to total_cents, in its own time, in any order. This is what makes the two-week rollout fine rather than dangerous.

Release 8 (contract). Once the deprecated-field counter has read zero for longer than the longest deploy cycle, remove total. Instrument the read; do not ask around.

The other three are ordinary and worth fixing anyway. Page 847 at size 500 reads 423,500 rows to return 500 — and that a client is on page 847 at all says it is walking the whole collection, which should be an export job (§13.8). sort=created_at is not a total order, so pagination is unstable across rows sharing a timestamp. And embedding the full customer in every order duplicates the same object up to 500 times per page and creates a second copy of mutable data (§6.4's embed-versus-reference rule) that will go stale.

Exercise 13.3 — Design the live layer. A logistics dashboard shows 400 vehicles moving on a map, for 8,000 concurrent dispatcher browsers. Positions update every 3 seconds. Choose the mechanism, compute the load, design the deploy behaviour, and say what happens when a dispatcher's laptop sleeps for an hour.

Solution 
VEHICLES, DISPATCHERS, UPDATE_S = 400, 8_000, 3
POSITION_BYTES = 48

def naive(vehicles, dispatchers, update_s, payload_bytes):
    msgs = vehicles / update_s * dispatchers
    return msgs, msgs * payload_bytes / 1e6

def batched(vehicles, dispatchers, update_s, payload_bytes):
    msgs = dispatchers / update_s                      # one batched frame per client per tick
    return msgs, msgs * vehicles * payload_bytes / 1e6

def filtered(vehicles, dispatchers, update_s, payload_bytes, visible_fraction=0.08):
    msgs = dispatchers / update_s
    return msgs, msgs * vehicles * visible_fraction * payload_bytes / 1e6

print(f'{"approach":<34}{"messages/s":>13}{"MB/s":>9}')
for name, fn in [('one message per vehicle per client', naive),
                 ('one batched frame per client', batched),
                 ('batched + only what is on screen', filtered)]:
    msgs, mbs = fn(VEHICLES, DISPATCHERS, UPDATE_S, POSITION_BYTES)
    print(f'{name:<34}{msgs:>13,.0f}{mbs:>9.1f}')

print(f'\nconnections: {DISPATCHERS:,}  at 12 KB each = '
      f'{DISPATCHERS * 12 / 1e6:.2f} GB across the fleet')
print(f'per node at 8 nodes: {DISPATCHERS // 8:,} connections')
print(f'reconnect storm on deploy, unstaggered: {DISPATCHERS:,} in ~1s')
print(f'staggered over 60s with jitter        : {DISPATCHERS // 60:,}/s')

approach                             messages/s     MB/s
one message per vehicle per client    1,066,667     51.2
one batched frame per client              2,667     51.2
batched + only what is on screen          2,667      4.1

connections: 8,000  at 12 KB each = 0.10 GB across the fleet
per node at 8 nodes: 1,000 connections
reconnect storm on deploy, unstaggered: 8,000 in ~1s
staggered over 60s with jitter        : 133/s

Server-sent events, batched, filtered to the viewport. Taking those three decisions in order:

SSE rather than WebSocket, because the data flows one way. The dispatcher's own actions — assigning a job, messaging a driver — are ordinary POST requests at a human's pace, and there is no reason to build a bidirectional protocol for them (§13.4). SSE's automatic reconnection is worth a great deal here, which the laptop question makes concrete.

Batch every tick, do not send per vehicle. One message per vehicle per client is over a million messages a second; one frame per client per tick is 2,667. Same information, the same bytes on the wire, and a factor of four hundred in message overhead — the batching is worth more than any protocol choice.

Filter to the viewport. A dispatcher looking at one region does not need the other 92% of vehicles, and sending only what is on screen cuts bandwidth by the same factor. The subscription becomes "this bounding box", updated when the map moves.

Deploys are the hard part, and they are a §14.9 problem. Eight thousand persistent connections die when a node restarts, and all of them reconnect at once — 8,000 connection setups in a second, against a fleet that is mid-deploy and has fewer nodes than usual. The design has to: deregister and drain (§14.9), send a close event telling clients to reconnect after a jittered delay, and roll one node at a time. Staggered over sixty seconds it is 133 reconnects a second, which is nothing.

And the sleeping laptop is the case that decides the protocol. After an hour the connection is long dead — a proxy or the OS killed it. On wake, the browser's EventSource reconnects automatically and sends Last-Event-ID, and this is where the design decision lies: do not replay an hour of position updates. They are worthless, and sending 1.2 million stale events would be a self-inflicted attack. The server should recognise a gap larger than a few ticks and respond with a full current snapshot instead of the backlog — which is the same principle as §3.4's "serve stale, but say so": what the dispatcher needs on wake is now, not history.

SECTION 14

Resilience

Every dependency in a distributed system is eventually slow, eventually wrong, and eventually gone. Resilience is not the absence of those events — it is the property that they stay local instead of becoming everyone's problem. This section is about the mechanisms that make that true, and about the uncomfortable fact that half of them, applied carelessly, are themselves the cause of the outage. Backend and API Design covers retries, timeouts, circuit breakers and rate limiting from the point of view of one service and its callers; here the subject is the whole call graph, where the arithmetic changes completely.

14.1 Why a Well-Behaved Service Still Fails

Start with the number that motivates everything else. A request that touches several services succeeds only if all of them do.

from math import prod

def chain_availability(per_service, depth):
    return prod([per_service] * depth)

print(f'{"depth":>6}{"99.9% each":>13}{"99.99% each":>13}{"min/month down at 99.9%":>26}')
for depth in (1, 3, 5, 10, 30):
    a3, a4 = chain_availability(0.999, depth), chain_availability(0.9999, depth)
    print(f'{depth:>6}{a3:>13.4%}{a4:>13.4%}{(1 - a3) * 43_830:>22,.0f} min')

 depth   99.9% each  99.99% each   min/month down at 99.9%
     1     99.9000%     99.9900%                    44 min
     3     99.7003%     99.9700%                   131 min
     5     99.5010%     99.9500%                   219 min
    10     99.0045%     99.9000%                   436 min
    30     97.0431%     99.7004%                 1,296 min

A thirty-service request path built from three-nines services is a two-nines system, down for most of a day per year, and no individual team is at fault. This is the same multiplication that disqualified two-phase commit in §11.6, and it has the same two answers: reduce the number of things that must succeed, or stop requiring all of them to.

The second answer is what this section is about. A dependency that is optional — a recommendation panel, a reviews block, a personalisation call — should not be able to fail a request, and turning a hard dependency into a soft one is worth more than any amount of reliability engineering on the dependency itself.

from math import prod

def request_availability(hard, soft, per_service=0.999):
    """Soft dependencies degrade the response; they do not fail the request."""
    return prod([per_service] * hard)

for hard, soft in [(10, 0), (5, 5), (3, 7), (2, 8)]:
    a = request_availability(hard, soft)
    print(f'{hard:>2} hard + {soft} soft: {a:.4%}  ->  {(1 - a) * 43_830:>5,.0f} min/month down')

10 hard + 0 soft: 99.0045%  ->    436 min/month down
 5 hard + 5 soft: 99.5010%  ->    219 min/month down
 3 hard + 7 soft: 99.7003%  ->    131 min/month down
 2 hard + 8 soft: 99.8001%  ->     88 min/month down

Ten hard dependencies is 99.0%; two hard and eight soft is 99.8%, an eightfold reduction in downtime with no change to any dependency. Classify every call as hard or soft, in writing, and make the soft ones structurally incapable of failing the request — a short timeout, a fallback value, and no retry. Most services have never done this exercise, and most find that half their "required" calls are not.

14.2 Timeouts, and the Deadline That Travels With the Request

A call with no timeout is not a call, it is a resource leak with a plausible cover story. The default is almost always wrong: many HTTP clients wait indefinitely, and a connection that will never answer holds a thread, a connection-pool slot and a chunk of memory until the process is restarted.

The number to choose it from is the dependency's own latency distribution, not a round figure.

import random

rng = random.Random(20260825)                    # a week of measured call latencies
LATENCIES_MS = sorted(rng.lognormvariate(3.0, 0.7) for _ in range(10_000))

def percentile(values, p):
    return values[round(p * (len(values) - 1))]

for p in (0.50, 0.95, 0.99, 0.999, 1.0):
    print(f'p{p:<7.1%} {percentile(LATENCIES_MS, p):>7.0f} ms')

print()
print(f'{"timeout":>9}{"calls cut":>12}{"mean hold":>12}{"worst hold":>12}')
for timeout in (40, 80, 150, 300, 1_000):
    cut = sum(1 for latency in LATENCIES_MS if latency > timeout)
    mean_hold = sum(min(latency, timeout) for latency in LATENCIES_MS) / len(LATENCIES_MS)
    print(f'{timeout:>7} ms{cut / len(LATENCIES_MS):>12.2%}'
          f'{mean_hold:>9.1f} ms{timeout:>9} ms')

p50.0%        20 ms
p95.0%        65 ms
p99.0%       103 ms
p99.9%       167 ms
p100.0%      359 ms

  timeout   calls cut   mean hold  worst hold
     40 ms      16.66%     22.3 ms       40 ms
     80 ms       2.77%     25.2 ms       80 ms
    150 ms       0.19%     25.9 ms      150 ms
    300 ms       0.01%     25.9 ms      300 ms
   1000 ms       0.00%     25.9 ms     1000 ms

Read the last two columns together, because that is the whole argument. Between an 80 ms timeout and a 1,000 ms one the mean hold barely moves — 25.2 ms to 25.9 ms, because almost every call is fast either way — while the worst-case hold grows twelvefold. The generous timeout buys 2.77% more successful calls and costs you a twelvefold increase in how long a single misbehaving dependency can hold each of your threads. That exposure is what fills a pool (§14.6), and it is invisible in every metric except the one nobody graphs.

So set the timeout just above p99, not near the maximum. Here that is roughly 150 ms: it fails 0.19% of currently-successful calls — which were the slowest calls in the distribution and were about to be retried or abandoned anyway — and it bounds every caller's exposure to something predictable. The instinct to set it high "so we do not fail good requests" is precisely backwards, because the slow requests are the ones filling your thread pool.

The harder half is that a timeout is meaningless in isolation, because timeouts compose badly:

def naive_chain(timeouts):
    """Each service sets its own timeout, independently, with no shared deadline."""
    return sum(timeouts)

def with_deadline(budget_ms, hops):
    """The caller's deadline travels with the request; each hop gets what is left."""
    remaining, allocation = budget_ms, []
    for hop in range(hops):
        share = remaining // (hops - hop)
        allocation.append(share)
        remaining -= share
    return allocation

print('client gives up after      : 1,000 ms')
print('sum of independent timeouts:', naive_chain([800, 800, 800, 800]), 'ms')
print('work done after the client left:',
      naive_chain([800, 800, 800, 800]) - 1_000, 'ms of pure waste')
print('with a propagated deadline :', with_deadline(1_000, 4), '= 1,000 ms total')

client gives up after      : 1,000 ms
sum of independent timeouts: 3200 ms
work done after the client left: 2200 ms of pure waste
with a propagated deadline : [250, 250, 250, 250] = 1,000 ms total

Every hop after the first 1,000 ms is work nobody will ever read, and it is being done during an incident, when capacity is exactly what you do not have. The fix is a deadline, not a timeout: the entry point computes an absolute instant by which the answer is useless, passes it down with every call (gRPC has this built in; over HTTP it is a header you define), and every service clamps its own timeout to what remains. A service that finds the deadline already passed should fail immediately without doing the work at all.

Three rules make deadlines work in practice. The deadline is absolute, not a duration — a duration restarts at every hop, which is the bug it exists to fix. Reserve a margin so the caller can send a proper error rather than being cut off mid-response. And a retry spends the same budget: two attempts at 400 ms inside a 1,000 ms deadline is a plan; two attempts at 800 ms is one attempt and a lie.

14.3 Retries, and the Multiplication Nobody Budgets For

A retry is the cheapest reliability mechanism available and the most common cause of a small problem becoming a large one. The reason is that retries multiply along a call chain.

def amplification(depth, attempts_per_hop):
    return attempts_per_hop ** depth

print(f'{"chain depth":>12}{"1 try":>8}{"2 tries":>10}{"3 tries":>10}')
for depth in (1, 2, 3, 4, 5):
    row = [amplification(depth, n) for n in (1, 2, 3)]
    print(f'{depth:>12}{row[0]:>8}{row[1]:>10}{row[2]:>10}')

print()
base_rps = 20_000
for depth, attempts in [(3, 1), (3, 2), (3, 3), (5, 3)]:
    load = base_rps * amplification(depth, attempts)
    print(f'depth {depth}, {attempts} attempt(s) per hop: '
          f'{load:>9,}/s reaching the deepest service ({load // base_rps}x)')

 chain depth   1 try   2 tries   3 tries
           1       1         2         3
           2       1         4         9
           3       1         8        27
           4       1        16        81
           5       1        32       243

depth 3, 1 attempt(s) per hop:    20,000/s reaching the deepest service (1x)
depth 3, 2 attempt(s) per hop:   160,000/s reaching the deepest service (8x)
depth 3, 3 attempt(s) per hop:   540,000/s reaching the deepest service (27x)
depth 5, 3 attempt(s) per hop: 4,860,000/s reaching the deepest service (243x)

Three retries at each of five hops is a 243-fold amplification. And it arrives at exactly the wrong moment: retries fire when the deep service is already failing, so the response to overload is a two-order-of-magnitude increase in the load causing it. This is the classic retry storm, and it is why a struggling service so often cannot recover even after the original trigger is gone — the load is now self-sustaining.

Three rules contain it, and the third is the one usually missing.

Retry at one layer, not every layer. Pick the layer that knows enough to decide — usually the one closest to the user, which knows whether the request still matters — and make every other layer fail fast. A retry in the HTTP client library, another in the service wrapper and another in the gateway is 8× amplification that nobody chose.

Retry only what is retryable. A 500 may be worth retrying; a 400 never is, because it will fail identically forever. A timeout is the ambiguous case and is exactly why §11.8's idempotency matters: you do not know whether the work happened.

Give retries a budget, not just a delay. Backoff spaces out one client's retries and does nothing to stop ten thousand clients retrying simultaneously. A retry budget caps retries as a fraction of successful requests — typically 10% — so a healthy system retries freely and a failing one cannot amplify at all:

class RetryBudget:
    """Allow retries only while they stay under a ratio of successful requests."""
    def __init__(self, ratio=0.10, minimum=10):
        self.ratio, self.minimum = ratio, minimum
        self.successes, self.retries = 0, 0

    def record_success(self):
        self.successes += 1

    def allow_retry(self):
        if self.retries < self.minimum or self.retries < self.successes * self.ratio:
            self.retries += 1
            return True
        return False

def simulate(total, failure_rate, budget):
    attempted, retried, failures = 0, 0, 0
    for i in range(total):
        attempted += 1
        failed = (i % int(1 / failure_rate)) == 0 if failure_rate else False
        if not failed:
            budget.record_success()
            continue
        failures += 1
        if budget.allow_retry():
            retried += 1
    return attempted, failures, retried

for name, rate in [('healthy (1% failing)', 0.01), ('degraded (50% failing)', 0.50),
                   ('outage (100% failing)', 1.00)]:
    attempted, failures, retried = simulate(10_000, rate, RetryBudget())
    extra = retried / attempted
    print(f'{name:<24} failures {failures:>6,}  retries {retried:>6,}  '
          f'extra load {extra:>6.1%}')

healthy (1% failing)     failures    100  retries    100  extra load   1.0%
degraded (50% failing)   failures  5,000  retries    500  extra load   5.0%
outage (100% failing)    failures 10,000  retries     10  extra load   0.1%

Look at the last row. With everything failing, the budget permits ten retries in total and then stops: the extra load during a full outage is 0.1%, not 100%. That is the property backoff alone cannot give you, because backoff delays a retry and a budget declines it. Run both.

14.4 Backoff and Jitter

Given that a retry is allowed, when it happens decides whether the retries of many clients collide. Fixed delays synchronise clients; exponential backoff spaces one client out; only jitter desynchronises the fleet.

import random

def delays(strategy, attempts, base_ms, rng):
    out = []
    for n in range(attempts):
        exponential = base_ms * 2 ** n
        if strategy == 'fixed':
            out.append(base_ms)
        elif strategy == 'exponential':
            out.append(exponential)
        elif strategy == 'full jitter':
            out.append(rng.uniform(0, exponential))
        elif strategy == 'decorrelated':
            previous = out[-1] if out else base_ms
            out.append(min(30_000, rng.uniform(base_ms, previous * 3)))
    return out

rng = random.Random(20260825)
for strategy in ('fixed', 'exponential', 'full jitter', 'decorrelated'):
    schedule = delays(strategy, 6, 100, rng)
    print(f'{strategy:<14}' + ' '.join(f'{d:>8,.0f}' for d in schedule), 'ms')

fixed              100      100      100      100      100      100 ms
exponential        100      200      400      800    1,600    3,200 ms
full jitter          7      128       73      270      685      243 ms
decorrelated       101      157      459      222      296      850 ms

Now the property that actually matters — what a fleet does, not what one client does:

import random
from collections import Counter

def delays(strategy, attempts, base_ms, rng):    # as above
    out = []
    for n in range(attempts):
        exponential = base_ms * 2 ** n
        if strategy == 'fixed':
            out.append(base_ms)
        elif strategy == 'exponential':
            out.append(exponential)
        elif strategy == 'full jitter':
            out.append(rng.uniform(0, exponential))
        elif strategy == 'decorrelated':
            previous = out[-1] if out else base_ms
            out.append(min(30_000, rng.uniform(base_ms, previous * 3)))
    return out

def collisions(strategy, clients, attempts, base_ms, bucket_ms=10):
    """How many clients retry in the same 10 ms window? A spike is a self-inflicted DDoS."""
    buckets = Counter()
    for client in range(clients):
        rng = random.Random(client)
        elapsed = 0.0
        for delay in delays(strategy, attempts, base_ms, rng):
            elapsed += delay
            buckets[int(elapsed // bucket_ms)] += 1
    return max(buckets.values()), len(buckets)

print(f'{"strategy":<14}{"worst 10ms burst":>19}{"windows used":>15}')
for strategy in ('fixed', 'exponential', 'full jitter', 'decorrelated'):
    worst, spread = collisions(strategy, 1_000, 6, 100)
    print(f'{strategy:<14}{worst:>19,}{spread:>15,}')

strategy         worst 10ms burst   windows used
fixed                       1,000              6
exponential                 1,000              6
full jitter                   158            504
decorrelated                   68            907

Exponential backoff without jitter is no better than a fixed delay for this purpose. A thousand clients that failed at the same instant — which is what happens when a shared dependency goes down — compute the same delay and retry at the same instant, forever, in ever-widening but perfectly synchronised waves. The retry storm survives every doubling. Adding randomness spreads the same thousand retries over five hundred windows instead of six, and drops the peak the dependency sees from 1,000 simultaneous retries to 158 — before it has recovered enough to serve any of them.

Fixed
Every client retries on the same cadence forever. Simple, and it converts one failure into a permanent synchronised load.
Exponential
Bounds one client's total attempts and gives the dependency time. Does nothing about synchronisation, which is the fleet-level problem.
Full jitter
uniform(0, base * 2**n). The best general default: the same expected backoff, with the synchronisation destroyed. This is the one to use unless you have a reason.
Decorrelated
uniform(base, previous * 3), capped. Each delay is drawn from a range set by the previous delay rather than the attempt number, so the fleet spreads out further still — 68 in the worst window above, against full jitter's 158 — at the cost of a schedule that is harder to reason about and can run long. A reasonable choice; not one worth arguing about.

Two details that are easy to get wrong. Cap the delay — unbounded exponential backoff reaches an hour by attempt 16, so a client that would have succeeded on retry 6 is instead asleep. And cap the total attempts against the deadline from §14.2, not against a count: three attempts is not a plan if the deadline expires during the second one.

14.5 Circuit Breakers

Retries and backoff assume the dependency will come back shortly. A circuit breaker is what you use when it will not: after enough consecutive failures it stops calling the dependency at all and fails immediately, which protects the caller — its threads, its latency, its own callers — and gives the dependency room to recover.

class CircuitBreaker:
    """Three states. `now` is injected: a breaker tested against the wall clock
    is a test that passes on a fast machine and fails in CI."""
    def __init__(self, failure_threshold=5, cooldown_s=30, trial_successes=2):
        self.failure_threshold, self.cooldown_s = failure_threshold, cooldown_s
        self.trial_successes = trial_successes
        self.state, self.failures, self.successes, self.opened_at = 'closed', 0, 0, None

    def call(self, operation, now):
        if self.state == 'open':
            if now - self.opened_at < self.cooldown_s:
                return 'rejected (open)', False           # fail fast: no call made
            self.state, self.successes = 'half-open', 0
        try:
            result = operation()
        except RuntimeError as exc:
            self.on_failure(now)
            return f'error: {exc}', True
        self.on_success()
        return result, True

    def on_failure(self, now):
        self.failures += 1
        if self.state == 'half-open' or self.failures >= self.failure_threshold:
            self.state, self.opened_at = 'open', now      # one trial failure re-opens

    def on_success(self):
        if self.state == 'half-open':
            self.successes += 1
            if self.successes >= self.trial_successes:
                self.state, self.failures = 'closed', 0
        else:
            self.failures = 0

def flaky(fails_until, clock):
    def operation():
        if clock[0] < fails_until:
            raise RuntimeError('upstream down')
        return 'ok'
    return operation

clock = [0]
breaker = CircuitBreaker()
operation = flaky(fails_until=40, clock=clock)
calls_made = 0

for now in range(0, 90, 5):
    clock[0] = now
    result, called = breaker.call(operation, now)
    calls_made += called
    print(f't={now:>3}s  {breaker.state:<10} {result}')
print(f'\ncalls actually made: {calls_made} of 18 requests')

t=  0s  closed     error: upstream down
t=  5s  closed     error: upstream down
t= 10s  closed     error: upstream down
t= 15s  closed     error: upstream down
t= 20s  open       error: upstream down
t= 25s  open       rejected (open)
t= 30s  open       rejected (open)
t= 35s  open       rejected (open)
t= 40s  open       rejected (open)
t= 45s  open       rejected (open)
t= 50s  half-open  ok
t= 55s  closed     ok
t= 60s  closed     ok
t= 65s  closed     ok
t= 70s  closed     ok
t= 75s  closed     ok
t= 80s  closed     ok
t= 85s  closed     ok

calls actually made: 13 of 18 requests

Three things in that trace are the whole design.

Between t=25 and t=45 no call was made at all. The breaker opened after five failures and rejected everything for the cooldown. Those requests failed in microseconds instead of waiting for a timeout, which is the point: the caller's threads stayed free, its latency stayed flat, and its own callers never noticed.

At t=50 exactly one request was allowed through. That is the half-open state, and it is what distinguishes a circuit breaker from simply giving up. A single probe costs nothing and answers the only question that matters.

A failure in half-open re-opens immediately, without waiting for the threshold again. A half-open probe against a service still on its knees must not become a second stampede.

Four practical notes, each of which has caused a real problem:

Break per dependency and per operation, not per process. One global breaker means a failing search backend stops your checkout. The unit should be roughly "one endpoint of one downstream service".

Count a rate over a window, not consecutive failures. Five consecutive failures never happens at 5% failure rate and 10,000 rps — the successes keep resetting the counter — and yet 500 requests a second are failing. A sliding window ("more than 50% of the last 100 calls") trips correctly under partial failure.

Decide what "open" returns, and make it useful. A breaker that returns an error has converted a slow failure into a fast one, which is worth a lot. A breaker that returns a cached value, a default, or a degraded response has converted it into a success — which is where the real value is, and it needs to be designed per call site (§14.1's soft dependencies).

A breaker and a retry interact. Retrying through an open breaker is free and pointless; retrying through a closed one is how it gets opened. Put the breaker outside the retry loop, so the retries count towards tripping it and a tripped breaker stops them.

14.6 Bulkheads

A circuit breaker limits how long you wait on a failing dependency. A bulkhead limits how much of your capacity that dependency can consume in the first place — the name is from ships, where a hull is divided so one flooded compartment does not sink the vessel. Without one, a single slow dependency takes down a service that does not even need it.

def shared_pool(threads, dependencies, slow_index, slow_ms, fast_ms, request_mix):
    """One thread pool for everything. Concurrency needed = arrival rate * service time."""
    used = 0.0
    for index, share in enumerate(request_mix):
        latency = slow_ms if index == slow_index else fast_ms
        used += share * latency / 1000
    return used, used > threads

def bulkheaded(threads, dependencies, slow_index, slow_ms, fast_ms, request_mix):
    """Each dependency gets its own slice. A slow one exhausts only its own."""
    per_dependency = threads // dependencies
    starved = []
    for index, share in enumerate(request_mix):
        latency = slow_ms if index == slow_index else fast_ms
        need = share * latency / 1000
        if need > per_dependency:
            starved.append(index)
    return per_dependency, starved

MIX = [900, 900, 900, 300]          # requests/s to each of four dependencies
used, exhausted = shared_pool(200, 4, slow_index=3, slow_ms=8_000,
                              fast_ms=20, request_mix=MIX)
print(f'shared pool of 200 threads: {used:,.0f} threads needed  exhausted: {exhausted}')
print('  -> every endpoint fails, including the three healthy ones')

per, starved = bulkheaded(200, 4, slow_index=3, slow_ms=8_000,
                          fast_ms=20, request_mix=MIX)
print(f'bulkheads of {per} threads each: dependencies starved: {starved}')
print('  -> dependency 3 fails; 0, 1 and 2 need',
      f'{900 * 20 / 1000:.0f} threads each and are unaffected')

shared pool of 200 threads: 2,454 threads needed  exhausted: True
  -> every endpoint fails, including the three healthy ones
bulkheads of 50 threads each: dependencies starved: [3]
  -> dependency 3 fails; 0, 1 and 2 need 18 threads each and are unaffected

The slow dependency needed 2,400 threads and there were 200. In the shared design it takes all of them, and the three healthy dependencies — which between them need 54 threads — get nothing. The service is completely down because one of its four dependencies got slow, and the three working endpoints are working perfectly with nowhere to run.

Bulkheads come in several forms, in ascending order of isolation and cost:

Concurrency limit
A semaphore per dependency: at most N in flight, the rest rejected immediately. Nearly free, no extra threads, and it is the one to start with. This is what the code above models.
Separate pools
A thread pool or connection pool per dependency. Stronger — a blocked call cannot consume another pool's threads — at the cost of context switching and memory.
Separate instances
Different processes or deployments for different classes of traffic: reads and writes, free tier and paid, batch and interactive. A crash or an OOM is now contained too.
Separate everything
Cells: a full stack per group of tenants, sharing nothing. The strongest isolation available and the most expensive; the blast radius of any failure is one cell.

The connection pool is the bulkhead people forget. A service with one 50-connection database pool shared by a fast user lookup and a slow report query has already built the shared-pool failure above — the reports take every connection and the lookups time out waiting for one. Two pools, sized separately, is a configuration change that prevents an entire class of incident.

The limit itself comes from Little's law and nothing else: concurrency = arrival rate × service time, plus headroom. Nine hundred requests a second at 20 ms is 18 concurrent; setting that bulkhead to 40 leaves room for a latency excursion and still guarantees the dependency cannot take more than 40 of your 200 threads no matter how badly it behaves.

14.7 Rate Limiting: the Four Algorithms

A rate limit protects a service from its callers — deliberate abuse, an accidental loop, or one tenant's batch job. Rate limiting and throttling are often used interchangeably and are worth separating: a rate limit rejects what exceeds the allowance, while throttling slows it — queueing or delaying rather than refusing. Throttling is gentler on a well-behaved client and dangerous under real overload, because a throttled request still occupies a connection and a thread (§14.6). The choice of algorithm decides how either one treats bursts, and the differences are large enough to matter.

class FixedWindow:
    """Simplest. Allows a 2x burst across a window boundary."""
    def __init__(self, limit, window_s):
        self.limit, self.window_s, self.counts = limit, window_s, {}

    def allow(self, now):
        window = int(now // self.window_s)
        self.counts[window] = self.counts.get(window, 0) + 1
        return self.counts[window] <= self.limit

class SlidingLog:
    """Exact, and stores one timestamp per request."""
    def __init__(self, limit, window_s):
        self.limit, self.window_s, self.log = limit, window_s, []

    def allow(self, now):
        self.log = [t for t in self.log if t > now - self.window_s]
        if len(self.log) < self.limit:
            self.log.append(now)
            return True
        return False

class SlidingCounter:
    """Two counters and a weighted estimate. The usual production choice."""
    def __init__(self, limit, window_s):
        self.limit, self.window_s, self.counts = limit, window_s, {}

    def allow(self, now):
        window = int(now // self.window_s)
        elapsed = (now % self.window_s) / self.window_s
        estimate = self.counts.get(window - 1, 0) * (1 - elapsed) + self.counts.get(window, 0)
        if estimate < self.limit:
            self.counts[window] = self.counts.get(window, 0) + 1
            return True
        return False

class TokenBucket:
    """Allows a controlled burst up to the bucket size, then a steady rate."""
    def __init__(self, rate_per_s, burst):
        self.rate, self.burst = rate_per_s, burst
        self.tokens, self.updated = float(burst), 0.0

    def allow(self, now):
        self.tokens = min(self.burst, self.tokens + (now - self.updated) * self.rate)
        self.updated = now
        if self.tokens >= 1:
            self.tokens -= 1
            return True
        return False

# 10 requests/second limit. The attack: 10 at the end of one window, 10 at the start
# of the next — 20 requests in a fraction of a second, both windows within their limit.
BOUNDARY = [59.9] * 10 + [60.1] * 10

print(f'{"algorithm":<18}{"allowed of 20":>15}{"verdict":>34}')
for name, limiter in [
        ('fixed window', FixedWindow(10, 60)),
        ('sliding log', SlidingLog(10, 60)),
        ('sliding counter', SlidingCounter(10, 60)),
        ('token bucket', TokenBucket(10 / 60, burst=10))]:
    allowed = sum(limiter.allow(t) for t in BOUNDARY)
    verdict = 'lets a 2x burst through' if allowed > 12 else 'holds the limit'
    print(f'{name:<18}{allowed:>15}{verdict:>34}')

algorithm           allowed of 20                           verdict
fixed window                   20           lets a 2x burst through
sliding log                    10                   holds the limit
sliding counter                11                   holds the limit
token bucket                   10                   holds the limit
Fixed window
One counter per window. Trivial and memory-free, and it permits twice the limit across a boundary, as above. Fine when the limit is a rough guard rail, wrong when it protects a hard capacity.
Sliding log
Exactly correct, and stores a timestamp per request per key — at a million keys and a thousand requests each, that is a billion timestamps. Correct and rarely affordable.
Sliding counter
Two counters and a linear interpolation between them. Within a couple of per cent of exact at a fraction of a per cent of the memory. The default choice, and what most gateways implement.
Token bucket
Two numbers per key, and the only one that expresses rate and burst separately. "10 per second sustained, 50 in a burst" is exactly what an API wants to offer, and it is impossible to say in any window-based scheme.

Choose between the last two on whether bursts are welcome. A token bucket lets a well-behaved client that has been idle spend its accumulated allowance — which is usually the desired behaviour for an API, since the client is not the problem. A sliding counter enforces smoothness, which is what you want in front of a resource that cannot absorb a burst at all.

Two things a limiter must do beyond counting. Say what happened: return 429, and a Retry-After telling the client when to come back — a limit the client cannot see turns into a retry storm (§14.3). And limit the right key: per API key for quota, per IP for abuse, per tenant for fairness, and per expensive-operation for protection. A single global limit protects the service and lets one caller consume everyone's share, which is a fairness bug wearing a resilience costume.

14.8 Enforcing a Limit Across a Fleet

The implementations above hold state in one process. With twenty gateway nodes and a per-process limiter, the effective limit is twenty times what you configured — and dividing by the node count is wrong too, because traffic is never balanced perfectly and a rebalance changes the divisor.

def local_limits(global_limit, nodes, distribution):
    """Each node enforces global_limit/nodes. What does the client actually get?"""
    per_node = global_limit / nodes
    allowed = sum(min(share, per_node) for share in distribution)
    return per_node, allowed

EVEN = [50] * 20
SKEWED = [220, 150, 120] + [30] * 17          # sticky sessions, hashed routing, retries

for name, distribution in [('even', EVEN), ('skewed', SKEWED)]:
    demand = sum(distribution)
    per_node, allowed = local_limits(1_000, 20, distribution)
    print(f'{name:<8} demand {demand:>5,}/s  per-node cap {per_node:>5,.0f}  '
          f'allowed {allowed:>6,.0f}/s  ({allowed / 1_000:.0%} of the intended limit)')

even     demand 1,000/s  per-node cap    50  allowed  1,000/s  (100% of the intended limit)
skewed   demand 1,000/s  per-node cap    50  allowed    660/s  (66% of the intended limit)

Under skew the client is cut off at 66% of the limit it was sold, while the service is running at 66% of the capacity it provisioned. Both sides lose, and nobody can see why. Three workable designs:

Centralised counter
Every node increments a counter in Redis. Exactly correct, and it adds a network round trip to every request and makes the limiter store a hard dependency of the request path — so it needs its own bulkhead and a fail-open policy.
Local with periodic sync
Each node enforces locally and reports its usage every second; allowances are redistributed to where the traffic actually is. Approximate for one second, no per-request round trip. The usual answer at scale.
Sticky routing
Route a key consistently to one node (§8.4), so its limiter is authoritative with no coordination at all. Free and exact, and it inherits every hot-key and rebalancing problem partitioning has.

Decide fail-open or fail-closed explicitly, because the default is whatever the code happens to do. A rate limiter for abuse protection should probably fail closed — if you cannot tell whether this is an attack, do not serve it. A rate limiter for fairness between paying tenants should fail open — a Redis blip must not take down the API. Write the choice down next to the limit.

14.9 Graceful Shutdown

Every deploy stops processes. On a fleet deploying several times a day, shutdown is not an edge case — it is a routine event happening constantly, and doing it badly produces a steady background of errors that everyone learns to ignore.

The naive sequence loses requests, and the reason is a race nobody sees until they look for it:

def shutdown(sequence, in_flight=12, arrival_rate=40, drain_s=15, deregister_lag_s=5):
    """Return (requests lost, requests completed) for each shutdown ordering."""
    if sequence == 'stop immediately':
        return in_flight + arrival_rate * deregister_lag_s, 0
    if sequence == 'drain, then deregister':
        # still in the load balancer's pool while draining: new work keeps arriving
        return arrival_rate * deregister_lag_s, in_flight
    if sequence == 'deregister, then drain':
        # the lag is spent still serving; only work arriving in that window is served
        return 0, in_flight + arrival_rate * deregister_lag_s
    raise ValueError(sequence)

for sequence in ('stop immediately', 'drain, then deregister', 'deregister, then drain'):
    lost, completed = shutdown(sequence)
    print(f'{sequence:<26} lost {lost:>4}  completed {completed:>4}')

stop immediately           lost  212  completed    0
drain, then deregister     lost  200  completed   12
deregister, then drain     lost    0  completed  212

Deregistration is not instantaneous, and that lag is the whole problem. A load balancer learns a node is gone through a health check that runs every few seconds, or through a registry update that propagates asynchronously. In between, it keeps sending traffic. So the correct sequence has five steps and the first two are the ones usually missing:

1
Fail the readiness check on SIGTERM, while continuing to serve normally. This is what tells the load balancer to stop sending new work.
2
Keep serving for longer than the deregistration lag — two or three health-check intervals. This is the step that turns lost requests into zero, and it is counter-intuitive: the process is deliberately doing nothing but waiting.
3
Stop accepting new connections, and close idle keep-alive connections with Connection: close so clients reconnect elsewhere rather than reusing a socket that is about to vanish.
4
Finish in-flight requests, up to a drain timeout. Stop background consumers too — a queue worker must finish or return its current message, not abandon it.
5
Flush and exit. Write-behind buffers (§9.4), metrics, traces and logs are all lost otherwise, and they are exactly what you will want if the deploy goes badly.

Three details decide whether this works. The drain timeout must be shorter than the orchestrator's kill timeout — Kubernetes sends SIGKILL after terminationGracePeriodSeconds, and a 60-second drain under a 30-second grace period is an ungraceful shutdown with extra steps. Readiness and liveness are different checks: readiness says "send me traffic", liveness says "I am not wedged", and returning failure from the liveness probe during shutdown gets the process killed rather than drained. And long-lived connections need their own plan — a WebSocket or a streaming response cannot simply be drained, so the server must send a close frame and let clients reconnect, staggered, or a deploy becomes a synchronised reconnect storm (§14.4).

Exercises

Exercise 14.1 — Diagnose the outage. A checkout service calls four dependencies. At 09:00 the recommendations service — used only to show a "you might also like" panel — starts responding in 30 seconds instead of 40 ms. By 09:02 checkout is entirely down, including for users who never see the panel. The recommendations service recovers at 09:10; checkout does not recover until it is restarted at 09:40. Explain every part of that timeline and give the four changes that would have prevented it.

Solution 
TIMELINE = [
    ('09:00', 'recommendations latency 40ms -> 30s',
     'the trigger; a dependency got slow, not down'),
    ('09:00-09:02', 'threads accumulate in the shared pool',
     'Little\'s law: 200 rps x 30s = 6,000 threads needed, pool has 200'),
    ('09:02', 'checkout is fully down',
     'no threads left for payments, inventory or pricing (§14.6)'),
    ('09:02+', 'clients retry, doubling arrival rate',
     'retry amplification against an already-saturated pool (§14.3)'),
    ('09:10', 'recommendations recovers, checkout does not',
     'the queue is now self-sustaining: retries alone exceed capacity'),
    ('09:40', 'restart clears it',
     'the only thing that drops the backlog — the missing mechanism is load shedding'),
]
for when, what, why in TIMELINE:
    print(f'{when:<12} {what}\n{"":12} -> {why}')

print()
def threads_needed(rps, latency_s):
    return rps * latency_s

for latency in (0.04, 1.0, 30.0):
    print(f'recommendations at {latency:>5.2f}s: '
          f'{threads_needed(200, latency):>7,.0f} threads needed (pool = 200)')

09:00        recommendations latency 40ms -> 30s
             -> the trigger; a dependency got slow, not down
09:00-09:02  threads accumulate in the shared pool
             -> Little's law: 200 rps x 30s = 6,000 threads needed, pool has 200
09:02        checkout is fully down
             -> no threads left for payments, inventory or pricing (§14.6)
09:02+       clients retry, doubling arrival rate
             -> retry amplification against an already-saturated pool (§14.3)
09:10        recommendations recovers, checkout does not
             -> the queue is now self-sustaining: retries alone exceed capacity
09:40        restart clears it
             -> the only thing that drops the backlog — the missing mechanism is load shedding

recommendations at  0.04s:       8 threads needed (pool = 200)
recommendations at  1.00s:     200 threads needed (pool = 200)
recommendations at 30.00s:   6,000 threads needed (pool = 200)

The trigger is slowness, not failure, and that is what makes it so damaging. A dependency that returns an error frees the thread immediately; a dependency that takes 30 seconds holds it. Nothing in the system was designed to fail, so nothing did — it just stopped having anywhere to run.

The four changes, in order of how much they would have helped:

1. A bulkhead on recommendations (§14.6). A semaphore of 20 concurrent calls means recommendations can consume at most 20 of the 200 threads no matter how slow it gets. Checkout's other three dependencies are untouched, and the panel simply does not render. This change alone converts the outage into a cosmetic degradation.

2. A timeout matched to the dependency (§14.2). A 30-second wait for a 40 ms call is a timeout that was never set, or was set to a client-library default. At 200 ms, each thread is held 150× less time — 40 threads instead of 6,000 — which is survivable on its own.

3. Make it a soft dependency (§14.1). The panel is decorative. It should have a short timeout, a fallback (an empty panel, or a cached generic list), and no retry, and its failure should never propagate. This is the change that should have existed before the incident, and the one that is cheapest to make.

4. A circuit breaker (§14.5). After the first seconds of failures, stop calling recommendations entirely and serve the fallback. It also explains the 09:10–09:40 gap: with a breaker, recovery is automatic at the next half-open probe, and no restart is needed.

And the reason the restart was required at all is that nothing shed load. Once the arrival rate exceeded capacity, the backlog grew without bound and every request in it was already past its deadline by the time it was served — work being done for clients that left. A concurrency limit that rejects immediately when the queue is full (§3) turns "down until restarted" into "degraded while the dependency is slow".

Exercise 14.2 — Build a resilient client. Write a client wrapper combining a deadline, a bulkhead, a circuit breaker, retries with full jitter, and a retry budget — in the correct order, with the interactions right. Demonstrate that (a) retries stop when the deadline is spent, (b) the breaker opens and the retries stop with it, and (c) the bulkhead rejects rather than queueing.

Solution

The ordering is the exercise. From the outside in: deadline, bulkhead, retry loop, budget, breaker, call. Every one of those positions is load-bearing.

The deadline is outermost because it governs all attempts, not each one. The bulkhead is outside the retry loop — otherwise a retry acquires a second permit and a retrying client can consume the whole limit by itself. The breaker is inside the retry loop so that failed attempts count towards tripping it, and so that once it trips, the remaining retries are rejected in microseconds rather than being attempted.

import random

class Rejected(RuntimeError):
    pass

class ResilientClient:
    def __init__(self, breaker, concurrency=10, budget_ratio=0.10,
                 max_attempts=3, base_delay_ms=50, seed=20260825):
        self.breaker, self.limit = breaker, concurrency
        self.in_flight = 0
        self.max_attempts, self.base_delay_ms = max_attempts, base_delay_ms
        self.budget_ratio, self.successes, self.retries = budget_ratio, 0, 0
        self.rng = random.Random(seed)

    def allow_retry(self):
        if self.retries < 10 or self.retries < self.successes * self.budget_ratio:
            self.retries += 1
            return True
        return False

    def call(self, operation, now, deadline, trace):
        if self.in_flight >= self.limit:                       # bulkhead: reject, never queue
            trace.append('bulkhead: rejected immediately')
            return 'rejected'
        self.in_flight += 1
        try:
            elapsed = 0.0
            for attempt in range(1, self.max_attempts + 1):
                if now + elapsed >= deadline:                  # deadline governs all attempts
                    trace.append(f'attempt {attempt}: deadline spent, giving up')
                    return 'deadline exceeded'
                result, called = self.breaker.call(operation, now + elapsed)
                if not called:
                    trace.append(f'attempt {attempt}: {result}')
                    return 'circuit open'                      # no point retrying an open breaker
                if not result.startswith('error'):
                    self.successes += 1
                    trace.append(f'attempt {attempt}: {result}')
                    return result
                trace.append(f'attempt {attempt}: {result}')
                if attempt == self.max_attempts or not self.allow_retry():
                    trace.append(f'attempt {attempt}: no retry (budget or attempts exhausted)')
                    return 'failed'
                delay = self.rng.uniform(0, self.base_delay_ms * 2 ** (attempt - 1)) / 1000
                elapsed += delay + 0.4                         # the delay plus the call itself
                trace.append(f'          backoff {delay * 1000:.0f} ms (full jitter)')
            return 'failed'
        finally:
            self.in_flight -= 1


class CircuitBreaker:
    def __init__(self, failure_threshold=5, cooldown_s=30, trial_successes=2):
        self.failure_threshold, self.cooldown_s = failure_threshold, cooldown_s
        self.trial_successes = trial_successes
        self.state, self.failures, self.successes, self.opened_at = 'closed', 0, 0, None

    def call(self, operation, now):
        if self.state == 'open':
            if now - self.opened_at < self.cooldown_s:
                return 'rejected (open)', False
            self.state, self.successes = 'half-open', 0
        try:
            return operation(), True
        except RuntimeError as exc:
            self.failures += 1
            if self.state == 'half-open' or self.failures >= self.failure_threshold:
                self.state, self.opened_at = 'open', now
            return f'error: {exc}', True


def always_fails():
    raise RuntimeError('upstream 503')

def always_works():
    return 'ok'

print('--- (a) the deadline stops the retries')
client = ResilientClient(CircuitBreaker(failure_threshold=99), max_attempts=5)
trace = []
print('  result:', client.call(always_fails, now=0.0, deadline=1.0, trace=trace))
for line in trace:
    print('   ', line)

print('\n--- (b) the breaker opens, and the retries stop with it')
breaker = CircuitBreaker(failure_threshold=3)
client = ResilientClient(breaker, max_attempts=5)
trace = []
print('  result:', client.call(always_fails, now=0.0, deadline=60.0, trace=trace))
for line in trace:
    print('   ', line)
print('    breaker state:', breaker.state)
trace = []
print('  next request:', client.call(always_works, now=1.0, deadline=60.0, trace=trace))
for line in trace:
    print('   ', line)

print('\n--- (c) the bulkhead rejects rather than queueing')
client = ResilientClient(CircuitBreaker(), concurrency=2)
client.in_flight = 2                                  # two calls already running
trace = []
print('  result:', client.call(always_works, now=0.0, deadline=60.0, trace=trace))
for line in trace:
    print('   ', line)

--- (a) the deadline stops the retries
  result: deadline exceeded
    attempt 1: error: upstream 503
              backoff 4 ms (full jitter)
    attempt 2: error: upstream 503
              backoff 64 ms (full jitter)
    attempt 3: error: upstream 503
              backoff 37 ms (full jitter)
    attempt 4: deadline spent, giving up

--- (b) the breaker opens, and the retries stop with it
  result: circuit open
    attempt 1: error: upstream 503
              backoff 4 ms (full jitter)
    attempt 2: error: upstream 503
              backoff 64 ms (full jitter)
    attempt 3: error: upstream 503
              backoff 37 ms (full jitter)
    attempt 4: rejected (open)
    breaker state: open
  next request: circuit open
    attempt 1: rejected (open)

--- (c) the bulkhead rejects rather than queueing
  result: rejected
    bulkhead: rejected immediately

Read the three traces against the ordering.

(a) Five attempts were budgeted and only three were made: the deadline ended it, because each attempt costs its own latency plus its backoff, and the client tracks the running total rather than counting attempts. A client that counts attempts alone will reliably blow through its caller's deadline (§14.2) — five attempts at 400 ms is two seconds, whatever the configuration file says.

(b) The breaker tripped on the third failure, and attempt 4 was rejected in microseconds instead of being made. That is the interaction the ordering buys: the retries fed the breaker, and the breaker then stopped the retries. The next request is rejected too, without touching the dependency — which is the entire point, and is what gives the dependency room to recover.

(c) The bulkhead rejected immediately rather than waiting for a permit. Queueing for a bulkhead defeats it: the caller's thread is held while it waits, which is precisely the resource the bulkhead exists to protect. A rejection here should map to a fallback or a 503 with Retry-After, not to an exception the caller has no plan for.

What is deliberately not here: a fallback value. Every one of these mechanisms converts a slow failure into a fast one, and only a fallback converts it into a success. The wrapper is the cheap half of resilience; deciding what each call site does when the wrapper says no is the half that determines whether users notice.

Exercise 14.3 — Set every number. For a payment API — 5,000 requests/s, a 2-second client deadline, a payment processor whose latency is p50 90 ms / p99 600 ms / p999 4 s and which has roughly one 5-minute outage a month — choose and justify: the timeout, the retry policy, the circuit-breaker thresholds, the bulkhead size, and the rate limit. Then state what a caller experiences during the monthly outage.

Solution 
RPS, DEADLINE_MS = 5_000, 2_000
P50, P99, P999 = 90, 600, 4_000

timeout_ms = 800                      # just above p99
attempts = 2                          # 2 x 800 = 1,600 ms, inside the 2,000 ms deadline
budget_used = attempts * timeout_ms

print('timeout        :', timeout_ms, 'ms  (p99 =', P99, 'ms, p999 =', P999, 'ms)')
print('attempts       :', attempts, f'-> {budget_used} ms of a {DEADLINE_MS} ms deadline')
print('margin left    :', DEADLINE_MS - budget_used, 'ms for backoff and our own work')
cut_off = 'between p99 and p999' if P99 < timeout_ms < P999 else 'the wrong slice'
print('cut off        :', cut_off, '- under 1% of calls, and the slowest ones')

concurrency = RPS * (timeout_ms / 1000)
steady = RPS * (P50 / 1000)
print('\nbulkhead       :', f'{steady:,.0f} concurrent at p50,',
      f'{concurrency:,.0f} at the timeout')
print('               : size it at', f'{steady * 2:,.0f}',
      '- 2x steady state, far below the timeout-case worst')

failures_per_window = 0.5
print('\nbreaker        : >50% of the last 100 calls failing, 30s cooldown, 3 trial successes')
print('               : at', f'{RPS:,}', 'rps a 100-call window fills in',
      f'{100 / RPS * 1000:.0f} ms — fast detection, and a rate not a streak')

print('\nrate limit     : token bucket, per API key: 100/s sustained, 300 burst')
print('               : sum of key limits may exceed', f'{RPS:,}',
      'rps — the limit is fairness, the bulkhead is capacity')

outage_s = 5 * 60
print('\n--- the monthly 5-minute outage ---')
print('t=0.0s   first failures; each caller waits', timeout_ms, 'ms, retries once, fails at',
      f'{budget_used} ms')
print('t=0.02s  breaker opens (100 calls at', f'{RPS:,}', 'rps)')
print('t=0.02s+ every call fails in microseconds, not', f'{budget_used} ms')
print('         threads held:', f'{concurrency:,.0f} -> ~0')
print('t=30s    one half-open probe; still failing; re-opens immediately')
print('t=300s   probe succeeds twice; breaker closes; full traffic resumes')
print('caller sees:', f'{outage_s // 30}', 'probes over',
      outage_s // 60, 'minutes, and a fast 503 the rest of the time')

timeout        : 800 ms  (p99 = 600 ms, p999 = 4000 ms)
attempts       : 2 -> 1600 ms of a 2000 ms deadline
margin left    : 400 ms for backoff and our own work
cut off        : between p99 and p999 - under 1% of calls, and the slowest ones

bulkhead       : 450 concurrent at p50, 4,000 at the timeout
               : size it at 900 - 2x steady state, far below the timeout-case worst

breaker        : >50% of the last 100 calls failing, 30s cooldown, 3 trial successes
               : at 5,000 rps a 100-call window fills in 20 ms — fast detection, and a rate not a streak

rate limit     : token bucket, per API key: 100/s sustained, 300 burst
               : sum of key limits may exceed 5,000 rps — the limit is fairness, the bulkhead is capacity

--- the monthly 5-minute outage ---
t=0.0s   first failures; each caller waits 800 ms, retries once, fails at 1600 ms
t=0.02s  breaker opens (100 calls at 5,000 rps)
t=0.02s+ every call fails in microseconds, not 1600 ms
         threads held: 4,000 -> ~0
t=30s    one half-open probe; still failing; re-opens immediately
t=300s   probe succeeds twice; breaker closes; full traffic resumes
caller sees: 10 probes over 5 minutes, and a fast 503 the rest of the time

Every number above comes from a measurement, and that is the point of the exercise — none of them is a round figure chosen because it looked reasonable.

The timeout is p99 plus a little, and the attempt count is derived from the deadline rather than chosen. Two attempts at 800 ms is 1,600 ms of a 2,000 ms budget, leaving 400 ms for backoff and the service's own work. Three attempts would not fit, so the retry policy is decided by the timeout, not configured independently — and this is the calculation that most retry configurations skip.

The bulkhead is sized from steady state, not from the worst case. At p50, 5,000 rps needs 450 concurrent calls; at the timeout it would need 4,000. Sizing for 4,000 means provisioning for a pathology and letting the processor consume everything when it happens. Sizing at 900 — twice steady state — absorbs a real latency excursion and hard-caps the damage.

The breaker uses a rate over a window, not consecutive failures, because at 5,000 rps a 5% failure rate never produces five in a row while still failing 250 requests a second (§14.5). A 100-call window fills in 20 ms, so detection is effectively instant.

The rate limit is about fairness, not capacity, and that distinction decides its shape. Per-key limits deliberately sum to more than the fleet can serve — most keys are idle most of the time — and the bulkhead and load shedding are what protect capacity. A token bucket lets a merchant with a quiet morning process a legitimate batch in the afternoon, which is behaviour you want to permit.

And during the outage, the caller's experience is the design's real output. For 20 milliseconds, callers wait 1.6 seconds and fail. For the remaining 4 minutes 59 seconds they get an immediate 503 with Retry-After, no threads are consumed, the rest of the API is unaffected, and recovery is automatic on the probe after the processor returns. Compare that to the same outage with no breaker: five minutes at 4,000 concurrent held threads, which is not a payment outage, it is a total one. The mechanisms in this section did not prevent a single failed payment — they confined a processor's outage to the payments path and made it end without a human.

SECTION 15

Operations

A design that cannot be observed cannot be operated, and a system nobody can see inside fails in ways nobody can explain. This section is about the parts of a system that exist for the people running it: knowing what it is doing, finding out why when it stops, changing it without breaking it, and learning from the times it broke anyway. These are design decisions, not an afterthought — instrumenting a system after it is built produces exactly the metrics that were easy to add rather than the ones that answer questions.

15.1 Monitoring Answers "Is It Broken?"; Observability Answers "Why?"

The distinction is not pedantry, and it decides what you build.

Monitoring
Watching a known set of signals for known failure modes. You decided in advance what to measure, so it can only tell you about problems you anticipated. Cheap, essential, and blind to everything else.
Observability
Being able to ask new questions of a running system without deploying anything. It is a property of how much context the system emits, and the test is whether you can answer a question you did not think of beforehand.

The practical difference is cardinality — how many distinct things a signal can distinguish — and it is also where the cost lives:

def series(dimensions):
    total = 1
    for _, values in dimensions:
        total *= values
    return total

BASE = [('endpoint', 40), ('status code', 8), ('method', 5)]
print(f'{"metric labels":<44}{"time series":>14}')
print(f'{"endpoint x status x method":<44}{series(BASE):>14,}')
for name, values in [('+ instance (200 pods)', 200), ('+ customer id (50,000)', 50_000)]:
    BASE.append((name, values))
    print(f'{name:<44}{series(BASE):>14,}')

metric labels                                  time series
endpoint x status x method                           1,600
+ instance (200 pods)                              320,000
+ customer id (50,000)                      16,000,000,000

Adding a customer id as a metric label turns 1,600 time series into 16 billion, which no metrics system will store and which is why "just add a label for it" is the most expensive suggestion in a design review. High-cardinality questions — "what happened to this customer's request?" — belong in traces and logs, which are sampled and indexed rather than aggregated.

That gives the division of labour between the three signals:

Metrics
Cheap, aggregated, low cardinality. Constant cost per series regardless of traffic, so they can be kept for years. Answer "how many" and "how fast", never "which one".
Logs
High cardinality, high volume, expensive to store and search. Answer "what exactly happened to this request". Structured — key-value, not prose — or they cannot be queried.
Traces
One request's path across every service, with timing per hop. The only signal that answers "where did the 2 seconds go" in a distributed call graph, and the one most systems lack.

Start with metrics, add tracing before you think you need it, and treat logs as the expensive one. Tracing is the signal that is hardest to retrofit, because it requires context propagation through every service and every client library — and it is the signal that turns a four-hour investigation into a four-minute one (§15.3).

15.2 The Signals Worth Alerting On

Most dashboards measure what is easy. Two small, standard sets measure what matters, and between them they cover nearly everything.

RED = [('Rate', 'requests per second'),
       ('Errors', 'failed requests per second, and as a proportion'),
       ('Duration', 'the latency distribution — p50, p95, p99, p999')]
USE = [('Utilisation', 'proportion of time the resource is busy'),
       ('Saturation', 'how much work is queued and waiting'),
       ('Errors', 'error events for that resource')]

print('RED — for anything serving requests:')
for name, meaning in RED:
    print(f'   {name:<14}{meaning}')
print('\nUSE — for anything with a finite capacity (CPU, disk, pool, queue):')
for name, meaning in USE:
    print(f'   {name:<14}{meaning}')

print('\nsaturation leads utilisation, which leads errors:')
for utilisation, queue, errors in [(0.60, 0, 0.000), (0.85, 3, 0.000),
                                   (0.95, 40, 0.002), (0.99, 900, 0.180)]:
    print(f'   utilisation {utilisation:>5.0%}   queued {queue:>4}   errors {errors:>6.1%}')

RED — for anything serving requests:
   Rate          requests per second
   Errors        failed requests per second, and as a proportion
   Duration      the latency distribution — p50, p95, p99, p999

USE — for anything with a finite capacity (CPU, disk, pool, queue):
   Utilisation   proportion of time the resource is busy
   Saturation    how much work is queued and waiting
   Errors        error events for that resource

saturation leads utilisation, which leads errors:
   utilisation   60%   queued    0   errors   0.0%
   utilisation   85%   queued    3   errors   0.0%
   utilisation   95%   queued   40   errors   0.2%
   utilisation   99%   queued  900   errors  18.0%

Saturation moves first, and that is why it is the signal to alert on. By the time the error rate is visible the system is already failing; the queue started growing minutes earlier. This is the same argument §3.6 makes about shedding on concurrency rather than on errors, and §10.9 makes about alerting on message age rather than depth.

Averages are the other place dashboards mislead, and the demonstration is worth doing:

LATENCIES = [20] * 990 + [4_000] * 10          # 1% of requests are terrible

def percentile(values, p):
    ordered = sorted(values)
    return ordered[min(len(ordered) - 1, int(len(ordered) * p))]

mean = sum(LATENCIES) / len(LATENCIES)
print(f'mean  {mean:>8,.0f} ms')
for p in (0.50, 0.95, 0.99, 0.999):
    print(f'p{p:<5.1%}{percentile(LATENCIES, p):>8,} ms')

users_affected = sum(1 for latency in LATENCIES if latency > 1_000)
print(f'\nrequests over 1s: {users_affected} of {len(LATENCIES)} '
      f'({users_affected / len(LATENCIES):.1%})')
print('the mean says 60 ms and hides all of them')

mean        60 ms
p50.0%      20 ms
p95.0%      20 ms
p99.0%   4,000 ms
p99.9%   4,000 ms

requests over 1s: 10 of 1000 (1.0%)
the mean says 60 ms and hides all of them

A mean of 60 ms describes a system where one request in a hundred takes four seconds. Alert on percentiles, and remember that a user making twenty requests to render one page has a good chance of hitting the p99 at least once — the tail is the experience, not an outlier.

Two rules for alerts themselves, because an alerting system that cries wolf is worse than none:

Every alert must be actionable and must name the action. An alert with no runbook trains the on-call engineer to acknowledge and ignore, and that habit is what makes them miss the real one.

Alert on symptoms, not causes. "p99 latency above the SLO" is worth waking someone for; "CPU above 80%" is not, because a system can be at 90% CPU and perfectly healthy. Cause-based alerts multiply as the system grows and are the main source of alert fatigue — page on the SLO burn rate (§3.2), and let everything else be a dashboard or a ticket.

15.3 Distributed Tracing

In a monolith, a stack trace answers "where did the time go". Across twelve services it does not exist, and without tracing the answer is assembled by hand from twelve sets of logs.

SPANS = [
    ('gateway',        0,   840, 0),
    ('  auth',        2,     18, 1),
    ('  orders',      22,   790, 1),
    ('    postgres',  26,    14, 2),
    ('    pricing',   42,   120, 2),
    ('    inventory', 165,   38, 2),
    ('    shipping',  205,  600, 2),
    ('      carrier-api', 210, 590, 3),
    ('  render',      815,   22, 1),
]
WIDTH, TOTAL = 56, 840
print(f'{"span":<18}{"start":>7}{"ms":>7}  timeline')
for name, start, duration, depth in SPANS:
    left = round(start / TOTAL * WIDTH)
    bar = round(duration / TOTAL * WIDTH) or 1
    print(f'{name:<18}{start:>7}{duration:>7}  {" " * left}{"=" * bar}')

leaf = max((s for s in SPANS if s[3] == 3), key=lambda s: s[2])
print(f'\nthe answer: {leaf[0].strip()} accounts for {leaf[2]}ms of {TOTAL}ms '
      f'({leaf[2] / TOTAL:.0%})')

span                start     ms  timeline
gateway                 0    840  ========================================================
  auth                  2     18  =
  orders               22    790   =====================================================
    postgres           26     14    =
    pricing            42    120     ========
    inventory         165     38             ===
    shipping          205    600                ========================================
      carrier-api     210    590                =======================================
  render              815     22                                                        =

the answer: carrier-api accounts for 590ms of 840ms (70%)

Seventy per cent of the request is one call to an external carrier API, four levels down. No metric on any individual service would show that: each one reports its own latency, all of them look busy, and shipping appears slow when it is merely waiting. A trace is the only signal that attributes time across a call graph, and this is the question it exists to answer.

Three things decide whether tracing works at all:

Context must propagate through everything. The trace id travels in a header — the W3C traceparent standard — and any hop that drops it severs the trace there. Queues are the usual gap: a message must carry the trace context in its metadata, or the asynchronous half of the system is invisible (§10).

Sample, and sample intelligently. Tracing every request at scale costs more than the system. Head-based sampling decides at the entry point — cheap, and it throws away the interesting requests along with the boring ones. Tail-based sampling decides after the trace completes, keeping everything that errored or was slow plus a small percentage of the rest, which is what you actually want and costs more to run.

Put the trace id everywhere. In every log line, in every error response, in the support ticket. A user reporting "my order failed at 14:32" is a needle in a haystack; a user quoting a trace id is one query.

And traces have a second use that is worth as much as debugging: they document the system. A service map derived from real traces shows the calls that actually happen, including the ones nobody remembered — which is the evidence §12.2 wants for finding boundaries, and it is more truthful than any architecture diagram.

15.4 Deploying Without Downtime

Every deploy is a controlled change to a running system. Three strategies, and they differ in how much they cost and how quickly they can be undone.

def strategy(name, instances, minutes_per_instance=2):
    PLANS = {                    # downtime_instances, extra_capacity, blast_radius, rollback
        'recreate':   (instances, 0.00, '100% of users',   'redeploy the old version — slow'),
        'rolling':    (0,         0.00, '100% by the end', 'another full rollout — slow'),
        'blue-green': (0,         1.00, '100% at the cut', 'switch the router back — seconds'),
        'canary':     (0,         0.05, '1-5% of users',   'route back — seconds'),
    }
    down, extra, blast, rollback = PLANS[name]
    return (f'{down * minutes_per_instance} min', f'{extra:.0%}', blast, rollback)

print(f'{"strategy":<12}{"downtime":>10}{"extra capacity":>16}{"blast radius":>18}   rollback')
for name in ('recreate', 'rolling', 'blue-green', 'canary'):
    down, extra, blast, rollback = strategy(name, instances=20)
    print(f'{name:<12}{down:>10}{extra:>16}{blast:>18}   {rollback}')

strategy      downtime  extra capacity      blast radius   rollback
recreate        40 min              0%     100% of users   redeploy the old version — slow
rolling          0 min              0%   100% by the end   another full rollout — slow
blue-green       0 min            100%   100% at the cut   switch the router back — seconds
canary           0 min              5%     1-5% of users   route back — seconds
Recreate
Stop everything, start the new version. Acceptable only where downtime is acceptable — and note that it is the only strategy where the two versions never coexist, which is occasionally a genuine requirement.
Rolling
Replace instances a few at a time. No extra capacity and no downtime, and both versions run simultaneously for the whole rollout — which is the constraint §13.7 and §6.10 exist to satisfy. Rolling back is another slow rollout.
Blue-green
Run a complete second fleet, verify it, switch the router. Rollback is a routing change measured in seconds, which is its whole value. Costs double capacity during the deploy, and the database still has to serve both.
Canary
Send a small percentage of traffic to the new version and watch. The only strategy that limits the blast radius of a bad release — 1% of users see the bug instead of all of them — and the only one that gives real production evidence before committing.

Canary is the one worth building properly, because it is the only strategy that turns a deploy from a leap into a measurement. The mechanism is a comparison, not a wait:

def canary_gate(baseline, canary, tolerance=1.2):
    checks = []
    for metric in ('error_rate', 'p99_ms'):
        ratio = canary[metric] / baseline[metric] if baseline[metric] else float('inf')
        checks.append((metric, baseline[metric], canary[metric], ratio, ratio <= tolerance))
    return checks, all(passed for *_, passed in checks)

SCENARIOS = [
    ('healthy release',    {'error_rate': 0.002, 'p99_ms': 240}, {'error_rate': 0.002, 'p99_ms': 250}),
    ('latency regression', {'error_rate': 0.002, 'p99_ms': 240}, {'error_rate': 0.002, 'p99_ms': 900}),
    ('new error path',     {'error_rate': 0.002, 'p99_ms': 240}, {'error_rate': 0.031, 'p99_ms': 245}),
]
for name, baseline, canary in SCENARIOS:
    checks, ok = canary_gate(baseline, canary)
    print(f'{name:<20}{"PROMOTE" if ok else "ROLL BACK"}')
    for metric, base, cand, ratio, passed in checks:
        print(f'   {metric:<12}baseline {base:<8} canary {cand:<8} '
              f'{ratio:>5.2f}x  {"ok" if passed else "FAIL"}')

healthy release     PROMOTE
   error_rate  baseline 0.002    canary 0.002     1.00x  ok
   p99_ms      baseline 240      canary 250       1.04x  ok
latency regression  ROLL BACK
   error_rate  baseline 0.002    canary 0.002     1.00x  ok
   p99_ms      baseline 240      canary 900       3.75x  FAIL
new error path      ROLL BACK
   error_rate  baseline 0.002    canary 0.031    15.50x  FAIL
   p99_ms      baseline 240      canary 245       1.02x  ok

Compare the canary against the baseline running at the same moment, not against yesterday's numbers. Traffic varies by hour and by day, so an absolute threshold produces false alarms at the daily peak and misses real regressions at 4 a.m. A ratio against concurrently-running old instances controls for all of it.

Two things that make a canary honest. It needs enough traffic to be significant — 1% of a hundred requests a second is one request a second, and ten minutes of that cannot distinguish a 0.2% error rate from a 2% one. And it must run long enough to see slow failures: a memory leak, a cache filling, a nightly job. A canary that passes in five minutes has tested startup, not operation.

And the promotion must be automatic. A canary that requires a human to read a dashboard and decide is a canary that gets promoted at the end of the day because everyone wants to go home.

15.5 Feature Flags: Separating Deploy From Release
