assignment
consensus-backed store: one driver, one ride
events
log of trip events (outbox relay)

The relationships between them are the model's eighteen, and each is a labelled, directed statement in §19.4's list. Read the absences too, because that is what a good container diagram tells you: the apps call only the gateway (and the only thing that reaches back to them is the live-updates fleet), each store has a single writer (location for the geo-index, matching for assignments, trips for the event log), payments is reached only through the event log, and only payments talks to the payment provider. Those are design decisions (§12.4's coupling, §12.10's boundaries) made visible. What the diagram does not show is that the assignment store is a consensus group across three zones, that the gateway has a load balancer in front of it, or that the platform runs in two regions for data residency. Those belong to a deployment diagram, drawn once per environment (§19.3, §19.5).

19.7 Requirements as a Document

§1.1 said requirements come first and most of them are not about features. This subsection is about writing them down so the design can be checked against them, and it follows the arc42 template, which is the most widely used structure for architecture documentation and whose first and tenth sections cover exactly this.

Requirements overview, quality goals, and stakeholders

arc42's Introduction and Goals section holds three things, and it is worth taking them in the order the template does:

Requirements overview
A "short description of the functional requirements, driving forces, extract (or abstract) of requirements", with links to the full requirements documents rather than a copy of them. The template's advice is to keep the excerpts "as short as possible" and to balance readability against redundancy.
Quality goals
"The top three (max five) quality goals for the architecture whose fulfillment is of highest importance to the major stakeholders." The template is emphatic that these are goals for the architecture: "Don't confuse them with project goals. They are not necessarily identical." A project goal is to ship by March; a quality goal is that the system answers within five seconds at peak.
Stakeholders
A table of "all person, roles or organizations that should know the architecture, have to be convinced of the architecture, have to work with the architecture or with code, need the documentation of the architecture for their work, have to come up with decisions about the system or its development", each with their expectations. Its stated reason: "Otherwise, you may get nasty surprises later."

The limit of three to five quality goals is the most useful discipline in the section, because it forces the ranking that §1.1 said the design cannot do without. A system cannot be maximally available, consistent, cheap, fast and quick to change at once: §4.3's CAP theorem is one instance of that, and every choice in §6 to §14 was a case of it. Naming the top few is deciding which ones win when they conflict. The template's motivation reads: "you should know the quality goals of your most important stakeholders, since they will influence fundamental architectural decisions. Make sure to be very concrete about these qualities, avoid buzzwords."

The concreteness is the difficulty. Every project has quality goals, and most write them as adjectives: fast, scalable, secure, reliable. An adjective cannot be tested, so it cannot be met or missed, and it cannot conflict with another adjective in a way that forces a choice. The remedy the template offers is in its tenth section, Quality Requirements: the top goals are restated as scenarios, and the remaining, lesser requirements (those "which will not create high risks when they are not fully achieved (but might be nice-to-have)") are listed in an overview, "by describing categories or topics" such as those in ISO 25010 or arc42's own quality model.

The same discipline applies to the other pieces §1.1 named. Constraints are the fixed points you did not choose (a regulator, a corporate standard, a legacy system that must keep working) and go in the template's second section, because they eliminate options and a design reviewed without them will be reviewed against the wrong space. The out-of-scope list of §20.1 earns its place for the same reason: what the design deliberately does not cover is as informative as what it does.

19.8 Quality Scenarios

A quality scenario is how a vague goal becomes a checkable one. The arc42 text states the purpose: "Quality scenarios make quality requirements concrete and allow to decide whether they are fulfilled (in the sense of acceptance criteria). Ensure that your scenarios are specific and measurable." Each one is, in effect, a measurable requirement: something a test, a dashboard or a calendar can confirm or refute.

Usage scenario and change scenario

It names two kinds that together cover most of what matters:

Usage scenario
Also called an application or use-case scenario. It "describe[s] the system's runtime reaction to a certain stimulus", including its efficiency and performance. Example: "The system reacts to a user's request within one second."
Change scenario
It describes "the desired effect of a modification or extension of the system or of its immediate environment", and the effort or duration of the change is measured. Example: "additional functionality is implemented ... and the effort or duration of the change is measured."

A scenario is a measurable requirement

The template gives two forms. The short form has three parts: context/background, source or stimulus, and metric or acceptance criteria. The long form, favoured by the Software Engineering Institute, has eight: a scenario ID and name, then source (who or what initiates it), stimulus (the triggering event), environment (the operational condition it occurs in), artifact (the building blocks affected), response (what the system does) and response measure (the metric by which the response is judged). The parts that matter in both are the same two: a stimulus that can be reproduced, and a measure that can be read off a dashboard. A scenario without the second is an adjective in a table.

That structure can be checked mechanically, at least for the failures that are visible without understanding the domain. The linter below flags a missing part, a measure with no number in it, and the buzzwords the template warns against. The scenarios come from the numbers of §20.1:

import re

FIELDS = ('source', 'stimulus', 'environment', 'artifact', 'response', 'measure')
BUZZWORDS = ('fast', 'quick', 'scalable', 'robust', 'reliable', 'highly available', 'secure', 'user-friendly',
             'efficient', 'flexible', 'easy', 'seamless', 'real-time')

def lint(scenario):
    problems = [f'missing {field}' for field in FIELDS if not scenario.get(field, '').strip()]
    measure = scenario.get('measure', '')
    if measure and not re.search(r'\d', measure):
        problems.append('the measure contains no number')
    elif measure and not re.search(r'\d\s*(ms|s|seconds?|minutes?|hours?|days?|%|per|/|requests?|GB|MB|engineer-days?)', measure):
        problems.append('the measure has a number but no unit')
    text = ' '.join(scenario.get(f, '') for f in FIELDS).lower()
    problems += [f'buzzword "{w}"' for w in BUZZWORDS if re.search(rf'\b{re.escape(w)}\b', text)]
    return problems

SCENARIOS = {
    'S1 matching latency (usage)': dict(
        source='a rider', stimulus='requests a ride at the daily peak (300,000 drivers online, 75,000 position updates per second)',
        environment='normal operation, one region', artifact='matching and assignment',
        response='a driver is assigned and both parties are notified',
        measure='p99 of request-to-assignment at most 5 s, over every 5-minute window'),
    'S2 zone failure (usage)': dict(
        source='the infrastructure', stimulus='one availability zone becomes unreachable',
        environment='the daily peak', artifact='the assignment store',
        response='a new leader is elected and assignments continue; no assignment is lost or granted twice',
        measure='ride requests fail for at most 30 s; 0 drivers assigned two rides'),
    'S3 new region (change)': dict(
        source='the business', stimulus='launches in a new region with its own data-residency rules',
        environment='design time', artifact='deployment configuration and partition keys',
        response='the region goes live without changing the matching code',
        measure='at most 5 engineer-days'),
    'X1 "should be fast"': dict(source='a user', stimulus='opens the app', environment='', artifact='the system',
        response='the system responds quickly', measure='fast enough for a good user experience'),
    'X2 "highly available"': dict(source='the infrastructure', stimulus='a server fails', environment='production', artifact='the platform',
        response='the platform stays highly available', measure='reliable and scalable'),
    'X3 unit missing': dict(source='an analyst', stimulus='requests a report', environment='month end', artifact='reporting',
        response='the report is delivered', measure='within 30'),
}
for name, scenario in SCENARIOS.items():
    problems = lint(scenario)
    print(f'{name:<30}', 'ok' if not problems else '; '.join(problems))

MINUTES_PER_YEAR = 365.25 * 24 * 60
print(f'\nwhat a 99.99% target permits: {MINUTES_PER_YEAR * 0.0001:.1f} minutes of unavailability a year, {30 * 24 * 60 * 0.0001:.1f} minutes in a 30-day month')

S1 matching latency (usage)    ok
S2 zone failure (usage)        ok
S3 new region (change)         ok
X1 "should be fast"            missing environment; the measure contains no number; buzzword "fast"
X2 "highly available"          the measure contains no number; buzzword "scalable"; buzzword "reliable"; buzzword "highly available"
X3 unit missing                the measure has a number but no unit

what a 99.99% target permits: 52.6 minutes of unavailability a year, 4.3 minutes in a 30-day month

The first three pass and the last three fail for different reasons: X1 has no environment and a measure that is a feeling, X2's measure is two more buzzwords ("reliable and scalable"), and X3 has a number and no unit, which makes it unfalsifiable ("30" what?). The linter cannot tell whether a scenario is sensible, only whether it is checkable, and that is the right division of labour: a person decides whether five seconds is the right target, and a tool notices when nobody wrote one. The last line connects the scenario to a number a design can be checked against. A 99.99% availability goal is four minutes and a bit per month, which is why S2's thirty-second failover is a scenario the design must be able to meet: a single failover that takes five minutes has already spent the month's budget (§3.2's error budget, made concrete).

A design review can then run the scenarios against the design as a checklist, which is how the template suggests using them, as "architecture analysis or evaluation". Take S2 and walk the design: which container holds the state that must not be lost (the assignment store), what makes a new leader elected within the window (the consensus group of §5.4), and what happens to in-flight requests during the election (they are retried with an idempotency key, §11.8). A scenario that the design cannot walk through is a defect found at review time, which is when it is cheapest.

19.9 Architecture Decision Records

Diagrams and requirements answer what and for what. Neither records why this and not the alternative, and that is the piece that disappears first. Nygard identified the failure in 2011: "One of the hardest things to track during the life of a project is the motivation behind certain decisions. A new person coming on to a project may be perplexed, baffled, delighted, or infuriated by some past decision. Without understanding the rationale or consequences, this person has only two choices: blindly accept the decision ... [or] blindly change it." Both are bad, and the post explains why: blind acceptance means "the development team becomes afraid to change anything and the project collapses under its own weight", and blind reversal risks "damaging the project's overall value without realizing it" (for example, "the decision supported a non-functional requirement that hasn't been tested yet.").

An architecturally significant decision, one record at a time

His answer is the architecture decision record, an ADR: "a short text file in a format similar to an Alexandrian pattern ... Each record describes a set of forces and a single decision in response to those forces." The rules he set out are few, and each has a reason:

Only significant decisions
An architecturally significant decision is one of "those that affect the structure, non-functional characteristics, dependencies, interfaces, or construction techniques." Choosing a variable name is not one; choosing a message broker is.
One decision per record
"One ADR describes one significant decision for a specific project." The decision is "the central piece", so the same force may appear in several records.
In the repository, as text
"Under doc/arch/adr-NNN.md", in "a lightweight text formatting language like Markdown", so it is reviewed and versioned with the code that it constrains.
Numbered, never reused, never deleted
"ADRs will be numbered sequentially and monotonically. Numbers will not be reused." A reversed decision is kept as a superseded decision, marked as such: "It's still relevant to know that it was the decision, but is no longer the decision."
One or two pages
"We will write each ADR as if it is a conversation with a future developer", in full sentences, because a record nobody reads records nothing.

The format: title, context, decision, ADR status, ADR consequences

The format has five parts (title, context, decision, status and consequences). The title is a short noun phrase. The context "describes the forces at play, including technological, political, social, and project local. These forces are probably in tension, and should be called out as such. The language in this section is value-neutral. It is simply describing facts." The decision "describes our response to these forces. It is stated in full sentences, with active voice. 'We will ...'" The ADR status is "proposed" until stakeholders agree, "accepted" once they do, and later "deprecated" or "superseded" with a reference to the replacement. And the ADR consequences section "describes the resulting context, after applying the decision. All consequences should be listed here, not just the 'positive' ones. A particular decision may have positive, negative, and neutral consequences, but all of them affect the team and project in the future."

The last requirement is the one people skip, and it is the one that makes a record worth reading. An ADR whose consequences are all positive is advocacy, not a record: a reader eighteen months later needs to know the costs that were accepted, since those are what explain the next problem. Here is an ADR from the capstone written in that shape, together with the record it replaced, checked by a small tool that enforces the mechanical rules:

import re

ADRS = {
    4: """# ADR 4: Store driver assignments in the trips database
Status: Superseded by ADR 7

## Context
The system must never assign one driver to two rides. Trips already live in a partitioned relational database, so a unique constraint on the driver is the cheapest way to enforce this.

## Decision
We will record the assignment as a row in the trips database and enforce uniqueness with a constraint on (driver_id, active).

## Consequences
The rule is enforced by a mechanism the team already runs. Every assignment attempt becomes a write to the trips partition, and at peak those writes contend with trip updates on the same rows.
""",
    7: """# ADR 7: Grant assignments through a consensus-backed store
Status: Accepted. Supersedes ADR 4.

## Context
Load tests at the daily peak (75,000 position updates and thousands of assignment attempts per second) showed that ADR 4's constraint serialises assignments behind trip updates and breaks the 5-second matching target. The one rule that must be linearizable is that a driver has at most one ride; everything else may be eventually consistent.

## Decision
We will grant each assignment with a compare-and-set on a consensus-backed store keyed by driver id, with a lease that expires if the trip service does not confirm the assignment. Positions stay in an eventually consistent in-memory index.

## Consequences
Only the assignment rule pays for consensus, and it no longer contends with trip writes. Matching now depends on the availability of the assignment store, so an outage there stops new assignments; we accept that rather than allow a driver to be assigned twice. The team must operate a consensus group (a cost in on-call load), and expired leases need a reconciliation job.
""",
    9: """# ADR 9: Use a message broker
Status: Accepted

## Decision
We will use a message broker.
""",
}

SECTIONS = ('Context', 'Decision', 'Consequences')

def lint_adrs(adrs):
    problems = []
    numbers = sorted(adrs)
    if len(set(numbers)) != len(numbers):
        problems.append('a number was reused')
    for n in numbers:
        text = adrs[n]
        head = re.match(r'# ADR (\d+): (.+)', text)
        if not head or int(head.group(1)) != n:
            problems.append(f'ADR {n}: the title line does not carry its own number')
        for section in SECTIONS:
            if f'## {section}' not in text:
                problems.append(f'ADR {n}: no "{section}" section')
        status = re.search(r'^Status: (.+)$', text, re.M)
        if not status or not re.match(r'(Proposed|Accepted|Deprecated|Superseded by ADR \d+)', status.group(1)):
            problems.append(f'ADR {n}: status is missing or not one of proposed / accepted / deprecated / superseded')
        if re.search(r'## Decision\s+(?!We will)', text):
            problems.append(f'ADR {n}: the decision is not stated as "We will ..."')
        replaced_by = re.search(r'Superseded by ADR (\d+)', text)
        if replaced_by:
            other = int(replaced_by.group(1))
            if other not in adrs:
                problems.append(f'ADR {n}: superseded by ADR {other}, which does not exist')
            elif f'Supersedes ADR {n}' not in adrs[other]:
                problems.append(f'ADR {n}: superseded by ADR {other}, but ADR {other} does not say it supersedes ADR {n}')
        length = len(text.split())
        if length > 700:
            problems.append(f'ADR {n}: {length} words; the format asks for one or two pages')
        if '## Consequences' in text and re.search(r'## Consequences\s*$', text.strip(), re.S):
            problems.append(f'ADR {n}: an empty consequences section')
    return problems

print('index:')
for n in sorted(ADRS):
    title = re.match(r'# ADR \d+: (.+)', ADRS[n]).group(1)
    status = re.search(r'^Status: (.+)$', ADRS[n], re.M).group(1)
    print(f'  ADR {n:>2}  {title:<58} {status}')
print('\nlint:')
for problem in lint_adrs(ADRS) or ['no problems']:
    print(' ', problem)

index:
  ADR  4  Store driver assignments in the trips database             Superseded by ADR 7
  ADR  7  Grant assignments through a consensus-backed store         Accepted. Supersedes ADR 4.
  ADR  9  Use a message broker                                       Accepted

lint:
  ADR 9: no "Context" section
  ADR 9: no "Consequences" section

Superseded decisions: reading the history in both directions

ADRs 4 and 7 pass: a superseded record points at its replacement and the replacement says what it replaces, which is what lets a reader walk the history in either direction. ADR 9 fails two checks that Nygard's rules imply: it has no context (a decision without forces is an assertion) and no consequences (no costs recorded). It also names no alternative, which no linter can see and a reader will notice at once. The specific failure to notice is that ADR 9 would pass a reviewer's glance. It exists, it is numbered, it is short, and it uses "We will". Only a check for the required parts, or a reader asking "why?", finds it empty.

Notice what ADR 7 records that no diagram could. The container diagram of §19.6 shows an assignment store; it cannot say that the first attempt put assignments in the trips database, that it failed a load test at the peak, or that the team knowingly made matching depend on the store's availability instead of accepting a double assignment. Someone proposing to "simplify" by moving assignments back into the trips database will find the objection in the repository, with the numbers, before they find it in production.

19.10 Putting It Together

The three artefacts fit into one document, and arc42's twelve sections are a convenient skeleton for it. The mapping from what this section taught is direct:

1. Introduction and Goals
Requirements overview, the top quality goals (three to five), stakeholders (§19.7).
2. Constraints
The fixed points: regulation, standards, mandated technology.
3. Context and Scope
The system context diagram (C4 level 1), and the external interfaces (§19.3).
4-5. Solution Strategy, Building Blocks
The container diagram (C4 level 2), and component diagrams only where they add value.
6. Runtime View
Dynamic diagrams for the few flows that cross many containers (§19.5).
7. Deployment View
The deployment diagram, one per environment, holding the replicas, zones and load balancers the container view leaves out.
8. Crosscutting Concepts
How the whole system does authentication (§18), observability (§15), resilience (§14), and other things every container repeats.
9. Architecture Decisions
The ADRs: "important, expensive, large scale or risky architecture decisions including rationales" (§19.9).
10. Quality Requirements
The quality overview and the scenarios (§19.8).
11-12. Risks and Glossary
Known risks and technical debt, and the vocabulary the domain uses.

Four habits keep such a document alive, and they are the difference between an artefact and an archive:

Keep it beside the code and review it with the code. A design document in a wiki is a design document nobody updates. The model, the ADRs and the scenarios belong in the repository, and a change that alters a container, adds a relationship or reverses a decision is incomplete until its record is in the same pull request.

Generate what can be generated. §19.4's model produces its views; component and code diagrams are best produced from the code itself, which is the C4 site's advice; a lint like the ones above runs in CI and fails when an ADR is malformed or a scenario has no number. What cannot be generated (the reasons) is the only part that needs a human.

Draw the two recommended diagrams and stop. A context and a container diagram, current, are worth more than eight diagrams of which six are stale. Add a dynamic or deployment diagram when a specific reader needs one, and delete it when it stops being true rather than leaving it to mislead.

Record decisions when they are made. An ADR written at the time takes ten minutes and captures the alternatives that were actually considered. The same record reconstructed a year later is a plausible story. Write it in the pull request that implements the decision.

What this section does not do is tell you what to design. That is the rest of the course, and it ends where the next course begins: System Design in Practice takes the method of §1.5, the fundamentals of §2 to §19 and the artefacts of this section, and applies them to a series of worked problems, each from requirements with numbers through to a design that can be defended in front of a reviewer.

Exercises

Exercise 19.1 — Find what is wrong with the model. The model below has three defects that a view would expose or a consistency check should catch. Write the check, find them, and fix the model.

PEOPLE = {'customer': 'Customer'}
SYSTEMS = {'shop': 'Web shop', 'bank': 'Bank'}
CONTAINERS = {
    'web': ('shop', 'Serves pages', 'web application'),
    'api': ('shop', 'Business logic', 'service'),
    'db':  ('shop', 'Orders', 'relational database'),
}
RELATIONSHIPS = [
    ('customer', 'web', 'browses'), ('web', 'api', 'calls'), ('api', 'db', 'reads and writes'),
    ('api', 'cache', 'looks up prices'),                # ?
    ('bank', 'db', 'writes settlements'),               # ?
    ('customer', 'bank', 'pays'),                       # ?
]
Solution 
PEOPLE = {'customer': 'Customer'}
SYSTEMS = {'shop': 'Web shop', 'bank': 'Bank'}
CONTAINERS = {'web': ('shop', 'Serves pages', 'web application'), 'api': ('shop', 'Business logic', 'service'),
              'db': ('shop', 'Orders', 'relational database')}
RELATIONSHIPS = [('customer', 'web', 'browses'), ('web', 'api', 'calls'), ('api', 'db', 'reads and writes'),
                 ('api', 'cache', 'looks up prices'), ('bank', 'db', 'writes settlements'), ('customer', 'bank', 'pays')]

def check(people, systems, containers, relationships, scope):
    problems, known = [], set(people) | set(systems) | set(containers)
    for a, b, what in relationships:
        for end in (a, b):
            if end not in known:
                problems.append(f'({a} -> {b}, "{what}"): {end!r} is not in the model')
        if a in known and b in known:
            a_sys = containers[a][0] if a in containers else a
            b_sys = containers[b][0] if b in containers else b
            # an external system reaches the platform through an interface it calls, never into another system's store
            if b in containers and containers[b][2].endswith('database') and a in systems and a_sys != b_sys:
                problems.append(f'({a} -> {b}, "{what}"): an external system writes straight into a container\'s data store')
            # a person talking to a system outside the scope of this model belongs in the landscape, not here
            if a in people and b in systems and b != scope:
                problems.append(f'({a} -> {b}, "{what}"): a person connects to {b!r}, which is outside the scope {scope!r}')
    return problems

for problem in check(PEOPLE, SYSTEMS, CONTAINERS, RELATIONSHIPS, scope='shop'):
    print(problem)

(api -> cache, "looks up prices"): 'cache' is not in the model
(bank -> db, "writes settlements"): an external system writes straight into a container's data store
(customer -> bank, "pays"): a person connects to 'bank', which is outside the scope 'shop'

The three defects are of three kinds. api -> cache mentions an element that was never declared: either a container is missing (add cache with its technology) or the arrow is wrong; the consistency check of §19.4 catches this class before any picture is drawn. bank -> db is a modelling error: an external system does not write into a container's database, it calls an interface, so the relationship should run from the bank to an api-level container (a settlement webhook), and the arrow into the data store is the design smell that a container diagram exposes ("no service writes another service's store" is the rule the diagram was supposed to make visible). customer -> bank says the customer pays the bank directly, which is a true fact about the world and belongs in the context view as a person-to-system relationship, but is not something the shop does. Decide whether it is part of the shop's scope; if the customer's card is charged by the shop's own payment container, the relationship goes through it. Fix the first by adding the container, the second by re-pointing it at the API, and remove the third from the shop's model. A model that will not pass such a check draws a diagram that cannot be trusted.

Exercise 19.2 — Turn adjectives into scenarios. Rewrite these requirements as scenarios that pass the linter of §19.8, choosing numbers you can defend. (a) "Search should be fast." (b) "The service must be highly available." (c) "It has to scale." (d) "It should be easy to add a new payment method."

Solution 
import re
FIELDS = ('source', 'stimulus', 'environment', 'artifact', 'response', 'measure')
BUZZ = ('fast', 'scalable', 'highly available', 'easy', 'reliable', 'quick', 'flexible')

def lint(sc):
    out = [f'missing {f}' for f in FIELDS if not sc.get(f)]
    m = sc.get('measure', '')
    if not re.search(r'\d\s*(ms|s\b|seconds?|minutes?|%|per|/|engineer-days?|x\b)', m):
        out.append('measure needs a number and a unit')
    text = ' '.join(sc.get(f, '') for f in FIELDS).lower()
    out += [f'buzzword {w}' for w in BUZZ if re.search(rf'\b{w}\b', text)]
    return out

REWRITES = {
    '(a) search latency': dict(source='a shopper', stimulus='submits a query', environment='peak evening traffic, 2,000 queries/s',
        artifact='search service', response='the first page of results is returned', measure='p95 at most 300 ms, p99 at most 800 ms'),
    '(b) availability': dict(source='the infrastructure', stimulus='any single machine or zone fails', environment='production, all day',
        artifact='the checkout service', response='requests continue to be served by the remaining capacity',
        measure='99.95% of checkout requests succeed per calendar month (about 22 minutes of budget)'),
    '(c) scaling': dict(source='marketing', stimulus='a campaign multiplies traffic', environment='a planned launch',
        artifact='the web tier and the database', response='the system absorbs the load by adding instances, with no code change',
        measure='handles 5x the current peak (10,000 requests/s) with p99 at most 1 s, scaled out within 15 minutes'),
    '(d) new payment method': dict(source='the product team', stimulus='asks to add a payment method', environment='design time',
        artifact='the payment module', response='a new provider is integrated behind the existing interface',
        measure='at most 5 engineer-days, with 0 changes to the order service'),
}
for name, sc in REWRITES.items():
    print(f'{name:<26}', 'ok' if not lint(sc) else lint(sc))

(a) search latency         ok
(b) availability           ok
(c) scaling                ok
(d) new payment method     ok

Each rewrite names a stimulus someone can reproduce and a measure someone can read off a graph or a calendar. (a) turns "fast" into two percentiles at a stated load, since a single average hides the tail (§15.2). (b) turns "highly available" into a monthly success rate whose error budget can be computed (99.95% of a month is about 22 minutes), which is what makes the target something a deployment can spend. (c) says by how much ("5x the current peak") and how quickly, since "scales" without a factor cannot be tested. (d) is a change scenario measured in effort, and its second clause (0 changes to the order service) is the design constraint it imposes. The general rule the four share: a scenario is a test the design must pass, and if you cannot describe the test, you do not yet have a requirement.

Exercise 19.3 — Write and lint an ADR. Your team is choosing between a single shared PostgreSQL database for all services and one database per service. You choose one database per service. Write the ADR (title, context with at least two forces in tension, decision as "We will ...", status, and consequences that include at least two costs), and say what would have to change for you to supersede it.

Solution 
ADR = """# ADR 12: Give each service its own database
Status: Accepted

## Context
Forty engineers now work in one codebase against one PostgreSQL database. Schema changes need sign-off from every team that reads the tables, deployments are serialised behind the slowest migration, and a slow query in reporting has already exhausted the connection pool for checkout. Against that, a shared database gives us joins across all data, one backup story, and transactions that span domains. The product roadmap adds three new services this year.

## Decision
We will give each service its own database and forbid direct access to another service's tables. Data needed across services will be obtained through that service's API or from the events it publishes.

## Consequences
Teams can change their schema and deploy on their own schedule, and a runaway query can only exhaust its own service's pool. Cross-service joins are no longer possible in SQL, so the reporting team must build read models from events, and some reports will be eventually consistent. Transactions that span services become sagas, which are harder to reason about and to test. We take on the operational cost of many databases: backups, upgrades, monitoring and access control, each times the number of services.
"""
import re
have = {s: f'## {s}' in ADR for s in ('Context', 'Decision', 'Consequences')}
print('sections present         :', have)
print('status line              :', re.search(r'^Status: (.+)$', ADR, re.M).group(1))
print('decision starts "We will":', bool(re.search(r'## Decision\s+We will', ADR)))
costs = [w for w in ('cost', 'harder', 'no longer', 'eventually consistent') if w in ADR.split('## Consequences')[1]]
print('costs recorded           :', costs)
print('words                    :', len(ADR.split()), '(the format asks for one or two pages)')

sections present         : {'Context': True, 'Decision': True, 'Consequences': True}
status line              : Accepted
decision starts "We will": True
costs recorded           : ['cost', 'harder', 'no longer', 'eventually consistent']
words                    : 204 (the format asks for one or two pages)

The context names two forces in tension, the pain of coupling (sign-offs, serialised deploys, the exhausted pool) against what the shared database gave for free (joins, one backup story, cross-domain transactions), and it states them neutrally, as the format asks. The decision is one sentence in the active voice, plus the rule that makes it real (no reading another service's tables). The consequences list benefits and the costs that will cause tomorrow's problems: no SQL joins, reporting becomes event-driven and eventually consistent, sagas replace transactions, and operational work multiplies. What would supersede it: an ADR is superseded when its context changes. If the number of services falls (a consolidation of the kind §12.5 describes), if a domain needs cross-service transactions strongly enough that sagas prove unaffordable, or if the operational cost of many databases outweighs the isolation, a new ADR is written that says so, cites this one as superseded, and records what was learned. This one stays in the repository as the record of why it was once right.

Exercise 19.4 — Which artefact does each fact belong in? For each statement say whether it belongs in the system context diagram, the container diagram, a deployment diagram, a dynamic diagram, a quality scenario, or an ADR, and defend the one you find hardest. (a) "The platform depends on an external maps provider." (b) "The assignment store runs as three replicas across three zones." (c) "Matching must reach a p99 of 5 s at 300,000 drivers." (d) "We rejected a single relational database for assignments because of contention at peak." (e) "A cancelled ride passes through six steps across four services." (f) "Positions are kept in an in-memory geospatial index."

Solution 
PLACEMENT = [
    ('(a) depends on a maps provider',           'system context',   'an external system directly connected to the platform; no technology'),
    ('(b) three replicas across three zones',    'deployment',       'replication and zones vary by environment; the container view omits them on purpose'),
    ('(c) p99 5 s at 300,000 drivers',           'quality scenario', 'a measurable target with a stimulus; it is checked, not drawn'),
    ('(d) rejected one relational database',     'ADR',              'a decision and the forces behind it: exactly what a diagram cannot show'),
    ('(e) cancellation across four services',    'dynamic diagram',  'a numbered flow across containers; recommended only for complicated recurring flows'),
    ('(f) in-memory geospatial index',           'container diagram','a data store and its technology: the level where technology choices are named'),
]
for statement, artefact, why in PLACEMENT:
    print(f'{statement:<44}{artefact:<18}{why}')

(a) depends on a maps provider              system context    an external system directly connected to the platform; no technology
(b) three replicas across three zones       deployment        replication and zones vary by environment; the container view omits them on purpose
(c) p99 5 s at 300,000 drivers              quality scenario  a measurable target with a stimulus; it is checked, not drawn
(d) rejected one relational database        ADR               a decision and the forces behind it: exactly what a diagram cannot show
(e) cancellation across four services       dynamic diagram   a numbered flow across containers; recommended only for complicated recurring flows
(f) in-memory geospatial index              container diagram a data store and its technology: the level where technology choices are named

Five of the six have one obvious home. (b) is the one that goes wrong most, because "three replicas" feels like architecture and ends up on the container diagram, where it makes every environment's diagram wrong for some environment. The C4 site's own note is the rule: the container diagram "says very little about deployment aspects such as clustering, load balancers, replication, failover, etc because it will likely vary across different environments." The statement that the assignment store exists and is consensus-backed is a container fact; how many copies run where is a deployment fact; and why we chose consensus at all is an ADR (ADR 7 in §19.9). One system, three documents, each answering one question and none repeating another.

SECTION 20

Capstone: Designing a Ride-Hailing Platform

Everything in this course has been a mechanism in isolation. This section uses them together on one system, end to end, following §1.5's method: clarify, estimate, model, build the simplest thing that works, then find each bottleneck in turn and say what fixing it cost. The system is a ride-hailing platform — chosen because it exercises almost every part of the syllabus and because its hardest requirement, matching a rider to a nearby driver in seconds, has no comfortable answer.

20.1 The Requirements, and the Numbers They Imply

Start where §1.1 says to start: separate what it does from the conditions under which it must do it.

FUNCTIONAL = [
    'a driver goes online and streams their position',
    'a rider requests a ride from A to B',
    'the system matches them to a nearby driver within seconds',
    'both track the trip live',
    'the fare is computed and charged at the end',
    'both see their trip history and receipts',
]
NON_FUNCTIONAL = [
    ('scale',        '3,000,000 drivers, 300,000 online at peak; 12,000,000 riders'),
    ('position rate','every online driver reports every 4 seconds'),
    ('matching',     'p99 under 5 seconds from request to assignment'),
    ('availability', '99.99% for request-a-ride; 99.9% for history'),
    ('consistency',  'a driver must never be assigned two rides — this is the hard one'),
    ('durability',   'a completed trip and its payment must never be lost'),
    ('residency',    'EU trip data stays in the EU'),
]
OUT_OF_SCOPE = ['fraud detection', 'driver onboarding', 'pricing strategy',
                'the mobile apps themselves', 'accounting and tax']

for label, items in [('FUNCTIONAL', FUNCTIONAL), ('OUT OF SCOPE', OUT_OF_SCOPE)]:
    print(label)
    for item in items:
        print(f'   - {item}')
print('\nNON-FUNCTIONAL — these decide the design')
for name, value in NON_FUNCTIONAL:
    print(f'   {name:<14}{value}')

FUNCTIONAL
   - a driver goes online and streams their position
   - a rider requests a ride from A to B
   - the system matches them to a nearby driver within seconds
   - both track the trip live
   - the fare is computed and charged at the end
   - both see their trip history and receipts
OUT OF SCOPE
   - fraud detection
   - driver onboarding
   - pricing strategy
   - the mobile apps themselves
   - accounting and tax

NON-FUNCTIONAL — these decide the design
   scale         3,000,000 drivers, 300,000 online at peak; 12,000,000 riders
   position rate every online driver reports every 4 seconds
   matching      p99 under 5 seconds from request to assignment
   availability  99.99% for request-a-ride; 99.9% for history
   consistency   a driver must never be assigned two rides — this is the hard one
   durability    a completed trip and its payment must never be lost
   residency     EU trip data stays in the EU

One line in that list is worth more than the rest combined: a driver must never be assigned two rides. It is a uniqueness constraint under concurrency, and it is the single requirement in the system that cannot be satisfied by eventual consistency (§4.4). Everything else — positions, history, fares, receipts — tolerates staleness measured in seconds. Identifying that one requirement early is what stops the whole system being designed to a standard only one part of it needs.

Now §1.2's arithmetic:

ONLINE_DRIVERS, POSITION_EVERY_S = 300_000, 4
RIDES_PER_DAY, PEAK = 4_000_000, 3
POSITION_BYTES, TRIP_BYTES = 60, 2_000

positions_s = ONLINE_DRIVERS / POSITION_EVERY_S
rides_s = RIDES_PER_DAY / 86_400
print(f'{"driver positions/s":<30}{positions_s:>14,.0f}')
print(f'{"position writes/day":<30}{positions_s * 86_400:>14,.0f}')
print(f'{"ride requests/s (average)":<30}{rides_s:>14,.0f}')
print(f'{"ride requests/s (peak)":<30}{rides_s * PEAK:>14,.0f}')
print(f'{"position data/day":<30}{positions_s * 86_400 * POSITION_BYTES / 1e9:>12,.1f} GB')
print(f'{"trip data/year":<30}{RIDES_PER_DAY * 365 * TRIP_BYTES / 1e12:>12,.1f} TB')
print(f'\nposition writes are {positions_s / (rides_s * PEAK):,.0f}x the ride-request rate')

driver positions/s                    75,000
position writes/day            6,480,000,000
ride requests/s (average)                 46
ride requests/s (peak)                   139
position data/day                    388.8 GB
trip data/year                         2.9 TB

position writes are 540x the ride-request rate

The position stream is five hundred times the ride-request rate, and that ratio is the whole shape of the system. Seventy-five thousand writes a second is far past a single relational node (§6.1), while 139 ride requests a second at peak is trivial. These are two completely different systems and must not share a store — which is the first architectural decision, and it comes from arithmetic rather than from taste.

20.2 The Data Model, and the Store for Each Part

§1.5 puts the data model before the diagram, because access patterns choose the stores (§6.1) and the partition keys (§8.3) — the two decisions that are hardest to reverse.

DATA = [
    ('driver positions', 'write 75k/s, read by geographic proximity, TTL 30s',
     'in-memory geospatial index (Redis)', 'geo cell', 'seconds'),
    ('trips (active)', 'write on state change, read by trip_id and by driver_id',
     'relational, partitioned', 'trip_id', 'strong'),
    ('trips (history)', 'append-only, read by user, never updated',
     'relational, partitioned by user; cold trips to object storage', 'rider_id', 'eventual'),
    ('driver assignment lock', 'one writer wins; must be linearizable',
     'a consensus-backed store (§5.4)', 'driver_id', 'LINEARIZABLE'),
    ('payments', 'write once per trip, must never be lost',
     'relational + outbox (§11.2)', 'trip_id', 'strong'),
    ('trip telemetry', 'append-only, queried by time range, downsampled',
     'time-series store (§6.7)', 'trip_id + time', 'eventual'),
    ('receipts and maps', 'write once, read rarely, large',
     'object storage (§6.7)', 'blob key', 'n/a'),
]
print(f'{"data":<24}{"partition key":<16}{"consistency":<14}store / access')
for name, access, store, key, consistency in DATA:
    print(f'{name:<24}{key:<16}{consistency:<14}{store}')
    print(f'{"":54}{access}')

data                    partition key   consistency   store / access
driver positions        geo cell        seconds       in-memory geospatial index (Redis)
                                                      write 75k/s, read by geographic proximity, TTL 30s
trips (active)          trip_id         strong        relational, partitioned
                                                      write on state change, read by trip_id and by driver_id
trips (history)         rider_id        eventual      relational, partitioned by user; cold trips to object storage
                                                      append-only, read by user, never updated
driver assignment lock  driver_id       LINEARIZABLE  a consensus-backed store (§5.4)
                                                      one writer wins; must be linearizable
payments                trip_id         strong        relational + outbox (§11.2)
                                                      write once per trip, must never be lost
trip telemetry          trip_id + time  eventual      time-series store (§6.7)
                                                      append-only, queried by time range, downsampled
receipts and maps       blob key        n/a           object storage (§6.7)
                                                      write once, read rarely, large

Four of those rows deserve their reasoning stated.

Positions are not durable and should not be. A driver's location from thirty seconds ago is worthless, so this is an in-memory store with a TTL, not a database. Losing the entire position index means every driver's next report rebuilds it within four seconds — which reframes the 75,000 writes a second from a durability problem into a memory-bandwidth one.

The assignment lock is the only linearizable thing in the system (§4.4), and it is deliberately tiny: one key per driver, held for seconds. §5.7's advice is being followed exactly — consensus is expensive, so use it for the smallest possible thing and let everything else be eventual.

Trip history is partitioned by rider_id, not by trip_id. The dominant query is "my last twenty trips", and §8.3's rule says to partition by the entity the queries are about. Partitioning by trip_id would spread perfectly and make the only query anyone runs a scatter-gather.

And telemetry goes to a time-series store because of its shape, not its volume: append-only, always queried by time range, and less valuable as it ages — §6.7's downsampling turns years of it into gigabytes.

20.3 The Simplest Thing That Works

§1.5 step four: draw the smallest design, then break it deliberately.

SIMPLE = [
    ('mobile apps', 'HTTPS + a persistent connection for live updates'),
    ('load balancer', 'layer 7, least-connections (§2.4)'),
    ('API service', 'stateless (§2.2), several instances'),
    ('PostgreSQL', 'trips, drivers, riders, payments'),
    ('Redis', 'driver positions, with a geospatial index'),
]
for component, note in SIMPLE:
    print(f'{component:<16}{note}')

def sanity(positions_per_s, ride_requests_per_s):
    return [
        ('75k position writes into Redis', positions_per_s < 200_000, 'fine — Redis handles it'),
        ('75k writes into PostgreSQL', positions_per_s < 20_000, 'NO — this is why they are separate'),
        ('139 ride requests/s', ride_requests_per_s < 5_000, 'fine on one node'),
        ('matching scans all drivers', False, 'NO — 300k drivers per request is hopeless'),
    ]

print()
for check, ok, verdict in sanity(75_000, 139):
    print(f'{check:<34}{"OK " if ok else "FAIL"}  {verdict}')

mobile apps     HTTPS + a persistent connection for live updates
load balancer   layer 7, least-connections (§2.4)
API service     stateless (§2.2), several instances
PostgreSQL      trips, drivers, riders, payments
Redis           driver positions, with a geospatial index

75k position writes into Redis    OK   fine — Redis handles it
75k writes into PostgreSQL        FAIL  NO — this is why they are separate
139 ride requests/s               OK   fine on one node
matching scans all drivers        FAIL  NO — 300k drivers per request is hopeless

Two failures, and they are the two the rest of this section is about. Position writes cannot go into the relational database, and matching cannot scan every driver on every request. Everything else in the simple design survives at this scale — which is §1.5's point: the simple design is not a strawman, it is most of the answer.

20.4 Matching: the Hard Part

Finding nearby drivers is a geospatial query at 139 requests a second against an index taking 75,000 writes a second. A linear scan is out of the question:

import math

def scan_cost(drivers, requests_per_s):
    return drivers * requests_per_s

def cell_cost(drivers, requests_per_s, cells, neighbours=9):
    per_cell = drivers / cells
    return per_cell * neighbours * requests_per_s, per_cell

CITY_DRIVERS, REQUESTS = 300_000, 139
print(f'linear scan      : {scan_cost(CITY_DRIVERS, REQUESTS):>14,.0f} distance calcs/s')
for cells in (1_000, 100_000, 1_000_000):
    cost, per_cell = cell_cost(CITY_DRIVERS, REQUESTS, cells)
    print(f'grid, {cells:>9,} cells: {cost:>14,.0f} distance calcs/s  '
          f'({per_cell:>6.1f} drivers per cell)')

linear scan      :     41,700,000 distance calcs/s
grid,     1,000 cells:        375,300 distance calcs/s  ( 300.0 drivers per cell)
grid,   100,000 cells:          3,753 distance calcs/s  (   3.0 drivers per cell)
grid, 1,000,000 cells:            375 distance calcs/s  (   0.3 drivers per cell)

A grid turns 41.7 million distance calculations a second into a few thousand, and the table shows the trade rather than a single answer: a coarse grid still examines three hundred drivers per cell, and a very fine one examines almost none but searches nine nearly-empty cells and will often have to widen the radius to find any candidate at all. A hundred thousand cells — three drivers each, twenty-seven examined per request — is the shape that works.

The mechanism is the one every geospatial index uses: divide the world into cells, index each driver by their cell, and search only the cell containing the rider plus its eight neighbours — because a driver just over a cell boundary may still be the closest one.

import math

CELL_DEGREES = 0.01                       # roughly 1.1 km of latitude

def cell(lat, lon):
    return (int(lat / CELL_DEGREES), int(lon / CELL_DEGREES))

def neighbours(cell_id):
    y, x = cell_id
    return [(y + dy, x + dx) for dy in (-1, 0, 1) for dx in (-1, 0, 1)]

INDEX = {}
DRIVERS = [('d1', 52.520, 13.405), ('d2', 52.523, 13.412), ('d3', 52.499, 13.401),
           ('d4', 52.600, 13.500), ('d5', 52.521, 13.399)]
for driver_id, lat, lon in DRIVERS:
    INDEX.setdefault(cell(lat, lon), []).append((driver_id, lat, lon))

def nearby(lat, lon, radius_km=2.0):
    found = []
    for cell_id in neighbours(cell(lat, lon)):
        for driver_id, dlat, dlon in INDEX.get(cell_id, []):
            km = math.hypot((dlat - lat) * 111.0, (dlon - lon) * 68.0)
            if km <= radius_km:
                found.append((round(km, 2), driver_id))
    return sorted(found)

rider = (52.5205, 13.4050)
print('rider cell      :', cell(*rider))
print('cells searched  :', len(neighbours(cell(*rider))))
print('drivers examined:', sum(len(INDEX.get(c, [])) for c in neighbours(cell(*rider))),
      'of', len(DRIVERS))
print('nearby (km, id) :', nearby(*rider))
print('d4 excluded     :', 'd4' not in [d for _, d in nearby(*rider)], '- 9 km away')

rider cell      : (5252, 1340)
cells searched  : 9
drivers examined: 3 of 5
nearby (km, id) : [(0.06, 'd1'), (0.41, 'd5'), (0.55, 'd2')]
d4 excluded     : True - 9 km away

Three of five drivers were even examined, and the distant one was never considered. At city scale that ratio is what makes the query possible at all. Real systems use a hierarchical cell system — Uber's H3, Google's S2, or a geohash — which handles the two problems this toy version has: cells are not equal in area as latitude changes, and a fixed cell size is wrong for both a dense city centre and a rural area. A hierarchy lets the search start small and widen until it finds enough candidates.

The index lives in memory and is rebuilt continuously, which is what makes 75,000 writes a second affordable. And note the shape of the read: nine cell lookups, each a hash-table hit, then a distance calculation on a few dozen candidates. That is not a database query, and trying to make it one is the mistake this subsection exists to prevent.

20.5 Assignment: the One Place That Needs Consensus

Matching produces candidates. Assignment must pick exactly one, and must guarantee that no driver is assigned twice — the requirement §20.1 identified as the hard one.

class AssignmentStore:
    """A linearizable compare-and-set per driver. `now` is injected (§5.4)."""
    def __init__(self, lease_seconds=15):
        self.holder, self.expires = {}, {}
        self.lease_seconds = lease_seconds

    def acquire(self, driver_id, trip_id, now):
        current = self.holder.get(driver_id)
        if current is not None and self.expires[driver_id] > now:
            return False, f'held by {current} until t={self.expires[driver_id]}'
        self.holder[driver_id] = trip_id
        self.expires[driver_id] = now + self.lease_seconds
        return True, f'assigned to {trip_id} until t={self.expires[driver_id]}'

    def confirm(self, driver_id, trip_id, now):
        if self.holder.get(driver_id) != trip_id:
            return False
        self.expires[driver_id] = now + 3_600        # the driver accepted; hold for the trip
        return True

store = AssignmentStore()
print('two riders race for the same driver at t=0:')
for trip in ('trip-A', 'trip-B'):
    ok, note = store.acquire('driver-7', trip, now=0)
    print(f'   {trip}: {"WON " if ok else "lost"}  {note}')

print('\ndriver-7 never responds; the lease expires:')
print('   at t=10:', store.acquire('driver-7', 'trip-C', now=10)[1])
print('   at t=16:', store.acquire('driver-7', 'trip-C', now=16)[1])

print('\nthe driver accepts, so the lease is extended for the trip:')
print('   confirmed:', store.confirm('driver-7', 'trip-C', now=17))
print('   trip-D at t=20:', store.acquire('driver-7', 'trip-D', now=20)[1])

two riders race for the same driver at t=0:
   trip-A: WON   assigned to trip-A until t=15
   trip-B: lost  held by trip-A until t=15

driver-7 never responds; the lease expires:
   at t=10: held by trip-A until t=15
   at t=16: assigned to trip-C until t=31

the driver accepts, so the lease is extended for the trip:
   confirmed: True
   trip-D at t=20: held by trip-C until t=3617

Four properties in that small object are load-bearing.

A compare-and-set, not a read-then-write. Two concurrent requests both reading "driver-7 is free" and both writing an assignment is the classic race, and the only fix is an operation the store performs atomically. This is what §5.2's quorum and §5.4's Raft exist to provide, and it is why the assignment store must be consensus-backed rather than a cache.

A lease with an expiry, not a permanent lock. A driver whose phone dies mid-offer must not be locked out forever, and there is no reliable way to detect that they are gone (§5.5). A fifteen-second lease means the failure resolves itself, and the injected now is what makes that testable in a single deterministic run.

The lease is extended on acceptance, not replaced. A confirmed assignment holds the driver for the trip's duration, and the transition is the same key — so there is no window between "offer accepted" and "driver marked busy" in which a second offer could slip through.

And this is the only linearizable operation in the system. One key, held for seconds, on a store designed for it — while position updates, trip history, telemetry and receipts are all eventual. §5.7 makes exactly this argument: the way to afford consensus is to need it in one place.

20.6 The Trip: an Event-Driven Flow

A trip is a sequence of state changes, several of which have downstream consequences in other services. That is §11's subject, and the outbox is what makes it correct.

STATES = ['requested', 'assigned', 'driver_arrived', 'in_progress', 'completed', 'paid']
CONSEQUENCES = {
    'assigned':       ['notify rider', 'notify driver', 'start ETA updates'],
    'driver_arrived': ['notify rider'],
    'in_progress':    ['start telemetry recording', 'stop showing other offers'],
    'completed':      ['compute the fare', 'release the driver lease', 'trigger payment'],
    'paid':           ['email the receipt', 'update driver earnings', 'update analytics'],
}

def transition(state, outbox):
    for consequence in CONSEQUENCES.get(state, []):
        outbox.append((state, consequence))          # committed WITH the state change
    return state

outbox = []
for state in STATES:
    transition(state, outbox)

print(f'{"state":<18}events published')
for state in STATES:
    events = [c for s, c in outbox if s == state]
    print(f'{state:<18}{events if events else "-"}')
print(f'\ntotal events in the outbox: {len(outbox)}')
print('every one committed in the same transaction as the state change (§11.2)')

state             events published
requested         -
assigned          ['notify rider', 'notify driver', 'start ETA updates']
driver_arrived    ['notify rider']
in_progress       ['start telemetry recording', 'stop showing other offers']
completed         ['compute the fare', 'release the driver lease', 'trigger payment']
paid              ['email the receipt', 'update driver earnings', 'update analytics']

total events in the outbox: 12
every one committed in the same transaction as the state change (§11.2)

Every consequence is an outbox row written in the same transaction as the state change, so there is no ordering of a crash that leaves a trip marked completed with no payment triggered, or a payment triggered for a trip that was rolled back. The Backend and API Design course builds the relay against a real database; here the point is that the trip's own transaction is the only place the system is required to be atomic, and everything downstream is an at-least-once consumer with a dedup receipt (§11.8).

The payment flow is a saga, because it spans services and cannot be one transaction:

def run_saga(steps, fail_at=None):
    trace, done = [], []
    for name, do, undo in steps:
        if name == fail_at:
            trace.append(f'FAIL  {name}')
            for undo_name, undo_fn in reversed(done):
                trace.append(f'UNDO  {undo_name}: {undo_fn()}')
            return 'compensated', trace
        trace.append(f'ok    {name}: {do()}')
        done.append((name, undo))
    return 'completed', trace

STEPS = [
    ('compute fare',    lambda: '18.40 EUR',            lambda: 'fare voided'),
    ('charge rider',    lambda: 'auth_3c captured',     lambda: 'refund issued'),
    ('credit driver',   lambda: '14.72 EUR credited',   lambda: 'credit reversed'),
    ('release driver',  lambda: 'lease released',       lambda: None),
]
for failure in (None, 'credit driver'):
    outcome, trace = run_saga(STEPS, fail_at=failure)
    print(f'--- fail_at={failure!r}: {outcome}')
    for line in trace:
        print('   ', line)

--- fail_at=None: completed
    ok    compute fare: 18.40 EUR
    ok    charge rider: auth_3c captured
    ok    credit driver: 14.72 EUR credited
    ok    release driver: lease released
--- fail_at='credit driver': compensated
    ok    compute fare: 18.40 EUR
    ok    charge rider: auth_3c captured
    FAIL  credit driver
    UNDO  charge rider: refund issued
    UNDO  compute fare: fare voided

The compensation for a captured charge is a refund, not a rollback (§11.7) — money left the rider's account and came back, and both appear on their statement. That is the honest cost of spanning services, and the alternative, two-phase commit across payments and driver earnings, is disqualified by §11.6's arithmetic before anything else.

Note the ordering, which is deliberate. release driver is last because it is the only irreversible step: once the driver is back in the matching pool they may be assigned a new trip, and no compensation can undo that. §11.7's rule — order the steps so the irreversible ones come last — is doing real work here.

20.7 Serving Live Updates

Both rider and driver watch the trip move. That is §13.4's problem at the scale of every trip in progress.

CONCURRENT_TRIPS = 250_000
WATCHERS_PER_TRIP = 2
UPDATE_EVERY_S = 4

def push_load(trips, watchers, update_s, payload_bytes=120):
    connections = trips * watchers
    messages = connections / update_s
    return connections, messages, messages * payload_bytes / 1e6

connections, messages, mbs = push_load(CONCURRENT_TRIPS, WATCHERS_PER_TRIP, UPDATE_EVERY_S)
print(f'{"concurrent connections":<28}{connections:>14,.0f}')
print(f'{"messages/s":<28}{messages:>14,.0f}')
print(f'{"bandwidth":<28}{mbs:>12,.1f} MB/s')
print(f'{"connections per node (x40)":<28}{connections / 40:>14,.0f}')
print(f'{"memory at 12 KB each":<28}{connections * 12_000 / 1e9:>12,.1f} GB across the fleet')

for poll_s in (4, 1):
    poll_requests = connections / poll_s
    empty = 1 - min(1.0, (1 / UPDATE_EVERY_S) / (1 / poll_s))
    print(f'\npolling every {poll_s}s: {poll_requests:>10,.0f} HTTP requests/s, '
          f'{empty:>4.0%} returning nothing, staleness up to {poll_s}s')
print(f'\nSSE: {messages:>10,.0f} messages/s, 0% empty, staleness ~0 '
      f'— and no request overhead at all')

concurrent connections             500,000
messages/s                         125,000
bandwidth                           15.0 MB/s
connections per node (x40)          12,500
memory at 12 KB each                 6.0 GB across the fleet

polling every 4s:    125,000 HTTP requests/s,   0% returning nothing, staleness up to 4s

polling every 1s:    500,000 HTTP requests/s,  75% returning nothing, staleness up to 1s

SSE:    125,000 messages/s, 0% empty, staleness ~0 — and no request overhead at all

Read the last three lines together, because they are the argument. Polling at the update interval matches SSE's message count exactly and adds up to four seconds of staleness plus the full cost of an HTTP request for each one; polling fast enough to be comparably fresh means four times the requests, three-quarters of which return nothing. Push wins on freshness at the same message count, and on cost at the same freshness — there is no polling interval at which it loses.

So: server-sent events, one per watcher, following §13.4's rule that the data flows one way. The rider's own actions — cancelling, messaging the driver — are ordinary requests at human pace. SSE brings automatic reconnection with Last-Event-ID, which is what a phone moving between cells needs, and it costs no custom protocol.

Two consequences that must be designed for rather than discovered:

The connection tier is stateful (§2.2) in the specific sense that a connection is bound to one instance. A deploy therefore disconnects half a million clients, and unstaggered they all reconnect at once. §14.9's sequence applies — fail readiness, keep serving, drain, close with a jittered reconnect hint (§14.4) — and one node is rolled at a time.

And a client that reconnects after a gap gets a snapshot, not a backlog. A phone in a tunnel for five minutes does not want seventy-five stale positions; it wants the current one. This is the same decision as §3.4's "serve stale, but say so", applied to a stream.

The design is now complete enough to trace every part of the course through it.

§10 asynchronism    telemetry, receipts, analytics and notifications all off the request path

§19 documenting     the container diagram of §19.6, and ADR 7 recording why assignment left the trips database

Three of those connections are worth expanding, because they are where the design is decided rather than assembled.

§4's consistency decision is the architecture. One linearizable key and everything else eventual is what makes the system affordable. A design that made trip state, positions and history all strongly consistent would be correct and would cost perhaps two orders of magnitude more, for a guarantee nobody needs on any of them.

§12's boundaries each have a specific justification (§12.1). Matching is separate because its workload — in-memory, geospatial, 75,000 writes a second — is nothing like the rest, and it must scale on its own. Payments is separate because it has a different availability requirement, a different compliance surface, and a team that ships to a different cadence. Trips is the core and is deliberately one service, because a trip's state changes are one transaction and splitting them would buy a distributed transaction and nothing else.

And §14's soft-dependency classification is what keeps the system up. Surge pricing, ETA prediction and driver ratings are all soft: a short timeout, a fallback (base fare, a distance-based ETA estimate, a hidden rating), and no retry. Only the assignment store and the trip database are hard dependencies of "request a ride", which is why that flow can be 99.99% while the services it consults are not.

20.9 What Fails, and What It Costs

Every design has failure modes. Naming them is the difference between a design and a diagram (§1.5).

FAILURES = [
    ('the position index is lost',
     'no drivers are visible for up to 4 seconds', 'self-healing — every driver re-reports',
     'LOW'),
    ('the assignment store loses quorum',
     'no new rides can be assigned; trips in progress continue', 'the availability floor of the system',
     'HIGH — this is the SPOF (§2.6)'),
    ('a region fails',
     'that region cannot serve; riders elsewhere unaffected', 'fail over, or the region is down',
     'MEDIUM — bounded by design (§15.6)'),
    ('the payment provider is down',
     'trips complete; charges queue in the outbox', 'nothing user-visible for hours',
     'LOW — this is what async buys (§10.1)'),
    ('a hot city at rush hour',
     'one geographic cell is 30% of traffic', 'subdivide the cell; it is a hot partition (§8.5)',
     'MEDIUM'),
    ('a surge of position writes',
     'the index falls behind; matching uses stale positions', 'shed position updates first (§3.6)',
     'LOW — positions are the most sheddable thing here'),
]
print(f'{"failure":<34}{"severity":<26}mitigation')
for failure, effect, mitigation, severity in FAILURES:
    print(f'{failure:<34}{severity:<26}{mitigation}')
    print(f'{"":34}effect: {effect}')

failure                           severity                  mitigation
the position index is lost        LOW                       self-healing — every driver re-reports
                                  effect: no drivers are visible for up to 4 seconds
the assignment store loses quorum HIGH — this is the SPOF (§2.6)the availability floor of the system
                                  effect: no new rides can be assigned; trips in progress continue

                                  effect: that region cannot serve; riders elsewhere unaffected

The assignment store is the single point of failure, and that is a deliberate, stated trade. It is the price of the one requirement that cannot be relaxed. What can be done is to bound its blast radius: one consensus group per city rather than one globally, so losing a group stops assignments in one city instead of everywhere (§2.6's cells).

def blast(cities, group_per_city=True):
    if group_per_city:
        return 1 / cities, 'one city cannot assign; everywhere else is unaffected'
    return 1.0, 'no ride can be assigned anywhere in the world'

for cities, per_city in [(600, False), (600, True)]:
    fraction, effect = blast(cities, per_city)
    print(f'{"one group per city" if per_city else "one global group":<22}'
          f'{fraction:>8.2%} of users affected   {effect}')

one global group       100.00% of users affected   no ride can be assigned anywhere in the world
one group per city       0.17% of users affected   one city cannot assign; everywhere else is unaffected

And the failure the design handles best is the payment provider, which is worth noticing because it is the one that would be most damaging in a synchronous design. Charges accumulate in the outbox and are relayed when the provider returns; trips complete normally; nobody notices for hours. That is entirely a consequence of §10.1's decision to take payment off the request path, made at the very start.

20.10 What Is Deliberately Missing

A design is also what it leaves out, and saying so is part of finishing it.

Surge pricing
Named as out of scope in §20.1. It is a pricing and modelling problem whose systems requirement — a cached multiplier per cell, refreshed every few minutes — is a paragraph, and whose difficulty is entirely elsewhere.
Fraud detection
A stream-processing problem consuming the same event log (§11.3, §16), and a different subject. The design accommodates it by publishing events rather than by anticipating it.
Routing and ETAs
A graph problem over road networks, solved by a specialised service. The system design contribution is that it is a soft dependency with a distance-based fallback (§14.1).
The matching policy
Nearest driver? Shortest total wait? Highest acceptance probability? That is an optimisation question, and the design's job is to make it a changeable one — which is why §15.5's feature flags and §15.4's canary matter here more than anywhere else in the system.

The last one is the most important omission to state. The matching mechanism — a geospatial index, candidate selection, a leased assignment — is a system-design problem and is solved above. The matching policy is a business question that will change every quarter for the life of the product, and the design's contribution is that changing it requires no architectural change: it is a scoring function behind a flag, canaried at 1%, compared against the baseline on assignment time and acceptance rate.

That is the general lesson this capstone exists to deliver. Almost none of the difficulty was in choosing components. It was in identifying the one requirement that could not be relaxed, giving it the smallest possible mechanism, and letting everything else be eventual, asynchronous, cached and degradable — which is what every section of this course has been building towards.

Exercises

Exercise 20.1 — Change one requirement. For each change, say what breaks, what you would redesign, and what stays the same.

(a) Riders may now book a ride up to 7 days in advance.
(b) The p99 matching requirement tightens from 5 seconds to 500 milliseconds.
(c) Drivers may accept two rides at once (shared rides).
(d) EU trip data must never leave the EU, including backups and analytics.
Solution 
CHANGES = [
    ('(a) advance booking',
     'nothing in matching — a scheduled ride is a delayed request',
     'add a scheduler: a durable timer that publishes a ride-request event at T-10min',
     'the whole live path is unchanged; this is a new producer, not a new system'),
    ('(b) p99 500ms',
     'the assignment round trip and the driver-response wait no longer fit',
     'pre-compute candidate sets per cell; offer to several drivers in parallel',
     'the index, the lease and the trip flow are unchanged'),
    ('(c) shared rides',
     'the assignment lease is wrong — it assumes exclusivity',
     'the lease becomes a counted semaphore (capacity 2) with the same CAS discipline',
     'still ONE linearizable key per driver; the constraint changed, not its nature'),
    ('(d) strict residency',
     'the global analytics warehouse and cross-region backups are now illegal',
     'per-region storage AND per-region analytics; only aggregates cross the border',
     'the design is already partitioned by region; the leak is in the derived systems'),
]
for label, breaks, redesign, unchanged in CHANGES:
    print(f'{label}\n   breaks   : {breaks}\n   redesign : {redesign}\n   unchanged: {unchanged}\n')

(a) advance booking
   breaks   : nothing in matching — a scheduled ride is a delayed request
   redesign : add a scheduler: a durable timer that publishes a ride-request event at T-10min
   unchanged: the whole live path is unchanged; this is a new producer, not a new system

(b) p99 500ms
   breaks   : the assignment round trip and the driver-response wait no longer fit
   redesign : pre-compute candidate sets per cell; offer to several drivers in parallel
   unchanged: the index, the lease and the trip flow are unchanged

(c) shared rides
   breaks   : the assignment lease is wrong — it assumes exclusivity
   redesign : the lease becomes a counted semaphore (capacity 2) with the same CAS discipline
   unchanged: still ONE linearizable key per driver; the constraint changed, not its nature

(d) strict residency
   breaks   : the global analytics warehouse and cross-region backups are now illegal
   redesign : per-region storage AND per-region analytics; only aggregates cross the border
   unchanged: the design is already partitioned by region; the leak is in the derived systems

(a) is the easy one and it is worth doing first to establish the pattern. A scheduled ride is not a new kind of ride; it is a ride request that arrives later. The addition is a durable scheduler — a table of timers, or a delayed message (§10) — that publishes the ordinary request event ten minutes before the pickup. Everything downstream is unchanged, which is the sign of a boundary in the right place (§12.1).

(b) is the one that forces real redesign, and the interesting part is where the time actually goes. Five hundred milliseconds does not permit: a cell lookup, a candidate scoring pass, a consensus write, a push to the driver, and a human tapping "accept". The last item alone is seconds. So the requirement can only be met by changing what "matched" means — offer to several drivers simultaneously and let the first acceptance win (which the compare-and-set already handles correctly), and pre-compute ranked candidate sets per cell so the request path is a lookup rather than a computation. The lease mechanism does not change at all, which is the point: it was designed for a race, and this makes the race deliberate.

(c) is the one that tests whether the assignment design was right. A shared ride means a driver can hold two trips, so the lease is no longer a mutex — it is a semaphore with capacity two. The compare-and-set becomes "increment if below capacity", which is the same linearizable operation on the same single key. Nothing else moves, and that is the strongest evidence that putting the constraint in one small consensus-backed key was the correct decision (§5.7).

(d) is the one that catches people out, because the primary path already complies. Trips are partitioned by region and the leader is in-region, so the transactional system is fine. The violations are in the derived systems: a global analytics warehouse, cross-region backups, a search index in another region, and the position stream if it flows to a central pipeline. Data residency is almost always broken in the pipeline, not the database — which is why §20.1 listed it as a non-functional requirement rather than assuming it followed from the partitioning.

Exercise 20.2 — Design a different system. Apply §1.5's method end to end to a system of a different shape: a collaborative document editor for 5 million users, with up to 50 simultaneous editors per document, offline editing, and full version history. Work through requirements, estimates, data model, the hard part, and the failure modes.

Solution
