1. REQUIREMENTS — the ones that decide the design
   concurrency   up to 50 simultaneous editors, character-level
   offline       edit offline; converge on reconnect — this is the hard one
   history       every version, restorable, forever
   latency       a local keystroke must render immediately — 0 ms, not "fast"
   consistency   all editors converge; no edit is ever lost
   availability  99.9%; a document must open even if collaboration is down

2. ESTIMATE
   documents                    150,000,000
   concurrent editors               100,000
   operations/s                     400,000
   ops/day                   34,560,000,000
   at 40 bytes each, per day      1,382.4 GB

3. DATA MODEL
   document operations (the log)   append-only log, partitioned          document_id
   document snapshots              object storage, every N ops (§11.4)   document_id + version
   document metadata + ACLs        relational                            document_id
   presence (who is editing)       in-memory, TTL 30s                    document_id

4. THE HARD PART: convergence
   NOT a lock — a lock makes offline editing impossible and typing laggy
   NOT last-writer-wins — it discards characters someone typed (§4.7)
   CRDTs or OT: a merge that is commutative, associative and idempotent (§4.7)

The requirement that decides everything is offline editing, and it decides it by elimination. Two users editing the same paragraph on separate laptops, on a plane, must both converge when they reconnect — and there is no coordination available, so every design that involves agreement is ruled out before it is considered. No lock, no leader, no consensus. That leaves exactly one family of answers: a merge function that converges without communication, which is §4.7's CRDT.

The second requirement, a zero-latency keystroke, rules out the rest. A character must appear as it is typed, so the edit is applied locally first and synchronised afterwards — which means the client holds authoritative state and the server is a relay and a durable log rather than the source of truth. That is an unusual shape, and it follows directly from the two requirements above.

Everything else is machinery this course has already built. The operation log is §11.3's event sourcing — the document is the fold over its operations, which gives full version history for free rather than as a feature. Snapshots every N operations bound the replay cost (§11.4). Presence is an in-memory TTL store exactly like §20.4's position index. Documents are partitioned by document_id (§8.3), because every operation and every read is scoped to one document — an unusually clean partition key.

And the failure modes:

A client is offline for a month. Its operation log diverges far from the server's, and the merge is still correct — that is what a CRDT guarantees — but the client may be replaying against a document that has since been deleted or had its permissions revoked. Convergence is not authorisation, and that check has to happen on reconnect rather than being assumed from the merge.

A CRDT's metadata grows. Tombstones for deleted characters cannot be discarded while any replica might still be offline (§4.7). The practical answer is a garbage-collection horizon: after a bounded period, an offline client must re-sync from a snapshot rather than merge.

Fifty simultaneous editors on one document is a hot partition (§8.5). All fifty connect to the instance holding that document's session, which is a deliberate affinity — and it is §2.3's legitimate case, because the state is a cache of the log and losing it costs a reload rather than data.

And the collaboration service can fail without the document failing. Opening and reading a document is a read of the log plus the latest snapshot, which needs nothing from the real-time tier. §3.4's graceful degradation: the document opens read-only with a banner, rather than not opening.

You started this course able to build a system that works. You can now design one that keeps working when it is large, when a third of it is broken, and when the people who built it have moved on — and, just as importantly, you can say why each part of it is there.

What you can now do

  1. Turn a vague request into a design you can defend. Separate functional from non-functional requirements, ask the questions that decide the architecture, estimate peak load and three-year storage in two minutes, and know which numbers eliminate which options.
  2. Scale deliberately rather than reflexively. Vertical first, horizontal when a number forces it, statelessness as the property everything depends on, and Amdahl's law as the reason a serial fraction caps you long before the hardware does.
  3. State an availability target as a duration and know what it costs. Nines in minutes per week, SLIs precise enough that two people compute the same number, error budgets as permission rather than as a threshold, and burn-rate alerting instead of a breach nobody can act on.
  4. Choose a consistency model per operation. The three meanings of the word, CAP stated correctly, the model hierarchy, the session guarantees, and the discipline of making one thing linearizable so everything else can be eventual.
  5. Reason about agreement and its price. Quorums, split-brain, fencing tokens, Raft, failure detection, logical clocks — and §5.7's more useful conclusion, which is how to avoid needing consensus at all.
  6. Pick a data store from access patterns. Relational by default and for good reasons, key-value and document for what they trade away, wide-column and the LSM tree, graph for real traversals, and object storage, search and time-series for the workloads a general-purpose database serves badly.
  7. Read a query plan. Selectivity, composite-index column order, covering and partial indexes, and the ability to tell a missing index from stale statistics from a LIMIT doing its job.
  8. Replicate and partition on purpose. Single-leader, multi-leader and leaderless; synchronous, asynchronous and semi-synchronous; the three lag anomalies and their fixes; partition-key choice, consistent hashing, hotspots and the rebalancing you will have to do.
  9. Cache without serving lies. The arithmetic that says whether a cache is worth building, the five strategies, why delete-on-write races, how a stampede becomes an outage, why LRU is defeated by a scan, and what must never be cached at all.
  10. Move work off the request path safely. Queues versus logs and why the difference matters, worker-pool sizing from Little's law, ordering within a partition, fan-out on write versus on read, at-least-once as the only real guarantee, dead letters, and back pressure that propagates.
  11. Build event-driven systems that stay correct. The outbox instead of a dual write, event sourcing and CQRS, two-phase commit and why it blocks, sagas with compensating actions, idempotent consumers, and event schemas that outlive the code that wrote them.
  12. Put service boundaries where the language changes, recognise a distributed monolith by its symptoms, and know that merging services is a legitimate fix rather than a retreat.
  13. Make failure local. Deadlines that travel with the request, retry budgets rather than just backoff, jitter that desynchronises a fleet, circuit breakers, bulkheads, four rate-limiting algorithms, and a graceful shutdown that loses nothing.
  14. Operate what you designed. Metrics, logs and traces with the right thing in each, saturation as the signal that leads, canaries compared against a live baseline, feature flags that separate deploy from release, and blameless postmortems whose actions actually get done.
  15. Process data that never stops arriving. Bounded versus unbounded data, MapReduce's partition-combine-recompute model, event time against processing time, windows and watermarks with their trade between latency and completeness, triggers and accumulation modes, exactly-once as replayable sources plus idempotent or transactional sinks, and reprocessing from the log instead of building a second system.
  16. Count what is too big to store. The Count-Min sketch with its one-sided error and its additive bound, HeavyKeeper for ranked lists, HyperLogLog for distinct counts, the mergeability that lets them span shards and windows, and the discipline of sizing each from the smallest number you need to trust.
  17. Say who is calling, and for whom. OAuth 2.0's four roles, the authorization code flow with PKCE, client credentials for services, refresh-token rotation, the ID token and what a client must validate in it, audience-restricted tokens between your own services, and the RFC 9700 checklist.
  18. Leave a design that can be understood and checked. The C4 model's abstractions and the two diagrams worth keeping current, requirements as scenarios with measures, and architecture decision records that name their costs.

That is the working set. There is no part of a normal distributed system you should now find arbitrary.

The five ideas that keep recurring

Strip away the mechanisms and the same small number of ideas appear in every section. They are worth carrying forward on their own.

Compute it
Almost every disagreement about a design is settled by arithmetic somebody has not done. Requests per second, bytes per item, the availability product across a chain, the break-even hit rate, the concurrency Little's law demands. Two minutes of estimation beats an hour of opinion.
Make the strong requirement small
Consensus, linearizability and transactions are expensive. The systems that afford them need them in one place — one key, one partition, one operation — and let everything around it be eventual. §20's ride-hailing design is one linearizable key in a system of millions of writes a second.
At-least-once, applied idempotently
Exactly-once delivery is not achievable, and every system that claims it is doing this instead. Once you see it, the outbox, the projector offset, the payment idempotency key and Kafka's transactions are all one construction.
Fail fast, locally, and say so
Slow failure is worse than fast failure, silent degradation is worse than a visible error, and an unbounded queue is worse than a rejection. Every mechanism in §14 converts a slow, spreading failure into a fast, contained one.
The smallest design that meets the requirements
Every component is something to run, monitor, upgrade and be woken by. A system serving ten thousand users from one machine is a correct design, and the ability to defend leaving something out is the skill this course was really teaching.

Where to go next

Read the papers. Almost everything here has a primary source that is shorter and clearer than its summaries: Raft's In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm, Amazon's Dynamo paper for leaderless replication, Google's Spanner and Bigtable, and the Google SRE book for SLOs, error budgets and cascading failure. The newer sections have primary sources of the same kind: Dean and Ghemawat's MapReduce paper and Akidau and colleagues' Dataflow Model paper for §16, the Count-Min, HyperLogLog and HeavyKeeper papers for §17, and RFC 6749, RFC 7636 and RFC 9700 for §18, all short enough to read in an evening.

Operate something. No amount of reading substitutes for being paged. A system you have failed over, drained, canaried and post-mortemed teaches you things no design document contains — and it is the difference between knowing what a bulkhead is and knowing when you needed one.

Then design something and write down what you traded. The habit this course is built around is not choosing components; it is being able to say, for every component, which number forced it and what it cost you. A design defended that way is one somebody else can check, extend, and argue with — which is the whole point.
